author_feedback: We thank the AC and all reviewers for their constructive feedback. 1.Ground-Truth Curation & Baseline Fairness (R1, R3) We clarify that our annotations are not raw algorithmic outputs. Initial volumetric labels were generated using Ref. 23, followed by rigorous visual QC and correction by 20 trained raters using ITK-SNAP. Cases with extensive segmentation errors, abnormal intensity distributions, or severe artifacts were excluded. Corrected cases took ~20 minutes each, with ~1–3% of voxels modified. Final labels were approved by 8 experienced radiologists. Overall, ~3–5% of cases were excluded, leaving 7,662 scans. Surface targets were derived from these labels following Ref. 25.While off-the-shelf baselines (SynthSeg and Recon-all-clinical) were not retrained, the comparison remains fair: both our annotations and the baselines are built on FreeSurfer anatomical conventions. For the adult data used in our study, Ref. 23 uses FreeSurfer-derived QC labels, while the baselines are trained on FreeSurfer-related labels. Thus, all methods are evaluated under a common anatomical convention and a single reference standard. 2.LUT Construction & Leakage Control & “Physics-Informed” Augmentation (R1, R2) For each training scan, we compute class-wise intensity statistics, i.e., mean mu_k and standard deviation sigma_k, from voxels of tissue class k and store them in the LUT. During augmentation, for a source image I_src, we compute source statistics, sample target statistics of the same class from the LUT, and remap voxels with L(v)=k as described in Sec. 2.1.To prevent data leakage, the LUT is computed only from the training set. In our work, “Physics-Informed” means simulating structured acquisition shifts (LUT-based contrast remapping, random bias fields, Gamma transforms, and partial-volume effects) rather than arbitrary perturbations. 3.Prompt Conditioning & Hard Routing (R1, R2, R3) uBrain uses controlled prompts for predefined medical concepts, rather than free-form text, to provide stable anchors for modality-adaptive encoding (MAE) and task-driven decoding (TDD). Unlike orthogonal one-hot vectors, text embeddings capture semantic correlations across modalities and tasks (Fig. 4). Modality embeddings guide soft MoME expert aggregation through cross-attention, whereas task embeddings drive hard Automatic Pathway (AP) routing. For each AP module l, the router produces logits z_l = W_l p_task + b_l over M=5 paths, and softmax(z_l) gives intermediate activation probabilities. During training, a hard Gumbel-Softmax with temperature tau=1.0 produces one-hot path selection while preserving differentiability through the straight-through estimator. During inference, we select the maximum-probability path by argmax. Thus, Fig. 4(c) correctly shows hard path selection, not soft mixing. 4.Novelty & Baselines (R1, R2, R3) We will cite and discuss Vox2Cortex, SegRecon, and prior MoME methods. Unlike these works, which primarily target MRI surface reconstruction, with an auxiliary volumetric component often limited to simple filled-WM segmentation, or focus on lesion segmentation, uBrain uses MAE and TDD in one prompt-driven model to unify multimodal inputs and multiple co-equal anatomical outputs, rather than merely coupling volume and surface. Table 3 shows that MAE+TDD alone improves over SwinUNETR baseline before GMM augmentation, supporting the architectural efficacy of MAE and TDD. Since no single foundation model matches our broad input-output scope, we compare against strong task-specific SOTA baselines (SynthSeg and Recon-all-clinical). 5.Evaluation Metrics (R2) We agree regional metrics are vital. Due to space limits, we reported standard average metrics (Dice, ASSD). The revised Supplementary Material will include detailed ROI-level metrics (e.g., hippocampus, ventricles) and HD95.Our current results demonstrate broad multimodal potential as a unified framework, with rigorous clinical deployment validation as future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers generally acknowledge the merit in proposing a unified, prompt-driven framework for brain image analysis across multiple modalities and tasks. However, significant concerns were raised across all reviews, focusing on the novelty of the unified approach in light of prior work, the clarity and justification of certain methodological components, and the issue of baseline comparison given the unique ground truth generation. Specifically, the lack of comparison against other recent unified/foundation models and the insufficient detail for reproducibility weaken the paper’s claims. | The rebuttal successfully resolves the concerns regarding data leakage and ground-truth definitions. I recommend accepting this paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I want to start acknowledging that I agree with the reviewers in highlighting that merging tasks is a worthwhile endeavour and a great strength of the paper. Similarly, I can understand why two of the reviewers decided to accept after rebuttal as some concerns have been successfully addressed and I also agree that a large-scale evaluation is a great strength in itself. Having said that, I cannot help but side with reviewer #2 in terms of major concerns not addressed. My decision is made on the basis of considering this submission a methodological paper and expecting a few different things from it: Methodological rigour. Having read the paper and rebuttal, I am unconvinced of the following claim: “Unlike orthogonal one-hot vectors, text embeddings capture semantic correlations across modalities and tasks”. Figure 4 does show that the embeddings are clustered but it does not provide evidence on whether single categorical variables, passed through an encoder would be equivalent. Similarly, “‘physics-Informed’ means simulating structured acquisition shifts” is a fairly loose interpretation of what physics-informed means and misleading. If data augmentation was truly “physics-informed”, I would have expected that the authors would exploit properties from magnetic resonance and x-ray tomography. Furthermore, whether linear scaling based on Gaussian distributions is novel is arguable, too. The same could be said for most of the methodological contributions beyond unifying segmentation and cortical reconstruction. A comprehensive and rigorous evaluation. I do agree with the authors that a rebuttal is not the place to address new experiments, but the lack of proper comparisons in the original manuscript is a major concern, nonetheless. With this I am echoing reviewer #2’s complaints about baseline concerns. Moreover, I also agree that not addressing crucial evaluation metrics for downstream tasks (even if it could be due to rebuttal policy) downgrades the author’s contributions. Evaluation, in general, should cover relevant metrics to understand the applicability of a new method. Limiting the evaluation to metrics that do not provide the whole picture is still a major concern, whether a rebuttal allows for it or not. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Given mixed opinions, I carefully reviewed the paper and rebuttal. While novelty concerns are mostly addressed, I still oppose acceptance for the following reasons: 1.Missing baselines: I highly disagree with the author’s response that only one baseline is relevant for comparison. Comparisons to the following methods would have been highly relevant and are currently missing to judge the presented work against the state-of-the-art: SuperSynth (contrast-agnostic multi-task model), PhySeg [a] and GOUHFI [b] (contrast-agnostic segmentation), Anatomix [c] and Brain-ID [d] (contrast-agnostic brain MRI foundation models). 2.Potentially biased results: the only baseline was not even retrained on the authors’ data. Using a common list of labels is not a safeguard against annotator bias (human or automated), which often have different ways of segmenting the same regions. Right now, it is unclear whether the reported gains come from methodological improvements or labelling differences. 3.Unclear methods/limited reproducibility: as noted by reviewers, the method description remains largely superficial and omits key information about the main contributions (modality MoME, dynamic pathway rerouting). Combined with the lack of code release, this makes this work not reproducible. 4.Insufficient literature review: for MICCAI, even a concise literature review should be conducted. Here, decades of previous works are reduced to two lines citing all learning-based segmentation works together [9–16]. 5.The augmentation pipeline after GMM sampling (partial-volume, bias field, gamma transform) is directly taken from SynthSeg and should be explicitly acknowledged. Overall, the work is promising, but these major issues make it unsuitable for acceptance at MICCAI in its current form. title: AC-MIL: Weakly-Supervised Atrial LGE-MRI Quality Assessment via Adversarial Concept Disentanglement
reviewer_1_strengths: Strengths: Well-motivated problem clear clinical relevance (interpretability for LGE-MRI) the concept seems to be novel thoughtful design: adversarial residual branch and spatial diversity constraint are conceptually sound and address known issues (leakage, entanglement) solid experimental protocol (10-fold CV, multiple metrics, ablations) qualitative analyses (UMAP, attention maps) support interpretability claims

reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The problem is clinically meaningful. Image quality in atrial LGE-MRI directly affects downstream analysis and clinical usability, so reliable and interpretable quality assessment is of practical importance. 2.The method has a certain degree of novelty. The paper attempts to decompose the MIL feature space into clinically meaningful concept dimensions (e.g., sharpness, myocardial nulling, aortic enhancement, and residual factors), which goes beyond conventional black-box quality assessment models. 3.The method offers interpretability. The spatial attention heatmaps provide localization of potential quality-defect regions, which improves trustworthiness and makes the model output more aligned with clinical expectations.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Training and implementation details are insufficient. The manuscript does not provide a sufficiently complete description of the hyperparameter settings, which limits reproducibility and makes it difficult to assess the sensitivity of the reported performance to the training configuration. 2.The paper does not clearly specify the source institution(s), the total number of samples, the train/validation/test split ratios, or the sample distribution across quality levels. These details are essential for judging the reliability of the experimental conclusions and whether the dataset is balanced. 3.The manuscript does not adequately explain how the quality levels were defined by experts, nor whether inter-rater agreement was assessed. Since label reliability is central to a quality assessment task, the expert grading criteria and their consistency should be described much more clearly. 4.Ethics and compliance information is missing. As a medical imaging study, the paper should provide information regarding ethics approval, data access authorization, and related compliance procedures to improve transparency.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Methodological Novelty: The combination of an unsupervised residual branch with predefined clinical concepts is an elegant solution to the completeness problem often found in Concept Bottleneck Models. The use of a Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) to enforce feature orthogonality and prevent the residual branch from trivially relearning known semantics is well-executed. 2.Clinical Interpretability: By breaking down the opaque MIL pooling process into specific radiological failure modes, the framework provides highly actionable feedback for clinical technicians, directly addressing the “black box” criticism of standard deep learning approaches. 3.Strong Qualitative Validation: The manuscript provides compelling visual and statistical evidence supporting its architectural claims. The UMAP projections, Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) boxplots, and visual attention maps (Figure 3) effectively demonstrate that the Spatial Attention Diversity (L_SAD) successfully forces spatial specialization. 4.Rigorous Ablation: The ablation study (Table 1) clearly isolates the impact of the CBM, SAD, and Adversarial components, providing transparency regarding the performance trade-offs inherent in enforcing interpretability.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Performance Trade-off: As shown in Table 1, the inclusion of the Spatial Attention Diversity (L_SAD) penalty actually decreases the overall Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) from 0.68 to 0.66.While the authors logically justify this as a “necessary trade-off” to prevent shortcut learning and ensure true anatomical alignment, the manuscript would benefit from a deeper discussion on why spatial overlap inherently degrades the metric and how this trade-off might affect clinical deployment. 2.Lack of Expert Validation on Attention Maps: While the Jensen-Shannon Divergence proves the attention maps are distinct from one another, there is no quantitative validation that these maps accurately localize the correct artifacts. A small-scale reader study or expert scoring of the attention maps would strongly validate the clinical utility claim. 3.Dataset Diversity: The manuscript evaluates 775 LGE MRI scans but does not specify if this is a multi-center or single-center dataset. If it is single-center, claims of generalizability may be overstated, especially given the known variability in LGE-MRI acquisition protocols across different institutions.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the meta-reviewer and reviewers for their constructive feedback and address the major concerns below. M, R1, R3, R4: QWK drop, 0.68 -> 0.66.The 0.68 QWK row is not the model “without adversarial loss”; it is AC-MIL with CBM+adversarial erasure. The full model adds Spatial Attention Diversity (SAD), resulting in QWK=0.66.Thus, the reduction is due to SAD, not adversarial erasure. SAD penalizes overlap between concept-specific attention maps, reducing shortcut correlations and enforcing spatial disentanglement. As shown in Fig. 3, this yields more spatially separated and anatomically consistent attention maps. We performed paired analysis on existing out-of-fold predictions. For the reported setting (λSAD=0.1), the QWK reduction is statistically significant (paired permutation p=0.008<0.05), indicating a measurable cost. When SAD regularization is reduced (λSAD=0.05), the difference is not significant (p=0.30>0.05), showing that the trade-off is controlled by regularization strength. We chose λSAD=0.1 to prioritize interpretable, anatomically consistent concept separation while maintaining competitive QA performance relative to ABMIL and HAMIL-QA, rather than maximizing raw QWK. Thus, the full model reflects a principled interpretability–performance trade-off rather than instability. M, R4: Fig. 2a and “AUC = 0.96.” This appears to stem from a misinterpretation of Fig. 2a. We do not report a Sharpness adversarial AUC of 0.96.Fig. 2a shows adversaries predicting predefined concepts from the unsupervised branch; curves near chance indicate that predefined concept signals are not recoverable from the unsupervised branch above chance. Thus, Fig. 2a supports reduced leakage rather than demonstrating leakage. We will clarify the caption and text to avoid confusion. M, R2, R4: concept labels and weak supervision. The concept labels were manually assigned by expert readers at the volume level; they were not derived from the global quality score. The method is weakly supervised because AC-MIL uses only volume-level quality and concept grades, without slice-, patch-, or pixel-level supervision. Inter-rater agreement is available only on a subset. On a 50-case subset independently scored by 5 raters, ICC/weighted κ was 0.74 for fibrosis-assessment quality and 0.62–0.72 across the concept categories. We emphasize that these are limited subset estimates and not full-dataset reliability measurements for all 775 scans. R1: method clarity and stop-gradient. As reported in Sec. 2.4, the asymmetric stop-gradient prevents task-level gradients from forcing predefined concept branches to encode final QA information, reducing concept leakage. We will make this motivation more prominent. R2, R3: dataset, split, and ethics. The manuscript reports 775 LGE-MRI scans with stratified 10-fold CV: 10% test per fold and 10% of the remaining training portion for validation/early stopping. We will additionally clarify quality-grade distribution, scanner/source details under data-use restrictions, and the omitted IRB/ethics approval, consent/waiver, and data-use statements. This was a presentation omission, not a lack of IRB/data-use compliance. R1, R4: baselines and interpretability comparisons. ABMIL and HAMIL-QA were selected because they are directly aligned with weakly supervised MIL-based quality assessment, with HAMIL-QA being the closest prior atrial LGE-MRI QA method. Generic interpretable classifiers are not directly comparable because they do not address the hierarchical weakly supervised volume/slice/patch setting. We will clarify this choice. R1, R3: single-dataset evaluation. We agree that multi-center validation would strengthen generalizability. However, to our knowledge, no public dataset exists for atrial LGE-MRI quality assessment with both ordinal QA and concept-level labels. The dataset used in this work is in-house; code will be released upon acceptance, and dataset access will be explored through institutional MOU agreements.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers agreed that the paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and proposes an interpretable framework for atrial LGE-MRI quality assessment with some interesting ideas. However, the main concerns centered on the strength of the empirical validation. In the rebuttal, the authors should (1) explain and justify the QWK drop from 0.68 to 0.66 when adding the SAD loss, with statistical significance testing; (2) clarify whether the sharpness adversarial branch AUC of 0.96 constitutes information leakage; (3) describe how concept-level labels were annotated and report inter-rater agreement if available. | The rebuttal is sufficient in addressing the concerns of the reviewers, though R1 maintained rejection based on single-centre limitation. The limitation is noted but can be accepted for a MICCAI paper with techinical novelty, which is on bottleneck modeling and spatial attention diversity, and can be interesting for discussion at the conference. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Although the paper proposes an interesting framework for atrial LGE-MRI quality assessment, the clinical motivation is not fully convincing: unlike real-time ultrasound QA, it remains unclear how the predicted quality concepts would be used to meaningfully adjust MRI acquisition or improve downstream clinical decision-making. In addition, the validation is limited to a single in-house dataset (considering there are so many public atrial LGE MRI resource in MICCAI challenge, such as LA challenge 2018, LAScarQS 2021, CARE 2023, etc), the gains over existing methods are modest, and the interpretability claims still lack strong external or clinician-validated evidence. Therefore, despite the positive aspects of the method, I am not convinced that the current evidence is sufficient for acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal addressed the main concerns about the SAD trade-off, the adversarial leakage interpretation, and the concept-label annotation process. In the final version, please add the promised details on dataset composition, splits, ethics approval, inter-rater agreement, and clearly state the limitation that the evaluation is based on a single in-house dataset.

title: ADAPT: Adaptive Profiling Transformers for Efficient Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: Authors introduce an adaptive view-profiling mechanism that dynamically allocates slices to diagnostically informative views based on learned attention scores. This is a thoughtful design choice because it attempts to prioritize clinically relevant anatomical regions while maintaining computational efficiency, potentially allowing the model to extract richer contextual information without processing the full 3D volume. The proposed pathology-driven morphology augmentation strategy is another interesting attempt to incorporate disease progression knowledge into the training process by simulating atrophy-related morphological variations along the NC–MCI–AD continuum. Finally, the paper presents empirical evaluation across multiple AD classification tasks while also reporting substantial reductions in computational cost compared to other models.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: First, the experimental design relies primarily on training and testing within the ADNI dataset, which may not adequately evaluate the model’s ability to generalize across acquisition protocols and study cohorts. Since ADNI contains multiple phases with different scanners and imaging protocols, it would be more informative to treat ADNI-1, ADNI-2, and ADNI-3 as separate domains for training and testing, which would better reflect real-world cross-cohort generalization. Second, the manuscript does not report the sample size and class distribution for the additional datasets used in the experiments (AIBL, MIRIAD, and OASIS). Without this information, it is difficult to interpret the reported performance or assess whether the datasets are balanced, which is important for judging the reliability of the accuracy results. Third, the evaluation focuses mainly on binary classification tasks (e. g. , AD vs. NC or NC vs. MCI), whereas a three-class classification setting (AD vs. MCI vs. NC) would be more clinically meaningful and more consistent with the diagnostic continuum of Alzheimer’s disease.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper has several notable strengths. First, it presents a well-motivated framework that bridges the gap between 2D efficiency and 3D volumetric modeling in Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis. The idea of achieving 3D-level performance using a computationally efficient 2D-based design is practically important, especially for real clinical settings with limited GPU resources. Second, the view-specific transformer architecture is a meaningful contribution, as it explicitly separates within-slice, within-view, and cross-view relationships. This structured modeling of multi-view MRI data is a reasonable way to capture spatial dependencies that are often missed in standard 2D approaches. Third, the adaptive view-profiling strategy adds an intelligent mechanism to prioritize more informative slices based on learned attention, which aligns well with the clinical notion that not all slices contribute equally to diagnosis. Finally, the pathology-driven morphology augmentation is a useful data-centric contribution that helps improve robustness by simulating disease progression patterns, and the reported results across multiple AD-related classification tasks suggest consistent performance improvements over baseline methods.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper has several limitations. First, some components are related to prior work on multi-view and slice-based transformer/CNN models for MRI analysis, such as multi-view CNNs and slice-attention methods used in Alzheimer’s disease classification, but the comparison with these methods is not clearly discussed. Second, the efficiency claims are mainly supported by GFLOPs reduction, without detailed evaluation of real-world latency or memory usage in clinical settings. Third, similar pathology-aware augmentation strategies have been explored in earlier work on brain atrophy simulation and disease progression modeling, but the paper does not clearly compare against them.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for recognizing ADAPT’s clinical motivation, view-profiling design, pathology-driven augmentation, and consistent gains. We address the concerns below: 1) Cross-cohort setup and cohort reporting (R1, AC). Our robustness claim is based on external-cohort testing, not an ADNI-only evaluation. ADNI was used for training/validation/model selection; AIBL, MIRIAD, and OASIS were held-out test cohorts never used for model selection. ADNI-1/2/3 phase-wise splitting is useful but remains intra-consortium; testing on independent studies/institutions more directly supports cross-institutional generalization. We will report external cohort composition: AIBL 413 scans (363 NC/50 AD), MIRIAD 523 (177 NC/346 AD), and OASIS 2157 (1692 NC/465 AD). Reliability comes from subject-level disjoint ADNI splits, model selection only on ADNI validation data, and consistent gains across external cohorts with different sizes/class balances, reducing the chance that improvement is due to one favorable test set. For three-class AD/MCI/NC, our binary tasks cover AD vs. NC for standard separation and NC vs. MCI for early-stage discrimination, where differences are subtler. Joint three-class evaluation is valuable but complementary to our main claim. 2) Efficiency beyond GFLOPs (R2, AC). We profiled inference under matched hardware settings. ADAPT runs at ~52 ms/volume with only 0.43 GiB peak GPU memory. Compared with the closest multi-view baseline M3T, ADAPT is ~4.9× faster (52 vs. 254 ms), uses ~56× less memory (0.43 vs. 24.3 GiB), and requires ~1/10 GFLOPs (92.5 vs. 934.4), while achieving higher accuracy across all cohorts in Table 1.Compared with nnMamba, ADAPT is slower in latency (52 vs. 25 ms) but uses ~6× less memory and ~5× fewer GFLOPs with higher accuracy. Thus, our claim is a favorable accuracy-memory-complexity trade-off, not merely GFLOPs reduction. We will add the numbers to Table 1.3) Positioning against prior work (R2, AC). ADAPT is related to multi-view/slice-attention MRI models, but differs mechanistically. Compared with M3T [8] and MTr-Net [21], prior multi-view/2.5D methods use fixed plane processing and do not learn to reallocate slice budget across multi-views according to disease relevance. ADAPT couples view-specialized encoders with learned adaptive slice allocation while keeping total computation fixed. Under the same morphology-augmentation setting, ADAPT outperforms M3T across all four cohorts with ~1/10 GFLOPs. Compared with MSA3D (Chen et al., 2022), which uses attention to weight/fuse slice features while retaining a 3D global-feature branch, ADAPT changes which slices are sampled and uses a 2.5D transformer without full-volume 3D convolution. For pathology-aware augmentation, we claim that the morphology perturbation is only a training-time regularizer to increase NC-MCI-AD morphological variability. 4) Presentation and reproducibility revisions (R3, AC). R3’s concerns mainly involve readability/organization rather than method/result validity. We will revise Fig. 1 to make the pipeline explicit: MRI slicing → SAE shared encoding → DS-AE view-specific encoding → IntraCAE within-view fusion → InterCAE cross-view fusion → classification/adaptive profiling, with consistent colors for embeddings, attention blocks, and view streams. We will bold the best values in Tables 1-3, reformat Tables 1-2, and combine Figs. 2-3 into one NC-vs-AD attention visualization with row/column labels (views/encoder-stage attention maps) and explicit reference in Sec. 3.3.We will also define acronyms at first occurrence, release code upon acceptance, and report missing details including hardware, preprocessing, and latency/memory protocol. These revisions directly address R3 and do not alter the method, experiments, or conclusions. Chen, L., Qiao, H., & Zhu, F. (2022). Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis with brain structural MRI using multiview-slice attention and 3D convolution neural network.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a clinically motivated ADAPT framework that aims to achieve 3D-level AD diagnosis performance with 2D-level computational cost. The view-specific transformer, adaptive view profiling, and pathology-driven morphology augmentation are well aligned with the goal of balancing accuracy, efficiency, and clinical relevance. The evaluation relies heavily on ADNI, and the paper does not clearly report sample sizes and class distributions for the additional datasets. A clearer cross-cohort setup, such as treating ADNI phases or external cohorts as separate domains, would better support the claimed robustness. The positioning against prior work needs clarification. Several components overlap with existing multi-view, slice-attention, and pathology-aware augmentation methods, but the paper does not sufficiently compare with or discuss these related approaches. This makes it harder to judge the true methodological novelty. The efficiency and experimental claims should be better supported. GFLOPs reduction alone is not enough to demonstrate practical efficiency; latency, memory usage, and clearer reporting of tables/figures and experimental settings are needed. | The rebuttal satisfactorily addresses the main concerns by clarifying the held-out external cohort setup, reporting cohort composition, adding latency and memory evidence beyond GFLOPs, distinguishing ADAPT from prior multi-view/slice-attention and augmentation methods, and resolving presentation/reproducibility issues. Therefore, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Following the rebuttal, all three reviewers agreed to accept the paper, including R3, who had initially rejected it. The authors credibly addressed the main concerns by clarifying the cross-cohort setup and showing the efficiency claim using latency and memory measurements rather than GFLOPs alone. Overall, the methodological design, external-cohort validation and favourable accuracy-efficiency trade-off justify acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem: how to retain strong 3D diagnostic performance for Alzheimer’s disease classification while substantially reducing computational cost. I find the overall framework well motivated, and the three main components of ADAPT, namely the view-specific transformer design, adaptive view profiling, and pathology-driven morphology augmentation, are well aligned with this goal. The rebuttal adequately addresses the main concerns raised in the reviews and meta-review. In particular, the authors clarify that the evaluation is not limited to ADNI-only testing: ADNI is used for training/validation/model selection, while AIBL, MIRIAD, and OASIS are treated as held-out external cohorts. This substantially strengthens the robustness claim. The rebuttal also improves the efficiency argument by reporting latency and peak GPU memory in addition to GFLOPs, which makes the practical trade-off much clearer and more convincing. I also appreciate the improved positioning relative to prior multi-view and slice-based methods. While the individual components are related to existing ideas, the paper’s contribution lies in a coherent and practically meaningful integration: learning how to allocate limited slice budget across views while maintaining a lightweight 2D/2.5D design. In this sense, the work is not purely incremental engineering, but a thoughtful methodological refinement with demonstrated empirical value. There are still some limitations. The novelty is moderate rather than radical, and some important implementation and reporting details should have been clearer in the original manuscript rather than only in the rebuttal. A three-class AD/MCI/NC setting would also have strengthened the clinical scope. However, I do not view these as fatal weaknesses. The paper presents a solid technical contribution, a strong efficiency-accuracy trade-off, and encouraging external-cohort results that are relevant to the MICCAI community. Overall, I believe the paper is sufficiently strong for acceptance.

title: AEGIS: Anatomy-Embedded Group-Invariant Segmentation for Fair Medical Foundation Models
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed method is innovative and addresses an important issue in medical image segmentation, which is the unfairness across different demographic groups. The use of a 2D slice-based PEFT paradigm is a novel approach that allows for efficient fine-tuning of segmentation models while improving fairness. The experimental results on the three datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of AEGIS in improving fairness while maintaining segmentation performance. This work has the potential to make a significant impact on the field of medical image segmentation and contribute to more equitable healthcare outcomes.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Some of the references should be the published papers, instead of arXiv preprints. 2.In the introduction, the authors use references [11, 12, 14, 15, 18] to support the claim that foundation models suffer from unfairness. However, some of the references do not involve foundation models. 3.The word “genuine” is too absolute. 4.The authors use \tau=2 as the pixel threshold, but it is not clear how this threshold is determined. Additional ablation studies on the choice of \tau or other explanations would be helpful to understand its impact on the performance of the proposed method. 5.The authors claim that their 2D slice-based PEFT paradigm can support large batches. However, the key factor that determines the batch size is the GPU memory. Besides, I am curious about whether this method can be expended to 3D segmentators, and how to process the 2D results to obtain the final 3D segmentation results? 6.The font size of the figures is too small, which makes it difficult to read the details. It is recommended to increase the font size for better readability. 7.The authors only use DSC and EAGap as evaluation metrics, other metrics regarding the trade-off between accuracy and fairness should also be considered, such as ES-Dice. 8.I am curious about the input bounding box prompt. How is the bounding box generated? 9.GroupDRO is an algorithm designed for classification tasks, what backbone is used for the segmentation task? 10.In table 2, the nnU-Net reports a DSC of 53.9, which is much lower than the results reported in the challenge website. It would be helpful to clarify the reason for this discrepancy, such as whether the same training and testing data are used, and whether the same evaluation metrics are applied. 11.The authors claim that their method achieves Pareto-optimal results, but no theoretical analysis is provided to support this claim.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The study addresses an important concern in FMs regarding awareness of the fairness by introducing several mechanisms (ACFA and HADW) in a framework named as AEGIS. Isolation of anatomical features represented with sensitive attributes by ACFA module is a moderately novel approach and purifies the optimization for a fairer model construction. HADW is then applied to purified features for dynamically adjusting the loss weighting by considering data from worst-performing sub-groups and reduces the disparities across members inside sub-groups. These mechanisms allow for smaller disparity gaps while retaining segmentation performance as higher as possible. Proposed framework is extensively tested on three different use-cases in comparison with existing/well-known models. The method outperforms those off-the-shelf models mostly in subgroup disparities without sacrificing on segmentation performance evaluated by Dice score. The ablation study also verifies the positive performance contribution of the components. The paper is well organized and the methodology is explained clearly.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: In the paper, the major flaw is the misleading analysis for Pareto Frontier (PF). According to Figure 2 (a-c), it is claimed that AEGIS outperforms other systems in terms of utility-fairness trade-off performance, which is indicated as performance-fairness PF, but there is only one operating point/model for each system. Contrary; given a system, PF is constructed as a subset of non-dominated points/models among all points/models generated by that system. So, each model should be a different realization of the system (AEGIS, MedSAM etc.) regularized by some fairness hyper-parameter (lambda) or system threshold etc., and surviving/non-dominated points should create the frontier. The comparative analysis should be then performed between system frontier curves based on specialized metrics/tools (hypervolume, uniformity/fairical etc.). This part must be revised in the paper accordingly by dropping the claim or changing it to reflect true Pareto optimality analysis. Otherwise, the current plot is just a visualization of Table 1 and misleading about the superiority of the AEGIS on Pareto optimality. That would be also a good extension to test the proposed framework with different FMs and sensitive attributes higher than two members (non-binary) such as race (Harvard FairSeg has this attribute with three sub-groups as Asian, Black, White). The current analysis is only based on MedSegX and sensitive attributes with two sub-groups. A comprehensive analysis with these factors would make the framework more generalizable under different conditions. Qualitative examples would be supportive to perform visual analysis on predicted segmentation masks across the systems in consideration. The code and the in-house HNSCC cohort data (if possible) should be also made public for reproducibility purpose. Although the method is clearly explained, the reproducibility is lack because of unavailable data. It is intuitive but that would be better to put sub-captions (a, b,..) inside Figure 2 to match what a-c is in the text.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses the fairness-aware degradation problem in medical foundation models, particularly in the context of PEFT for HNSCC segmentation via adaptation of large pre-trained segmentation models. The proposed modules, representation alignment and loss reweighting, are conceptually intuitive and align with the problem-specific solution. Avoiding adversarial training reduces optimization instability, particularly under PEFT settings. Experiments on in-house and OOD datasets, and ablation study, validate the evaluation analysis.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Fairness objective is not clearly or formally defined. What notion of fairness the method is truly optimizing? Fairness metric choice is limited. The evaluation primarily focus on the EA Gap. The paper does not sufficiently justify why this metric is preferred over standard fairness metrices in medical image segmentation fairness. The proposed method builds on the MedSegX. However, the baseline MedSegX already achieves comparable or better performance on overall Dice score, EA Gap for minority subgroups (e.g., Female and Young). This raises concern over whether the observed fairness EA gap reduction stems from genuine fairness optimization or from degraded baseline subgroup performance introduced by the proposed modifications. A clear analysis and justification is required. Minor weaknesses: Hyperparameters are fixed without sufficient justification or sensitivity analysis. Page 3, τ is set to 2; page 4, β = 0.9; λalign = 0.1, λf air = 1.0, and λbg = 0.05, and T =0.1, the lower temperature value plays a significant role.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for the careful reading. R1/R2:Pareto-front claim. A:We thank the reviewers for identifying this issue.We agree that “Pareto Front/Pareto-optimal” is too strong for Fig.2(a-c),because each method is one operating point rather than a frontier obtained by sweeping a fairness-control parameter.We will revise the title,caption,and conclusion to“performance-fairness trade-off analysis”and remove the formal Pareto-optimality claim. Frontier-level tools such as hypervolume/uniformity are thus not applicable to Fig.2(a-c).This is a terminology correction,not a change to the empirical conclusion:AEGIS remains in the favorable high-Dice/low-gap region, reducing the maximum EA Gap while preserving competitive/best overall Dice. R1/R4:Fairness objective and metrics. A:We respectfully disagree that our evaluation is unsupported or based on one non-standard metric.Medical segmentation fairness has no universally adopted metric analogous to Dice/HD95;metrics should match the fairness notion and task.Our notion is group-wise segmentation accuracy parity:reducing group-conditioned Dice disparities while preserving overall Dice.This objective is implemented in Eq. (1):L_task preserves utility,while L_align and L_fair reduce inter-group feature conflicts and emphasize historically underperforming subgroups.EA Gap, defined in Sec.3.2,directly measures the largest subgroup-level Dice deviation targeted by AEGIS.The evaluation is not “only EA Gap”:Table 1 reports overall Dice,subgroup Dice,and EA Gap jointly.ES-Dice is a useful complementary composite metric derived from overall performance and group disparities;since its ingredients are already reported,it requires no extra experiments.Our decomposed reporting is more transparent because it shows which subgroup improves and whether utility drops,rather than collapsing them into one score. The results do not indicate fairness via uniform degradation:HNSCC preserves overall Dice while reducing all gaps;PI-CAI improves both overall Dice and site gap;Harvard-FairSeg shows marginal overall-Dice change while improving the lower-performing older subgroup and reducing the age gap.Thus, gains come from improving/preserving underperforming subgroups with little or no overall-Dice loss,not from uniformly degrading all groups. R1/R4:Implementation details. A:GroupDRO use the identical MedSegX-PEFT backbone.The box prompt follows MedSegX:a GT-derived tight box with up to 20-pixel perturbation during training and no perturbation during evaluation for all prompt-based methods.This is an oracle protocol for controlled benchmarking,not a deployment assumption.AEGIS follows the MedSegX 2D protocol:3D MRI volumes are sliced into 2D axial images;Dice is computed on 2D predictions and averaged over samples/subgroups.We did not use the official PI-CAI 3D detection/diagnosis pipeline;leaderboard numbers are not directly comparable to our Dice-based OOD segmentation evaluation,explaining the apparent nnU-Net discrepancy.τ=2 affects only foreground-prototype construction.β=0.9 stabilizes EMA,T=0.1 focuses on harder groups,and λ_align/λ_fair/λ_bg balance fairness terms with L_task.These values were chosen from validation performance/training stability,then fixed for all reported test evaluations. R1/R2:Scope,presentation,and reproducibility. A:More foundation models,non-binary attributes,and qualitative masks would strengthen generality.Under rebuttal rules we do not add new results,but the submission already covers one foundation-model backbone,three datasets,in-domain/OOD settings, and gender/age/site attributes. We will update arXiv-only references where possible,separate FM-specific from broader bias evidence,replace “genuine”,enlarge figure fonts, and improve readability.Fig.2 already includes sublabels (a-f);we will make them more visible.We will release all code upon acceptance;private HNSCC data may be requested by email subject to institutional approval and a data-use agreement.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Disparate scores from reviewers, who also differentially report utility (R4: MedSegX performs as well or better on test cases, R1: “improve[s] fairness and maintains seg performance”). Rebuttal with author’s response is sensible here to attempt to clarify. | All reviewers are in agreement. However, please fix the error noticed by R4.I have determined this to be acceptable conditional on a fix in the camera ready. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reading the rebuttal, I recommend Accept. The paper gives a concrete PEFT framework for fairness-aware medical segmentation. Its two main parts are easy to identify: ACFA changes the feature space used by the segmentation model, and HADW changes how subgroup errors are weighted during training. The experiments on the in-house HNSCC cohort and the two external datasets show smaller subgroup gaps while keeping Dice in a similar range, and the ablations indicate that both parts contribute. The main concerns raised in the reviews were about the way the results were presented rather than about a clear failure of the method. In particular, the Pareto-frontier analysis was misleading because the paper showed one operating point per method, not a frontier over multiple settings. The rebuttal addressed this point by agreeing to revise the claim and presentation. There is also a remaining notation issue: the reported EAGap values appear to follow a max-min subgroup gap, while the equation in the paper defines a deviation from the overall Dice. This should be fixed in the camera-ready version. Overall, the method is technically reasonable, the experiments support the main empirical claim, and the remaining issues are concrete manuscript corrections. I would therefore support acceptance, with the expectation that the authors revise the Pareto-frontier language and correct the fairness-gap definition in the final version. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a fairness-aware framework AEGIS for adapting medical foundation models. They demonstrate performance using metrics that reviewers found insufficient and by overstating claims for the Pareto-Front performance analysis. During the rebuttal, the authors clarified these two points, especially: 1/ they proposed to change the claims for the Pareto-Front / Pareto-optimal issue ; 2/ they provide clarification on their choice of fairness objective and metrics. Additional points were mentioned by the authors, providing details on the implementation. Therefore, I recommend acceptance of this paper.

title: Anatomically Consistent TMJ Disc Segmentation via Semantic Anchoring and Clinical Priors
reviewer_1_strengths: The targeted problem is practical and challeging. The module designs are very clear and interpretable, for example the use of MedDINOv3 in PSA module. MOL is effectively used to help with the performance improvment.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The explanation of some method designs and experimental settings is insufficient. , such as the temperature in softmax function, the ratios of sampled points. The proposed framework is a 2D segmentation model in essence, although the PSA module aggregate adjacent slices. As we know, 3D segmentation models are advantageous over 2D models in anatomical inconsistency performances. I suggest the authors add some metrics of continuity or topology accuracy to further prove the effectiveness of their method, such as, number of connected components, fragmentation score.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: a) The writing of this paper is easy to understand and there are few spelling or grammatical error. b) The quantitative and qualitative experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method, and the article achieves SOTA performance in comparative experiments. c) The method tries to describe the network architecture as well as the objective functions thoroughly. d) Considering the specific difficulties of the TMJ task, the proposed TSIC utilizes object detection foundation model and adjacent-slice features to produce an enhanced similarity based localization map, overcoming the challenge in localizing small targets. Besides, it adaptively adjusts boundary predicions at the point level to resolve the issue of boundary ambiguity. e) The innovative introduction of auxiliary metadata effectively enchance the performance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: a) In ‘Introduction’ section, the review of current methods is insufficient, lacking more detailed introduction of relevant specific approaches on TMJ task. Meanwhile, foundation models such as MedSAM and MedDINOv3 are mentioned. What’s the advantages and disadvantages of them compared to general model. b) The comparison methods in experiments are not up-to-date. It only compares against old methods like the standard UNet and its very basic variants and new but less effective SAM-based model. If possible, more state-of-the-art methods specifically for TMJ Segmentation tasks should be included for comparison. c) In ‘Application’ section, predicted masks and images are concatenated for downstream diagnostic tasks, the setting should be discussed. Besides, more state-of-the-art medical image classification methods should be taken into account, rather than very basic ResNet. Actually, more detailed experimental elaboration and corresponding tabulated comparison results should be included. d) Although the writing of this paper is easy to understand, there are still some minor writing issues can be corrected. For example, the first line of ‘Ablation Study’ section references a non-existent ‘Table 2(a)’. The architecture diagram uses two different representations for the ground truth: ‘Mgt’ and ‘GroundTruth’, Although they are used in different modules, the notation should remain consistent if there is no change. e) The submission does not mention open access to source code or data. Although it’s allowed, the ‘Method’ section should be more specific in the absence of source code. While the paper provides a detailed description of the implementation process, it lacks more intuitive mathematical formulations.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and challenging problem, namely TMJ disc segmentation, which is difficult due to small object size, low contrast, and high anatomical variability. The proposed framework is well-motivated and technically sound. The combination of semantic anchoring in foundation model feature space and metadata-guided refinement is a thoughtful design that directly targets both localization and boundary ambiguity. The method effectively incorporates clinical prior knowledge. This adds interpretability and domain relevance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The proposed method partially relies on empirical design choices and task-specific clinical priors. While these components are effective for the current dataset, it remains unclear whether the approach can generalize to external datasets. Therefore, validation on independent external datasets is necessary to demonstrate the robustness and generalizability of the method. The current evaluation mainly focuses on integrating the proposed method into baseline models, rather than comparing with recent dedicated TMJ disc segmentation methods. As a result, it is difficult to properly assess the relative performance level of the proposed approach within the current state of the field. We note that although the proposed method achieves notable improvements over the baselines, there is still room for further performance gains. Providing an analysis of failure cases or samples with large segmentation errors would be beneficial for better understanding the limitations of the method and guiding future improvements. In the ablation study, we observe that the performance gains mainly stem from the MOL and PSA components, while the contribution of C-MPR appears relatively limited. Moreover, MOL also plays an important role in supporting PSA. This raises a practical concern for clinical deployment: whether MOL can be consistently obtained for all patients. In cases where MOL is partially missing, it remains unclear whether the model can still maintain stable performance.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank Reviewers 1,2,3 (R1,R2,R3) and the Meta-Reviewer (M) for the constructive feedback. [M,R2,R3: Baseline rationale] We agree that recent TMJ methods need more discussion. For example, Liu et al. use a topology-preserving multi-branch decoder with joint loss, and Hu et al. extend TransUNet with edge enhancement and cross-slice attention. However, without a public TMJ benchmark, paper-level SOTA comparison is unreliable due to different datasets/settings, and fair reproduction is difficult without released code/protocols. We therefore used strong, widely validated, reproducible baselines for a fair test across CNN, self-configuring, Transformer, and foundation-model families. [M,R3: External validity] We acknowledge the lack of external TMJ validation as a limitation. Suitable cohorts are scarce because no public TMJ benchmark exists. As a sanity check, our pipeline improved Dice from 0.82 to 0.89 on a structurally similar knee meniscus task, but this was not treated as external validation due to anatomical/task mismatch. Within available TMJ data, we used patient-level 5-fold CV on a relatively large cohort for fair evaluation and observed consistent gains across backbones. Future work will pursue multi-institutional validation. [M,R3: C-MPR] C-MPR is a boundary refinement module, not the main localization component, so its effect is clearer in HD95 than Dice. Comparing Exp. 3 and Exp. 6 in Table 2, adding C-MPR lowers HD95 from 6.01 to 5.27 (↓12.3%), supporting its role in reducing boundary outliers after localization. [M,R3: MOL dependency] MOL is routinely assessed in TMJ evaluation [23] and is naturally recognized during closed/open-mouth MRI acquisition, so missingness is unlikely. Nevertheless, if unavailable, the model can operate as the no-MOL variant (Table 2, Exp. 5), which still outperforms the vanilla backbone, showing that MOL improves performance but is not strictly required. [R1,R2,R3: Code] Model code will be released for implementation clarity and reproducibility. [R1: Empirical design choices] Most method-specific settings were chosen through qualitative inspection and empirical validation. The actual softmax temperatures are τ=0.05 for MOL=0 and τ=0.1 for MOL=1, yielding sharper and broader localization, respectively (the reversed description will be corrected). For point sampling, we follow PointRend [11] with 75% uncertainty-based samples and a 25% coverage pool, where 25% is drawn from PSA-defined salient regions and the rest remains random. We will clarify these details. [R1: Topology metrics] Thank you for the suggestion. We agree and will reflect topology metrics, such as CC, FS, and Euler, in the released evaluation code for additional verification. [R2: Related-methods] We agree that these methods need better context, as they serve different roles rather than a direct pros/cons comparison. Prior TMJ-specific studies are mostly CNN-based adaptations to TMJ MRI and were too briefly summarized. MedSAM is a strong recent medical segmentation baseline, while MedDINOv3 is both a representative foundation model and the semantic feature source for PSA. We will clarify this distinction and expand the TMJ-specific discussion. [R2: Application settings] This pilot study tested the diagnostic value of predicted masks while limiting classifier effects. We used ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 as a simple baseline, trained for 50 epochs with learning rate 6e-5 and batch size 16.Masks were concatenated with close/open MRI pairs as 4-channel inputs and improved AUROC. SOTA-oriented classifiers remain future work. [R2: Typos] Thanks for catching these. We will fix them. [R3: Failures] Thank you for the suggestion. During qualitative analysis, we observed failures, including over-segmentation into adjacent retrodiscal tissue when the posterior disc margin appeared intermixed and hard to distinguish. Given the tiny disc size, even small spill-over can affect metrics under severe anatomical ambiguity.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: N/A Justification(s): There is clear consensus among reviewers that the work presents a well-designed and interpretable framework with clinical relevance. There is strong empirical performance demonstrated with improvements over baselines and clear presentation. However, all reviewers also acknowledge limitations in evaluation of the work, the fact that the evaluation is limited to a single dataset with no external validation making the generalization potential unclear and there is a lack of comparison with strong baselines. In rebuttal, the authors should focus on strengthening the state of the art comparison by clarifying why the given baselines were chosen and comparing with more reject relevant approaches. If additional experimental results on external datasets exist, these should be reported and if not the authors should give a strong justification for limiting the work to the single dataset, acknowledging the limitations of this. The authors should also clarify the dependence on MOL and whether this can be consistently obtained given the apparent strong need for it. The contributions of the components should also be clarified given the apparently small contributions of C-MPR. | N/A Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): R1 kept the same recommendation of Accept, while R2 changed from Weak Accept to Accept. Both reviewers were satisfied with the rebuttal, in which the authors addressed initial concerns regarding the paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): TISC introduces an anatomically and clinically consistent framework for the challenging task of temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disc segmentation from MRI by coupling deep foundation feature anchoring with clinical metadata. The initial reviewer concerns regarding baseline rationale, missing external validation, and metadata dependency were comprehensively and convincingly resolved during the rebuttal phase. Specifically, the authors clarified that paper-level SOTA comparisons are structurally restricted due to the lack of a standardized public benchmark, while successfully demonstrating that their method degrades gracefully and maintains stable performance even if clinical metadata is completely absent.

title: Anatomy- and Site-Guided 3D Patch Diffusion for Robust MRI Harmonization
reviewer_1_strengths: The investigators appropriately generated a curated, robust training dataset assembled from multiple public repositories of multi-site international medical imaging studies and a robust clinical cohort of patients with Alzheimer’s disease for testing. Methodological refinement is demonstrated in (1) performing ablation studies to optimize classifier-free guidance, (2) assessing site variability of supposedly site-invariant anatomical priors, and (3) assessing harmonization performance of clinically meaningful structure-cognition correlations. However, further methodological detail is needed as specified below.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Although the presented 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework is intriguing, and training and testing datasets are robust, greater clarity is needed on methodological reasoning and details throughout the paper. Derivation of anatomical representations that are supposedly site-invariant is a critical step in the proposed framework for structural MRI harmonization. As such, greater detail should be provided on how Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) tests in Ablation Study 2 demonstrate site-invariance of the anatomical conditioning map. What specific distribution pairs were MMDs calculated between? How was MMD averaged per site when MMDs were calculated on inter-site discrepancies? Presumably MMDs were calculated on same subject, same map (raw vs. anatomical map), between sites, e. g. , subject1-site1-raw histogram vs. subject1-site2-raw histogram or subject1-site1-anatomical histogram vs. subject1-site2-anatomical histogram. However, such detail should be explicitly specified for clarity and reproducibility in the paper. Visual or tabulated results, rather than single summary p-values, would also be helpful for interpretation. As is, the site-invariance of anatomical representations is questionable. In Task 1, the dependent variable in the linear mixed-effects model is not stated – a model formula should be provided for clarity. Presumably, the site fixed effect and subject random effect predicted GM and WM volumes normalized to intracranial tissue volume. If so, why were whole tissue volumes chosen for site- and subject-effect modeling as opposed to more specific memory- or disease-related regional volumes as in Task 2? Gross whole-GM and whole-WM tissue volumes are likely less sensitive to small scanner-specific differences in tissue boundaries than small regional volumes like the hippocampus or entorhinal cortex. Normalizing GM and WM volume to total intracranial tissue volume (GM+WM) may have further reduced sensitivity to site or scanner effects. Why was normalization to whole tissue volume chosen? Overall, it’s unclear if the proposed 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework is a superior method or step forward for structural MRI harmonization, relative to existing published techniques. STGAN and HACA3 outperform the proposed framework in matched-subject harmonization performance (SSIM, WD, PCC). STGAN, HACA3, and basic preprocessing outperform the proposed framework in mixed-effects modeling of brain tissue volumes, albeit not consistently. HACA3 is also the best-performing method for cognitive associations in 3/8 regions assessed, whereas the proposed diffusion framework is the clear best-performer in only 2/8 regions (possibly 3/8 if including middle temporal, though it is difficult to discern a difference between STGAN and Diffusion for middle temporal in Fig. 3). For what tasks or under what circumstances would the authors recommend the proposed framework be utilized over STGAN or HACA3? While the curated training and clinical datasets are robust in spanning multiple international sites and studies, re-training and evaluating methods on all full available datasets would increase confidence in results.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.This paper presents a well-motivated and technically sound framework that combines patch-based processing with conditional diffusion, which is a meaningful extension for high-resolution MRI harmonization tasks. The use of overlapping patches is particularly practical, as it addresses both memory constraints and the loss of fine anatomical detail often observed in full-volume or latent-space methods. 2.The introduction of anatomy-guided diffusion through gradient and high-frequency-derived maps is a novel and interesting design choice. This explicitly enforces structural consistency across sites and provides a principled way to disentangle anatomical information from scanner-specific contrast variations. 3.The incorporation of manifold-constrained classifier-free guidance is a thoughtful addition that improves sampling stability while maintaining subject-specific features. This reflects careful consideration of the trade-off between the strength of harmonization and anatomical fidelity.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.This paper does not sufficiently quantify the contribution of the proposed anatomical map components. While gradient and high-frequency features are claimed to guide harmonization, no ablation studies isolate their individual effects (e.g., removing gamma perturbation, gradient, or frequency components). This makes it difficult to assess whether the performance gains stem from the anatomical guidance or from the diffusion framework itself. 2.Although the method achieves strong global performance, the regional analysis reveals inconsistencies. Specifically, certain clinically important ROIs, such as the posterior cingulate and entorhinal cortex, show slightly worse correlations with MMSE compared to baseline methods, suggesting that the harmonization may not uniformly preserve region-specific information. This raises concerns about its reliability for localized analyses. 3.The novelty of the framework is somewhat incremental relative to recent diffusion-based harmonization approaches. Prior work on conditional diffusion for medical image translation and harmonization (e.g., diffusion-based MRI synthesis and style transfer methods) has already explored conditioning mechanisms and structural guidance, and the current work primarily extends these ideas through patch-based processing and feature engineering rather than introducing a fundamentally new formulation.

author_feedback: Dear Reviewers, Area Chairs, and Program Chairs, We thank you for the careful reading and constructive feedback. We address the main points below. To preserve anonymity, the GitHub repository is not included in the submission but is already prepared and will be made public after the review process. It contains the full training and inference code, pretrained weights, the exact train/test splits data, and all evaluation scripts used in the paper. 1) Clarification of the anatomical map / site-invariance analysis. We agree that this is a central step and should be described more explicitly. In Ablation Study 2, MMD was computed between every pair of acquisition sites (si ,sj), not between matched subjects. For each site, we pooled the histogram feature vectors from all scans acquired at that site, and computed the RBF-kernel MMD separately for raw-image histograms and anatomical-map histograms. Thus, each value corresponds to one site-pair comparison. The “per-site” summary is the average of that site’s MMD values against all other sites. The paired t-test compares raw vs. anatomical-map MMD on the same site pairs, so the reduction directly reflects lower inter-site discrepancy for the anatomical map. For brevity, we do not reproduce the full pairwise table here. Our anatomical map is intended as a simple low-level prior that suppresses scanner contrast while preserving structure, inspired by recent work on anatomical priors (10.1016/j.neuroimage.2025.121297). Gradient magnitude and high-frequency content are chosen because they are less tied to site-specific intensity statistics than raw signal, and random gamma perturbation further reduces leakage of contrast cues into the conditioning map. 2) Mixed-effects model in Task 1.For each method, we fitted a linear mixed-effects model with site as a fixed effect and subject as a random intercept: tissue_ratio ~ site + (1 | subject) The dependent variable is the GM or WM tissue ratio. These ratios are normalized by total intracranial volume, defined as GM + WM + CSF, to reduce inter-subject size differences and make comparisons across sites and harmonization methods more comparable. 3) Comparison with STGAN / HACA3 and when our method is most useful. We agree that no single method dominates every metric. Our claim is not that diffusion is uniformly best, but that it is the most consistent method in our experiments and provides a strong balance between harmonization and preservation of biologically meaningful signals. In the tissue-level analysis, our method is the only one that consistently achieves both low marginal R² and high conditional R² across GM and WM, whereas STGAN and HACA3 are stronger in one tissue but less consistent in the other. In the cognition analysis, our method achieves the highest global mean absolute correlation and improves over the preprocessed baseline. This is also consistent with Fig. 2, where our method shows fewer over- and under-segmentation errors than the Anatomy Target, suggesting more robust anatomical preservation. At the same time, we acknowledge that STGAN and HACA3 can be stronger in specific metrics or regions. 4) Nature of the contributions / ablations. We appreciate the request for more component-level justification. The manuscript already includes three targeted analyses: guidance ablation (CFG vs. CFG++), the site-invariance test for the anatomical prior, and downstream clinical preservation analyses. Together, these support the full design: patch-based high-resolution synthesis, anatomy-guided conditioning, and manifold-constrained guidance. We also performed an additional internal ablation of the anatomical representation components: removing the gradient component caused a marked SSIM drop (-0.28 drop), indicating that gradient information is the main contributor; removing the high-frequency component did not significantly reduce SSIM, suggesting a smaller contribution. Other components could also merit further investigation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework for multi-site MRI harmonization conditioned on an anatomical map and site-specific embeddings. Evaluation includes traveling-subject data and a clinical cohort with cognition-related downstream analyses. The reviewers all acknowledge that the problem is practically important, that the combination of anatomical conditioning with site embeddings is a sensible disentanglement strategy, and that the evaluation scope is substantial. All three reviewers recommend Weak Reject (3), but the AC finds that these rejections are based on somewhat different reasons. R1 provides the most detailed and consistent critique (and the AC weighs it more into the current decision): the MMD-based evidence for site-invariance of the anatomical maps is ambiguously described (which distributions are compared, how results are averaged, and only p-values are reported), and the linear mixed-effects model formula for Task 1 is not stated. More importantly, R1 argues that the proposed method does not clearly outperform STGAN and HACA3 across the reported metrics; STGAN and HACA3 win on matched-subject SSIM/WD/PCC, the baselines can win on mixed-effects tissue volumes, and HACA3 is best for cognitive correlations in more ROIs than the proposed method. This undermines the significance claim. R2 argues that the construction of the anatomical map is under-justified: it amounts to gradient-style feature engineering and the paper does not explain why this particular construction is preferred. R3 notes that there is no component ablation isolating the contributions of the gradient, high-frequency, and gamma-perturbation parts, that certain clinically important ROIs (posterior cingulate, entorhinal cortex) show worse MMSE correlations than baselines, and that the novelty is incremental relative to existing conditional-diffusion harmonization work. Most of R1 and R2’s concerns can be addressed through clarification and re-analysis of existing results (MMD pair specification, mixed-effects formula, discussion of when to use the proposed method vs. STGAN/HACA3). R3’s request for finer ablations of the anatomical-map components is the one concern that would typically require new experiments, but it is not on its own decisive. Given the uniform but moderate rejection score and the substantial amount of work the paper represents, I recommend inviting the authors to respond in rebuttal before a final decision. While preparing the rebuttal, the authors should carefully read reviewers’ comments and the MICCAI rebuttal guidelines. | All three reviewers opened at weak reject in the initial review but they all gave different reasons. The rebuttal did a good job clarifying the site-invariance (MMD) analysis and the mixed-effects model, and reframing the contribution as the most consistent and balanced method rather than the best on every metric, which moved R1 to accept. The harder concerns, though, are only partly resolved on the submitted manuscript: R2’s point that the anatomical map is under-motivated gradient feature engineering and R3’s point that the paper lacks a component ablation and shows regional inconsistencies are answered mainly by a new ablation run during the rebuttal. Weighing the one engaged accept (which I weigh the most in the initial review) against two non-response reviewers, and the authors overall effective rebuttal given the 4000 limit, I lean toward accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper originally received consistent “weak reject” reviews with clear avenues for rebuttal. The extensive work that was put into the methodology and experimentation was recognized by the AC. I believe the authors have adequately addressed the concerns that led to weak rejects, including both novelty and clarification of the contrast-agnostic space. I recommend that this paper be accepted. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have adequately addressed the reviewers’ questions and concerns.
