title: BiC-ODE: Bidirectionally Coupled Neural ODEs for Rapid Laminar Surface Reconstruction of the Human Cortex from 5T MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: The topic of this submission is within the scope of this conference and of potential interest to its audience. The work described here is an incremental but noteworthy advance over previous work by a similar group of authors. The text is straightforward to understand for a reader with knowledge in recent approaches for image analysis.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: For more medically-inclined readers, it would be interesting to learn which anatomical layer(s) are represented by this somewhat ominous “hypointense band”. What is the anatomical (clinical) relevance of this work?
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: （1）The method is specifically designed for the unique high-contrast low-signal band present in 5T FLAIR images. （2）The proposed SOVR metric is reasonable and practical, effectively quantifying the preservation of the nested ordering of the four cortical surfaces. （3）The experimental comparisons are comprehensive, including multiple deep learning methods and ablation studies, with results showing advantages in metrics such as ASSD, HD90, and SOVR.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: （1）The paper claims that “bidirectional coupled deformation” is the core innovation. However, in the actual implementation, it merely concatenates the features of the WM and pial surfaces and feeds them into a shared network. This “coupling” approach is relatively simplistic and lacks theoretical depth or significant mechanistic innovation, differing little from standard multi-task joint prediction. The technical contribution of the “Cross-Surface Coupling” section appears significantly overstated. （2）The authors only cite a paper currently “under review” as the method for generating the silver standard, without providing any specific description, validation, or open-source code for that method. This substantially undermines the reproducibility and credibility of the experimental results. Reviewers cannot determine whether the silver standard itself is accurate, nor can they assess whether BiC-ODE offers genuine improvement over that optimization method. （3）The method was validated exclusively on 5T FLAIR data from a single institution and was not tested on 3T, 7T, or 5T data from other vendors. For a deep learning model, this is a major limitation; it fails to demonstrate the method’s generalizability across different acquisition conditions, field strengths, or populations. （4）The authors did not directly compare BiC-ODE against the optimization method used to generate the silver standard (e.g., in terms of accuracy, inference time, robustness). Readers cannot judge whether the deep learning method genuinely outperforms the traditional approach, nor evaluate the suitability of the silver standard as a reasonable supervision target.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The method introduces several novel components, particularly the bidirectional coupled information exchange between surfaces and the dedicated loss functions for hypointense band modeling. This appears to be one of the first approaches specifically designed for cortical hypointense band modeling, making it a genuinely novel contribution to the field.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Silver standard ground truth. The authors use silver standard hypointense band surfaces generated by an optimization method that is currently under review (provided as supplementary material). While using an algorithmic silver standard is generally acceptable when it is well-validated, relying on an unpublished and unreviewed method as the evaluation reference raises concerns about the reliability of the results. Since the referenced paper is anonymized — suggesting it may be from the same group — the authors presumably have access to manual annotations. I would encourage the authors to use manual labels as ground truth, or at minimum provide a more thorough justification for why the silver standard is sufficiently reliable for this purpose. Cross-surface coupling is not evaluated in the ablation study. The bidirectional coupled information exchange is a core architectural contribution, yet its individual impact is not isolated in the ablation study. It would be informative to understand how much of the performance gain is attributable to this design choice versus the specialized loss functions.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Reviewers and AC for their constructive feedback. We address the core concerns below. 1.Silver-Standard Reliability & Comparison (AC, R1-3) The silver-standard surfaces were generated by an energy-function optimization method (detailed in the supplement) that incorporates geometry- and image-guided terms. Crucially, this optimization method demonstrates excellent agreement with clinician-validated manual annotations (Dice ~96.0%/~95.4% on the primary/cross-site datasets) and high test-retest repeatability (ASSD <0.1 mm). Since manual labels are only local masks, this highly accurate method serves as our whole-cortex evaluation ground truth. This optimization method is not a competing baseline but our supervisory signal. BiC-ODE’s primary contribution is successfully matching this clinician-validated standard (Tables 1-2, Fig. 2) while reducing the optimization’s hours-long computation to seconds-level inference for large 5T cohorts. 2.Rationale & Ablation of bidirectional coupling (AC, R2, R3) We will refine claims about the coupling module. The inner and outer hypointense-band surfaces are adjacent boundaries defining a thin intracortical band. If each surface deforms independently using only local features, they develop inconsistent relative positions and severe ordering violations. BiC-ODE therefore explicitly conditions each surface’s velocity field on its counterpart to reconstruct a strictly coupled pair. We report the requested coupling ablation here. Removing cross-surface coupling (each surface concatenates only its own features) worsened ASSD/HD90 and increased SOVR to ~17% compared with BiC-ODE. This confirms that bidirectional conditioning is physically essential for preserving relative positions, proving the performance gain is not merely due to specialized loss functions. 3.Clinical relevance (R1, R3) We define the hypointense band as an MRI-visible, signal-defined band on 5T FLAIR, not as a specific anatomical layer. Nevertheless, prior studies (Refs.[1–3]) suggest that intracortical contrast reflects regional cyto-/myeloarchitectonic variation. The supplement shows preliminary clinical relevance: epilepsy patients had lower hypointense-layer thickness ratio than healthy controls, suggesting that these multi-layer metrics may complement conventional WM/pial morphometry for cortical microstructural disorders. 4.Cross-site generalizability & Clarifications on claims & Other concerns (R2,R3) (a) We tested BiC-ODE on the supplement’s cross-site 5T dataset, which was not used for training, obtaining comparable inner/outer ASSD (~0.14/0.17mm), HD90 (~0.31/0.36mm), and SOVR (~2.5%), supporting cross-site generalizability; broader multi-vendor, 3T/7T validations are vital future work. (b) We will refine the Page 2 statement. While existing methods can be retrained on laminar-band targets, retraining alone does not explicitly model the two coupled hypointense-band boundaries and the required four-surface ordering. We will properly acknowledge joint surface methods such as Vox2Cortex. (c) WM/pial surface extraction is a shared upstream step; our runtime comparison focuses on hypointense-band reconstruction. (d) Detailed coupling/loss ablations will be considered in a journal version. (e) BiC-ODE and the supplement code will be released upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The most critical points to address in the rebuttal are the concerns regarding the silver standard ground truth and the lack of a direct comparison with the optimization method used to generate it. You must clearly justify its use or provide evidence of its reliability, as this undermines the credibility and reproducibility of the results. Second, the novelty of the bidirectional coupling lacks any theoretical justification or an ablation experiment. | The authors provided validation metrics on an external dataset and detailed the high agreement between their silver standard and manual annotations. An ablation experiment was presented to demonstrate that removing cross-surface coupling increases surface ordering violations. The final recommendation is to accept the manuscript. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes BiC-ODE, a bidirectional coupled neural ODE framework for reconstructing the inner and outer surfaces of the intracortical hypointense band in 5T FLAIR MRI, supervised by an optimization-derived silver standard and guided by task-specific depth, thickness, and intensity-band losses. The reviewers agree that this is among the first approaches to target hypointense band modeling, that the task is genuinely novel, and that the method performs well against relevant baselines while preserving the nested ordering of cortical surfaces. The principal concern across the reviews and the meta-review was the reliance on a silver standard generated by an as-yet-unpublished optimization method; the rebuttal addressed this by characterizing its agreement with clinician-validated annotations and clarifying that it serves as the supervisory signal rather than a competing baseline, with BiC-ODE’s contribution being to match this reference at a fraction of the computational cost, and the reviewer who weighted this concern most heavily found it sufficiently motivated. The authors are encouraged to retain the clearer, more measured description of the bidirectional coupling module and to incorporate the requested clinical motivation and acknowledgment of prior joint-surface methods in the camera-ready version. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This submission proposes a bidirectional neural ODE for reconstructing cortical hypointense bands in 5T MRI. R3 likved the methodologly on neural ODE. R1 and R2 noted issues with an unvalidated silver standard and missing ablation studies. The rebuttal clarified these concerns by showing agreemenrt between the silver standard and manual annotations, with an additional ablation study (note: no new experiments is allowed in the rebuttal, unfair to other submissions, discarding this study in this decision). The consensus is a positive impact and novelty in the method. For all these reasons, and with respect to the other submissions, the recommendation is towards Acceptnace.

title: BioFact-MoE: Biologically Factorized Mixture of Experts for Vision–Language Prognostic Modeling in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Use of domain knowledge: specific pathways are designed based on the clinical problem addressed, and evaluation is done wrt relevant treatment and clinical biomarkers. 2.Evaluation of impact of results on downstream task: strong for clinical impact, rather than focusing purely on quality of generated reports. 3.Ablation experiments of the proposed biological pathways to determine the most defining factors.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.There are a lot of design choices made in the proposed BioFact-MoE and MoE survival models. The majority appears to be based on prior work, but this is not made explicitly clear. The paper would benefit from a better clarification of the main contribution(s) and thus the novelty, and parts that are either existing work or secondary design choices. Its now unclear which of the exact components results in specific improvements in performance. Why are so many different design choices needed over the state of the art? It would have been stronger if the authors introduced clear contributed components rather than a complete framework, and systematically evaluate the effect of these components over / in combination with the state-of-the-art. Maybe the complexity of design such a complete new framework is not needed, and one specific design choice would be sufficient to result in an improvement. The ablation experiments also suggest that the biological factorization is the main driver, hence it would have been clearer to just focus on that component. 2.Private dataset with limited descriptions, making it difficult to assess the results. Its unclear how this data was acquired, which sources of variation could be present, what the patient characteristics are, etc. Mentions of “comparable clinical stage” are not interpretable, the role of TACE is discussed often but we dont know what clinical practice for these patients is and thus when they got TACE or not. 3.A 2D ResNet is a relatively simple / outdated choice for the image-only survival model. An improved, 3D model, such as a SwinTransformer or ConvNext 2.0 would be more suitable. 4.It would have been stronger to compare the performance to liver MRI specific VLMs such as https://doi. org/10.3390/app152312578 or https://doi. org/10.1016/j. ebiom. 2025.106060 and non-liver specific but MRI specific VLMs, instead of the now more general purpose VLMs used. 5.It would have been stronger to perform a cross-validation than a single split. Its also unclear over what the mean and std of the AUCs are computed, and it would have been better to have confidence intervals. Its therefore not entirely clear whether the proposed method really gives a statistical significant improvement over the baselines.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.A key strength is the idea of biological factorization. Instead of using one mixed representation from images and reports, the model separates liver-related and tumor-related information using different experts. Most prior work groups information based on general meaning or tasks, not based on these clinical factors. 2.The model is interpretable and clinically meaningful. It can show whether a patient’s risk is mainly driven by liver condition or tumor biology 3.The paper uses LLMs to split reports into liver and tumor parts and combines this with anatomy-based image masking. This avoids the need for manual labeling. 4.Comprehensive validation and ablation strategy - The paper compares against several baselines and includes ablation studies to show what each part of the model contributes.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.No external validation cohort - Although the data comes from two hospitals, it appears to be combined and then split for training and testing. A separate external validation cohort would be important to ensure generalizability. 2.Unclear evaluation of LLM outputs - It is not clear whether the LLM used for report decomposition was evaluated. For the biological factorization to be meaningful, the liver/tumor separation needs to be reasonably accurate. 3.Limited statistical reporting - While p-values and mean±std are reported, there is little detail on the statistical tests used or multiple comparison corrections, especially for biomarker and subgroup analyses (t-tests/bootstrap for statistical significance). 4.No dedicated discussion section - A separate discussion section would help better explain the background, novelty and the significance of the results. reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Clear clinical motivation: Not only does the model achieve a better performance, but it also increases transparency and interpretability of the predictions. Good deep-learning comparison: The authors compared their architecture to multiple (6) deep learning baselines In-depth analysis: chapters “3.4 Biological Validation” and chapter ”3.5 Ablation Study” expand the article beyond the core section and reveal many interesting connections. (https://doi.org/10.1002/hep.510280322) non-disclosed LLM version: The authors used the LLM Qwen3 to preprocess radiology reports, but didn’t specify the specifc version. author_feedback: We thank the Meta-Reviewer and reviewers for constructive feedback. We address the central concern - methodological novelty - and the specific technical points. 1.Novelty vs. joint segmentation+classification (R1, R2, Meta). R2 cites Huang 2024 [1] and Ryu 2021 [2] as overlapping prior work. However, BioGuide differs in what the auxiliary task is, in how it is implemented, and in what it delivers for segmentation. (a) [1,2] use disease-level labels (MS vs. NMOSD; four hepatic lesions). BioGuide instead encodes fine-grained radiological signs - blurring, transmantle sign, lobar location - the precise descriptors radiologists use, tightly coupled to lesion morphology. To our knowledge, no prior work uses radiological signs as auxiliary targets. (b) Unlike [1,2], where classification is primary and segmentation gains are marginal, segmentation is critical for MS and FCD. [2]: JI rises only from 68.5±10.3 to 70.0±10.9 with benign/malignant labels and does not improve with 4-class labels (68.5±12.2). [1]: joint-model precision is below baseline (73.9 vs. 74.1 for UNet); no small-cluster detection is reported, and Fig. 10 shows only refinement of already-detected large clusters. For dispersed pathologies like MS, finding all clusters matters more than refining contours. BioGuide improves every metric, including detection. (c) Architecture: [1] uses a dual-branch backbone with a Lesion Guidance Module; [2] requires user clicks. BioGuide is a single MLP at the bottleneck - no backbone change, no user input - validated on two SOTA backbones, four datasets. Knowledge-blind ablations (Random/Shuffled) isolate medical semantics from architectural regularization and are absent from both cited works. 2.Zero-vector for healthy patches (R1.1). “Temporal Lobe” is a binary property of a lesion, not the patch’s location. It describes lesion location, which directly influences morphology (e.g., temporal lesions are typically larger than occipital ones). All-zero labels for healthy patches are equivalent to the standard “no-object” target in multi-label detection. 3.Bottleneck placement (R1.2). Lesion characteristic vectors are provided as binary labels at the patient level, therefore, the precise spatial coordinates of “Blurring” are unknown. The model is not asked to localize “Blurring” voxel-wise, only to determine whether it exists in the patch. The bottleneck captures the highest-level, spatially compressed semantic context, ideal for this task. Backpropagating the patch-level loss through the encoder forces early and mid-level filters to become sensitive to clinically relevant signs. 4.”Fair” baseline with a yes/no head (R1.3). This is exactly what Random Noise and Shuffled Medical Labels test: identically-sized MLP heads, jointly trained, isolating signal content from the act of adding a head. A “lesion yes/no” head is a degenerate case of shuffled-label control. A shuffled-label vector containing at least one non-zero entry still provides the model with a global signal that a lesion exists within the patch. 5.PCA (R2,R3). Fold clustering in the baseline indicates the model memorizes fold-specific intensity distributions - poor generalization. BioGuide breaks this and reorganizes the latent space by radiological signs, the desired outcome. Better generalization is confirmed quantitatively: in Table 2, BioGuide trained on 70% data outperforms the baseline trained on 100% - data efficiency, not overfitting. Due to the 8-page limit, additional PCA figures could not be included but will be made available on GitHub upon acceptance. 6.”Marginal” MS gains (R2). MS gains (Dice +1.1%, detection +2.1%) are modest but consistent across all folds. MS lesions are higher-contrast on FLAIR and the nnU-Net baseline is already near-optimal. For FCD, where lesions are subtle and heterogeneous, gains are larger, precisely because clinical descriptors carry more discriminative information there.

title: Brain-Specialized Self-supervised Learning: Neuroanatomy-Aware Spatial Priors for 3D Brain MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: The study appropriately identifies the limitations of standard self-supervised learning objectives for natural images when applied to brain MRI, and proposes a spatial prior that better captures the anatomical regularity and low-texture characteristics of this domain. The model is pretrained on a large-scale unlabeled dataset of 6,811 T1-weighted scans collected from multiple cohorts, which supports strong generalizability. The training framework is computationally efficient, as it aligns representations in the latent space without relying on a heavy decoder for pixel-level reconstruction. The approach is thoroughly evaluated across multiple benchmarks, and the analysis provides useful insights into why ROI-based priors may fail at the selected patch level due to mixed-region tokens and label noise.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The distance-based weighting is implemented as a simple linear function, which may not adequately capture complex neuroanatomical relationships or long-range dependencies. A more flexible non-linear formulation could potentially improve the modeling of spatial interactions. 2.The framework is restricted to T1-weighted MRI, and its applicability to other important modalities such as FLAIR, T2, or PET is not examined, limiting its broader relevance. 3.The treatment of symmetric anatomical regions remains unclear. Although distant patches are decorrelated, the method does not explicitly address whether this negatively impacts regions that are anatomically similar but spatially separated, such as bilateral structures. 4.The analysis of patch size is limited, as the study does not include a systematic evaluation of how different patch resolutions influence the effectiveness of the proposed distance-based prior.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The proposed Distance-Modulated Patch Decorrelation (DIS) introduces no additional annotation requirements and incurs minimal computational overhead, making it well suited to the abundance of unlabeled brain MRI data. It offers a more flexible and scalable alternative to traditional ROI-based anatomical priors. 2.The effectiveness of DIS is clearly demonstrated through analyses of patch similarity decay over spatial distance and ROI purity evaluation, which also explain why ROI-based priors fail under fine-grained patch representations. 3.Notably, the method shows pronounced improvements in subtle-signal tasks such as MCI classification and brain tumor grading, aligning well with the needs of early-stage clinical diagnosis.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Marginal gains on the core task. On the primary AD vs. NC classification task, the method shows no improvement over iBOT. The advantages are mainly observed in MCI vs. NC and BraTS tumor grading, raising questions about its general effectiveness on more established benchmarks. 2.Lack of statistical significance testing. No statistical significance analysis (e.g., p-values) is reported when comparing the proposed method with baselines. Without such tests, it is unclear whether the observed improvements are statistically meaningful or simply due to random variation. 3.Incomplete ablation studies. The paper does not conduct combinatorial ablations of different loss components, making it difficult to disentangle the independent contributions and potential synergistic effects of each module. 4.No hyperparameter sensitivity analysis. The loss weights are both fixed at 1, without investigating their impact on performance. In addition, the masking ratio and EMA momentum are set to default values, and no parameter sensitivity experiments are provided to validate the robustness of these choices.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This manuscript uses a distance-aware regularizer that uses 3D patch-center geometry to modulate patch decorrelation, which is a natural fit for volumetric neuroimaging where spatial organization matters. The distance weighted decorrelation term is lightweight and easy to add to existing teacher–student ViT pipelines. This simplicity is interesting compared with heavier pixel reconstruction or atlas-dependent supervision. Specially, the equation in Section 3.4 is straightforward and likely reproducible in principle. Authors evaluated their work on ADNI AD/NC, ADNI MCI/NC, OASIS-3 AD/NC, and BraTS grading. The results are not good enough, but this comparison is interesting. The ablation (Table 2) is the strong part of this manuscript. It isolates the effects of masked token learning, CLS discrimination, the proposed distance prior, and an ROI-based alternative. This Table 2 supports that the spatial term contributes beyond the base hybrid SSL setup. Rather than showing downstream results, the authors analyze distance-dependent patch similarity and investigating why atlas-based ROI priors fail at the chosen 14 14 14 patch granularity. Specially, Fig 3 shows a plausible explanation for why a seemingly more anatomical prior can degrade performance. This analysis is a good addition.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: SSL is rapidly evolving, but the related work section does not sufficiently discuss recent papers. It is unclear why more up-to-date methods, especially in 3D medical SSL, are not included. The authors should better justify their choice of references and clearly position their work with respect to the latest developments in this area. Authors did not share their code for reproducibility. In a field like SSL, where implementation details can significantly affect performance, it is very important to provide code along with proper comments and guidelines. This would allow others to reproduce the results and build upon the work. The paper has compared the results with set of baselines. While the paper includes standard methods such as MAE, SimMIM, and iBOT, it does not fully evaluate against several relevant recent SSL approaches specifically designed for 3D medical imaging. Recent literature continues to show rapid progress in this area. All downstream tasks are classification tasks. But this manuscript centered on patch-level spatial structure in 3D MRI. Need a clear argument why they only chose only classification as downstream tasks and not included tasks, which are local representation quality matters more directly, such as segmentation, fine-grained region-level analysis. The results in Table 1 also raise some concerns. The improvements over strong baselines are fairly modest and inconsistent across settings, which makes it difficult to assess the true value of the proposed approach. The authors should do more to explain these gaps and make a clearer case for why their method matters. It is still unclear why this work is necessary and whether it represents a meaningful step forward or a new direction for SSL.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. 1.Empirical evidence and statistical support(Rmeta, R2, R3) We acknowledge that DIS does not uniformly outperform iBOT across all benchmarks and does not improve over iBOT on ADNI AD/NC. Our results should therefore be interpreted as showing task dependent benefits rather than uniform superiority. DIS is a patch level spatial regularizer designed to reduce spurious similarity among distant patches. Therefore, its benefit is expected to be clearer when disease cues are subtle, spatially distributed, or heterogeneous. In line with this interpretation, DIS improves over iBOT on ADNI MCI/NC from 0.69 to 0.71 AUC and on BraTS from 0.59 to 0.73 AUC. Although performance was evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation, formal statistical significance testing between methods was not performed. Therefore, we do not claim statistically significant superiority and interpret the observed gains conservatively. 2.Ablation design and hyperparameter sensitivity(Rmeta, R1, R2) Regarding ablation, the masked token objective is the base pretext task, not an optional auxiliary loss. It creates the masked student/unmasked teacher asymmetry. Without it, the two views would be nearly identical under the same augmentation pipeline, making the CLS objective less informative. Since DIS is defined on patch representations learned in this masked view setting, removing masked token learning would change the pretraining objective rather than isolate DIS. Thus, Table 2 uses a progressive ablation design. This design tests whether DIS provides additional benefit beyond the base SSL objectives and whether a distance-aware prior is preferable to an atlas derived ROI prior at the selected patch granularity. For controlled comparison, the masking ratio and EMA momentum followed standard MAE/iBOT-style settings and 14×14×14 patches were used to balance resolution, token length and computation. Sensitivity to λ_cls, λ_sp and patch size was not exhaustively explored, which is a limitation of the submitted study. 3.Baseline scope and downstream evaluation(Rmeta, R3) We acknowledge the limited baseline scope and absence of segmentation evaluation. Our experiments were designed to isolate the proposed spatial prior under matched backbone and training conditions, rather than to provide an exhaustive benchmark of all recent 3D SSL systems. MAE and SimMIM represent masked image modeling baselines, while iBOT is the closest teacher-student token level SSL framework to DIS. This comparison allows the effect of the distance-modulated spatial prior to be examined under a controlled setting. We also agree that segmentation would more directly assess local representation quality. In the submitted study, we focused on classification to evaluate the pretrained encoder under controlled transfer settings, because segmentation performance can be affected by decoder design, resolution recovery and task specific optimization. The submitted patch-level similarity decay and ROI purity analyses provide representation-level evidence that DIS changes patch representations as intended. 4.Spatial prior design and modality scope(R1) We used a simple linear distance weight as a minimal, monotonic and parameter free spatial prior. The goal is not to model nonlinear anatomy or bilateral symmetry, but to reduce spurious similarity between distant patch tokens in low texture 3D MRI. DIS uses soft distance-modulated decorrelation rather than hard negatives, so homologous regions can remain similar when supported by image evidence and the base SSL objectives. The ROI prior degraded performance, suggesting that rigid atlas constraints can be noisy at 14×14×14 patch granularity due to mixed region patches. Evaluation on FLAIR, T2, PET, explicit symmetry modeling and learnable distance priors were outside the scope of the submitted experiments. 5.Reproducibility To support reproducibility, we plan to release the source code upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The overall recommendation from the three reviewers is borderline, with one weak accept and two weak rejects. The authors need to make rebuttal to address the following concerns: First, the empirical evidence presented in the paper is unconvincing for the majority of reviewers: performance gains over strong baselines are modest and inconsistent, with no improvement on the primary AD vs. NC classification task, and no statistical significance testing is reported. Other major concerns include an incomplete comparison with recent 3D medical SSL methods, the absence of evaluation on segmentation tasks that would directly reflect patch-level representation quality, and insufficient ablation of individual loss components and hyperparameter sensitivities. | The paper proposes a neuroanatomy-aware self-supervised learning framework with a distance-modulated patch decorrelation prior. While the initial reviews were mixed, the author rebuttal effectively clarified the scope of the contributions and the limitations. After rebuttal, Reviewer #2 raised their score to Accept, joining Reviewer #1’s Weak Accept. After reading the paper, I think that the strengths of this work lie in a lightweight, well-motivated spatial regularizer that demonstrably improves patch discriminability in low-texture 3D brain MRI, particularly on subtle-disease tasks like MCI classification and tumor grading. The ablation and representation analyses also convincingly explain why the proposed prior outperforms rigid atlas-based ROIs. The rebuttal’s conservative interpretation of results and commitment to code release further strengthen the case. Overall, the paper provides a domain-appropriate inductive bias that advances representation learning for brain MRI, which I think can be considered as acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper correctly identifies a key limitation of generic SSL for 3D brain MRI and proposes a lightweight, effective spatial prior (DIS) that improves performance on subtle-signal tasks such as MCI classification and tumor grading. All three reviewers gave scores of 4, 3, and 3 (no Strong Reject), and the authors’ rebuttal honestly acknowledges the method’s task-dependent benefits. The remaining concerns are addressable and do not undermine the core contribution. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After considering the rebuttal and updated reviews, I lean toward rejection. The rebuttal clarifies the intended scope of the contribution; however, several important concerns remain insufficiently addressed, including the lack of statistical validation, sensitivity analysis, limited downstream evaluation, and only task-dependent rather than consistent improvements over strong SSL baselines. Therefore, I do not think the paper sufficiently crosses the acceptance threshold in its current form.

title: BrainAnytime: Anatomy-Aware Cross-Modal Pretraining for Brain Image Analysis with Arbitrary Modality Availability
reviewer_1_strengths: Unlike models that assume fixed inputs, this work is motivated by the clinical modality escalation pathway, making it highly relevant for real-world diagnostic workflows where data is often incomplete. The model is pretrained on a massive dataset 3D scans, ensuring high robustness and generalization. It provides a novel way to incorporate prior medical knowledge into a self-supervised learning framework.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the framework is titled “BrainAnytime,” the PACM importance weights are specifically tuned for Alzheimer’s Disease using Braak staging. Its generalizability to other neurodegenerative diseases or brain tumors, where different regions are salient, is not explored. The PACM strategy requires registering input volumes to the MNI152 space to apply the atlas. The authors do not discuss how registration errors—which are common in patients with severe cortical atrophy—might propagate and affect the importance scoring. In RCMD, T1, T2, and FLAIR are pooled into a single group. Since these sequences capture distinct pathological features, grouping them might dilute sequence-specific information that could be useful for cross-modal alignment.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper is well organized and clearly presented The proposed pathology-aware curriculum masking module is novel and well-motivated. The authors conducted thorough comparison and ablation experiments.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: See additional comments below
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper has fairly reasonable clinical formulation and relevance of missing modalities, and the scale and diversity of data and extensive benchmarking also stand out. The PACM and RCMD modules are also clinically motivated (anatomy relevant prior for masking, bridging gaps between MRI and PET). There’s also consistently high performance over strong missing modality baselines and inclusion of ablation studies.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: First, the paper does not explain why tau-PET as a core AD biomarker is not included. Second, while pre-training is on diverse datasets, evaluation is only on ADNI, which has similar distribution to training datasets. Inclusion of more out-of-distribution independent external datasets could be helpful to strengthen the claim of the generalizability. Third, the paper does not explain or why using RCMD is optimal over many grounded alternatives (CLIP style, token-level alignment, masked cross-reconstruction (standard in MultiMAE)), nor ablations on them, since there’s no ablation on the effectiveness on specifically cross-modal alignment when PET is not present. Fourth, it’s also not sure whether dynamic score is better than static score in PACM. Fifth, label efficiency is better demonstrated with comparison with baselines.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal

The paper addresses the important problem of handling arbitrary modality availability in brain image analysis, and the proposed framework with multi-modal masked autoencoding, cross-modal distillation, and pathology-aware masking represents a substantial methodological contribution. The thorough evaluation across multiple modalities and downstream tasks are also good points for the paper.

title: Bridging EEG to fMRI: Semi-Supervised Functional Connectivity Translation via Latent Alignment
reviewer_1_strengths: The motivation is laid out clearly: the authors give a reasonable account of why signal-level EEG-to-fMRI regression is fragile (HRF variability, ROI-wise independence) and why FC-space translation could sidestep those issues. The method follows logically from this setup — FC construction feeds into Stage I self-reconstruction, which then initialises Stage II cross-modal alignment, and the paper reads as a coherent pipeline rather than a loose collection of modules. On the numbers side, Table 1 shows gains over every included baseline, and the ablation in Table 2 confirms that each of the three main components (Stage I pretraining, latent alignment, hierarchical-order supervision) contributes positively. I also appreciate that the authors went beyond reconstruction metrics and ran a downstream AD classification experiment (Table 3, frozen encoder + MLP), which at least makes the practical intent of the representation concrete.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The comparison set is too narrow for the claims made. The introduction itself discusses [13] and [14] as prior EEG-to-fMRI methods, yet neither appears in Table 1 — only NeuroBOLT [15] plus four generic graph models. Calling this “strong baselines” in the abstract is hard to justify when the two most directly relevant prior methods are missing. 2.The downstream AD experiment is the weakest link in the evidence chain. Seven EEG datasets are pooled into a single 217 AD / 146 NC split, but several of the cited sources raise questions: PearlNeuro [6] is a database of middle-aged at-risk individuals, not a clean AD-vs-NC benchmark; AD-Auditory [12] involves auditory entrainment rather than standard resting-state; and the APAVA reference [23] is a methods paper on EEG FC topology, not a dataset descriptor. Without knowing how labels were assigned and whether the 5-fold split controls for source identity, the Table 3 improvements could partly reflect dataset or label confounding rather than genuine representational quality. 3.The paired data used in Stage II (115 subjects, 831 sessions aggregated from six sources) is not described at a level that allows external verification. In particular, [5] reads as a research paper on NODDI microstructure, not a standard data release, so it is unclear exactly which sessions it contributes and how they were obtained. 4.Baseline fairness is also only partial. The proposed method starts from source-localised multi-band EEG FC and benefits from large-scale unpaired pretraining, while NeuroBOLT operates at the signal level and its FC is computed post-hoc. Table 1 therefore shows that this particular pipeline works well, but the comparison is not apples-to-apples enough to support broad superiority claims. 5.The novelty is more in the combination than in the individual pieces. The hierarchical-order FC construction follows [32], the source localisation and PEC pipeline draws heavily on [10], and the teacher–student alignment idea is well established. What is new is putting these together for EEG-to-fMRI FC translation — a valid contribution, but the paper sometimes overstates it.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The shift from signal-level to FC-space translation is the paper’s clearest conceptual contribution and is well-argued: hemodynamic response variability and temporal-scale mismatch destabilise point-wise regression, whereas FC aggregates over extended windows and captures inter-regional structure directly. 2.The asymmetry between available data modalities is a fundamental constraint in this domain. Exploiting tens of thousands of unpaired recordings for Stage I pretraining while reserving scarce simultaneous EEG-fMRI pairs for cross-modal alignment only is the right inductive bias, and the two-stage separation is clean and principled. 3.The comparison covers both signal-level SOTA (NeuroBOLT) and four graph-level methods of increasing modeling capacity, all evaluated under identical subject-independent splits and the same FC extraction pipeline, enabling fair comparison across paradigms. 4.Freezing the EEG encoder and training a lightweight MLP for Alzheimer’s disease classification on seven independent EEG datasets is a well-designed transfer test.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The hierarchical FC operator Ψ is critically under-specified. The paper describes high-order FC as correlation between pairs of ROI connectivity profiles and associated FC as correlation between first-order and high-order profiles, but provides no formal definition, no equation, and no illustration. The resulting three-channel hierarchical representation A_hier is central to Stage I supervision and Stage II decoding, yet a reader cannot reconstruct it from the text alone. Citing reference [32] is insufficient; the paper must be self-contained. This is a significant reproducibility concern. 2.No statistical significance testing is provided. All FC translation results (Table 1, Table 2) are from a single 7:1:2 split on 115 subjects. Given the high variance (PR std ~0.12), the reported improvements over baselines may not be statistically significant. Paired tests (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank on per-subject metrics) or confidence intervals over multiple random splits are necessary to support the claim of consistent improvement. 3.The 115-subject paired dataset is aggregated from six protocols with substantially different cognitive states (resting state, auditory oddball, visual oddball, sleep, eyes open/closed). FC profiles are known to differ systematically across task conditions, and the paper describes the Stage II split only as subject-level 7:1:2 without stating whether it is paradigm-stratified. If subjects from the same paradigm appear in both train and test, the reported FC translation metrics may reflect within-paradigm generalization rather than true cross-subject transfer. The paper does not report performance broken down by paradigm, making it difficult to assess how robust the method is across acquisition conditions. This should be discussed, and paradigm-stratified evaluation or at least per-paradigm reporting would substantially strengthen the experimental section. 4.The KL divergence over embeddings is non-standard. Equation 3 applies softmax to 128-dimensional graph-level embeddings and computes KL divergence between the resulting distributions, treating embedding dimensions as categories with no clear probabilistic interpretation. The rationale for this formulation over alternatives (MMD, cosine loss alone, contrastive loss) is not given, and no ablation isolates its contribution from the cosine loss in Eq. 2.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The problem is important because EEG is much cheaper and easier to collect than fMRI. There is mobile EEG nowadays. Predicting fMRI-like network information from EEG could be useful for clinical studies and screening. It is a good idea to work at the FC instead of the raw signal. EEG and fMRI have very different temporal resolution, so direct signal prediction is difficult. FC-level translation seems more stable and more meaningful. The semi-supervised setup is reasonable because paired EEG-fMRI data are limited. Using large unpaired EEG and fMRI datasets before training on paired data is a good idea. The proposed method performs better than the benchmarked methods, and the ablation study supports the main parts of the model.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The Transformer module is not tailored for the symmetric FC matrices. FC matrices have the upper and lower triangles contain duplicate information. If the model uses the full N×N matrix, it may waste memory and computation by processing the same edges twice. This needs clarification. Second, the method is limited to use static FC, so the high temporal resolution of the EEG not benefited. This makes the impact of the method limited. Third, the EEG FC construction is confusing. The paper mentions slow envelope fluctuations below 1 Hz, but also uses five EEG frequency bands. This should be stated clearly. Fourth, the paper does not report EEG channel counts, montages, sampling rates, or how these differ across datasets. This is important because the method relies on EEG source localization before computing ROI-level FC. Fifth, the hierarchical-order FC operator Ψ is not clearly defined. The authors should provide exact equations and clearly state which FC matrices are included.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their feedback. Below, we concisely address the reviewers’ concerns: Q1.Comparison fairness & baselines, R1.We agree that [13] and [14] should be discussed more explicitly. We selected NeuroBOLT [15] as the most comparable signal-level EEG-to-fMRI baseline because [13] requires strict EEG-fMRI alignment flags/events, unavailable in parts of our data, making reproduction unreliable; [14] and [15] are from the same group; [15] is newer, more robust, and better suited for resting-state comparison, while [14] has no released code. [15] uses raw signals as intended, so the comparison evaluates signal-level vs. FC-level paradigms under the same FC metric. Q2.Dataset transparency & clarification, R1/R2.Given limited paired subjects and heterogeneous paradigms, we used a random subject-level split across all paired data instead of paradigm-specific training, which makes the task more challenging and indirectly supports cross-paradigm generalization. Stage II data are simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings, totaling 115 subjects/831 sessions: NATVIEW 22/392, Oddball 17/102, NODDI 15/15, rest & sleep 33/255, Eyes Open/Closed 8/8, and Simultaneous EEG-fMRI 20/59.One session is one simultaneous run. The split is subject-level: train/val/test = 80/12/23 subjects and 582/83/166 sessions. For AD evaluation, it is supportive evidence, not definitive clinical validation. We only selected AD or NC subjects; other diseases or ambiguous diagnoses were excluded. Metadata contain 363 subjects from 461 EEG records, with 217 AD/146 NC subjects. AD/NC counts are ADFSU 160/12, PearlNeuro 0/78, ADFTD 36/29, ADSZ 24/24, BrainLat_EEG 20/28, AD-Auditory 17/10, and APAVA 12/11.The 5-fold split is subject-level. We will add source-wise tables, label rules, corrected citations, and discuss paradigm/source heterogeneity. Q3.Hierarchical operator Ψ, R2/R4.Although Ψ is described conceptually, explicit equations are needed. Given first-order fMRI FC C∈R^(N×N), high-order FC is H_ij=corr(C_(i,:),C_(j,:)), measuring similarity between ROI-wise connectivity profiles. Associated FC is S_ij=corr(C_(i,:),H_(j,:)), capturing cross-order similarity. The target is A_hier=Ψ(C)=[C,H,S]. Ψ is deterministic with no learned parameters. Q4.Statistics & KL, R2.Statistical evidence was insufficiently reported. We had conducted paired Wilcoxon tests on existing held-out predictions but omitted them due to space. Despite large PR variance, our method significantly outperforms all baselines in PR (p<0.001) and MSE (p<0.05). For KL, we will clarify that it is not a decisive latent-alignment loss, but an auxiliary teacher-student distillation regularizer. It softly encourages the EEG student embedding to follow the fMRI teacher’s latent distribution, while cosine similarity and reconstruction remain the main constraints. Q5.Prior components vs. contribution, R1.We follow [10] for standard EEG/fMRI preprocessing. Inspired by [32], we construct hierarchical fMRI FC targets to capture richer connectivity patterns. Our contribution is integrating these into semi-supervised EEG-to-fMRI FC translation: FC-space graph-to-graph mapping, unpaired representation learning, and frozen fMRI-teacher-guided EEG alignment. Q6.Other clarifications, R4.For symmetric FC, full N×N is used not to model duplicated edges independently, but to keep each ROI’s row-wise connectivity profile as a node feature for graph encoding. Upper-triangular inputs are more efficient but lose this ROI-wise structure. EEG FC captures temporal dependencies over a window, though not moment-to-moment dynamics. Most EEG datasets use a 19-channel 10–20 montage, with a few exceptions; after source localization, all data are mapped to the same ROI space, so acquisition differences do not change the model input. Finally, δ/θ/α/β/γ are carrier bands, while “<1 Hz slow envelope fluctuation” refers to envelope dynamics used for PEC.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Overall, the reviewers appreciated the novelty of treating EEG to fMRI translation as a graph matching problem, noting that signal-level inference is not robust. They also appreciated the teacher-student alignment approach and downstream AD classification task. However, they raised several concerns about the paper clarity, method reproducibility, and fairness of the experimental comparisons. The authors should clearly address these and the other reviewer concerns in their rebuttal. | The authors have done a good job addressing the main critiques. This work would be of interest to MICCAI. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have addressed several concerns, the claims on comprehensive evaluations should be further clarified. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This is a borderline paper in my track. One reviewer still maintained a negative recommendation and raised several concerns. title: CalcSeg: Confidence-aware 3D Latent Context Curriculum Learning For Myocardial Scar Segmentation From Single-Stack LGE-CMRs
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is quite well written and overall easy to follow. Whilst the parts of the pipeline are not new, the specific combination proposed is interesting, suitable to the task at hand and sound. The results are believable and the improvement over SOTA seems substantial.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Limited validation. Despite having access to different datasets (some public, some private), the authors merged them when performing their validation. This reduces the chances of independent inter-paper comparisons, which are one of the limiting factors for research in LGE segmentation. Questionable experimental setting. The authors state “We quantify the segmentation performance using Dice Similarity Coefficient computed over the myocardium for the complete dataset and 6 known difficult cases, and the percentage error in scar volume. ” This is very problematic to me: what was the training/validation/test split? Was there one? The paper doesn’t mention this very crucial piece of information. Issues with uncertainty estimation. The paper claims that epistemic uncertainty “progressively decreases with the stages” of UCL, and uses this as evidence that the curriculum is working as intended. However, in Fig. 3 the y-axis is labelled “mean uncertainty”, and the mean across the whole test set (left panel) appears approximately stable across stages while only the std shrinks. This would indicate that UCL homogenises uncertainty across samples, not that it reduces it. The authors should (i) discuss this finding thoroughly and (ii) clarify exactly how the plotted “mean uncertainty” and its spread computed (per-sample MC-Dropout std aggregated how, over what?). Misuse of the term “unsupervised”. The paper repeatedly describes the proposed curriculum as “unsupervised”, but the difficulty score relies on the per-sample errors against the ground-truth segmentation. This requires labels and is therefore not unsupervised in the sense the term is normally used in the curriculum learning literature, where “unsupervised CL” refers to difficulty estimation without access to labels.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Myocardial scar segmentation is a challenging and important problem for the medical imaging community. The presented method shows improved performance against the baselines, both quantitatively and qualitatively. The idea of using curriculum learning for the myocardial scar segmentation is promising.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: I find the paper to be written in a very confusing way. Particularly the section on “3D Latent Context Modeling” is very hard to understand, while being one of the contributions of the paper. It is unclear whether the latent representation z represents 2D or 3D features, it’s also not represented anywhere in Fig. 1 to aid understanding. Some variables are never defined, such as C in the softmax formula, B, and F. The “disentangled slice-wise self-attention” is never clearly described. The description of this module is dense and lacks clarity regarding the data flow, with the naming not exactly matching between text and figure. This makes the architectural novelty difficult to verify or reproduce. The “custom residual decoder” used is also never described. The loss function and curriculum scoring are introduced abruptly and are not explained with sufficient clarity. Several terms are defined mathematically, but the paper does not provide enough intuition for why these components are combined, how the weights were chosen, or how the resulting optimization behaves during training. The experimental results section provides very little analysis of the results. The ablation study is limited. It shows that each component helps, yet it does not disentangle whether the curriculum or the attention module is responsible for most of the gain on the hard cases, missing a combination where only UCL is used. Further, there is no discussion on why CaucSeg outperforms the baselines. The paper reports improvements over ScarNet, the myocardial scar segmentation SOTA method, but the experimental section does not sufficiently explain why the proposed method is better. In particular, it is unclear whether the gains come from the confidence-aware curriculum, the 3D latent context module, or simpler training effects. The empirical evaluation is incomplete with respect to recent literature. In particular, the paper does not compare against or cite a recent relevant method, ScarElastic [1], which appears closely related and has reported strong performance on myocardial scar segmentation. Additionally, the manuscript includes a baseline denoted as “ScarNet (Sup. CL),” but does not provide a citation or sufficient detail to clearly identify this method. Clarifying the identity of this baseline and including relevant recent methods such as [1] would strengthen the empirical evaluation. In Fig. 1 the images only show the myocardium with all the other tissues being masked. Is this a preprocessing step in the pipeline? No description of such masking is present in the dataset dataset section, which makes it confusing as to what is the actual input to the model. [1] Zou, R., Li, Y., Zhou, N., Guan, X., Li, G., Xie, D., … & Luo, C. (2025). ScarElastic: continuous elasticity field modeling for myocardial scar delineation in LGE-CMR. npj Digital Medicine .
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: he slice-wise self-attention module is an intelligent solution to the “anisotropy problem” in CMR. By performing latent fusion on 2D features rather than using full 3D convolutions, the authors effectively capture out-of-plane context without the computational overhead or sensitivity to breath-hold displacements common in 3D-UNet architectures. The shift from supervised to model-adaptive curriculum learning is a timely contribution. The integration of epistemic uncertainty into the difficulty score allows the model to prioritize samples where the “ground truth” might be ambiguous (e.g., the gray zone of fibrosis), which is a common clinical reality in LGE-CMR.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Terminology Ambiguity: The authors refer to the curriculum as “unsupervised.” While the difficulty scoring is automated, the segmentation task is supervised. This distinction should be clearer to avoid confusion with self-supervised or unsupervised segmentation methods. Parameter Sensitivity: The difficulty score D_i depends on three weighting parameters \gamma_j. The manuscript lacks a sensitivity analysis or a clear heuristic for selecting these weights. Given that curriculum learning can be sensitive to the order of sample introduction, this is a significant omission.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for all valuable feedback and constructive suggestions. Our responses to the major questions are summarized below. [M,R1,R3] Clarification on “Unsupervised” Curriculum Learning (UCL) Our intent was to distinguish our approach from manually annotated difficulty ratings, i.e., scores are computed automatically using Dice, uncertainty and scar burden error rather than clinician-assigned labels. Although uncertainty provides an unsupervised signal, we agree that it may be confused with typical unsupervised training methods that do not use ground-truth label supervision. We will update the terminology with semi/weakly-supervised. [M,R1] Data Splits & Evaluation Protocol All metrics are computed on the independent test set, including 6 clinically challenging cases from a site, explicitly flagged by experts. The train-val-test split was 7:1:2. The uncertainty is computed as the mean standard deviation across 100 MC-Dropout samples per subject, yielding one scalar per subject. Fig.3 shows mean and standard deviation of these uncertainty values. The overall mean (left, Fig.3) appears relatively stable since high-confidence cases dominate the test set (ratio 22:6). In contrast, when stratified by difficulty (right, Fig.3), uncertainty decreases substantially across stages for the clinically challenging subgroup. We will clarify this in the revised paper. [M,R2] Please note that z is a 2D per-slice latent representation produced independently for each slice, with ‘F’ total slices, yielding a 3D tensor prior to self-attention (SA). The disentangled slice-wise SA is a standard transformer operation [7,22] applied across slices “performing explicit 2D-to-3D latent feature fusion on the encoded latent representation z.” The term “disentangled” describes SA alternating between spatial and slice-wise attention, following the space-time attention in Arnab et al., 2021. All notations (B=batch size, F=total slices, C=projection dimension), and the “custom residual decoder” referring to an employed ResNet-based decoder instead of the standard MedSAM decoder will be clarified. [R1] We appreciate the suggestion to keep validation separated between public and in-house datasets wherever dataset sizes allow. However, current public LGE datasets are relatively small, particularly for difficult cases, motivating us to incorporate private institutes’ data. Fully separated validation remains valuable for future work as larger public datasets become available. [R2] The improved performance of our method over the baselines stems from combining the two proposed modules: slice-wise SA & UCL. Tab.1 includes results from ScarNet with CL, which uses a 2D transformer backbone and is analogous to the UCL-only ablation. Tab.2 shows that our SA improves overall segmentation performance, UCL particularly improves difficult cases, and their combination yields the best overall performance. These findings suggest SOTA methods underperform since they lack richer 3D context, operating on isolated 2D slices and random batch selection. Thanks for referring to ScarElastic. Our framework could be easily incorporated on top of ScarElastic by using it as an alternative backbone. We will include this reference in our revised manuscript, and will clarify that “ScarNet (Sup.CL)” denotes ScarNet[30] trained with CL. Masking is a preprocessing step applied prior to training and inference, as stated in the dataset section. The loss function and curriculum scoring are independent from the architectural design, as described in the method section. The focal loss parameters followed [Lin et al., 2018] with related values provided in the parameter setting section. [R3] Based on our empirical findings, the parameters are stable as they are automatically derived from each metric’s scale via the inverse of its order of magnitude. This ensures all metrics are in the same numerical range and no single metric dominates. We will clarify this in the revised paper.
