title: CALM: Interpretable Cross-Modal Alignment for Biomarker Discovery from Unpaired Data
reviewer_1_strengths: Unlike conventional approaches that rely on paired multimodal data from the same individuals, the proposed method learns cross-modal relationships from disjoint cohorts, improving its applicability in scenarios where paired data are scarce. By leveraging a shared latent space together with class-conditional distribution alignment, the model is able to establish meaningful inter-modal relationships even in the absence of explicit pairing. The use of linear projections allows for direct interpretation of region–pathway associations, which is advantageous over black-box models for biomarker discovery and mechanistic insights. The model trained on fully disjoint unimodal datasets can be transferred to unseen paired datasets, demonstrating strong generalization capability. The identified associations between immune/metabolic pathways and specific brain regions offer cross-scale (brain–gene) insights relevant to the study of brain disorders.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper does not clearly specify the form of the final classifier (e. g. , whether a linear classifier or another architecture is used). This omission makes the overall pipeline less transparent and may affect both reproducibility and interpretability. The biological validation of the findings remains limited. It would be beneficial to incorporate external resources (e. g. , the Allen Brain Atlas) to further corroborate the reported brain region–gene pathway associations, thereby strengthening the reliability and biological relevance of the conclusions.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Novel and practically relevant problem setting. The paper addresses the important and underexplored problem of learning imaging-genetics associations from completely unpaired datasets. This is practically meaningful because many large public datasets are unimodal and disjoint, making paired multimodal analysis difficult in real-world settings. 2.Interpretable model design. A major strength of the work is that interpretability is built into the architecture itself. By using per-entity encoders and linear projections, the method preserves explicit correspondence between brain ROIs and genetic pathways, allowing direct extraction of an association matrix. This is more meaningful than typical latent fusion approaches where feature interactions become difficult to interpret. 3.Well-motivated objective formulation. The combination of class-conditional distribution alignment, supervised contrastive learning, and orthogonality regularization is conceptually coherent. The objective is designed not only to align the two modalities, but also to maintain class discrimination and avoid degenerate solutions in the projection matrices. Reasonable experimental validation. The paper includes comparisons against several relevant baselines as well as ablation studies that isolate the contribution of the key loss terms. In addition, the method is evaluated on an independent paired external dataset, which strengthens the empirical validation. 5.Validation of biological consistency. The learned association matrix shows high correlation with a paired-data baseline (r = 0.87), and the identified pathway-ROI relationships are discussed in the context of established ASD literature. This gives additional support that the learned cross-modal associations are not purely algorithmic artifacts.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Important hyperparameter choices are under-justified. The method depends on several potentially sensitive hyperparameters, including the weights of the CMMD, contrastive, and orthogonality losses, as well as the contrastive temperature. Although these values are reported, the paper does not clearly explain how they were selected, nor does it provide a sensitivity analysis. This makes it difficult to assess how robust the reported performance is to these design choices. 2.The performance gain over the ablations is relatively modest. CALM achieves the best overall results, but the margin over the strongest ablation variants is small in Table 1.While the method is conceptually appealing, the empirical advantage of using the full objective over simpler variants is not yet entirely convincing. A stronger discussion of when each component materially helps would improve the paper. 3.Reproducibility is limited by insufficient architectural detail. The paper states that pretrained autoencoders and classifiers are used, but the exact architecture and pretraining protocol of these encoders are not described in sufficient detail in the main text. Since the encoder design is important for preserving interpretability and for the second-stage alignment, clearer implementation details would improve reproducibility. 4.Biological interpretation remains largely qualitative. The discussion of the discovered pathway-ROI associations is interesting, but the biological interpretation is mostly narrative and literature-supported rather than quantitatively validated. Additional statistical or biological validation would make the interpretability claim stronger.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The main strengths of the paper are: (1) The paper tackles a clinically relevant and practical problem by learning cross-modal associations from completely unpaired imaging and genetics data. (2) The method is conceptually simple and well-structured, combining distribution alignment and contrastive learning in a clear and reasonable way. (3) The experimental evaluation is relatively comprehensive, including external validation on a paired dataset and analysis of association stability.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weaknesses of the paper are: (1) The paper has many formatting issues. For example, the reference formats are inconsistent; the citation of Fig. 3(b) is problematic; the subsection ‘Regularization (L_{orth})’ is missing a colon; the font styles around symbols S(i) and P(j) are inconsistent, etc. The authors need to thoroughly check the manuscript themselves. (2) There’s a lot of unnecessary italic styling throughout the paper. Italics should really be used only when you want to emphasize a key point. (3) There are too few baseline comparisons, only three. And the performance gain of CALM over its own ablations is very limited. Also, why is the Ablation L_{OT} using the loss from Ref [3]? What’s the reason? (4) The association matrix A = W_I^T W_G is just the product of two parameter matrices. Why does that directly quantify pairwise relationships between brain regions and genetic pathways? What’s the interpretability there? Also, why set the latent dimension d = 6? There’s no justification for this choice, and no parameter analysis for this value.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the important problem of learning cross-modal associations from unpaired imaging and genetic data. We address the major critiques below. 1.Construction of the Association Matrix (Rev 3): Each column of W_I (resp. W_G) defines how a brain ROI (resp. genetic pathway) contributes to each shared latent dimension. L_orth keeps these rows near-orthonormal to maximize the variance captured by these dimensions. L_cmmd and L_con align the two modalities along these shared dimensions. A large entry A_{r,p} implies that ROI “r” and pathway “p” load similarly onto the latent dimensions, indicating that they co-vary in the aligned space. This is analogous to CCA but without paired samples. Columns of W_I / W_G correspond one-to-one to ROIs / pathways, so A can be viewed as an ROI-pathway association matrix. 2.Hyperparameter Selection (Revs 2 & 3): Hyperparameters were tuned via grid search with 5-fold CV on the unpaired ABIDE and SSC datasets, covering latent dimension d, batch size, learning rate, loss weights (λ_cmmd, λ_con, λ_orth), and contrastive temperature. The ACE dataset was never seen during hyperparameter selection, and Table 1 confirms CALM’s generalizability to it. Latent dimension d had the largest impact on performance: larger values tend to overfit the modest training set. Loss weights and contrastive temperature were robust across reasonable ranges and can serve as defaults in future studies. 3.Clarity of Model Architecture (Revs 1 & 2): Both the imaging and genetics branches use the same autoencoder design. Each brain ROI (n_I = 246, 4 morphometric values) and genetic pathway (n_G = 177, 6 phenotypic traits) is encoded independently (preserving a one-to-one correspondence) by a 3-layer per-entity MLP into a 6-dim embedding. A mirrored decoder reconstructs the input. Each encoder also has a 2-layer MLP classifier. Encoders are pretrained with MSE reconstruction and BCE losses. Code will be released upon acceptance. 4.Comparison and Ablation (Revs 1 & 3): Our baselines span key alternative approaches: SUE (NeurIPS 2025) for unpaired cross-modal alignment, UNSEEN (NeurIPS 2023) for missing-modality settings, and G-MIND as an imaging-genetics-specific baseline. SUE requires paired data for fine-tuning, yet CALM still achieves statistically better accuracy and AUC than all three. None of the baselines outputs interpretable ROI/pathway associations, the central deliverable of CALM. Although classification performance is similar across CALM and its ablations, each loss imposes a specific constraint on A. L_cmmd aligns intra-class imaging and genetic distributions, giving A biological relevance. L_con pulls the intra-class samples together across modalities while pushing the inter-class samples apart, anchoring the alignment to the diagnostic axis. Together, they “organize” the latent space, making the associations stable and reproducible across CV folds and consistent with paired results. We note that AUC only evaluates single-modality classification and does not reflect the cross-modal alignment achieved by ‭L_cmmd‬ and ‭L_con‬. L_OT in Table 1 replaces L_cmmd with the Sinkhorn OT loss as a separate ablation. 5.Biological Validation (Revs 1 & 2): As our paper introduces a new framework to link unpaired datasets, we focus on methodology and provide a preliminary demonstration in autism, using single-modality cohorts (ABIDE, SSC) and a matched cohort with both modalities (ACE). Results show (1) high concordance between associations in unpaired and paired scenarios (Fig. 2a) and (2) stability and reproducibility across CV folds (Fig. 2b). As suggested, we are pursuing quantitative validation against the SFARI gene database and the Allen Brain Atlas. 6.Formatting (Rev 3): We will fix inconsistent superscript fonts, a missing colon in the regularization subheading, broken Fig. 3(b) citation, extra italic emphasis, and reference list format.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I recommend an Invite for Rebuttal based on the mixed reviewer scores. All reviewers commended the paper for tackling a highly practical and novel problem setting by learning cross-modal associations from completely unpaired imaging and genetics datasets. The proposed method was praised for its conceptually coherent design, its strong generalization to unseen external paired datasets, and its built-in interpretability achieved through linear projections. However, several technical and presentation concerns must be rigorously addressed in the rebuttal. First, the authors need to provide comprehensive implementation details regarding the exact architecture and pretraining protocols of the autoencoders and classifiers used in the pipeline. Second, critical design choices and hyperparameters, particularly the chosen latent dimension size and the various loss weights, require thorough justification and a sensitivity analysis. Reviewers also questioned the modest performance gains of the full model over its ablation variants and requested justification for the limited number of baseline comparisons. Furthermore, the rebuttal must explicitly clarify the mathematical rationale behind using the product of the parameter matrices to directly quantify pairwise relationships and defend its interpretability. Finally, the authors must commit to resolving the manuscript’s formatting inconsistencies and excessive italicization, and they should discuss potential avenues for stronger quantitative biological validation, such as incorporating external resources like the Allen Brain Atlas. | Although the proposed framework addresses the highly practical problem of learning cross-modal associations from completely unpaired imaging and genetics datasets , reviewers remain unconvinced due to the modest empirical gains over ablation baselines. While the authors provided helpful architectural details and hyperparameter justifications during the rebuttal, the biological validation of the discovered associations remains largely qualitative rather than quantitative. Consequently, given these lingering concerns regarding the strength of the experimental evidence and the lack of robust biological validation, the paper ultimately falls below the acceptance threshold. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This manuscript presented a method to align unpaired cross modal data for biomarker discovery. Reviewers found this method to be a practical solution to a novel problem set with a conceptually coherent design. The weaknesses were missing implementation details, some design choices not being justified, and there being only a few baseline comparison methods. Overall the reviewers found the rebuttal addressed most points except for the modest gains in the full model over ablation studies which lead to questions about if the full model is really necessary. Additionally the biological validation of the method was qualitative only. I recommend for acceptance because on balance the negatives (modest gains in ablation experiment, limitations on comparisons) are outweighted by the strength of the novel design which is conceptually interesting. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal addresses the reviewer’s concerns well. The work addresses a core challenge by learning cross-modal associations from completely unpaired imaging and genetics data. Overall, the reviewers are positive and I recommend acceptation.

title: Cardiac Motion Transfer with Adaptive Physics Constraint
reviewer_1_strengths: The problem is clinically meaningful. Combining lesion visibility and motion dynamics is a useful direction for infarction assessment. The adaptive weighting idea is technically sensible and better motivated than a fixed hard physics penalty. The method is clearly structured and easy to follow at a high level. The paper includes multiple baseline comparisons and ablations, and the reported gains are consistent across several metrics.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The contribution is mainly an adaptive weighting of a physics-guided loss, not a fundamentally new synthesis framework. The evaluation protocol is not sufficiently clear. In particular, the paper does not explain well how direct image-quality metrics are computed without real dynamic LGE ground truth. Reverse validation is interesting but indirect, and it cannot fully replace direct validation of dynamic lesion fidelity. The paper uses a large private clinical dataset but does not visibly report ethics approval, patient consent, or governance details. The study is limited to 2D slices, with no discussion of through-plane motion or 3D consistency.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Clear motivation and clinical relevance: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem in dynamic lesion assessment by connecting cine MRI and LGE MRI. Technical innovation: The proposed dLGE-MRI framework introduces a noise-adaptive physics weighting mechanism that adjusts the physics constraint using a virtual residual likelihood-based strategy. Comprehensive evaluation: The paper includes comparisons against nine methods, ablation studies, and evaluation on a private myocardial infarction dataset of 850 subjects. Good presentation: The manuscript is well organized and visually clear, with supporting figures and tables that make the experimental setup and results easy to interpret.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Missing justification: Since the LGE image already provides structural/anatomical prior to adapting cine-derived deformation to LGE deformation learning, the manuscript should better explain the role of myocardial mask. If feasible, an ablation study without the mask would help clarify its contribution. Lack of limitations discussion: The manuscript would be stronger if it included a brief discussion of the framework’s limitations and assumptions. The ablation results also need more interpretation. For example, please provide intuition for why removing the physics constraint degrades image quality. There is no discussion section. Limited temporal visualization of results: Since this is a dynamic LGE MRI problem, showing only selected frames makes it harder to assess motion preservation over the full cardiac cycle. If feasible within space constraints, additional temporal visualization or supplemental dLGE sequences would strengthen the evidence that the method preserves lesion-wall motion.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The proposed method is compared to a wide range of methods from the literature.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Presentation clarity: Section 2 would benefit from improved clarity. The notation is often confusing, especially in Section 2.3, where several symbols appear without being properly introduced, making the methodology difficult to follow. Figure 2 is also unclear and does not help clarify the approach. Experimental validation: The experimental validation relies solely on a private dataset, which makes it difficult to assess the practical relevance and generalizability of the proposed methodology. The ablation study for the weighting strategy shows only marginal qualitative and quantitative improvements; evaluating this component on additional datasets would help substantiate its impact. reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the meta-reviewer and three reviewers for their valuable feedback. Upon closer reading, we note that the meta-review may be more relevant to another work, and we kindly seek your further guidance. We appreciate the reviewers’ encouragement: “thoughtful and technically solid paper”[R1], “clinically meaningful”[R1,R2], “novel strategy”[R4], recognition of our experiments: “comprehensive evaluation”[R2], “compared to a wide range of methods”[R3], and presentation guidance: “easy to follow at a high level”[R1], “well organized”[R2], “would benefit from improved clarity” [R3]. The main concerns cover five aspects: validation, limitation discussion, method design, experimental details and presentation. Validation: 1)“evaluation protocol is not sufficiently clear”[R1]; 2)“reverse validation”[R1,R4]; 3)“private dataset”[R3]; “downstream clinical applicability”[R4]. A: To our knowledge, this is an early exploration of dynamic LGE synthesis, providing a potential means to assess dynamic motion of LGE lesions. But given the absence of real dynamic LGE in practice, direct evaluation metrics are unsuitable. 1) Referring to the evaluation protocols in motion transfer works LIA [25] (TPAMI) and LIA-X [26], we adopt the IS metric for identity consistency and the IQ metric for perceptual image quality based on content and local distortions. 2) We design a reverse validation strategy: a generative model is trained on the synthesized dynamic LGE, and its outputs are compared with real static LGE during testing. 3) We also thank R3, R4 for their insightful suggestions: -Public dataset: Existing public datasets (e.g., ACDC, MM) contain only cine-MRI for segmentation and motion tracking, but not direct validation of dynamic LGE generation. Even so, we have validated our physics-constrained module on motion tracking tasks using these datasets with better performance. -Downstream clinical value: Our clinical collaborators have similarly encouraged this direction. Preliminary results indicate that dynamic deformation features better assess infarct damage and remodeling, enabling more precise risk stratification. We will report these findings in the journal version. Limitations:1)“limited to 2D slices”[R1,R2], “a linear-elastic model”[R4]; 2)“temporal visualization”[R2]; 3)“ignoring other pathologies”[R4]. A: 1) We have added discussion: the current model is limited by 2D slices and the linear-elastic assumption for computational efficiency, while 3D hyperelastic modeling can better capture the physiological features of the heart. 2) We have uploaded the LGE videos to GitHub for release after acceptance. 3) We agree that motion patterns vary across cardiac pathologies. Our physics loss is grounded in classic mechanical laws and remains disease agnostic. Following R4’s suggestion, extending our method to other conditions in future work would be clinically meaningful. Method design: 1)“the role of myocardial mask”, “why removing the physics constraint degrades image quality”[R2]; 2)“comparisons with methods incorporate physics losses” [R3]. A: 1) We have added interpretation: The myocardial mask enhances boundary clarity in dynamic LGE synthesis. Without the physics constraint, some physically implausible noisy motions are difficult to avoid. 2) We apologize that our comparisons focus on image generation methods, overlooking those with physics-based losses. Nonetheless, the “w/o AdaW” setting with lower performance in our ablation study corresponds to fixed-weight methods. Experimental details: 1)“ethics approval”[R1]; 2)“additional computational”[R4]. A: 1) We have added the information on ethics approval, patient consent, and data governance details. 2) Compared with baseline, the additional training cost comes from PINN, leading to about 1.5× longer training time, and 1.2 s extra inference time. Presentation: “use consistent font colors”[R2], “benefit from improved clarity”[R3]. A: We have clarified the notations, figures and related issues.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers agreed that the paper addresses a clinically relevant and challenging problem in AF-centric multi-label ECG classification, with reported improvements over multiple baselines on both private and public datasets. Strengths include the imbalance/correlation-aware loss, adaptive multi-scale fusion, and generally supportive ablation results. However, concerns remain regarding incremental novelty, unclear positioning against prior imbalance-aware and multi-scale ECG methods, insufficient implementation details, and missing analyses on patient-level splits, uncertainty, and hyperparameter sensitivity. In the rebuttal, the authors should clarify these experimental details, strengthen comparison to task-specific imbalance/correlation methods, and better justify the novelty of each component. | The rebuttal provides reasonable clarifications on the use of indirect/reverse validation, explains why direct metrics are difficult in this setting, adds ethics and governance details, and acknowledges the 2D and pathology-generalization limitations. Limitations remain, especially the indirect nature of validation and limited evidence for broader clinical applicability. However, these are partly inherent to this emerging task. Therefore, I support acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Key concerns persisted after rebuttal, including reliance on a single private dataset with no direct dynamic-LGE ground truth, only indirect reverse validation, marginal ablation gains, and unexamined effects of the 2D linear-elastic assumption. Given these unresolved limitations, the paper is not yet ready for publication and is recommended for rejection. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper addresses an important cardiac MRI problem and proposes a reasonable adaptive physics-weighted motion transfer method, with encouraging results on a large private dataset. However, the evidence remains insufficient for acceptance because the main dynamic LGE synthesis claim is validated only through indirect proxy metrics, without direct dynamic LGE ground truth, external validation, or comparison to relevant physics-informed cardiac motion methods. The rebuttal clarifies several points, but the remaining concerns require additional experiments and stronger validation rather than only camera-ready text changes.

title: CardioDiT: Latent Diffusion Transformers for 4D Cardiac MRI Synthesis
reviewer_1_strengths: The evaluation indicators are relatively comprehensive, covering commonly used qualitative and quantitative CMR volume assessment indicators, and further considering physiological rationality, planar anatomical consistency, geometric consistency and scalability, which is commendable.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The innovations are not clearly articulated. When applying 3D+t data from CMR to a diffusion transformer architecture, the mechanism by which this method handles spatiotemporal discontinuities and physiological inconsistencies is not clearly explained. It is recommended that the authors further clarify the design principles and innovative aspects of this method in addressing these key issues. 2.The authors point out that existing research enforces temporal consistency by decomposing spatial and temporal dimensions or introducing auxiliary mechanisms. This strategy introduces structural biases, thereby limiting the integration of the global context and leading to subtle spatiotemporal discontinuities or physiologically inconsistent cardiac dynamics. However, the experimental section does not directly compare this method with representative methods in references [11, 17], nor does it specifically analyze and verify the structural biases in these methods. 3.Regarding the choice of a phased modeling strategy: Why did the authors choose to first train a 3D VQ-GAN using 2D+t, then slice and encode the complete 3D+t volume data along the D direction, encoding each slice as a latent label, and finally stacking them to form a complete 3D+t latent volume data? Why not directly use the end-to-end approach of 3D+t to learn the latent representation and train it jointly with the 4D diffusion transformer? Please explain the rationale for this design choice. 4.The description of VQ-GAN is too brief, lacking explanation of the loss function, constraints, and specific strategies during training, affecting the understanding of the reproducibility of the entire framework. 5.Reference [15] is also based on a diffusion architecture, but this paper chooses to compare it with the 3D U-Net architecture. The basis for this choice is not clear enough. Furthermore, this paper is similar to reference [15] in its starting point and implementation method. It is recommended that the authors clearly explain the similarities and differences between this paper and reference [15] to highlight its uniqueness. 6.The comparison method in Figure 2 does not clearly indicate whether the experiment uses a public or private dataset, nor does it show the results of real images, affecting the completeness and credibility of the comparison. 7.None of the charts clearly indicate the data source (public or private datasets), nor do they explain the specific purpose of datasets such as ACDC (for training or evaluation), affecting the transparency and reproducibility of the experimental setup. 8.The description of the ablation experimental setup in Table 2 is insufficient, especially regarding the specific changes in model capacity from S to L (e. g. , number of layers, hidden layer dimension, number of parameters), which hinders the reader’s understanding of the impact of model size on performance. 9.For common applications of medical image synthesis (e. g. , data augmentation and privacy protection), it is recommended to supplement the discussion section with relevant explanations to clarify the applicability and potential value of this method in these practical applications. 10.In the discussion section, the authors mention that the framework does not depend on the temporal mechanism of a specific modality. It is recommended to further elaborate on the feasibility and potential challenges of extending it to other modalities to strengthen the argument for the generality of the method.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Methodological novelty: The proposed 4D diffusion transformer is well motivated for the task, enabling global spatiotemporal self-attention and avoiding space–time factorization. The results consistently support the benefits of this design. That said, the contribution should be considered in the context of closely related work by the authors, including a prior 4D diffusion approach based on a channel-merged 3D U-Net and a concurrent submission proposing a 3D variant of the transformer architecture. While the present work extends these ideas to a fully 4D setting and a different application, clarifying these relationships would strengthen the positioning of the contribution. Strong experimental design: The proposed method is thoroughly validated across three datasets (public and private), with both qualitative and quantitative evaluation. The reported metrics (FID, precision/recall, d-SSIM, AR, EF range, W2) cover complementary aspects of performance, including distributional similarity, structural consistency, and clinical plausibility. A targeted ablation study further explores the impact of model capacity.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Incomplete novelty framing and related work discussion: The introduction motivates the limitations of space–time factorization in prior work; however, a relevant study (later introduced in Section 2.4 as a baseline) already addresses this issue using a different architectural choice (channel-merged 3D U-Net). This work is not discussed upfront, and its conceptual relationship to the proposed method remains insufficiently clarified. Given the methodological similarities (e.g., use of a VQ-VAE latent representation and joint spatiotemporal modeling), a clearer positioning of the proposed approach with respect to this prior work would help better delineate the actual contribution.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The controlled experimental ladder from 2D+t factorized to 3D+t channel-merged to fully 4D diffusion provides a clear and well-motivated comparison structure. Few papers in cardiac generative modeling attempt this kind of progressive ablation across spatiotemporal coupling strategies, and the design itself should be useful as a template for future work in this area. The evaluation metric suite goes meaningfully beyond FID-only assessment. The inclusion of ejection-fraction distribution matching via Wasserstein distance, through-plane alignment (ARED), and domain-specific FID computed with CineMA foundation model features rather than ImageNet-pretrained Inception reflects careful thinking about what matters for cardiac MRI synthesis. CardioDiT-L achieves better distributional quality than the 3D+t U-Net baseline at roughly one-third the parameter count (177M vs. 578M) and less than half the VRAM, with the full pipeline fitting within 24 GB. This practical accessibility lowers the barrier for academic labs working with consumer-grade GPUs. The scalability ablation across three model sizes (S/B/L) with explicit reporting of parameter counts, inference times, and VRAM requirements provides useful engineering guidance and demonstrates that the framework has room to grow with additional compute.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The baseline comparison simultaneously changes the architecture class (U-Net to transformer) and the spatiotemporal coupling strategy (factorized to joint 4D), making it impossible to attribute improvements to 4D coupling specifically. A factorized DiT baseline (using separate spatial and temporal attention within the same transformer framework) would have isolated the variable the paper claims to study. Without this control, the central thesis that joint 4D modeling is the key driver of improvement remains plausible but not conclusively supported, and the evidence is equally consistent with transformers simply being more efficient than U-Nets for this task. All quantitative comparisons use only N=50 synthetic samples with no confidence intervals, bootstrap estimates, or significance tests. At this sample size, FID and precision/recall can exhibit substantial variance, and because all metrics are computed on the same 50 generated samples they are not statistically independent. The quantitative differences in Table 1 should therefore be treated as preliminary rather than established. The paper does not explain why N=50 was chosen or whether it reflects a computational constraint. The model achieves recall of 0.70 on the public dataset and 0.54 on the private dataset, meaning it fails to cover 30-46% of the real data distribution. For the paper’s stated applications of data augmentation and privacy-preserving sharing, systematically excluding nearly half the anatomical and pathological diversity is a serious limitation. The paper does not analyse which phenotypes or modes are missing, nor does it discuss the downstream consequences of this coverage gap. Despite the “fully 4D” framing used throughout the abstract and introduction, the VQ-GAN encodes 2D+t slices independently along the depth axis, meaning inter-slice spatial information is discarded before the transformer stage. The 4D coupling is introduced only at the diffusion model level. The paper does not test whether a 3D-aware autoencoder would improve results or analyze how much inter-slice information the current factorized encoding loses. The core transformer block architecture is specified only in supplementary material of a concurrent, unpublished submission that was not available for review. This means the reviewable novelty reduces to the 4D extension (positional encodings and patchification), and independent reimplementation from the main text alone is not possible. Additionally, the temporal standardization to 32 frames via cyclic repetition could inflate temporal consistency metrics by imposing artificial periodicity, yet no analysis of this effect is provided.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Novelty & baselines(R1/Q1,Q2,Q5;R2/Q1;R3/Q1). We agree related work should be clearer, will add [15] to the introduction and adjust novelty framing. [17] models only ED/ES phases; [15] uses the same latent encoding but a channel-merged LDM with a 3D U-Net denoiser, i.e. our 3D+t baseline. CardioDiT instead models the latent cine volume as spatiotemporal patches with global self-attention. This offers direct long-range slice-time coupling instead of indirect receptive-field growth, improving consistency and fidelity. 4D coupling & architecture(R3/Q1;R1/Q2). Do gains stem from 4D modelling or architecture? Our comparisons increase coupling progressively: 2D+t via inter-slice conditioning, 3D+t within the U-Net class, and CardioDiT via global attention over latent spatiotemporal patches. We do not claim that every gain isolates “4D coupling” independently of architecture; rather, a joint 4D transformer is an effective realization of such coupling. Moving from 2D+t to 3D+t improves consistency but reduces fidelity. Concurrent work (supplement) suggests that replacing U-Nets with transformers improves diffusion fidelity, here translated to 4D. An in-depth analysis of factorized transformer modules [11] is future work. Implementation & temporal processing(R1/Q4,Q8;R2;R3/Q5). Clarification on implementation and temporal metrics: We will revise Fig. 1/caption and Sec. 2.1-2.2 to explain inference/VQ decoding. The supplement details DiT architecture; code/configs will be public. The label y is zero as no labels were available; embedding dimension e matches the autoencoder. Temporal metrics used one cardiac cycle with detected key frames, so temporal consistency is not a metric artifact. Statistical Robustness(R3/Q2). We agree uncertainty estimates would strengthen interpretation and will temper claims. N=50 per model matches the 50 validation cases, ensuring equal real/synthetic sample sizes. Notably, feature metrics use 50 × 32 time-point vectors, not only 50 volume-level vectors. This improves stability relative to one feature vector per volume, and trends are consistent across data pools/ablations. Using the same 50 samples per model supports comparable metrics. We acknowledge that Tab. 1 differences are preliminary. Future work will synthesize larger cohorts and report significance where applicable. Scope. Several suggestions concern further analysis. We emphasize that the manuscript already provides a broad evaluation within the 8-page limit: multiple distributional and functional metrics, diverse private/public data pools, visual analysis, and ablations. We will expand the discussion on augmentation/privacy and on extension to other dynamic modalities. 4D modelling(R1/Q3;R3/Q4). Concerns regarding the “fully 4D” claim and the absence of end-to-end latent representation: “Fully 4D” refers to the DiT operating on the latent 3D+t volume. The 2D+t VQ-GAN follows cine CMR acquisition: anisotropic slices with coarse through-plane resolution but fine in-plane temporal detail. To our knowledge, no established 3D+t/4D VQ-GAN exists for this setting. Systematically comparing latent encoders is beyond scope. Diversity(R2;R3/Q3). Recall indicates imperfect coverage: Recall is a limited feature-space estimate, not direct phenotype diversity and should not be read as exactly 30% absent phenotypes. Within this limitation, CardioDiT has the best recall among compared methods. W2 was computed on validation samples, so it does not imply memorization and may reflect EF differences between splits. Clarifications(R1/Q1,Q6,Q7;R2). Public datasets were merged before training and evaluated jointly over all validation samples. Volumes were cropped to preserve cardiac content. Charts use public samples or samples generated from models trained on them. The 2D+t baseline shows discontinuities from independent slice synthesis, not breath-hold artifacts; hence, EF estimation is unreliable. All clarifications will be added in the camera-ready upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers agree the paper tackles an important problem in 4D cardiac MRI synthesis and includes a strong empirical evaluation across datasets with clinically relevant metrics. Two reviewers rated it Weak Accept, while one raised concerns about novelty and experimental attribution. The rebuttal should clearly position the contribution relative to closely related prior/concurrent work, justify whether gains stem from full 4D modeling rather than architecture changes, and clarify statistical robustness and implementation details. | The paper presents a well-motivated framework for 4D cardiac MRI synthesis. Reviewer opinions diverged after rebuttal: R1 moved to reject; R2 and R3 moved to accept. The central confound, that gains may reflect the transformer-over-U-Net advantage rather than 4D joint modeling per se, was not resolved experimentally, and the authors narrowed their claim accordingly. The authors are expected to incorporate the reframed novelty positioning, and add the clarified implementation and temporal processing details in the final version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal narrows the claim appropriately and two reviewers moved to Accept. R1 remains Reject, but the main remaining concern is attribution of gains rather than fatal unsoundness. Camera-ready should explicitly soften “fully 4D proves superiority” claims and state that the factorized-transformer control is future work. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This paper proposes CardioDiT, a full 4D implicit diffusion framework designed to address spatiotemporal consistency in cardiac MRI generation. However, the main conclusion that highlighting the role of full 4D modeling for improvement of anatomical and temporal consistency, is not well supported according to the current experiments. This is a non negligible issue that was not resolved in the rebuttal, leading the paper unacceptable for publication.

title: CARformer: Class-Aware Representation Learning for Small-Cohort, Imbalanced Psychiatric Disorder Classification in Brain MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: Well-motivated problem setting: The study targets a highly relevant and practically important clinical challenge, namely small-sample, imbalanced, and multi-disease classification in psychiatric neuroimaging. Methodological novelty: The “class-aware” design is conceptually interesting and appears well tailored to the problem setting. Rigorous experimental evaluation: The method is assessed on two independent and heterogeneous clinical sites, which strengthens the robustness of the findings and suggests good generalization potential. Promising empirical performance: The reported improvements are clear, especially for minority classes, with particularly notable gains on metrics such as AUPRC.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Insufficient methodological details: Critical implementation and design details are missing, which substantially weakens the rigor and reproducibility of the work. For example: (a) it is unclear how the logits from the CA-BoQ and the GAP are combined (e. g. , direct summation or weighted fusion), and why this design was chosen; (b) the initialization, update frequency, and update strategy of the confusion matrix W in the CAC module are not defined, leaving an important part of the method underspecified; (c) the manuscript does not discuss how the stability of the class-aligned queries is ensured during training. Lack of control for potential confounders: The paper does not provide sufficient evidence that the diagnostic groups are comparable at baseline, nor does it clearly state whether and how key covariates such as age and sex were controlled for in the training or analysis pipeline.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The motivation is well grounded. The paper tackles the problem under realistic clinical constraints, including small sample size, class imbalance, and limited single-site data, which makes the problem itself practically meaningful. 2.The dual-branch design is reasonable. The combination of global average pooling and CA-BoQ helps balance training stability and discriminability, which is a sensible design choice for this task.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The evidence for generalizability is insufficient. The experiments are conducted only on two sites from a single dataset, both from Japanese cohorts. There is no cross-dataset or cross-ethnicity validation, which limits the evidence for broader generalization. In addition, the set of baseline methods is relatively limited and somewhat outdated. 2.Important implementation details are missing. In particular, the paper does not clearly explain how the confusion matrix W is updated or how the corresponding weights are computed, which affects reproducibility and makes the CAC component harder to assess. 3.The interpretability claim is not sufficiently supported. The attention maps in Figure 2 do not appear to indicate stable and reproducible disease-related biomarkers across sites. This weakens the authors’ claims regarding spatial interpretability and biological consistency.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The authors propose a novel CARformer framework that integrates two complementary class-aware components to address multi-disorder discrimination under small-cohort, imbalanced psychiatric sMRI settings, which improves inter-class separability through class aware supervised contrastive supervision with confusion-informed negative re-weighting.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The introduction mentions co-morbidities and suggests that the methodology would be beneficial in determining overlap. However, the rest of the paper follows a traditional 3 group differential diagnosis path, all-be-it with the capability of handling different group sizes. There is no real explanation as to why the accuracy for HC or MDD is significantly different between hospitals. Given the proposed method is only better in 50% of the measures in the KUT dataset it suggests that CARFormer is not so much better than the other methods tested.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the Reviewers(Rs) and AC for their constructive feedback and for recognizing CARformer’s clinical motivation, class-aware methodological novelty, minority-class performance gains, and dual‑site evaluation in real‑world data conditions. We address the key concerns below and will add these clarifications and code-release information in the revised manuscript. Methodology Clarification: (R1 Q7.1a) CA-BoQ and GAP logits are fused by weighted additive logit blending, z=z_GAP+ α*z_BoQ, with fixed α=0.3.GAP provides a stable global classifier from the pretrained encoder, while CA-BoQ uses K learnable class-aligned queries and a diagonal per-query head to produce class-specific logits. (R1 Q7.1b; R2 Q7.2) We clarify that the CAC confusion matrix W is updated only from validation predictions. Before the first validation pass, CAC uses uniform negative-pair weighting with W_ij=1.After each validation epoch, W is computed from the row-normalized validation confusion matrix, clipped to [1,2], with diagonal entries reset to 1; subsequent epochs use exponential smoothing with decay = 0.5.In CAC, W_ij reweights only negative pairs between classes, while positive pairs remain as weight = 1.(R1 Q7.1c) Class-query stability is supported by both architectural and regularization designs: (i) class-aligned query slots with LayerNorm before/after cross-attention and a shared diagonal class-query head; (ii) a query-diversity penalty (λ_div = 10^-3) to reduce query collapse. CAC operates GAP-pooled features rather than query embeddings. Confounder handling (R1 Q7.2): Table 1 reports diagnostic-group demographics and scanner protocols for each SRPBS site (Tanaka et al., 2021). Although the cohort is not fully matched across diagnostic groups at baseline, potential confounding was mitigated through site-specific evaluations and subject-level stratified train/validation/test splits, preserving diagnostic distributions and balancing age and sex across subsets. Generalizability & baselines (R2 Q7.1) a) As a primarily methodological contribution, our experimental design was necessarily scoped by the availability of data. We note that the dataset we used is currently the only publicly available resource for the research community to study this clinically important problem. We will better justify this scope and explicitly discuss cross-dataset and cross-ethnicity limitations. b) Our baselines include 3D CNNs used for psychiatric sMRI classification (Zhang et al., 2023), BrainMVP (Rui et al., CVPR 2025) – a brain MRI pretraining model evaluated on brain MRI classification tasks and benchmarked against training-from-scratch and general/medical-domain SSL methods; and PCRLv2 (Zhou et al., TPAMI 2023), a strong medical-domain SSL framework. These represent task-relevant 3D sMRI classifiers and pretrained medical/brain MRI fine-tuning comparators, rather than only generic CNNs. Attention map (R2 Q7.3) UTO and KUT involve different disease contrasts, HC/MDD/BD versus HC/MDD/SZ, Fig. 2 visualizes CA-BoQ’s class-specific attention within each differential-diagnosis task, rather than testing invariant disease biomarkers across sites. Because competing diagnoses differ, discriminative evidence for the same class, such as MDD, may also differ across sites. Site performance differences (R3 Q7.2) We like to respectfully suggest that HC/MDD metrics should not be interpreted as the same binary task repeated across hospitals; MDD is contrasted with BD in UTO but with SZ in KUT, and sites differ in class distributions and acquisition protocols. CARformer is designed to improve class separation, in highly imbalanced KUT setting, it achieved best macro AUC/AUPRC and substantially improving minority-class MDD AUPRC from 0.196 with ResNet18 (the second-best macro baseline) to 0.700.Comorbidity/overlap clarification (R3 Q7.1) We clarify that comorbidity/symptom overlap is used as clinical motivation for the difficulty of 3-class psychiatric differential diagnosis.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This decision is grounded in the work’s clinically well-motivated research target on small-cohort imbalanced psychiatric disorder classification, the methodological novelty of the proposed CARformer framework, and valid dual-site experiments showing clear improvements for minority classes, alongside mixed but marginally competitive overall reviewer scores. To facilitate fair further evaluation, the authors must primarily address these key points: complete missing implementation details of CA-BoQ, GAP fusion and the confusion matrix update strategy, clarify unregulated clinical confounders like age and sex, respond to limited cross-dataset generalization and outdated baseline settings, justify unstable attention map interpretability and explain inconsistent model performance across experimental sites. | All three reviewers updated their final recommendations to Accept after reading the authors’ comprehensive rebuttal, which clarified key methodological details and improved the rationale and reproducibility of the CARformer framework. They found the authors’ explanation of confounding factor control aligned with common practices in clinical neuroimaging research and acknowledged that their initial concerns were partly due to a lack of familiarity with the dataset and task setting. Overall, they believe the authors’ responses have adequately addressed their comments. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Authors have adequately addressed all reviewers’ concerns. There is a consensus toward acceptance, which I agree with. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Based on the three post-rebuttal reviews, all reviewers are satisfied with the authors’ responses. Reviewer #1 finds the response comprehensive and substantive, noting that the manuscript has reached an acceptable level for publication. Reviewer #2 acknowledges that their initial concern has been adequately addressed and revises their assessment positively. Reviewer #3 confirms that the authors have adequately responded. Therefore, I recommend acceptance of this paper.

title: CineMesh4D: Personalized 4D Whole Heart Reconstruction from Sparse Cine MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: The main strengths of the paper are that it addresses an important problem, namely 4D whole-heart reconstruction from sparse multi-view cine MRI, and that it does so with a fairly complete end-to-end pipeline rather than focusing only on a single chamber or a single cardiac phase. The paper also explicitly models temporal coherence, which is appropriate for a 4D task, and the contour-based differentiable rendering supervision is a reasonable way to use sparse 2D cine views. Finally, the evaluation is reasonably broad, including geometric, contour, and temporal metrics as well as ablations.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Weaknesses also include the broad but insufficiently demonstrated clinical value, the under-described reference mesh generation process, and the relatively weak qualitative evaluation. The paper emphasizes “personalized” and “functional” reconstruction, but does not clearly define the clinical workflow or evaluate functional endpoints such as ejection fraction or EDV/ESV. In addition, the reference mesh generation pipeline is only described at a high level, which limits reproducibility and makes the reported errors harder to interpret. Finally, Fig. 3 and the supplementary video mainly show reconstructed meshes without clear side-by-side comparison to the reference mesh, making qualitative assessment less convincing.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1) Differentiated technical contribution: Beer–Lambert differentiable rendering loss is a principled, novel and physically motivated approach to supervise 3D mesh reconstruction from 2D contours. 2) The dual-context temporal block is good contribution and it is properly ablated. The design explicitly fuses global motion descriptors with local sliding-window temporal context, solving a common problem of jittery framewise predictions which proved by results showing lower mesh jitter and cleaner volume curves. 3) First end-to-end 4D whole-heart approach from multi-view sparse cine MRI without intermediate volumetric segmentation is actually a genuine gap in the literature. Most prior mesh reconstruction works focus on LV or biventricular models. This paper reconstructs LV, RV, LA, RA, myocardium, improving clinical relevance. 4) Good integration of classical and modern ideas: MeshVAE + GCN + Exphormer + LoRA + differentiable rendering + temporal modeling all support the central goal effectively without overengineering. The system feels balanced and practical. 5) Ablation across view combinations, pretraining strategy, and temporal block is comprehensive. 6) The rendering loss and dual context temporal block are a novel, well designed and goal focused contributions.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1) No comparison on a publicly available benchmark, all baselines are re-implemented without cross-study reproducibility, would like to see the blind testing on publicly available datasets like MMWHS, by using multi-planar reformation (mrp) the long and short axis views can be generated by this dataset which has whole heart segmentation anyway so it could prove generalizability of the proposed method. 2) The proposed method requires atlas based dense 3D segmentation to train MeshVAE. Training ground truth meshes come from a multi-step pipeline: 2D segmentations → atlas deformation → 3D segmentation → template mesh warping. This adds noise and biases that might limit generalization, yet little discussion is provided. 3) The paper notes that atrial reconstruction is less accurate due to sparse sampling. A more explicit failure-case analysis highlighting where the proposed method succeeds vs rest will show how much this method impacts and would strengthen the paper. 4) Since the loss compares against 2D ground-truth contours, any segmentation inconsistencies or label noise may misguide training. The paper doesn’t quantify sensitivity to segmentation errors.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: (1) The task this paper aims for is clinically meaningful for cardiac digital twins. (2) The results are strong, particularly on the temporal smoothness improvements.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1) The size of the dataset is a bit small, with only 57 test cases. (2) Insufficient literature review and comparison (3) The technique novelty should be further justified.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: N/A
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The reviewers generally view this as a solid and relevant contribution, with consistent strengths in problem formulation, technical design, and overall system completeness. In particular, the end-to-end 4D whole-heart reconstruction pipeline and the integration of temporal modeling and differentiable rendering are seen as meaningful steps toward practical clinical use. At the same time, several concerns are raised across reviews. These mainly relate to limited validation on public benchmarks, unclear generalization due to reliance on a multi-stage reference mesh pipeline, and gaps in positioning against recent prior work. Some reviewers also question whether the level of methodological novelty fully matches the claims, especially given similarities to existing approaches. I generally agree with the reviewers’ assessment. The paper is technically sound but the concerns around evaluation, benchmarking, and positioning are important and should be addressed by the authors to strengthen the submission.

title: ClinLoop: Human-AI Collaborative Agents for Multimodal Breast Cancer Diagnosis Under Incomplete Clinical Data
reviewer_1_strengths: Overall, the idea presented in the paper is interesting and novel. The proposed ClinLoop framework addresses the problem of missing modality for breast cancer diagnosis through a collaborative AI–expert approach, and the reported performance is supportive of its effectiveness.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) How is model performance affected by the experts’ level of expertise and years of experience? 2) Additionally, how many experts were involved in this study? Are multiple clinicians involved in annotating the same case, and if so, how are potential discrepancies between their assessments handled? 3) The paper does not provide information on whether the code will be released.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The authors proposed ClinLoop, a human–AI collaborative workflow for multimodal breast cancer staging under real-world missing modalities. The idea is interesting and clinically relevant.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Statistical analysis, including p-values, should be provided to support the comparisons between methods.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Realistic clinical setting: The paper leverages data that constitutes realistic clinical scenarios where clinical data is typically not available for all patients in the cohort. 2.Addresses model uncertainty: The paper proposes a method to address uncertainty of AI methods by explicitly calibrating and deferring to a human for review 3.Incremental/active learning: The paper provides a way to use human provided feedback to improve the subsequent performance of the system
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Weak baselines: The paper assesses performance on single and multimodal models whose architecture or training scheme is not explicitly stated. The authors neither state if these are external baselines established in the literature. 2.Missing key methodological details: The paper does not provide much information of the various models used as components in the agentic framework. For instance, which encoders serve as the single and multimodal models. No details on how radiomic features are obtained for traditional classifiers. 3.No ablation of core contribution: The paper does not explicitly demonstrate which components of the framework contributes to the stated gains.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers (R1, R2, R3) and the Meta-Reviewer for recognizing the novelty and clinical relevance of the proposed ClinLoop framework. We are encouraged that R1 and R2 recommended acceptance, while R3’s weak-reject recommendation mainly concerns clearer experimental details and additional analysis. We are committed to releasing the code upon acceptance and reporting statistical analysis, including p-values, in the final paper. R1: Clinician expertise and reviewer variability. The clinician-in-the-loop stage involved three breast imaging/oncology clinicians with 12, 8, and 5 years of experience, respectively. Disagreements were resolved by consensus; unresolved cases were assigned lower confidence tags rather than treated as high-confidence gold labels. As described in Sec. 3.4, all deferred cases and a budgeted subset of high-impact samples are reviewed, and confidence-tagged labels are fed back for iterative updates. Together with the ensemble disagreement check in Sec. 3.2, model-level uncertainty pre-filters ambiguous predictions for prioritized review, while confidence-weighted retraining down-weights uncertain judgments. This design mitigates both model uncertainty and inter-reader variability across different expertise levels. R1/R2/R3: Code and reproducibility. We will release the training/evaluation code, configuration files, split-generation scripts, preprocessing instructions, and trained model recipes upon acceptance. The clinical images cannot be publicly released due to institutional governance, but we will provide sufficient implementation details to reproduce the method on comparable data. R2: Statistical analysis. We agree that statistical testing should be reported. The manuscript uses 5-fold patient-level cross-validation with a held-out calibration split and reports discrimination, calibration, and selective-prediction metrics. We have now performed paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across the five folds comparing ClinLoop with the strongest non-ClinLoop baseline. The main improvements are statistically significant (p<0.01). We will add mean±std and p-values for Macro-F1/Joint-Acc, ECE, and selective risk. R3: Baselines and methodological details. We agree that the baseline descriptions were too compressed. We will expand Secs. 4.1–4.3 to clarify that all deep baselines use the same patient-level folds, preprocessing, augmentation, optimizer, and training schedule. Single-modality baselines use 3D ResNet-50/MedicalNet for CT/MRI and EfficientNet-B4/ImageNet for DM. Missing-modality baselines include late fusion, MoE-style fusion, and modality dropout, all re-implemented under the same protocol. Radiomics baselines use an IBSI-compliant PyRadiomics pipeline with first-order, shape, and texture features (GLCM/GLRLM/GLSZM), ICC-based reproducibility filtering, LASSO selection, and 5-fold CV-tuned LR/SVM. LLM baselines use the same case inputs described in Sec. 4.3 and map outputs to TNM labels. For ClinLoop, CT/MRI use slice-based attention aggregation, DM uses a 2D CNN backbone, and multimodal fusion is conditioned on a modality mask to support arbitrary input subsets. R3: Ablation and component contribution. We agree that a dedicated ablation should be made explicit. We will add component-wise ablations for mask-conditioned fusion, ensemble/TTA uncertainty, conformal QA, modality-consistency checking, calibrated pseudo-labeling, and closed-loop clinician feedback. Tables 2 and 3 already show the benefit of the full loop; the added ablation will make the source of the gains clearer.

reviewer_2_strengths: The strongest aspect of this work lies in its rigorous, clinically grounded experimental design and thorough evaluation framework. Specific strengths include: 1.Large-Scale Multicenter Cohort and Rigorous External Validation: Cross-institutional generalization remains a critical challenge in medical AI. The authors assembled a substantial cohort across five institutions (two public, three internal). Rather than relying exclusively on internal cross-validation, they reserved two fully independent external centers (Ycenter and Qcenter) for unbiased out-of-distribution testing. This validation strategy provides robust empirical evidence of the model’s resilience to real-world distributional shifts. 2.Clinically Aligned Evaluation Metrics: Beyond relying on AUC alone, the authors report balanced accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. This multi-metric approach appropriately accounts for the class imbalance inherent in clinical datasets and directly reflects diagnostic utility, particularly in balancing false-positive rates with the reliable identification of true pCRs. 3.Comprehensive Ablation Analysis: Despite the methodological complexity—integrating graph-based modeling, adversarial domain adaptation, and retrieval-augmented generation—the ablation experiments (Table 3) are methodically designed. By isolating the clinical prior (CP), graph attention mechanism (PR), domain adversarial component (ADV), and the RAG framework, the authors demonstrate that each element yields measurable performance gains, particularly on external cohorts. This systematic validation confirms that the architectural choices are substantively motivated and functionally integrated rather than arbitrarily combined.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While the overall methodology is sound, the presentation of the proposed framework (particularly Figure 1) and the lack of critical implementation details require significant improvement: 1.Poor presentation clarity and severe text-figure mismatch in Figure 1: (a) Figure 1 lacks self-explanatory elements, leaving several visual components unexplained: 1) Unexplained abbreviations: Abbreviations such as Emb. and Tab. Enc. appear in the figure, but their full terms are not provided in the figure itself or the caption. 2) Unexplained symbols: The tag next to the nodes and the “scissors” symbol in Part C are not explained regarding their specific operations or states in either the figure or the caption. (b) There is a noticeable disconnect between the figure and the Methodology section, lacking terminology consistency: 1) Figure 1B uses descriptive module names like Self-Transformation, Linear Transformation, and Message Weighting, whereas Section 2.2 describes the process entirely using rigorous mathematical symbols. The visual elements lack a direct mapping to the equations, making it difficult to follow. 2) The figure introduces concepts not explained in the text: For example, the tag is shown in Figure 1A, but Section 2.1 (which introduces the prior graph construction) never mentions the concept of a “mask” or its specific implementation mechanism. 2.Missing implementation details of the MRI feature extractor: In Section 2.3, the imaging node initialization is defined as f-img(·). However, in the implementation details (Section 3.1), the authors only mention the cropping and concatenation sizes of the DCE-MRI images (192, 256, 256), omitting the specific architecture of the Imaging Backbone . This critical omission significantly hinders the reproducibility of the paper. 3.Privacy and compliance risks regarding LLM clinical deployment: The paper utilizes an LLM for retrieval and explanation but fails to specify whether it relies on calling an external API or local deployment. In real-world clinical Medical Image Computing (MIC) scenarios, transmitting sensitive data—including patient graph embeddings and multimodal features—to external LLM APIs (e.g., DeepSeek) poses significant privacy and compliance risks. Conversely, locally deploying a large-parameter LLM requires massive computational resources. The authors should clarify their deployment strategy. Furthermore, to truly demonstrate the clinical viability of the LLM framework, it is highly recommended to conduct validation experiments using a locally deployable, small-parameter LLM to assess whether the performance drop remains within an acceptable range.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers (R) for their feedback. We have clarified the concerns and will improve the writing accordingly. Q1.Lack description for image encoder. (R1,R2) Thank you for pointing this out. We omitted details of the MRI encoder in the manuscript. The MRI encoder is DenseNet-121, as specified in encoder.py of the anonymized code. We will add this clarification to manuscript. Q2.LLM mechanism and decision rule. (R1, R3) We thank the reviewers for the opportunity to clarify. PRAttn-RGCN is the diagnostic backbone, while the LLM-guided retrieval branch only provides auxiliary evidence by generating a schema-constrained retrieval plan over fixed similarity routes. Thus, the framework is not DeepSeek-specific, and any schema-compliant LLM can be substituted. For each query, the LLM receives the prompt together with patient’s sub-graph embedding, MRI/clinical/pathological embeddings, and edge-level attention weights. Finally, the LLM cannot “disagree” with PRAttn-RGCN because it does not produce a prediction. Any difference arises only between the PRAttn-RGCN output and the neighbor-derived estimate, which are combined deterministically: p_final = b·p_R-GCN + (1-b)·p_neighbors), b=0.7. PRAttn-RGCN remains the dominant decision source. Retrieval can adjust borderline cases but cannot override a confident backbone prediction. Q3.Clarification of clinical priors. (R3) Thank you for this insightful comment. Strong-prior edges are derived from breast cancer guidelines and expert consensus, representing clinically validated and stable medical facts. We keep them fixed to preserve such knowledge and reduce the risk of learning dataset-specific shortcuts under limited sample size or center bias. For less deterministic relations, soft priors are learnable but initialized with larger weights, while uncertain relations are weakly initialized and mainly learned from data. Priors are injected only as a first-layer log-bias to calibrate early R-GCN message passing, leaving deeper layers fully learnable. As shown in Table 3, adding clinical-prior improves AUC over vanilla R-GCN. Q4.Qcenter generalization and adversarial learning. (R3) Thank you for raising this point. We agree that Qcenter is a more challenging external domain, where our method still achieves the best at AUC, bACC and SEN. The adversarial branch is applied only to MRI to reduce protocol-related imaging bias, not all sources of external distribution shift. Its impact on pCR prediction is therefore limited, especially because prior studies and our analysis suggest that pathological factors dominate pCR prediction. This is also supported by Fig. 4, where few highly ranked edges are image-related. We will clarify that adversarial branch improves robustness when MRI bias is a major domain-shift source. Q5.Privacy risks regarding LLM. (R2) We used API-based LLM for three reasons. First, privacy risks are mitigated, as stated in Sec. 2.4, the LLM only receives de-identified embeddings and attention features, not raw patient data. Second, API-based use of properly de-identified medical data is already an established practice in healthcare AI workflows when privacy and governance requirements are met. Third, local deployment is limited by computational resources. Q6.Fig. 3 clustering and selection bias. (R1) Thank you for this observation. Fig.3 aims to visualize binary class separation across internal and external cohorts, not to claim that external sub-clusters are free from selection bias. We will clarify this interpretation. Q7.Writing details. (R2,R3) We will correct all typos related to Table 2; revise notation errors and ambiguities, such as clarifying that τ denotes the temperature coefficient and replacing it with t; and explain undefined abbreviations (Emb. as Embedding, Tab. as Table, and Enc. as Encoder). We will clarify as edge-prior mask and the scissors symbol denotes the gradient-reversal-based adversarial decoupling branch.
