title: Coarse-to-Fine Meta-Reweighting with Dynamic Retrieval for Adult-to-Pediatric Domain Adaptation in Tumor Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is well motivated. Pediatric glioma is underrepresented while adult glioma is a highly study task. This contrast highlights the potential impact of leveraging knowledge from adult data to improve pediatric applications. The proposed method is interesting. Finding the more representative samples could lead to improve optimization and help mitigate overfitting to the adult cohort. The method description and the figures are clear, and the paper is easy to follow The ablation results show that the independent elements of the proposed approach improve the performance and complement each other
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Comparison with state-of-the-art. The method shows improved results compared with several methods for training with noisy data, data scarcity, or domain adaptation. However, there are no comparisons against methods specifically developed for pediatric glioma segmentation, such as those proposed in the BraTS-PED 2023 challenge [a], which uses the same dataset as this work. Including such comparisons would provide a more task-relevant benchmark and better contextualize the contribution. Missing baseline with only pediatric images. The introduction explains how training with both populations will affect the performance on the underrepresented pediatric cohort. However, it is unclear how the method performs when it is only trained on pediatric data. The first row in Table 1 may correspond to this setting, but it could also be trained only on adult images. Clarifying this point is important for understanding the benefit of incorporating adult data. Moreover, when compared to the BraTS-PED 2023 challenge results, the reported performance looks substantially lower, even though those methods were trained using only pediatric data. While the results are not directly comparable since its different evaluation sets (official test vs. selected test subset), the difference with several of those methods, mainly in ET, is large enough to raise questions about the method’s performance against approaches designed for this task. The paper claims that the proposed approach has “lower computational and memory overhead” but does not include quantitative comparisons to support this statement The introduction says that there are only 99 labeled cases for pediatric glioma analysis suggesting that that is the total number of samples available, but that is only the number of cases in the version of the dataset used. The more recent BraTS-PET 2024 has 261 [b]. Also, section 2 says that BraTS 2024 is used but the number of patients match those of 2023. The order of sections 2.3, 2.4 and 3 is strange. The explanations of the baselines experiments are before the experimental setup. Also, section 2.3 should be closer to or merged with section 3.2 since they are highly related. [a] Fathi Kazerooni, Anahita, et al. “BraTS-PEDs: Results of the Multi-Consortium International Pediatric Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge 2023.” Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging 3.June 2025 issue (2025): 72-87. [b] Kazerooni, Anahita Fathi, et al. “The brain tumor segmentation in pediatrics (BraTS-PEDs) challenge: focus on pediatrics (CBTN-CONNECT-DIPGR-ASNR-MICCAI BraTS-PEDs). “ arXiv preprint arXiv:2404.15009 (2024).
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem. Pediatric brain tumor segmentation is clearly a low-data regime, and the manuscript is well motivated around the difficulty of leveraging adult data without simply inheriting adult-specific biases. The proposed formulation is intuitive and reasonably well matched to the problem. The idea of separating coarse tumor localization from fine pediatric-specific subregion refinement is sensible, and the use of the coarse mask as an auxiliary channel in the fine stage is clearly described. The dynamic retrieval mechanism is a potentially useful extension over fixed or arbitrary meta-sample selection. The method computes a mean pediatric gradient, scores pediatric cases by cosine similarity, and uses the top 10 as meta-cases for reweighting. The empirical section includes more than a single benchmark comparison. The paper provides an ablation study, comparisons against several reweighting/domain adaptation baselines, four-fold results, and backbone sensitivity experiments. Within the paper’s own experiments, the full method consistently improves over its internal baselines.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper has multiple reference-integrity problems. The manuscript states that it uses “BraTS 2021 (1,251 adult cases) [11],” but reference [11] in the bibliography is actually the 2024 BraTS post-treatment glioma challenge paper, not the standard BraTS 2021 adult pre-operative dataset. The baseline section also describes DA [6] as “supervised Domain Adaptation,” while the cited reference is explicitly titled Unsupervised domain adaptation for pediatric brain tumor segmentation. In addition, “L2RW [7]” is cited as a skin-lesion segmentation paper, whereas the standard L2RW reference is Ren et al., Learning to Reweight Examples for Robust Deep Learning (ICML 2018). I also note that MGR-DAS is described as [9] in the baseline section but appears as [10] in Table 2.Reference [1] is relevant, but poorly placed. It is a prior pediatric transfer-learning MICCAI paper, so it fits better as prior work on adult-to-pediatric adaptation than as support for the claim about tumor incidence. Several of the strongest claims are overstated relative to the actual evidence. In particular, the abstract states that the method “significantly outperforms state-of-the-art reweighting approaches, achieving a 10.7% improvement in Dice score and a 24.6 mm reduction in HD95.” Those numbers correspond to the gain over naive mixed training in Table 1, not the strongest competing reweighting baseline in Table 2, so the abstract wording is stronger than the evidence clearly supports. Likewise, the paper claims “state-of-the-art pediatric segmentation performance,” but it does not compare against the leading methods summarized in the BraTS-PEDs challenge results paper, where top pediatric approaches included nnU-Net/Swin UNETR ensembles, Auto3DSeg, and self-supervised nnU-Net variants. The evaluation protocol is ambiguous. Section 2.1 states that BraTS-PEDs is randomly divided into 70 training and 29 testing cases, but in the same paragraph it says the experiments are repeated under a 4-fold cross-validation scheme. Section 2.4 again refers to robustness evaluation using four-fold cross-validation. It is therefore unclear whether the main reported results are based on a fixed 70/29 split, cross-validation averages, or a mixture of both. In a 99-case pediatric dataset, this ambiguity is a major issue. Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation detail. The paper gives the high-level equations and some training settings, but several important details are absent: how sample-level gradients are computed in practice for 3D segmentation, whether gradients are computed over all parameters or a subset, how patch-level gradients are aggregated, how checkpoints are selected, and how hyperparameters such as retrieving 10 meta-cases every 5 epochs were chosen.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Well-designed two-stage strategy: Separates cross-domain consistent localization and pediatric-specific refinement, which is intuitive and effective. 2.Efficient reweighting: Avoids costly bi-level optimization and maintains low computation overhead, suitable for clinical deployment. 3.Clear writing and logical structure: The paper is well organized, with clear figures and formulas.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their insightful feedback and positive assessment of our coarse-to-fine meta-reweighting framework. We address the concerns below: (1) Comparison with BraTS-PED Challenge Winners (R1, R2): The top-performing methods in the BraTS-PED 2023 challenge, such as CNMCPMI2023 and Auto3DSeg, rely on ensemble pipelines that combine U-Net, Swin-UNETR, and ResNet architectures with larger model capacities and patch sizes. In contrast, our experiments use single U-Net or Swin-UNETR models with a smaller 64³ patch size and lower-parameter models due to limited computational resources, which may particularly affect ET performance in pediatric-only training. Nevertheless, as shown in Table 3(B), the proposed method consistently improves both backbones, indicating that it functions as a plug-and-play, backbone-agnostic learning framework. To directly address the reviewers’ concerns, we integrated the proposed method into the challenge-winning CNMCPMI2023 pipeline ( U-Net and Swin-UNETR with additional post-processing) on our split. This improved the average Dice score of the CNMCPMI2023 pipeline from 0.763 to 0.822, further demonstrating compatibility with SOTA ensemble pipelines. (2) Baseline Clarification (R1): The first row in Table 1 is indeed the pediatric-only baseline. We will clarify this explicitly in Table 1 caption. (3) Cross-Validation Ambiguity (R2): We would like to clarify that all main results are based on a fixed 70/29 pediatric train/test split for fair comparison with prior work. The additional 4-fold cross-validation experiments (25, 25, 25, and 24 testing cases) were conducted separately as a robustness analysis (only Table 3(A)). We agree Sec. 2.4 could be clearer, and we will revise it to avoid ambiguity. (4) Reference Inconsistencies (R2): We sincerely thank R2 for the meticulous audit. DA [6] is primarily an unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) study; however, the paper also reports all supervised DA results as an upper-bound reference. In our comparison, we selected the best-performing supervised DA from this paper. For L2RW [7], we cited the medical-image implementation paper (skin lesion) that applied L2RW, but we agree that the original ICML 2018 L2RW paper should also be cited. References [9] and [10] are conference/journal versions of the same work, and we will fix the numbering inconsistency, and the BraTS 2021 [11] citation will be corrected accordingly. (5) Reproducibility, Implementation Details, and Computational Efficiency (R1, R2, R3): Parameter-Efficiency: To minimize overhead, our method avoids bi-level optimization and restricts gradient computation to only over the encoder and decoder (∼4.45M parameters), excluding the ViT layers (∼100M parameters). As a result, our method requires 3.26 min/epoch, compared to 26.42 (MWN), 28.32 (L2RW), and 6.82 (MGR-DAS). We will add it to Table 2 Gradient Computation: We use micro-batching to compute sample-level gradients within 3D patches. Full implementation details will be available on GitHub upon acceptance, per MICCAI’s double-blind policy. (6) Meta-case Selection & Generalization (R3): Meta-cases are selected based on similarity to the average pediatric gradient G_ref (section 2.2 (i)), which prioritizes representative pediatric tumor patterns (e.g., missing/small edema regions) while reducing the influence of rare cases (e.g., large ED regions). Clinically, this helps the model focus on consistent pediatric characteristics rather than adult-dominant patterns. For testing on another dataset, we tested our method on pediatric brain tissue segmentation, and due to space limits, included only pediatric tumor segmentation. (7) Paper Organization (R1,R2): We agree that the organization of Secs. 2.3, 2.4, and 3 can be improved for readability. In addition, the reported 10.7% Dice improvement is relative to naive mixed training rather than the strongest competing (MGR-DAS), which is 8.5%. We will revise them in the revised version.

title: Contrast-Invariant Reference-Based Slice Thickness Estimation in MRI via Spectral Matching
reviewer_1_strengths: (1) The proposed method is simple but highly effective, applicable across arbitrary imaging contrasts, and capable of utilizing isotropic imaging data from different subjects at varying resolutions for comparison. (2) The experimental setup is comprehensive, reporting necessary statistical significance tests and runtime information. (3) The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated across multiple datasets.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) In actual acquisitions, a certain degree of oblique scanning may occur. The paper needs to further discuss the applicability of the method under such conditions. (2) The paper should further explain and investigate whether the proposed method remains robust in the presence of noise interference or motion artifacts. (3) It remains unclear whether the proposed method is sensitive to the choice of reference data. For instance, the impact of using different reference HR volumes on the estimated thick-slice thickness should be explored.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Contrast-Invariant Structural Representation: The use of the rank transform makes PRISM highly robust to global contrast changes. It addresses the practical variability often encountered in clinically acquired medical images. Flexibility and Efficiency: The method successfully estimates slice thickness without requiring anatomical alignment, paired data, or iterative optimization. This greatly enhances the practical applicability and efficiency of the proposed method compared to existing supervised or alignment-dependent approaches.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Difficulty in Visual Assessment (Fig 3): While Figure 3 demonstrates the results of the downstream super-resolution experiment, it is challenging to visually recognize the improvement in the provided images. The authors could better highlight the superiority of their method by providing error maps or zoomed-in residual images. Limitation in Evaluation Metrics: The paper primarily relies on PSNR and SSIM to quantify the results. However, considering the downstream task is super-resolution, it would be highly beneficial to evaluate or at least discuss the method’s ability to restore high-frequency components. Exploring metrics such as HFEN or LPIPS would make the evaluation much stronger. It would be helpful if the authors could discuss their rationale for metric selection or provide insights on high-frequency restoration in the rebuttal. Sensitivity of Rank Transform to Local Contrast: As briefly mentioned by the authors, while the rank transform is robust to global contrast differences, it can be sensitive to local contrast variations. For instance, in complex brain regions (e.g., near the gray matter and white matter boundary), the rank-transformed signal might experience a reversal in order between T1- and T2-weighted images. To fully justify the claim that the rank transform is more robust than other transformations, it would be beneficial for the authors to either provide visual examples of rank-transformed T1 and T2 images or provide a deeper discussion on how this local sensitivity impacts the overall performance. Limited Scope of Prospective Evaluation: The authors present a prospective result demonstrating that PRISM estimates a value closer to the target compared to other baseline techniques. While this is a positive and promising indicator, validating the method on such a specific, limited configuration is insufficient to fully demonstrate its prospective clinical utility and robustness. To convincingly support its clinical relevance, the evaluation should encompass a broader range of practical scenarios, or the authors should at least provide a deeper discussion or downstream super-resolution image.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Estimating slice thickness blindly is a severely ill-posed problem. The proposed method avoids the need for exact anatomical alignment or paired data by operating on whole-volume spectral statistics. This increases the method’s practical applicability across different subjects and contrasts. The use of the rank transform prior to spectral matching is a logical design choice. It suppresses global intensity and contrast variations while preserving the resolution-sensitive local orderings necessary to capture the blur signature. Furthermore, by framing the thickness estimation as a 1D exhaustive search over predefined standard deviations, the method sidesteps the convergence instability, degenerate solutions, and local minima that frequently plague gradient-based blind deconvolution algorithms. It is also computationally efficient, processing a full 3D brain volume in approximately 10 seconds.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The forward model explicitly parameterizes the continuous slice selection profile as a unit-area Gaussian. While this is a standard approximation in MRI super-resolution literature, true slice profiles—which are often generated by truncated sinc or SLR RF pulses—exhibit side lobes or flatter passbands. The paper would benefit from a simulation experiment evaluating the method’s robustness when the underlying ground-truth degradation deviates from a perfect Gaussian shape. Regarding the downstream super-resolution validation in Section 3.4, the experiments are performed exclusively using a specific pre-trained denoising diffusion null-space model. While the authors report that PRISM achieves PSNR and SSIM statistically indistinguishable from the true kernel, it remains unclear if the estimated kernels provide consistent improvements across other, more standard SR architectures, such as basic CNNs or TV-regularized reconstruction. Demonstrating that the estimated kernel acts as a consistent improvement across different solvers would strengthen the evaluation. In the real-world evaluation on OASIS-3 data (Section 3.5), the method estimates a mean thickness of 4.23 mm for data with a nominal 4 mm thickness. The authors hypothesize that this is due to PRISM capturing “additional contributions to the through-plane point spread function” relative to the reference. However, without an objective ground truth, this remains speculative. Including a physical phantom experiment where the true slice profile can be precisely measured would validate whether the method is accurately capturing scanner physics or merely exhibiting a systematic bias.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their constructive feedback. We address the main concerns below. Robustness and applicability (R1, AC). While we did not sweep multiple reference images, the experiments intentionally use a difficult reference setting: T2-w target volumes are compared with held-out T1-w references from different subjects, across multiple slice-thickness/gap settings. Despite mismatch in subject, contrast, dataset, and resolution, PRISM remains close to the true thickness and outperforms the baselines. This supports the claim that PRISM does not require matched or registered references. For oblique acquisitions, PRISM should be applied along the physical slice-selection direction from acquisition orientation metadata. Since the comparison uses volume-level spectra, this does not require registration. We will clarify that the HR reference should have comparable directional/anatomical spectral statistics, and that severe motion, slice dropout, or interpolation artifacts may bias spectral estimation. Rank-transform assumption and spectral matching (R2, AC). We appreciate the reviewer’s point that T1/T2 contrast differences can cause local tissue-order changes. Our claim is that the rank transform is invariant to monotonic intensity transformations and robust to global contrast differences, not invariant to every local contrast reversal. In PRISM, the rank transform is only the feature representation; the final comparison uses averaged 1D log spectra along the slice direction over the full in-plane field of view. Local ordering changes may alter the baseline feature spectrum, but are unlikely to mimic the through-plane high-frequency attenuation caused by thicker slices. This is directly tested by the cross-subject, cross-contrast experiments, where PRISM remains accurate across slice settings. Table 1 further supports this design choice: rank transform with spectral power error is consistently best or statistically indistinguishable from best, while alternative features/metrics are less stable. We will clarify this scope of contrast invariance. Downstream SR, metrics, and Fig. 3 (R2, R4, AC). We agree that Fig. 3 is visually dense. We will revise it using the existing reconstructions, adding zoomed insets around resolution-sensitive regions. The SR experiment was designed as a controlled forward-model ablation. The prior, weights, and random seeds are fixed; only the degradation model changes. Under this comparison, PRISM achieves PSNR/SSIM statistically indistinguishable from using the true kernel, whereas the naive and ESPRESO kernels do not. This supports the paper’s claim that PRISM can recover the benefit of the true forward model in downstream SR. Additional solvers or metrics are useful follow-up work, but they are additional experiments and are not permitted in the rebuttal. We will clarify that the SR result evaluates the estimated slice profile, rather than benchmarking SR architectures or perceptual metrics. Real-world evidence and Gaussian model (R2, R4, AC). We agree that the OASIS-3 real-data experiment is not phantom validation of the physical RF slice-selection waveform. Its purpose is to test behavior on real 2D acquisitions with known nominal thickness and gaps. PRISM estimates 4.23±0.05 mm for nominal 4 mm data, closer to metadata than ESPRESO or the spacing-equals-thickness assumption. The slight overestimate is consistent with PRISM estimating effective through-plane blur relative to the HR reference, including contributions beyond the nominal RF slice profile. Similarly, the Gaussian model is used as a compact one-parameter effective FWHM approximation, common in MRI SR modeling, not as a claim that all RF slice profiles are exactly Gaussian. The framework could be extended to non-Gaussian or measured profile dictionaries, which we will note as future work. All experiments use publicly available, de-identified datasets, and no new human-subject data were collected; we will make this explicit.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes PRISM, a simple and efficient contrast-invariant method for estimating slice thickness in thick-slice MRI by matching spectral characteristics between a low-resolution scan and a degraded high-resolution reference after rank transformation. The reviewers generally agree that this is a meaningful methodological contribution with practical potential, highlighting in particular that the method avoids the need for paired data or anatomical alignment, is computationally efficient, and may be useful for improving downstream super-resolution pipelines. At the same time, the current manuscript still requires clearer validation and discussion before it can be accepted. The main concerns focus on robustness under more realistic acquisition conditions, the assumptions behind the rank-transform formulation, and the strength of the downstream and prospective evidence. These issues do not appear fundamental and seem potentially addressable through clarification and better interpretation of the existing results. I therefore recommend invite for rebuttal. In the rebuttal, the authors should focus on clarifying the robustness and applicability of PRISM, discussing the limitations of the rank-transform assumption more explicitly, and better justifying the downstream and prospective validation. | This paper proposes PRISM, a contrast-invariant reference-based slice thickness estimation method for MRI, aiming to estimate the effective slice thickness of thick-slice MRI scans by matching spectral characteristics between a low-resolution target volume and a degraded high-resolution reference. The method uses rank transformation and 1D spectral matching to avoid the need for paired data, anatomical alignment, or supervised training. The reviewers recognized that the proposed method is simple, efficient, and practically useful. In particular, they appreciated its contrast-invariant formulation, registration-free design, computational efficiency, and potential utility for improving downstream super-resolution pipelines. The experiments across multiple datasets, slice-thickness settings, and downstream SR evaluation were also considered supportive of the main claims. The reviewers raised concerns about the robustness of the rank-transform assumption, sensitivity to reference data, applicability under realistic acquisition conditions such as oblique scans, noise, motion, and non-Gaussian slice profiles, as well as the limited scope of downstream and prospective validation. In the rebuttal, the authors clarified that PRISM is intended to be robust to global contrast differences rather than all local contrast reversals, and that the rank transform serves as a feature representation before whole-volume spectral matching. They also explained how PRISM can be applied along the physical slice-selection direction for oblique acquisitions, clarified the interpretation of the real-world OASIS-3 result as estimating effective through-plane blur, and justified the downstream SR experiment as a controlled forward-model ablation rather than a full SR benchmark. Although some limitations remain, including the Gaussian slice-profile approximation, limited prospective validation, and lack of broader SR solvers or perceptual high-frequency metrics, these issues mainly define the scope of the current work rather than undermining the core contribution. The method is mathematically sound, computationally efficient, and empirically consistent across the evaluated settings. Therefore, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Based on the positive post-rebuttal consensus where reviewers found their concerns sufficiently addressed, this paper is recommended for acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors convincingly addressed concerns by discussing limitations in formulation and applicability. I also find the concerns of R2 about limited evaluation scope to be unfounded, since the authors evaluate they method against relevant baselines in direct comparisons as well as for downstream SR scenarios, which is sufficient and meets the standards of the MICCAI conference. Overall, I recommend acceptance for this paper, since this mathematically sound method is novel and well-motivated and shows promising results in a thorough experimental setup.

title: CortexAdapt3D: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of General 3D Foundation Models for Cortical Surface Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: The CortexAdapt3D framework introduces a learnable relative positional bias and a cross attention module in the spectral domain, enabling efficient fine-tuning. The proposed framework is thoroughly evaluated and achieves consistent improvements across classification, regression, and parcellation tasks in cortical surface analysis.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: For the geodesic-aware patch construction, the similar ideas have been proposed in Surface Vision Transformer [1] and Spherical Transformer [2]. The related prior work should be discussed and compared. [1] Dahan, Simon, et al. Surface vision transformers: Attention-based modelling applied to cortical analysis. MIDL (2022). [2] Cheng, Jiale, et al. STF: A spherical transformer for versatile cortical surfaces applications. NeuroImage (2025).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: S1.Important and well-motivated research direction. Bridging the gap between large-scale 3D point cloud pre-training and cortical surface analysis is a timely problem. The paper correctly identifies three key domain mismatches — topology (Euclidean vs. geodesic proximity), positional encoding (absolute vs. relative), and feature richness (coordinates-only vs. derived neuroanatomical attributes) — and proposes a targeted component for each. Figure 1 effectively illustrates the motivation for geodesic patching and attribute incorporation. This systematic decomposition of the domain gap is a clear methodological contribution. S2.Comprehensive multi-task, multi-dataset evaluation with strong results. The paper evaluates on three distinct tasks (preterm classification, cortical parcellation, PMA age regression) across two independent datasets (dHCP, BCP), comparing against three categories of baselines: fully supervised from-scratch models (SphericalUNet, AGConv), full fine-tuning (PointMAE, PointDif), and state-of-the-art PEFT methods (IDPT, DAPT, PointGST). Tables 1-2 show consistent improvements across tasks and backbone choices. Notably, the improvement over full fine-tuning is substantial (Table 2: CortexAdapt3D Dice 89.90/89.96 vs. PointMAE full fine-tuning 75.01), which demonstrates that the domain-specific PEFT design provides genuine regularization benefit, not merely computational savings. S3.Principled domain-specific adapter design via cortical attribute conditioning. The ASMA module’s key insight — conditioning spectral modulation on neuroanatomically meaningful attributes (sulcal depth, cortical thickness, curvature) via cross-attention — is a well-motivated design choice that goes beyond generic PEFT methods. These attributes encode local brain morphology that cannot be inferred from coordinates alone, and their explicit integration provides the model with domain-specific inductive bias. The ablation in Table 3 (comparing with and without attribute conditioning: ACC 91.03 vs. 87.18 for PointDif) supports the claim that attribute awareness contributes meaningfully to performance. S4.Practical relevance for clinical deployment. The framework keeps the pre-trained backbone frozen, training only lightweight modules (RPB, ASMA, task head). This is appealing for clinical settings where labeled cortical data is scarce and computational resources are limited. The ability to leverage large-scale 3D pre-training from non-medical domains for specialized neuroimaging tasks addresses a real practical need.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: W1.ASMA’s spectral modulation mechanism builds closely on PointGST [4] — the novelty boundary should be clarified. The ASMA module (Sec. 2.4) follows the same spectral projection pipeline as PointGST (Liang et al., IEEE TPAMI 2025): project token features into a graph Laplacian eigenbasis, apply modulation, then project back. The principal difference is the cross-attention conditioning on cortical attributes. While this is a meaningful domain-specific adaptation (supported by the ablation in Table 3), the paper does not clearly delineate what is inherited from PointGST versus what is novel. A side-by-side comparison or explicit discussion would help the reader assess the incremental contribution. The paper’s framing presents ASMA as an entirely new component, which overstates the novelty. W2.No statistical significance testing — some performance gains are marginal. Tables 1-2 report single-point estimates without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or p-values. Some improvements are small: e.g., MAE 0.74 vs. 0.76 (Table 2, PointDif) is a 0.02-week difference. While other gains are more substantial (ACC 91.03 vs. 88.28, Dice 89.96 vs. 87.60), reporting variance over multiple random seeds would strengthen all claims and is expected practice for datasets of this size (hundreds of subjects). W3.Eigenbasis computation U is underspecified. Section 2.4 states “we project features into the spectral domain using the eigen basis of the graph Laplacian,” but does not clarify whether U is computed per-sample (preserving individual geometry but expensive and preventing batching) or on a template mesh (enabling batching but losing subject-specific information). This is a fundamental design choice affecting theoretical soundness. Clarifying this is essential for reproducibility and for understanding the method’s behavior. W4.Generalizability claims exceed experimental evidence. The abstract and conclusion claim CortexAdapt3D establishes “a unified, scalable paradigm.” However, both datasets contain only infant brain data. No experiments on adult cortical data, neurodegeneration, or pathological conditions are presented. The claims should be qualified to match the experimental scope.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Finding effective ways to adapt large 3D foundation models to cortical surface analysis is an important problem, and the proposed components are well-motivated.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper’s main weakness is a lack of clarity which makes it difficult to fully evaluate the contributions. The following points need to be addressed: ASMA design choice: What are the cortical-specific attributes used as input to ASMA (Page 4, first paragraph)? Additionally, how does ASMA compare to a simpler alternative, such as concatenating the cortical attributes directly to the input coordinates? Spherical U-Net for age regression: It is unclear how a U-Net architecture, which is typically used for segmentation or map prediction tasks, is adapted for age regression, which requires a single scalar output. Are additional layers added after the bottleneck or decoder? Could the model be overfitting due to having too many parameters for this task? The fully fine-tuned models perform surprisingly poorly. It would be helpful to understand why. For instance, how does fully supervised training of PointMAE or PointDif compare? The ablation study compares against spectral domain adapter fine-tuning without cortical attributes, which is an informative baseline. It would be valuable to include this condition in the main Table 2 experiments (parcellation and age regression) as well, unless this is equivalent to PointGST, in which case please clarify
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the constructive comments. We address the main concerns below. [R1,R2,R3] Prior work and relation to PointGST. Our contribution is not geodesic patching as standalone novelty, but adapting generic 3D pre-trained priors to cortical surfaces. For ICO-based cortical surfaces, topology-preserving patches are a natural domain adaptation, since Euclidean KNN can connect points across folds (Fig. 1). The ablation supports this: even with frozen patch embedding, changing only the patch construction improves generic-prior transfer. We will better discuss the cortical transformer works mentioned by R1.ASMA inherits the spectral projection–modulation–back-projection paradigm from PointGST, but differs in two cortical-specific aspects: we omit PointGST’s Euclidean local-basis branch, which does not respect intrinsic cortical topology, and introduce cortical-attribute-conditioned cross-attention. Thus, the ablation baseline is not exactly PointGST, but an empirically close PointGST-like spectral-adapter baseline without attribute conditioning. We will explicitly clarify inherited vs. new components. [R2,R3] Details of ASMA, patch sampling, eigenbasis, and RPB. ASMA uses sulcal depth, curvature, and cortical thickness as cortical attributes. Directly concatenating attributes with coordinates is possible in principle, but would alter the input distribution of the frozen pre-trained encoder and may weaken preserved generic priors; therefore, we inject attributes through a lightweight spectral adapter. All cortical surfaces are remeshed to ICO5 topology with 10,242 vertices and 20,480 faces. We construct 320 geodesic triangular patches; each patch contains 64 ICO5 faces and 45 vertices, not only three triangle corners. The input includes coordinates and cortical attributes. Connectivity is not explicitly fed into the backbone, but is used for topology-preserving patch assignment. The Laplacian eigenbasis U is computed per sample from the patch centers. Since N=320, using the full eigenbasis without truncation is computationally manageable. For RPB, B_ij is a scalar attention-logit bias for token pair (i,j), forming a bias matrix aligned with QK⊤. The pre-trained attention weights are frozen; only the added RPB MLP, computed from patch-center coordinates, is learnable during PEFT. We will define all symbols before use, including W_d/W_u as adapter down-/up-projection matrices and d_a as the adapter embedding dimension. [R3] Comparison methods and transfer setting. For age regression, we used the spherical-CNN encoder with global pooling and an MLP regression head, not the full U-Net decoder; we will rename it as spherical-CNN to avoid ambiguity. Point-MAE and PointDif are mainly pre-trained on ShapeNet, a synthetic object-level dataset with about 50K–57K shapes from 55 categories, rather than cortical surfaces. This domain gap and limited labeled infant data may make full fine-tuning prone to overfitting/catastrophic forgetting, while PEFT better preserves generic 3D priors and learns cortical-specific adaptation. [R2,R3] Statistical robustness, ablation scope, and claims. We initially reported point estimates due to space limits, as many key improvements are large. Nevertheless, we agree that statistical robustness is important for marginal differences. We will therefore add missing references and report mean±std and p-values from existing results. Our ablation was intentionally conducted on dHCP classification as a compact and sensitive setting to isolate component effects under the same transfer protocol. For dense prediction, the main BCP parcellation results already show a substantial gain over PointGST, with ACC improving from 71.14 to 91.91.We will restrict broader claims to the tested infant cortical tasks, leave adult/pathological cortical analysis as future work. [R1, R2, R3]-Reproducibility For sure, We will release the code after acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors should focus on addressing the lack of clarity and detail regarding the methodological contributions, particularly the Attribute-Aware Spectral Modulation Adapter (ASMA) and its relationship to prior work like PointGST. They must explicitly clarify the eigenbasis computation and whether it’s per-sample or template-based. This explanation impacts reproducibility and theoretical soundness. The other main concern is the generalizability claims which is limited to infant brain data. Reporting standard deviations for results will boost the performance claims especially for marginal gains. | The authors clarified the reviewers, specified the patch sampling and eigenbasis computations, and restricted their claims to infant data. Two reviewers upgraded their scores to accept after these clarifications, demonstrating that the primary concerns regarding reproducibility and methodological details were resolved. The paper is recommended for acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes CortexAdapt3D, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework that adapts generic 3D point-cloud foundation models to cortical surface analysis through geodesic-aware patch construction, learnable relative positional bias, and an attribute-aware spectral modulation adapter. The reviewers agree that adapting large 3D pre-trained priors to cortical surfaces is a timely and well-motivated problem, and that the multi-task, multi-dataset evaluation shows consistent improvements over supervised, full fine-tuning, and prior PEFT baselines. The rebuttal addressed the principal concerns in concrete terms, clarifying the per-sample eigenbasis computation, the patch construction and input representation, the relative positional bias and previously undefined notation, and the boundary between inherited and newly introduced adapter components. The main remaining reservation concerns novelty, as the contribution is best understood as a domain-specific adaptation of an existing spectral adapter paradigm; the authors are encouraged to retain the transparent inherited-versus-novel framing and to qualify the generalizability claims to the infant cortical setting actually evaluated. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This submission proposes a cortical surface analysis using fine-tuning of pre-trained models. R1 and R3 appreciated the multi-task performance. R2 noted the incremental nature of the method and heavy reliance on the existing PointGST. The rebuttal attempted clarifying the novelty of the components but the core concern on novelty remains. As is, the consensus appears to converge towards a lack of substantial technical innovation. For all these reasons, and with respect to the other submissions, the recommendtion is towards Rejection,

title: Counterfactual Contrastive Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The methodology is novel. I think its an interesting approach which generates counterfactual edits from distributional differences between classes, rather than from a classifier objective. This reduces sensitivity to classifier-specific artifacts and shortcut features. 2.The method is coherent and well motivated and the use of StyleGAN2 plus feature-space refinement is technically sensible. 3.The paper is well written and easy to follow. 4.The paper includes three medical imaging datasets, comparisons with established baselines, and a dedicated counterfactual comparison against several diffusion-based methods. The qualitative figures are easy to read, and the reported runtime advantage is substantial. 5.The results against CA baselines are strong. The proposed method appears to improve both reconstruction and swap quality, and the latent separation results suggest that salient informationis better concentrated in the salient variables than in prior approaches.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The main concern is how the paper is frames. The authors use the language of counterfactuals with no notion of identifiability or using structural causal models to derived counterfactuals under interventions. I think the paper paper should present itself more carefully as a generative editing framework rather than as a causal counterfactual method. 2.The paper is motivated by the claim that classifier-guided VCE methods can reproduce the biases and failure modes of the underlying classifier, but the experimental section does not directly substantiate this point. In particular, the paper does not include a controlled shortcut-feature or biased-classifier stress test demonstrating that classifier-based approaches produce misleading edits while the proposed method instead isolates the intended semantic factor. 3.Table 3,4 and 5 can be better organised and seperated rather than clumped together
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The authors address Visual Counterfactual Explanations for medical image classifiers, a direction with demonstrated clinical value for model interpretability, well-suited to the broader MICCAI community. The framing as classifier-free contrastive disentanglement as a means to counterfactual generation is a conceptually interesting alternative to the dominant classifier-guided paradigm and merits investigation. The paper is clearly written, well-structured with clearly motivated design choices, that makes the method and comparisons easy to follow. The choice of StyleGAN2 is well-motivated by its inherently disentangled StyleSpace, which offers per-attribute interpretability that current diffusion-based VCE methods largely lack. This is a meaningful architectural argument that deserves attention, even as diffusion models dominate the generative landscape.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Conceptual The authors frame the paper as Contrastive Analysis for Visual Counterfactual Explanations. The latter is generally understood as a means to understand black-box classifier behaviour [1], and as such VCE are tied to a given classifier. By reframing the problem to the domain level (a la “What would a healthy image of x look like?”) the authors answer a related but distinctively different question than their choice of focus on VCE implies (“Why did the classifier say that?”). While in itself potentially interesting, this mismatch raises questions about the clinical relevance, and the adequacy of the VCE framing for this contribution, thereby the adequacy for MICCAI. This conceptual gap also complicates the evaluation. VCE methods are typically assessed on their faithfulness to the underlying classifier [1,2]. Since the proposed method operates at the domain level rather than in the classifier’s weight-space, the choice to evaluate against a pretrained model and report accuracy or flip-rate metrics is ambiguous as observed changes might not reflect causal (i.e. the classifier’s actual) behaviour [1,2]. Technical Among others the method is evaluated on BloodMNIST, OCTMNIST. As the work references, both are subset of MedMNISTv2, and as such of 28x28 dimension. While the authors describe images where rescaled to 256x256, this original resolution seems insufficient to evaluate a generative method in a medical / clinical setting, and compare its quality with SOTA methods, rendering 2/3 of the evaluations ambiguous and the StyleGAN2 choice irrelevant. For clinical relevance, a domain level generative method needs to be assessed qualitatively by medical professionals [cf. 3]. The proposed method does not provide such insight. In general, the evaluation setup doesn’t seem to control for training stochasticity, reports appear to be on single runs, limiting the robustness of the conclusions. Novelty While of merit, StyleGAN2 approaches for counterfactual generation is a popular approach [4,5,6,7], as such the work is an application paper of established concepts with limited expansion on the topic, therefore providing ambiguous novelty for the MICCAI community. Inf Syst Front 2026 [5] Schutte et al., “Using StyleGAN for Visual Interpretability of Deep Learning Models on Medical Images”, NeurIPS workshop 2020 [6] Lang et al, “Training a GAN To Explain a Classifier in StyleSpace”, ICCV 2021 [7] Narayanaswamy et al., “Using generative AI to investigate medical imagery models and datasets”, EBioMedicine, 2024
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Extensive evaluation: experiments cover reconstruction quality, latent space disentanglement, and counterfactual generation; includes an ablation study; compared against 9 baseline methods in total Generalizability demonstrated across three diverse medical imaging datasets (brain MRI, blood cells, retinal OCT). Strong quantitative and qualitative results over related work Reproducibility: code is publicly available and the method is described in sufficient detail to re-implement.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Multi-stage training: (1) W-space disentanglement of common and salient factors, (2) F-space refinement. The motivation for splitting these two stages is not sufficiently justified. Hyperparameter selection (e.g., loss weights) is not described; given the multiple competing objectives and the constraint of not disrupting the pretrained GAN’s image generation, it is unclear how stable and sensitive the optimization is and whether the same settings transfer across the three datasets or require per-dataset tuning. Only single runs are reported with no standard deviations, making it difficult to assess result reliability. The F-space is not adequately explained: the choice of layer 8 is not justified, the distinction from W-space and W+-space is not made clear, and known limitations of F-space regarding editability are not discussed. The claim of faster editing is stated in the introduction but never substantiated in the results section. Blood-MNIST and OCT-MNIST have a native resolution of 28x28, yet the model is trained at 256x256; the impact of this large upscaling on results is not discussed. Table 4 uses a different set of comparison methods than Tables 1 and 2, making it impossible to draw consistent conclusions across experiments; the difference between the “swap” operation in Table 1 and the counterfactual generation in Table 4 is also unclear.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their insightful feedback. We address all comments below Conceptual concern (R1,R2): We acknowledge that our method is not a classical VCE approach, as it does not explain a specific classifier. Instead, it is a generative editing framework that can produce counterfactual examples, which we evaluate using standard VCE criteria with a pre-trained classifier. We will clarify this point in the article. Our work builds on the classical VCE definition from [9]: how an image from class c can be minimally and realistically modified so that a system predicts a different target class. Existing VCE methods rely on discriminative features learned by a pre-trained classifier. In contrast, we avoid classifier gradients and instead learn salient and common features at the distribution level to perform controlled edits, such as swapping and interpolation. Although our approach is classifier-free, we evaluate the generated (swapped) images with a pre-trained classifier, following prior VCE work, to verify whether the counterfactual edits induce the expected class changes. The fact that swapped images are mostly classified as the target class (Table 4) suggests that the learned salient factors capture meaningful discriminative patterns As stated in the conclusion, our method does not enable causal discovery, similarly to recent VCE approaches Novelty (R2): The methodological novelty does not lie in using StyleGAN2 as a backbone, but in the formulation of counterfactual generation. Unlike prior methods that search for directions in the W+ space maximizing classifier prediction changes, we decompose the W+ space into common and salient factors, generating counterfactual (swap) from distributional differences between classes rather than classifier objectives, as noted by R1 and R3 Datasets resolution (R2,R3): Datasets from MedMNIST+ are provided at 224×224 resolution and were resized to 256×256 to match the input requirements of StyleGAN2.We will clarify this in the revised manuscript Classifier failure modes (R1): We acknowledge that we did not include experiments on bias reproduction in classifier-guided VCE methods, as this has already been shown in prior work (e.g., [35]). We leave evaluation of our method on controlled bias datasets for future work Clinical relevance (R2): Qualitative results were assessed by expert medical doctors and biologists, but no formal multi-expert reader study was conducted. The focus was methodological development on MedMNIST+, with a future journal extension planned to include a full reader study Training stochasticity (R2, R3): We will update Table 4 to report mean and std over 5 training. Rankings and performance differences between methods remain very similar. For example, FR values are 0.955 (±0.02) for our method and 0.976 (±0.02) for ACE Clarifications (R3): We will clarify that we follow a two-stage training similar to [5], learning first common and salient factors in the W+ space, which is more regularized and editable, and refining details in the F space (layer 8 as in [5]) without changing the semantic edit direction learnt in the W+ space. We only use W+ and F space, with StyleGAN2 generators trained per dataset and then kept frozen. Hyperparameters are selected on validation sets (and not tuned on the test sets) and are the same for all datasets. Inference time is reported in Table 4.Similarly to previous CA works [1,7,10,22,34], we use summation instead of concatenation to avoid extra parameters (to map back to the W+ dimension) Tables (R1,R3): Tables will be reorganized with clearer, self-contained captions. Table 1 compares our method with contrastive baselines, while Table 4 evaluates counterfactuals against VCE-specific methods. We will clarify that the swap operation in Table 1 is equivalent to the counterfactual generation in Table 4.FID differences arise because Table 1 uses random X,Y pairs, whereas Table 4 fixes either Y or X using the images of Fig. 3
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper was reviewed by three experts in the field and received the following recommendations: two Weak Accepts and one Reject. While the reviewers noted several strengths, including the novelty of the classifier-free design and clear motivation, they also raised several concerns, including unclear claims regarding causal counterfactual framing and clinical value, insufficient evaluation with only single runs, and resolution issues in Blood-MNIST and OCT-MNIST. The authors are encouraged to address these concerns in the rebuttal. | After the rebuttal, two reviewers recommended acceptance, while one reviewer maintained a Reject recommendation. While the paper has some limitations, including the lack of a multi-expert reader study, it also demonstrates several strengths, including the novelty of the classifier-free design and clear motivation. Therefore, the paper is recommended for acceptance to MICCAI 2026.The authors are encouraged to incorporate the necessary changes discussed during the rebuttal process into the final camera-ready version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper has interesting points and innovation; R2’s concerns are valid, and the paper is borderline because of concerns of clinical relevance. If there were absolutely no chance of relevance, I feel it would be a reject; I will mark this as accept, acknowledging reviewer majority, but I agree that clinical relevance is questionable. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After going through the reviews as well as the authors’ rebuttal, I agree that, as acknowledged by the authors, there is a gap in the claim that requires reframing. I align with the reviewer’s post-rebuttal comment, and the paper needs substantial revision to appropriately revise its framing.

title: CPS4: Class Prompt Driven Semi-supervised Spine Segmentation with Class-Specific Consistency Constraint
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The integration of textual class prompts into semi-supervised spine segmentation is a significant and timely contribution. While VLMs have been explored in medical imaging, this work is the first to explicitly address the “cross-class interference” problem in multi-class spine segmentation by designing class-specific consistency constraints (token- and pixel-level attention losses). This moves beyond simple image-text alignment to fine-grained region-prompt binding. 2.The methodological design is logical and well-grounded. The two-stage approach effectively decouples the challenging task of learning robust vision-language alignment from the segmentation optimization. 3.Spine segmentation is critical for clinical applications but suffers from high annotation costs due to the multi-class nature (vertebrae + discs). By demonstrating superior performance with only 5% labeled data (achieving ~80.44% Dice), this work offers a practical solution to reduce the reliance on expensive expert annotations.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The method relies heavily on the quality and specificity of the textual class prompts (e. g. , “A magnetic resonance image of a {class name}”). The paper does not discuss the sensitivity of the model to prompt engineering variations (e. g. , synonyms, different sentence structures). In clinical settings, terminology can vary; the robustness of the method to such linguistic shifts is not evaluated. 2.The proposed framework requires a dedicated pretraining stage (Stage 1) before the actual semi-supervised segmentation training (Stage 2). The paper lacks a detailed analysis of the total computational cost (GPU hours) compared to end-to-end SSL methods. For practical deployment, the efficiency of generating 20 separate attention maps (for 20 classes) per unlabeled image during Stage 2 inference/training needs to be quantified. 3.The experiments are conducted solely on the MRSpineSeg dataset. While the results are impressive, the method’s generalizability to other modalities (e. g. , CT spine scans) or other multi-class anatomical structures (e. g. , abdominal organs) remains unproven. A cross-modality experiment or a discussion on potential domain shifts would strengthen the claims. 4.The dataset description notes that “Not all images contain 19 spinal structures. “ The method generates attention maps for all 20 classes for every unlabeled image. The paper does not explicitly explain how the framework handles cases where a specific vertebra is absent in the field of view. Does the VLM generate false positive attention maps for missing classes, and if so, how does the aggregation step mitigate this noise in the pseudo-labels?
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Overall, the motivation for this work is clear, the authors have well articulated their methodology, and the proposed approach has achieved promising experimental results.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The method heavily relies on class prompts, and the paper explicitly treats prompt-object consistency as the central issue. However, the prompt design is hard-coded to a single template, namely “A magnetic resonance image of a {class name},” without any prompt sensitivity analysis. As a result, it remains unclear whether the reported gains are robust to different textual formulations or are partially tied to this specific handcrafted prompt.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.This appears to be the first work to explicitly introduce textual class prompts into the semi-supervised spine segmentation domain. 2.The introduction of specific consistency constraints, namely the token-level and pixel-level losses, directly addresses the known issue of VLMs failing to focus on small or specific anatomical objects. The token-level loss aggregates attention activations toward the predicted spine unit, and the pixel-level loss prevents over-aggregation into subregions, ensuring the VLM covers the entire target unit. 3.The model achieves a Dice score of 80.44% using only 5% labeled data. It consistently outperforms established baselines like Mean Teacher (MT), MedCLIP, and MGCA across various labeling ratios (5%, 10%, 25%, 50%). 4.The ablation study clearly demonstrates that both token-level and pixel-level losses provide complementary gains, with the full model significantly outperforming the baseline.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The authors acknowledge that the MRSpineSeg dataset consists of volumetric (3D) images. However, the proposed architecture uses a 2D ResUNet. Spine anatomy is inherently 3D, and spatial consistency between adjacent slices is critical for identifying specific vertebrae (e.g., distinguishing T12 from L1). By treating slices as independent 2D inputs, the model ignores the rich volumetric context provided by the MRI. This is a step backward from the current state-of-the-art medical image segmentation, which typically employs 3D U-Net variants or Transformers to maintain anatomical continuity. The authors should justify why a 3D baseline (like nnU-Net) or a 2.5D contextual approach was not employed, and provide a comparison to prove that their text-guided pseudo-labels compensate for the lack of 3D spatial information. 2.The method generates pseudo-labels by “stacking” binary maps from the VLM and adding them to teacher predictions. However, the authors do not explain how they handle label conflicts. What happens if a pixel is predicted as both “L1” and “L1/L2 disc” by different class-specific maps? A simple summation of two potentially misaligned probability maps (in the loss function) does not seem mathematically sound - if both models are confident, the resulting “label” could exceed valid probability ranges or create highly noisy gradients. A more robust approach, such as Bayesian fusion or confidence-weighted averaging, is missing. 3.The method for aggregating 19+ class-specific attention maps into a single pseudo-label lacks a robust mechanism for handling overlapping predictions or false positives in slices where certain structures are absent. If the VLM is forced to produce a “T10” segmentation map for a slice that only contains “L5,” it will likely pick up noisy, similar-looking features. Stacking these “hallucinated” structures into the final pseudo-label could introduce significant systematic errors that the student network will then memorize. 4.The method relies on OTSU automatic thresholding to binarize attention maps into pseudo-labels. However, the paper lacks a sensitivity analysis or discussion on whether OTSU remains robust across different MRI qualities or if it tends to “over-segment” in noisy images. 5.Statement like “but no one has studied it yet.” (abstract). Such absolute statements can be risky; it is often safer and more professional for authors to claim to be “among the first” or “to the best of our knowledge.”
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Thanks to all reviewers for your careful reviews and appreciation of our work, such as novel framework (R1R2R3), significant contribution (R1), compelling motivation (R1R2), superior experiment (R1R2R3), and well writing (R1R2). Q1: Prompt Robustness (R1R2). A1: CPS4 is robust to synonyms and different sentence structures. For sentence structures, the prompts “A magnetic resonance image of a {class name}”, “A spine MR image containing {class name}”, and “The anatomical structure of {class name} in MRI” achieved mDice of 80.44, 80.35, 80.47.For synonyms, removing “Vertebra” or replacing it with “Spine”, e.g., “Lumbar Vertebra 1”, “Lumbar 1”, and “Lumbar Spine 1”, achieved mDice of 80.44, 80.32, 80.39.These small fluctuations demonstrate the robustness of CPS4. Q2: Efficiency Analysis (R1). A2: CPS4 requires no extra inference cost, since attention maps are generated only during training. On an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU, both CPS4 and baseline take 18 ms/image during inference. For training, CPS4 takes 13h34min in total, while the baseline takes 9h31min. The additional cost includes 2h31min for stage 1, 1h19min for attention map generation in stage 2, and 13min for the loss backpropagation.​ Despite additional cost, CPS4 brings a 6.19 mDice improvement under 5% labeled data. Q3: Generalizability (R1R3). A3: This work focuses on 2D spine segmentation. In our another work, we extended CPS4 and evaluated it on 3D semi-supervised spine segmentation, including 3D organ and 3D spine tasks. Using 3D nnUNet as the backbone, under 10% labeled data, CPS4 achieves 82.63 mDice on MACT organ dataset, outperforming MT and CLIP by 10.93 and 3.69; on MRSpineSeg dataset, CPS4 achieves 73.44 mDice, outperforming MT and CLIP by 7.07 and 3.81.Using 3D ResUNet as the backbone, under 10% labeled data, CPS4 achieves 82.06 mDice on MACT organ dataset, outperforming MT and CLIP by 8.95 and 2.33; on MRSpineSeg dataset, CPS4 achieves 72.64 mDice, outperforming MT and CLIP by 6.59 and 4.25.These results validate CPS4’s generalizability across different segmentation scenarios. Q4: Absent-Class Handling (R1R3). A4: After OTSU divides each attention map into foreground and background where each attention map is normalized to [0,1], we compute mean attention score of the foreground region. If this mean score is lower than 0.5, the class is regarded as absent, and its binary map is set to background. This reduces false-positive activations from missing classes. We will clarify this in the revised manuscript. Q5: Label Conflicts and Probability Maps Summation (R3). A5: For label conflicts, if a pixel is predicted as different classes after OTSU, we select the class with the highest score in attention maps, producing a non-overlapping text-guided label. For example, if both L1 and L1/L2 are activated at one pixel, but their original attention scores are 0.82 and 0.65, this pixel is assigned to L1.For probability maps summation, we add teacher prediction and text-guided label, normalize the added score, and apply argmax to obtain a one-hot pseudo label. For example, if teacher prediction is [0.7,0.2,0.08,0.02] and text-guided label is [1,0,0,0], their summation is [1.7,0.2,0.08,0.02]. After normalization, it becomes [0.85,0.1,0.04,0.01]. The final one-hot label is [1,0,0,0]. We will add these explanations in the revised manuscript and further evaluate Bayesian fusion and confidence-weighted averaging to assess their potential benefits over our fusion strategy. Q6: Sensitivity Analysis of OTSU (R3). A6: OTSU is robust to different MRI qualities. Gaussian noise is added to unlabeled MRI inputs during the text-guided label generation process in Stage 2.Standard deviations were set to 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, and CPS4 achieves mDice scores of 80.44, 80.31, 80.12, under 5% labeled data. Compared with the original result of 80.44 without noise, performance drops are only 0.00, 0.13, 0.32.These minor decreases indicate that OTSU is robust to different MRI qualities.

title: Cubic Structure-Aware Neural Radiance Fields for Zero-Shot Super-Resolution of Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging
reviewer_1_strengths: Key backgrounds on CMB lesions and SWI scans are well-written. Extensive ablation studies were performed, covering lattice sampling numbers, segmented attention, axis traversal strategies, and relative position bias. Downstream CMB segmentation was performed, further highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Current evaluation is limited. Other than NeRF, SR can be achieved using GAN or Diffusion-based methods [1]. However, only NeRF-based methods were compared in this paper. As far as I’m concerned, NeRF is not conventional for SR tasks. Evaluations were limited to datasets with small number of subjects (n=20 for HKCU-SWI-CMB and n=34 for private dataset). While I acknowledge the difficulty of collecting SWI scans, to see if the proposed method is clinically applicable, authors must validate their method on held-out dataset or use publicly available SWI scans (e. g. , ADNI, AIBL as described in [2]). Neither of these validation strategies was employed. There is no information regarding data splitting, which raises concerns about reproducibility. Data splitting information was only reported in Section 3: Applicability to Downstream Tasks. Then how did authors split the data used in Table 1? Following [2], further validation should have been performed using GRE MRI rather than MSD-T1.Some GRE scans are publicly available in ADNI and used in [2]. Since T1 MRI resolution is already much better than that of SWI, applying the proposed method to T1 is less meaningful. Given that the key motivation is addressing large slice thickness in imaging protocols, using GRE is a much more appropriate fit for this problem. [1] Z. Ji et al. “Deep learning-based magnetic resonance image super-resolution: a survey” Neural Computing and Applications, 2024. [2] T. Hassanzadeh et al. “A robust deep learning framework for cerebral microbleeds recognition in GRE and SWI MRI” NeuroImage: Clinical, 2025.

reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem (SWI anisotropy and small lesion detection). 2.The proposed zero-shot method does not require HR training data, making the method more practical and easier to deploy. 3.The proposed method combines cube-based sampling with a Transformer-enhanced NeRF to better capture structural information. 4.The paper includes a fairly complete experimental design, covering both SR reconstruction quality and downstream segmentation performance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper states LR data are generated by z-axis downsampling, but no details on slice profile or noise modeling. 2.Important imaging details (e.g., acquisition parameters and voxel size) are not provided. 3.The method is evaluated exclusively on synthetically downsampled data, without validation on real low-resolution acquisitions.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Zero-shot. No paired HR data needed — trains on the patient’s own LR volume only. 2.Spatial correlation. The proposed method replaces point-independent MLP, enabling information exchange among neighboring sampling points. 3.Comprehensive comparison. Multiple baselines, three datasets, three SR scales — thorough and convincing. 4.Good visualization. Axial, coronal, and sagittal views clearly show sharper details. 5.Clinical significance. The clinical problem is clearly stated and valid.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited baselines. No comparison with supervised SR methods or diffusion-based approaches. Only compares against interpolation and NeRF-family methods. 2.Slow inference. Zero-shot means training a separate model per patient. The paper doesn’t discuss inference time, but training 25000 iterations per volume is not trivial for clinical deployment.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments. Their concerns are addressed below. To Rev #1 W1(Why use NeRF and lack of comparisons to GAN/Diffusion methods): NeRF provides a zero-shot, subject-specific framework for 3D SR. Our CSANeRF is built upon this paradigm to address the practical challenge of scarce clinical SWI data. By training solely on a single subject’s LR volume without external supervision, our method is well suited to this data-limited setting. In contrast, GAN- and diffusion-based SR methods typically rely on large-scale supervised training, making them less suitable for the data-scarce scenarios considered in this study. Therefore, we compare CSANeRF with NeRF-based zero-shot baselines and interpolation methods, enabling a fair and controlled evaluation. W2 (Limited datasets) and W3(Data splitting): A key advantage of NeRF-based frameworks lies in their self-supervised, zero-shot formulation. The model is trained exclusively on a single subject’s LR volume, with the HR data completely withheld until final evaluation. Consequently, SR training does not rely on a conventional cross-subject train/test split or large-scale external datasets. The results in Table 1 report the average metrics across all subjects to validate the method’s performance. Regarding data splitting mentioned in Section 3, it pertains specifically to our downstream CMB segmentation experiments. W4(GRE vs. T1 validation): Our dataset selection was primarily driven by clinical relevance. Both SWI datasets used in our experiments were acquired from stroke patients, closely aligning with real clinical scenarios where SWI is the standard sequence due to its high sensitivity to CMBs. T1-weighted MRI has relatively high resolution. We used it as a benchmark for high-fidelity reconstruction to verify that CSANeRF can preserve fine anatomical structures without introducing artifacts. This further demonstrates the robustness of our method across different MRI contrasts. To Rev #2 W1(LR degradation modeling): You are correct that we adopted a simplified decimation strategy for downsampling along the z-axis, whereas real clinical MRI acquisition involves complex physical degradation. However, we adhered to the established protocol used in CuNeRF. It ensures a fair, controlled, and reproducible comparison with prior work. W2(Acquisition parameters): Both SWI datasets consist of stroke patients. The private dataset parameters are TR = 31 ms, TE = 7.2 ms, and voxel spacing = 0.6 × 0.6 × 1.5 mm³; the HKCU-SWI-CMB dataset parameters are TR = 17 ms, TE = 24 ms, and voxel spacing = 0.45 × 0.45 × 1.0 mm³. These details will be added to the final manuscript. W3(Validation on real LR acquisitions): We agree that validation on real LR acquisitions is ideal. However, in clinical practice, SWI is typically acquired at high resolution for reliable detection of subtle lesions such as CMBs, and real LR SWI volumes are rarely available for research. Nevertheless, validating our method on real LR MRI acquisitions from different imaging sequences and further exploring its potential to reduce patients’ multi-sequence MRI scan time in clinical practice will be an important direction for future work. To Rev #3 W1(Limited baselines): As discussed regarding Rev #1-W1, we aim to tackle the issue of insufficient training data. Supervised approaches, however, necessitate large-scale datasets, rendering them impractical for our specific application scenarios. Therefore, we did not include supervised SR methods in our experimental comparisons. W2(Slow inference): We fully acknowledge that NeRF-based methods are computationally intensive. To address this, CSANeRF has been optimized, significantly reducing the full convergence time to about 1.7 h per volume, compared to 2.5 h of the prior CuNeRF. Inference requires only 3–4 min to generate the final HR volume.
