All reviewers acknowledge this and recommend acceptance. There are no remaining concerns. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes CSANeRF, a cubic structure-aware Neural Radiance Fields method for zero-shot super-resolution of susceptibility-weighted imaging, aiming to address the thick-slice problem and improve the preservation of fine anatomical structures in clinical SWI scans. The reviewers recognized the clinical relevance of the problem, the advantage of the zero-shot setting without paired HR training data, and the technical contribution of combining cube-based sampling with Transformer-enhanced NeRF to better capture spatial correlations. The experimental design was also considered reasonably complete, including reconstruction quality evaluation, ablation studies, and downstream CMB segmentation validation. The reviewers raised concerns about data splitting, acquisition parameters, comparison with GAN/diffusion or supervised SR methods, validation on real LR acquisitions, and inference speed. In the rebuttal, the authors clarified that the method is trained on each subject’s LR volume in a self-supervised zero-shot manner, with HR data withheld for final evaluation. They also justified the comparison with zero-shot NeRF-based and interpolation baselines, provided acquisition details, explained the use of the CuNeRF degradation protocol, and reported the practical inference time. These clarifications effectively addressed the major concerns, and all reviewers supported acceptance after rebuttal. Therefore, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers recommend to accept this paper post-rebuttal. I agree with this assessment. The authors submitted a strong rebuttal clarifying the experimental setup / dataset choices and why comparison to supervised SR methods is not applicable in that application. This is a solid paper. The ablation studies as well as comprehensive evaluation not only on SWI but also on T1w images plus the actual downstream application (CMB lesion segmentation in SWI) convincing.

title: DEC-Net: A Multi-Task Distillation Expert Collaboration Network for Glioma Grading and Molecular Subtyping Using Multimodal MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is clearly written, logically organized, and experimentally thorough. The authors evaluate on both internal and external cohorts and provide ablation studies confirming the contribution of each module. The method’s performance remains strong under domain shift, suggesting good robustness.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Some methodological details could be clarified, for example, the rationale for center cropping (which may exclude boundary information) and whether inference used patch aggregation or whole‑volume prediction. The paper does not discuss its own limitations, and recent transformer‑ and foundation‑based multimodal approaches are omitted from comparison.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Strong Empirical Performance The proposed method demonstrates consistent performance improvements over existing approaches on both internal and external datasets. Notably, the model maintains its advantage even under domain shift, suggesting a certain level of robustness and generalization capability. 2.Public Availability of Code The authors provide publicly available code, which enhances the reproducibility of the work and facilitates future research building upon this method. 3.Comprehensive Ablation Study The paper includes a thorough ablation study evaluating the contribution of each proposed component. This analysis helps demonstrate that the individual modules are complementary and collectively contribute to the overall performance improvement.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient Analysis of Expert Routing Dynamics While the model successfully separates shared and task-specific experts, an in-depth analysis of their individual contributions is lacking. Providing a more granular investigation into how these experts are utilized across different tasks, along with an interpretability analysis of the routing mechanism, would significantly strengthen the justification for this architectural design. 2.Architectural Complexity and Presentation Clarity The proposed framework integrates multiple intricate modules, resulting in a relatively complex architecture that can be challenging to follow. While space limitations are acknowledged, a more streamlined explanation or supplementary visualizations detailing the data flow through these key components would greatly improve the paper’s readability and reproducibility. 3.Limited Scope of Baseline Comparisons The current experimental comparisons are primarily restricted to multi-task learning (MTL) methods. To comprehensively evaluate the proposed approach, the authors should include strong single-task baselines or more recent state-of-the-art architectures. This would rigorously demonstrate whether the performance gains stem from the multi-task synergy itself rather than merely the overall model capacity.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Clinically meaningful joint formulation. Non-invasive preoperative prediction of glioma grade together with IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion is of genuine clinical value, and jointly modelling the three tasks respects the biological coupling among the canonical diagnostic categories. Substantial multi-centre cohort with a genuinely held-out external test set. Training and cross-validation span two institutions (UCSF-PDGM and EGD, total n=1,214), and TCGA-GBM/LGG (n=167) is used exclusively as an external cohort. Many prior works report single-centre results only, and it enables a meaningful assessment of domain shift. External-test generalisation. On TCGA, DEC-Net leads the best competing baseline. Several baselines (e.g., MTAFNet, MFEFNet, MLNet) experience substantial AUC drops under domain shift, whereas DEC-Net degrades more gracefully. The relative ranking of methods also changes between internal and external evaluation, which is consistent with a genuine test of generalisation. Complete module ablation. Table 3 enumerates all eight on/off combinations of DRModule, PMoE, and D-Loss rather than the more common single-leave-one-out design. Reproducibility. Preprocessing is specified (SRI24 co-registration, 1 mm isotropic resampling, skull-stripping, z-score normalisation), optimiser (AdamW), learning rate (1e-4), batch size (8), epoch count (100), and loss weights (alpha=0.3, beta=0.1) are all reported. An anonymised code repository is linked.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.No statistical significance testing. Table 2 reports mean and standard deviation across cross-validation folds, but no paired statistical test (DeLong for AUC, McNemar for accuracy, or paired Wilcoxon on fold-level scores) is provided. Several internal-test “wins” fall within one standard deviation of the runner-up. Without paired testing, the claim of “consistently outperforms SOTA” on the internal cohort is not empirically supported. 2.Handling of a large fraction of Unknown labels is not stated, with a plausible confound in the D-Loss. Table 1 shows that IDH status is Unknown for 42% of EGD and 11% of TCGA, and 1p/19q status is Unknown for 68% of EGD and 18% of UCSF-PDGM. The paper does not state how these cases are handled during training and evaluation. This matters on two fronts. First, the effective per-task labelled sample sizes are materially smaller than the headline n=1,214; for 1p/19q in particular the labelled pool may be well below 700.Second, if P is estimated only from fully-labelled patients, it is computed on a biased subsample. 3.Unspecified fold stratification. UCSF-PDGM and EGD are acquired on different scanners and protocols. A random patient-level split mixes sites across train and validation folds, which allows the model to exploit site-specific cues (residual intensity distributions, etc.) and can inflate internal-test metrics. The paper does not state whether folds are patient-level only, site-stratified, or class-stratified, nor does it report per-fold site composition. 4.Unverified fairness of the nine SOTA baselines is unverified. The paper does not state whether the baselines were re-implemented in-house, whether they were trained under the same preprocessing pipeline, input size (128×128×128), modality set, and augmentation, whether they received the same hyperparameter-tuning budget, or how they handle Unknown labels. Several baselines (MTTU-Net, MDLNet, CMTLNet, MTAFNet, MLNet) are multi-task glioma methods whose original publications use different cohorts and label subsets. Simple re-implementation could systematically disadvantage them. 5.Methodological novelty is incremental. The EMA teacher-student mechanism is the Mean Teacher scheme of Tarvainen and Valpola (NeurIPS 2017) not the cited reference [27] which is a 2025 application paper. Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE) is not cited or contrasted. The D-Loss is a label-correlation regulariser from the multi-label classification literature. The paper’s contribution is therefore the combination applied to joint glioma profiling, which is a legitimate application-style contribution, but the current framing presents each component as novel without acknowledging the closest prior art. 6.Unexplained interactions in the ablation. In Table 3, the “PMoE + D-Loss” configuration underperforms “D-Loss only” on Grade AUC (91.68 vs 92.63) and 1p/19q AUC (82.37 vs 84.77), while the full three-module model then jumps to 95.11 and 85.45 respectively. This is a super-additive effect that is not discussed. 7.No calibration or operating-point analysis. For a method positioned to “support precise clinical decision-making”, calibration and a sensitivity-at-fixed-specificity table would strengthen the clinical framing.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer (MR) for their constructive comments. We address their concerns below. 1.Model Complexity and Performance(MR, R2Q2, R3Q1): The pre-trained network extracts tumor-relevant regions, the distillation framework enhances feature representation, the expert network mitigates inter-task interference, and the biologically guided D-Loss optimizes multi-task prediction. Together, these components improve glioma grading and molecular subtyping. Statistical tests on internal data show significant improvements: for AUC, significant differences are observed compared with several baseline methods (DeLong test, p < 0.05); for ACC, improvements are significant compared with all baseline methods (McNemar test, p < 0.05). 2.Rationale for Not Adopting Existing Tumor Segmentation Methods（MR）： Gliomas affect the whole brain environment. Focusing only on tumor segmentation masks is insufficient to capture the complete affected regions. Our approach captures comprehensive tumor-relevant areas without relying solely on existing segmentation methods. 3.Sensitivity (SEN) and Specificity (SPE) for Our Task (MR,R3Q7): Internal test SEN/SPE: Grade 88.14 ± 1.83 / 91.55 ± 2.47; IDH 84.99 ± 5.57 / 85.47 ± 2.79; 1p/19q 79.48 ± 5.25 / 79.89 ± 4.28.Due to space limits, these metrics were omitted from main tables but demonstrate superior performance over other methods. 4.Implementation and Inference Details (R1Q1): The center cropping effectively captures the core brain area while removing boundaries. During inference, we perform whole-volume prediction rather than patch-based aggregation. 5.Baseline Comparisons and Limitations (R1Q2, R2Q3): Our core contribution lies in multi-task learning , and our experiments mainly compare with recent SOTA multi-task methods. In our experiments, single-task results were evaluated. For ACC, multi-task synergy outperforms single-task baselines (Grade ACC 85–87% , IDH ACC 80–82%, and 1p/19q ACC 72–74%). We will add a brief discussion of limitations in the revised version. 6.Expert Routing Analysis (R2Q1): Full visualization of expert contributions is omitted due to page limits. We instead report the ratio of shared/task-specific expert selection: Grade (86/14), IDH (74/26), and 1p/19q (68/32). These results indicate that each task leverages different experts while showing task-related patterns, supporting the effectiveness of our routing mechanism. 7.Handling of Missing Labels (R3Q2): Samples with missing labels were excluded from model training, P-matrix estimation, and evaluation. We did not adopt pseudo-labeling, as unreliable pseudo-labels may introduce noisy prior knowledge and lead to model hallucination or error accumulation. As shown in Table 1, the valid annotated sample sizes are 1,166 for Grade, 910 for IDH, and 632 for 1p/19q. These counts are used for P-matrix estimation. 8.Cross-Validation Stratification (R3Q3): Our five-fold cross-validation is site-stratified. Each fold contains one-fifth of samples from both UCSF-PDGM and EGD, ensuring that data from different scanners and protocols are represented in every fold. Additionally, (1) bias-field correction was applied during preprocessing, (2) there are no strong site-specific correlations that could inflate metrics, and (3) external validation confirms the model’s robustness. 9.Fairness of Baseline Comparisons (R3Q4): To ensure a fair comparison, all nine SOTA baseline methods were evaluated under identical experimental settings, including the same preprocessing pipeline, fixed input size, consistent modality combination. 10.Citation and Methodology (R3Q5): We will add proper citations for EMA teacher-student and PLE. In our work, these components are adapted for glioma tasks, considering task correlations. Specifically, we introduce a shared-and-specific structure and a D-Loss guided by biological priors, which together constitute a novel application-oriented contribution for multimodal glioma analysis.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a multi-sequence MRI-based framework for glioma grading and molecular subtyping. However, the overall architecture appears overly complex, while only marginal improvements are observed compared with existing methods. To capture tumor-relevant regions, it is unclear why existing well-established tumor segmentation methods are not adopted, as many of them can already achieve highly accurate tumor delineation (e.g., Dice score > 0.9). In addition, class imbalance (e.g., IDH status) is a well-known challenge in glioma. Although focal loss is employed, it would be helpful to further report accuracy and recall for IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion, to better assess model performance. | The concerns regarding the paper have been addressed, and all reviewers agree to accept the paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes DEC-Net, a multi-task framework for joint glioma grading, IDH prediction, and 1p/19q prediction from multimodal MRI. All reviewers accepted the paper after rebuttal, which appears to have addressed the main concerns sufficiently. However, the authors should more carefully address class imbalance by including additional metrics, such as per-class performance, sen/spe, in the camera-ready version. They should also include statistical analyses for the comparisons and more clearly position their technical contributions relative to the existing literature. In addition, rows 4, 5, 6 of the ablation study show that the roles of DRModule and PMoE are not fully evident, and this should be better discussed. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes DEC-Net, a multi-task framework for glioma grading and molecular subtyping from multimodal MRI. Reviewers appreciated the clinical relevance, strong performance on both internal and external cohorts, and the comprehensive ablation studies. I agree with the reviewers that the method is technically sound and well validated. The rebuttal satisfactorily addressed concerns regarding unknown-label handling, cross-validation design, statistical significance testing, and baseline fairness. While some components build upon existing methods, the overall framework demonstrates clear practical value and strong generalization ability. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.

title: Decoding the Alzheimer’s Continuum: Interpretable Multi-gate Routing for Diagnosis and Transition Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: Figure 1 clearly illustrates that the proposed multi-task unified architecture effectively avoids the diagnostic probability conflicts caused by independent OVO classifiers. The analysis of the dual-gate routing mechanism reveals distinct expert activations for stable vs. progressive MCI, providing a basis for individual risk assessment. Integrating features like age, sex, and eTIV at Stage 2 has strong clinical relevance and significantly improves diagnostic accuracy.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The “2D slice + majority voting” strategy lacks justification. The authors must explain why a native 3D network was not used and address the potential loss of 3D spatial context. It is unclear whether the baselines in Table 1 benefit from the same SimMIM pre-training as the proposed model. The authors should unify these conditions or provide ablation studies to prove the architecture’s inherent superiority. The methods compared in Table 1 are relatively old. Quantitative comparisons with recent state-of-the-art models (e. g. , from 2024 or 2025) are needed to validate the paper’s novelty. Despite mentioning a long-tail distribution, the paper lacks specific strategies for handling imbalanced categories. A detailed per-class performance analysis should be added. The quantitative discussion on cross-cohort validation (Section 3.2) is inadequate. The paper needs to analyze how differing distributions of clinical priors across cohorts impact model generalization. Figure 2 fails to clearly highlight the core innovations (like the Adaptive Attention Fusion module). Visual cues such as borders or shading are needed to help readers quickly identify structural novelties. Equations (2) and (3) use code-style terminology (e. g. , Tokenize, Shift_W, DWConv). These must be replaced with standard, formal mathematical symbols.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper makes a compelling argument that diagnosis classification and stage transition prediction are complementary tasks that should be jointly modeled rather than treated independently. The ablation in Table 2 confirms that multi-task learning consistently outperforms single-task variants, lending empirical support to this design choice. Table 2 systematically dissects the contribution of multi-task learning, SimMIM pretraining, Tok-MLP, clinical priors (individually and combined), and fusion stage placement. Each component is shown to contribute meaningfully, and the ablations are well-structured. The finding that eTIV is the most impactful single clinical prior and that Stage 2 is optimal for fusion are informative design insights. The interpretability analysis is compelling. The expert-gate activation shift for AD-aligned experts when comparing stable vs. progressive MCI is a clear, interpretable signal. Good scale and multi-cohort validation. Using 12,037 scans across six cohorts with proper subject-level fold isolation and cross-cohort generalization testing strengthens the claims considerably. The preprocessing is thorough and welldocumented. Code availability.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The comparisons in Table 1 are not fair. Results for prior methods are cited from their original papers, which used different datasets, splits, and preprocessing. Why 2D slices? AD atrophy is inherently volumetric. Extracting sagittal slices and doing majority voting throws away 3D spatial information. This choice is never justified, and no 3D baseline is compared. Transition prediction metrics are incomplete: despite severe class imbalance (dominance of “Stability”), only aggregate accuracy and F1 are reported. The paper should report per-class metrics (precision, recall, F1) for each of the three diagnosis classes and each transition class. Aggregate metrics hide performance on the clinically most important subgroups. The cross-cohort experiment (Table 1, right) only tests NC vs. AD binary classification, which is the easiest discrimination task. Cross-cohort evaluation for the three-class and transition tasks would be far more informative. Several design choices are unjustified. Why 8 experts with this specific shared/aligned split? What’s the temperature τ? What’s the λ in Eq. 5? Was task loss weighting explored? Masking ratio 0.6, why?
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper proposes M³AD, a unified multi-task framework that jointly models the current Diagnosis Stage (DS) and the future DS Transition (e.g., Stability, Progression, Reversion) within a single architecture, rather than treating them as isolated classification problems. 2.The authors evaluate their method on a massive scale for neuroimaging, utilizing 12,037 T1-weighted MRI scans across six independent cohorts. This large-scale, multi-cohort approach, combined with a rigorous 5-fold cross-validation setup that explicitly confines all longitudinal scans of the same subject to a single fold to prevent data leakage, makes the empirical evaluation credible and robust.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The authors extract 2D sagittal slices from 3D MRI volumes and assign the subject-level diagnosis and progression labels to every single slice during training. However, Brain atrophy in early-stage Alzheimer’s (MCI) is highly localized (e.g., in the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex). Therefore, many lateral or extreme medial sagittal slices contain absolutely no pathological information. Assigning a “Progressive MCI” label to a healthy-looking slice introduces massive label noise during training, which degrades feature learning. 2.The authors claim the superiority of their multi-task framework, but fail to compare it with a vanilla multi-task learning baseline (e.g., a standard ViT with Hard Parameter Sharing using two task-specific linear heads). In Table 1, prior baselines are only evaluated on the diagnosis task, ignoring the transition task. In Table 2, the ‘Multiple Tasks’ setting only validates that training two tasks is better than one within the proposed architecture, but it does not justify the necessity of the complex components (like the multi-gate routing) over a simple multi-task approach.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing M3AD’s unified multi-task design that resolves NC/MCI/AD exclusivity (R1, R3), the component-wise ablations and interpretable expert-routing for stable vs. progressive MCI (R2), the clinical motivation (R3), and the multi-cohort subject-level evaluation (R2, R3). We respond by theme. [T1] 2D sagittal slices vs. 3D networks (R1.Q1, R2.Q2, R3.Q1) We agree early AD/MCI atrophy is spatially localized and some sagittal slices may carry limited pathological evidence. Our 2D sagittal design is not a claim of 2D superiority, but a resolution-preserving scalability trade-off. As noted in Raptor [1], 3D volumetric modeling incurs cubic-order computational costs and demands datasets orders of magnitude larger than 2D counterparts, motivating 2D-based alternatives. Under comparable memory, 3D training often requires heavy downsampling (e.g., ~80×96×80 in [2]), weakening subtle medial-temporal cues (hippocampal/entorhinal atrophy). Raptor’s Tab. 7 reports that sagittal-only embeddings already achieve competitive performance, while tri-axis (A+C+S) fusion yields further gains. This supports our sagittal-only design as a reasonable single-view choice under our memory and preprocessing constraints, and we acknowledge multi-view fusion as a clear future direction. Regarding label reliability, slice labels are weak supervision derived from subject-level diagnosis/transition labels. All slices and longitudinal scans of one subject stay within 1 fold; predictions use subject-level majority voting, mitigating isolated unreliable slices at inference though not training-time label noise. We will note this limitation in the revision. [T2] Table 1 and comparison fairness (R1.Q2/Q3, R2.Q1, R3.Q2) Table 1 is a reference comparison (see footnote); the controlled comparison is Table 2, where all variants share identical ADNI splits, preprocessing, and SimMIM pretraining. We will avoid overstating cross-study superiority and distinguish reference from controlled ablation. The Multiple Tasks rows in Table 2 report full M3AD under joint supervision, not a hard-sharing MTL baseline; they isolate the gain of joint over single-task training under the same routing. Hard-sharing MTL removes diagnosis-aligned experts and task gates, so cannot evaluate our routing. [2] has a different objective/protocol; [3] targets histopathology MIL. Neither addresses NC/MCI/AD exclusivity jointly with transition prediction; unified-protocol comparison remains future work. [T3] Class imbalance and cross-cohort scope (R1.Q4/Q5, R2.Q3/Q4) Class imbalance is handled via weighted cross-entropy (weight 1.0 for majority, higher for rare transitions: NC-to-AD progression, MCI-to-NC reversion). We will add this detail and report per-class precision/recall/F1 for both tasks. For external validation, transition prediction is limited by the lack of standardized longitudinal MCI follow-up labels, and 3-class cross-cohort diagnosis is complicated by heterogeneous MCI definitions. ADNI has more than 50 sites in its cohort study protocol, which provides intrinsic multi-center evaluation for both diagnosis and transition tasks. Extending external validation beyond NC/AD binary diagnosis remains future work. [T4] Hyperparameters (R2.Q5) τ=1.0/0.5 (pretrain/finetune); λ=0.5 in Eq.(5); 8 experts = 2 shared + 2 NC + 2 MCI + 2 AD; SimMIM mask 0.6; AdamW lr 1e-4/5e-5, wd 0.05, cosine + 10-ep warmup; task-loss 1:1.A full hyperparameter table will be included in the revision. [Minors] Figure and notation (R1.Q6/Q7) We will revise Fig. 2 to emphasize dual-gate MMoE routing and Stage-2 clinical prior integration, and replace the code-style Tok-MLP/UNeXt notation [4] with formal mathematical notation. We hope our responses address the reviewers’ concerns and thank them for their constructive feedback. Refs: [1] An et al., Raptor, ICML 2025.[2] Ding et al., Denseformer-MoE, IEEE TMI 2025.[3] Li et al., M4, MedIA 2025.[4] Valanarasu & Patel, UNeXt, MICCAI 2022.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper jointly models current AD diagnosis and future stage transition in a unified multi-task framework. The large-scale evaluation across six cohorts, the subject-level fold isolation, the detailed ablations, and the expert-routing analysis are clear strengths. The comparison in Table 1 is potentially unfair because prior results appear to come from different datasets, splits, and preprocessing pipelines, which weakens the claimed SOTA performance. In addition, the paper does not compare against a simple vanilla multi-task baseline, making it hard to tell whether the complex multi-gate MoE design is necessary. The 2D slice-based strategy needs strong justification. Assigning subject-level diagnosis and transition labels to all sagittal slices may introduce substantial label noise, especially for localized early AD pathology. The comparison is incomplete due to the absence of a 3D baseline and recent 2024/2025 baselines. The authors should further report per-class transition metrics and clarify key hyperparameters and cross-cohort results for the harder multi-class/transition tasks. | The authors have responded all reviewers’ questions. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The overall recommendation from the three reviewers, after rebuttal, leans toward acceptance, with R1 and R2 made their final recommendations to Accept and R3 maintaining a borderline Weak Accept. The reviewers acknowledged the strengths of the unified multi-task framework, the large-scale multi-cohort evaluation with rigorous subject-level isolation, and the interpretable expert-routing analysis for distinguishing stable versus progressive MCI. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a well-motivated work for joint AD diagnosis and status transition prediction, evaluated on a relatively large multi-cohort datasets. Implementations in terms of 2D slices hamper the significance of the proposed method.

title: Deep EM with Hierarchical Latent Label Modelling for Multi-Site Prostate Lesion Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Clinically important problem formulation: The paper addresses a challenge: real-world clinical datasets are rarely annotated by multiple raters on the same image, yet label heterogeneity across sites is pervasive. Rather than the classical multi-rater setup where disagreement is directly observable, the framework treats each site as a proxy annotator, inferring noise distributions. This is a pragmatic and reasonable adaptation to how multi-site data is actually collected. Principled generative model: The hierarchical formulation, latent clean mask as the unobserved truth, observed labels as site-conditioned noisy measurements, is theoretically coherent and draws meaningfully from the noise modeling literature (e. g. , confusion matrix-style annotator models), adapting it sensibly to the multi-site setting. Leave-one-dataset-out evaluation: The inclusion of a leave-one-site-out experiment is a commendable and well-designed validation choice. It directly probes the risk of the model collapsing toward a single site’s annotation bias and provides meaningful evidence of generalization across institutional protocols.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Hyperparameter sensitivity not analyzed: Given that these hyperparameters directly shape the learned noise model and the inferred latent consensus mask, showing their influence on downstream segmentation performance can strengthen the paper. Insufficient ablation study: Although it could be from limited pages, but the paper lacks ablations that isolate the contribution of the hierarchical structure from the noise modeling component. It is unclear whether the performance gains stem from the latent variable formulation, the site-specific noise model, or simply from multi-site data aggregation with soft labels. These components should be evaluated independently. Dataset effect not fully characterized: It is not demonstrated whether the learned site-specific noise parameters actually capture meaningful protocol or cohort differences (e. g. , scanner type, field strength, annotation guidelines). Authors might be able to analyze dataset-level distributional shift in an uninterpretable way. PIRADS-stratified analysis: Given that annotation noisiness likely varies systematically across PIRADS grades (with grade 3 lesions being substantially more ambiguous than grades 4 and 5) a stratified performance analysis across PIRADS categories would strengthen the evaluation. (minor) The Dice metric is incorrectly reported with units of mm, which should be unitless. The typo “nn” instead of “mm” also appears and should be corrected throughout. (minor) data details needed (e. g. , preprocessing steps)
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The design that formulates each site’s annotation as a noisy observation of an underlying clean annotation is well-motivated. The decomposition of label variability into global, site-specific, and case-level components provides a natural mechanism for partial pooling via the hierarchical Gaussian prior. The leave-one-site-out (LOSO) experiment clearly compares whether uncertainty generalizes across sites.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.There are report discrepancies between the text and the table, which can undermine the reliability of the results: a. ‘Supervised Dice decreases to 25.50/24.66/33.09% across Sites 1–3’, but the table reported 31.20% for site 3. b. ‘HierEM consistently improves generalisation, yielding higher Dice on Sites 1 and 2 (28.11 and 27.40 mm)’, but mm is clearly not the unit for Dice, and it should be 28.11/27.91%. c. ‘with lower HD95 (20.51 and 20.31 nn)’, nn is incorrect unit, and it should be 20.51/21.12 mm. 2.Dice for HierEM in site 1 has a very large standard deviation (21.88), if this was not a reporting error, the authors need to explain this finding. 3.The work was an extension of STAPLE, where multiple annotations of the same case were used to estimate annotator sensitivity and specificity. In this study, each case has exactly one annotation from one site and the sensitivity/specificity was pooled performance across cases within a site. This potentially assumes that all annotators at a given site perform identically, which is hardly achievable even under the same reading protocol. The authors should discuss this further and the influence of theoretical/realistic aspects of the design on the estimation of alpha and beta. 4.Minors: a. Misspelling like ‘generalisation’ was used throughout the paper, they don’t significantly affect reading but it’s good to correct them. b. The risk-coverage curve in fig.2 will benefit from an area under the curve-like metrics to help interpretation.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Multi site training an evaluation is a large problem in deep learning for medical image analysis. Performance typically drops when algorithms are validated in sites that they weren’t trained upon. HierEM is an elegant framework that addresses label bias between hospitals, to train a model that is more robust for site specific labeling. The method seems broadly applicable, on any scenario where multi institutional data is available. The sharing of the code, and extensive mathematical formulations are much appreciated.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The reported dices all seem rather low. As shown by the literature in the paper, this is because intra operator agreement is already topped at 0.4 dice for these type of annotations. As only an in house dataset is used, it is currently unclear if the method also extends to more moderate use cases, where annotations agree more.
reviewer_3_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
author_feedback: We thank the comments from the reviewers and the clear guidance from the AC. Reviewer 2: single annotation per case / STAPLE assumption We agree that annotators within the same site should not be identical, even under the same protocol, as suggested by R2.But we clarify that we do NOT assume uniform behaviour within sites. First, algorithmically, HierEM includes case-specific latent variables, u_k and v_k, in addition to the site-level variables (a_s, b_s) in Eq. 2, modelling the hierarchy of global, site-level, case-level variabilities. During training, the model specifies probabilities of observed labels given unknow latent clean label(Eq.1), and allows each case to move away from global and site averages by case variables (u_k, v_k) (eq.2). For reporting, site-level statistics can be estimated by pooled sensitivity and specificity over within-site annotators, but these do NOT assume all annotators at a given site perform identically. Second, from the data point of view, HierEM also addresses a different problem from classical STAPLE. STAPLE experiments used multiple annotations for every case, allowing individual-reader sensitivity and specificity to be estimated directly. Our HierEM is designed for multi-site data with single annotation for each case. It is noteworthy that, a site may involve multiple annotators, but each case is annotated only once. In practice, such single-annotation-per-case multi-site datasets are much more commonly available than datasets requiring multiple annotators to annotate every case. These within site annotators are expected to follow the same site-level annotation protocol, for example PI-RADS in dataset1 and Likert in dataset2, but their actual labelling behaviour may still differ due to individual judgement, experience. In HierEM, such residual case-wise discrepancies are not forced into a single site-level α/β. Instead, the case-level latent variables (u_k, v_k) allow the effective sensitivity and specificity, \alpha_{s,k} and \beta_{s,k}, to vary from case to case. Reporting results We sincerely thank R2 for identifying several typos and formatting issues. We are grateful for the careful reading and humbled by the attention to detail. Among these, we clarify that 1) the current value for Dice in Site3 is 31.20% both in table and text; and 2) the correct standard deviation for Site 1 should be 11.88 instead of 21.88.We will correct these. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we also added AURC to Fig. 2, with smaller area indicates lower risk. Ablation concerns of contribution of the hierarchical structure We use the same strong and efficient U-Net backbone across all methods to ensure a fair and controlled comparison. Since our method is agnostic to the segmentation backbone, this controlled setting reduces architectural differences as a potential factor. The experimental design is progressive and aims to demonstrate the contribution of site- and case-level modelling: we start with U-Net baseline, then add soft-label bootstrapping, flat EM modelling without case-level variables, and finally the proposed HierEM. The experiments serve not only as comparisons against relevant baselines, but also as an ablation of the main methodological components. We agree that a more systematic comparison study could further strengthen the work and will consider in future work. PIRADS-stratified analysis by reviewer1 This study included cases contain PI-RADS/Likert ≥3 lesions. We focus on comparing methods within this clinically meaningful lesion-positive population. We agree that PI-RADS/Likert-stratified evaluation would be clinically valuable, may potentially expand clinical applicability, although due to the fixed diagnostic patient cohort used in our test set, such stratification needs be carefully designed to reflect any intended real-world patient cohorts. Following the AC suggestion, we will acknowledge these.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes HierEM, a hierarchical expectation–maximization framework that treats each site’s annotation as a noisy observation of an underlying clean mask and decomposes label variability into global, site-, and case-level components. The reviewers agree that the problem is clinically important, the hierarchical generative formulation is theoretically coherent, and the leave-one-site-out evaluation is a clever design choice. Scores split 4/3/6.R1 and R2 raise concerns that are specific and grounded. R1 notes the paper lacks ablations isolating the contributions of the hierarchical structure, the site-specific noise model, and soft-label aggregation, and that no hyperparameter sensitivity or PIRADS-stratified analysis is reported. R2 identifies several discrepancies between the text and the tables (including wrong units and conflicting Dice numbers), flags an unexplained large standard deviation on Site 1, and raises a more substantive concern that extending STAPLE to a setting where each case has a single annotation implicitly assumes uniform annotator behavior within a site. R3 gives a Strong Accept, but the review is short and does not engage with the concrete details of the paper nor it justifies why the paper is outstanding, so I gave it less weight. R1’s review is also superficial and raised concerns that are somewhat generic. Given the split scores and somewhat unconvincing reviews (which is unfortunate for the authors and the community), I went through the paper myself and found R2’s point on the uniform-within-site assumption the most significant one; it touches the validity of the estimation that the whole framework rests on, and the authors should engage with it carefully, including possible clarification, implications, and any conditions under which the assumption is reasonable. The reporting discrepancies (units, conflicting Dice numbers, unexplained Site 1 standard deviation) are smaller in scope but should also be addressed, since they affect how the results are read. The ablation and sensitivity requests are harder to resolve in a rebuttal but are worth acknowledging. I invite the authors to respond before a final decision. Please refer to MICCAI rebuttal guidelines. Good luck. | I thank the authors and all three reviewers for their active participation in the rebuttal phase. Following the rebuttal, the authors effectively addressed the significant concerns raised during the initial review round, including inconsistencies in results, underlying assumptions of the method, and potential limitations. All three reviewers agreed that the paper should be accepted. Considering the merits in the paper, authors’ effective rebuttal, and the unanimous agreement from the reviewers, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Congratulations! Well done Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewer consensus achieved.

title: Deep Probabilistic Cerebrovascular Atlas
reviewer_1_strengths: 1, Methodological Exploration: The application of INR to overcome the partial volume effects and aliasing inherent in discrete voxel grids for highly variable vascular structures is an interesting engineering exploration. 2, Architectural Design: Introducing an MoE mechanism to theoretically decouple multi-scale spatial frequencies (e. g. , low-frequency global geometry of major arteries vs. high-frequency local details of distal branches) is a conceptually appealing approach to mitigating the spectral bias of standard MLPs (like SIREN).
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Summary: It appears the authors lack a practical understanding of real-world cerebrovascular challenges, which undermines the claimed clinical meaning of the work. 1.Insufficient Performance for Clinical Cerebrovascular Applications The results have severe vascular discontinuity and alignment errors, which limits the framework’s clinical applicability. 1.1 Dataset Limitations vs. Classic Methods: The model relies on the IXI MRA dataset resampled to a $256 \times 256$ in-plane resolution. At this resolution and field strength, the primarily visible structures are the macro-vasculature (large to medium arteries like the CoW). For these macro-structures, standard discrete processing methods (e. g. , Frangi-based vessel tracking, graph-cut methods, or conventional 3D CNNs) already achieve reliable performance. The necessity of a complex MoE-INR architecture is not fully justified given that the dataset does not clearly capture the micro-vascular details that INRs are theoretically designed to preserve. 1.2 Unclear Deviation Maps: The visual results presented in Figures 1, 2, and 3 are ambiguous, overly smoothed. Thus, it cannot provide sufficient evidence for reviewers to validate the method’s efficacy. Based solely on the visual performance in these figures, it appears the authors lack a practical understanding of real-world cerebrovascular challenges, which fundamentally undermines the claimed clinical significance of the work. This visual ambiguity is validated by the results in Table 1.An SSIM of 0.84 (reflecting an approximate 20% intensity reconstruction error), a Dice score of merely 0.71, and an Average Surface Distance (ASD) of 4.18 mm are highly problematic. Crucially, cerebrovascular imaging data is volumetrically dominated by macro-vasculature (large arteries). Because these large vessels constitute the vast majority of the target signal, baseline metrics are naturally inflated if the main arterial trunks are even partially captured. The fact that the proposed method still yields such subpar overall metrics. Despite the inherent statistical advantage provided by macro-vessel dominance, the method exposes severe algorithmic deficiencies. Consequently, the framework lacks the precision and reliability required for meaningful clinical tasks such as stroke localization or surgical planning. 1.3 Quantitative Discontinuities: The quantitative results in Table 1 show a whole-brain Connectivity Error of 183.69 ± 130.67, indicating notable vascular fragmentation. Furthermore, the framework yields a PSNR of 24.98 dB, an SSIM of 0.84, and an Average Surface Distance (ASD) of 4.18 mm. In cerebrovascular anatomy, where many medium vessels are 1-3 mm in diameter, an average error of 4.18 mm exceeds the size of the anatomical structures themselves, limiting the model’s ability to precisely quantify pathological deviations. 2.Limitations in Modeling Discrete Topological Mutations The framework relies on MoE and FiLM modulation to capture anatomical variability. However, it is limited to handle discrete topological changes. 2.1 On page 4, the modulation mechanism is described: “Following [10], the concatenated conditioning vector $\tilde{z} {i}=[z {i},c_{i}]$ is mapped to layer-specific scale ($\gamma$) and shift ($\beta$) parameters via a linear projection. “ 2.2 FiLM modulation applies global affine transformations (scaling and shifting) to the intermediate feature maps of the SIREN network. While modifying the frequency and phase of a continuous sine wave is effective for modeling global continuous morphing (e. g. , generalized widening or tortuosity due to aging), it is less suited for discrete local topological mutations. For example, the congenital absence of an A1 segment in the Circle of Willis is a binary (1-to-0) structural break. A global linear projection of a latent code cannot easily execute localized topological erasure without introducing artifacts (e. g. , semi-transparent vessels). The paper lacks theoretical or visual demonstration showing how FiLM and MoE accurately enforce these discrete topological graph changes. 3.Incomplete Baseline Comparisons The quantitative evaluation of the atlas reconstruction (Table 1) omits comparisons against standard clinical registration methods. 3.1 The Evidence: On page 5, the authors explain their baseline selection: “We compare VITAL against a state-of-the-art INR-based brain modeling baseline CiNeMA [9]. Traditional voxel-based registration methods are excluded as they do not employ a generative latent space for subject-specific reconstruction. “ 3.2 The Evidence: On page 5 (Preprocessing), the authors state: “For anatomical context, T1 images were segmented using FastSurfer [12] and rigidly registered to the MRA space via ANTs [4]. “ 3.3 The Critique: The authors use traditional registration tools (ANTs) for foundational data alignment but exclude state-of-the-art deformable registration methods (such as ANTs SyN) in their performance benchmarks. Since the primary metrics evaluated in Table 1 (e. g. , ASD and Connectivity Error) assess geometric alignment accuracy, the lack of a generative latent space in traditional methods does not justify excluding them from an alignment comparison. 4.Methodological Circularity in Clinical Anomaly Detection The experimental design for the TopCoW stroke dataset (Section 3) involves a circular dependency during the inference phase, which affects its clinical utility. 4.1 The Evidence: On page 7, the authors state: “Given the inherent imaging protocol variations between datasets and the severe morphological deviations in stroke subjects, relying solely on intensity reconstruction is prone to misalignment. Therefore, we employed supervised test-time adaptation using $\mathcal{L} {rec}+\mathcal{L} {seg}$ to investigate vascular anomalies, with the segmentation mask serving as a topological anchor. “ 4.2 The Critique: A primary objective of an anomaly detection system is to discover and segment abnormal vascular regions. By requiring the patient’s ground-truth segmentation mask ($\mathcal{L}_{seg}$) during the test-time adaptation phase to achieve alignment, the algorithm relies on the intended output to process the input. A model that requires a pre-existing mask of the anomaly to perform localization cannot be directly applied to a real-world diagnostic workflow. 5.Terminology Mismatch: “Spatio-Temporal Evolution” vs. Cross-Sectional Interpolation The manuscript uses longitudinal terminology to describe cross-sectional data manipulations. 5.1 The Claim: In the Abstract, the authors declare: “. . . we construct the first continuous spatio-temporal neural atlas of the human cerebrovascular system. . . “ and on page 7: “Fig. 4 presents the spatiotemporal evolution of VITAL atlas spanning the adult lifespan from 20 to 80 years. “ 5.2 The Reality: The dataset description on page 5 states: “In this study, we used MRA scans and corresponding T1 images from healthy adults (19-87 years old) in the IXI dataset [6]. “ The methodology relies on computing target latent codes via “Gaussian kernel regression over the trained population” (page 5). 5.3 The Critique: The IXI dataset is strictly cross-sectional, containing single-timepoint scans of different individuals at various ages. Modeling true “spatio-temporal evolution” generally requires longitudinal data (repeated scans of the same subjects over time). Interpolating a latent code between subjects of different ages mathematically generates a cross-sectional age-related morphological mean, rather than a longitudinal aging trajectory. 6.Inconsistencies Regarding Discretization and Partial Volume Effects The motivation for utilizing an Implicit Neural Representation is to bypass the limitations of discrete grids; however, the preprocessing pipeline partially conflicts with this objective.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: the work is thorough and well explained/organized with clear applications and strong well presented results
reviewer_2_weaknesses: -I found the notion of “population-level conditioning” introduced in the paper somewhat unclear. From my understanding, the conditioning appears to be performed at the patient level. This distinction should be clarified, as it is important for interpreting the proposed method. -Although the challenge of modeling vasculature across different scales is well recognized, the paper does not provide sufficient ablation studies to demonstrate how the MoE architecture effectively addresses this issue. In particular, it is unclear how the number of experts is selected. Figure 2c provides some qualitative insight, but it is based on a single sample and does not constitute a comprehensive evaluation.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This is a very well-written and comprehensive piece of work. The main novelty lies in the application. The overall framework based on which this method is developed, i.e., CINA/CINeMA, has already been around for a while and is popular for atlas construction but has never been applied to cerebrovascular atlas construction. In terms of the framework, the authors further incorporate an MoE architecture beyond the original CINeMA, and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the overall performance of the proposed method. The motivation for the MoE architecture is well-explained. For an 8-page short paper, the authors provide a lot of experimental results to support the usefulness of the MoE architecture (Table 1), characterization of how the proposed MoE architecture work indeed result in different experts specializing in different areas of the vasculature (Fig. 2(c)), and usefulness for downstream tasks (clear separation of Normative vs. Pathological in Fig. 3(c)). Key design choices are well-justified. For example, the authors employ a label-stratified coordinate sampling approach to ensure sufficient sampling of the foreground coordinates, which are relatively sparse.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Although the application of INR to cerebrovascular atlas construction is quite new and, in fact, first of its kind, the novelty of the method itself is somewhat limited. From a method stand point, the authors are aware and acknowledge previous works, e.g., CINeMA [9] and MoE for INR [5], which greatly influenced this work. The proposed method does not introduce much new stuff beyond a combination of [9] and [5]. There are also some ambiguities in the description of the method. 1.In Section 2.1, what is vessel intensity value I(x) referring to? Is it the intensity values of the MRA images? 2.Also in section 2.1, the author claim that affine transformation is used. However, the formulation of the transformation is rotation plus translation makes it sounds like a rigid transformation is used? It would be helpful to clarify. 3.Fig. 2(b) and the discussion thereof are hard to follow. There are a lot of information in Fig. 2(b) and I believe it would be helpful to provide more explanation. author_feedback: We sincerely thank all experts for their constructive comments [R1,R2,R4]. We are encouraged that R2 and R4 found our work well-motivated, technically sound, and of clear interest to MICCAI. We clarify all key concerns below. Scope [R1]. Several concerns appear to arise from interpreting VITAL as a segmentation, diagnostic, or surgical-planning system. This is not our intended claim. VITAL is a continuous probabilistic population atlas and normative reference: it models healthy population variability and enables atlas-to-subject comparison, not a standalone diagnostic, segmentation, or navigation tool. Circularity in TopCoW analysis [R1]. This concern follows from the same scope misinterpretation. The masks used in test-time adaptation contain only observed vessel and brain-region labels, which can be obtained from existing segmentation tools. They don’t contain anomaly labels, lesion masks, stroke labels, or ground truth about pathology. The deviation map is computed after atlas projection as the mismatch between the healthy population prior and observed anatomy (Figs. 1 and 3). So the mask anchors alignment; it doesn’t supervise the deviation map. We will clarify this more. Metric interpretation [R1]. The metrics measure atlas-to-subject reconstruction quality of a probabilistic population prior, not supervised segmentation accuracy. Extremely high Dice might indicate memorization of individual topology rather than a meaningful population prior, the opposite of what a normative atlas should achieve. Table 1 should be read mainly as an ablation: MoE (K=4)+Lmoe improves over CiNeMA across most metrics, including PSNR (+3.2 dB), SSIM (+0.05), ASD (-0.98 mm whole-brain, -0.52 mm CoW), conn. error (-112), and center. distance (-0.95 mm). We will revise the wording to avoid implying surgical-grade precision, which is not claimed. Baseline comparisons [R1]. Table 1 evaluates conditional reconstruction within generative atlas frameworks; CiNeMA is the closest comparable baseline. Fig. 2 includes NLR/MultiMorph to illustrate population-level wash-out in discrete atlases, not to claim superiority over deformable registration in a geometric alignment benchmark. ANTs was used solely for intra-subject (T1 to MRA) rigid preprocessing to align anatomy labels, which is a standard procedure, and not as an atlasing baseline. Age-conditioned vs. longitudinal terminology [R1]. We agree that IXI is cross-sectional and that spatio-temporal evolution overstates the design. We will use age-conditioned atlas and cross-sectional lifespan morphological modeling instead. The intended contribution, a continuous implicit function conditioned on age modeling population-level morphological variation across the adult lifespan, is a standard approach in normative brain atlasing. Topology Mutation [R1]. FiLM alone does not guarantee deterministic binary graph edits, but VITAL uses spatial latent codes rather than a single global latent code for local variation without global compensation, with MoE partitioning cross-scale capacity. Anatomical variants are represented probabilistically: congenital absences appear as regions of low vessel probability and high uncertainty rather than hard topology deletions. Clarifications [R2,R4]. 1) VITAL conditions at two levels: z encodes subject-specific variation; c encodes population-level covariates. 2) K=4 was selected as a capacity-cost trade-off supported by the ablation in Table 1 (K=2 vs. K=4); Fig. 2c is qualitative and representative, not a comprehensive evaluation. 3) Yes, it should be ‘vascular’. 4) I(x) denotes MRA intensity. The transformation is rigid to avoid over-warping sparse vascular branch. 5) Fig. 2b shows VITAL assigns more mass to high vessel probability than voxel-based atlas methods, indicating less spatial wash-out. 6) SIREN mitigates spectral bias, but a monolithic SIREN shares one parameter set across scales, causing capacity competition; MoE explicitly partitions this capacity (Fig. 2c).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes VITAL, an implicit neural atlas with a Mixture-of-Experts architecture for cerebrovascular modeling, applied to anomaly analysis on stroke subjects. Several substantive concerns are raised across the reviews. The methodological novelty appears limited as the approach largely combines CINeMA and MoE-for-INR, and warrants stronger articulation. More fundamentally, the anomaly analysis exhibits a circular dependency where the test-time adaptation relies on the patient’s segmentation mask through L_seg, and the validity of the resulting deviation maps as a clinical signal needs to be defended. The reported metrics, including an average surface distance exceeding the diameter of medium cerebral vessels, are also difficult to contextualize given the omission of standard deformable registration baselines. Further concerns include the characterization of cross-sectional latent interpolation as “spatio-temporal evolution,” and ambiguities in population-level versus subject-level conditioning and in the transformation formulation. The rebuttal should address the major reviewers’ concerns including these points. | This paper proposes VITAL, an implicit neural atlas with a Mixture-of-Experts architecture for continuous probabilistic modeling of the cerebrovascular system, applied to atlas-to-subject deviation analysis on stroke data. The reviewers acknowledge that applying INR to cerebrovascular atlas construction is the first of its kind and clinically relevant, and that the MoE design is well motivated and supported by ablations. The rebuttal clarified the intended scope as a probabilistic population atlas and normative reference rather than a standalone diagnostic system; under this scope, the masks in test-time adaptation function as alignment anchors and the metrics are appropriately read as an ablation against the closest generative atlas baseline. The authors are encouraged to revise the “spatio-temporal evolution” terminology and to soften wording suggesting surgical-grade precision, as committed. The novelty lies primarily in adapting existing components, but the application is genuinely new for this anatomy and the empirical support is convincing. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers summarized strengths of your work, novel aspects and noted that your solution to the specific application area may be of potential interest. The rebuttal helped to clarify open issues and misunderstandings. Would the paper be accepted, authors are strongly encouraged to improve the final write-up by including recommendations by reviewers, in particular to improve clarity in order to avoid misunderstandings. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Based on the reviewers’ evaluations, the authors’ rebuttal, and the initial meta-review, the paper is recommended for acceptance. While Reviewer #1 raised serious concerns about clinical utility, insufficient performance, and terminology, two other expert reviewers (R2 and R4) found the work well-motivated, technically sound, and of clear interest to the MICCAI community. The rebuttal convincingly clarified the scope as a probabilistic population atlas and normative reference, not a standalone diagnostic or segmentation tool, and addressed the major points by revising the “spatio-temporal” terminology to cross-sectional age-conditioned modeling, explaining the role of the mask in test-time adaptation, and contextualizing the metrics as an ablation of the MoE architecture relative to the closest INR baseline. The accepting reviewers’ post-rebuttal assessments reaffirmed their support, noting that the responses resolved ambiguities and underscored the novelty and relevance of applying implicit neural representations to cerebrovascular atlas construction.

title: Detail Consistent Stage-Wise Distillation for Efficient 3D MRI Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The major strong points are: Domain-specific subband selection - unlike standard “match-all” high-frequency distillation methods used in natural image processing, the authors propose a selection strategy specifically matched to MRI characteristics (Section 2.2). The exclusion of the high-frequency subband S (HHH) is motivated by the fact that this band is typically dominated by acquisition noise and artifacts in MRI. This introduces a domain-specific inductive bias, allowing the compact student model to focus its limited capacity on structurally relevant features rather than scanner-specific noise. Decision to perform feature alignment in the spatial domain - by reconstructing detail-only features via Inverse Discrete Wavelet Transform (IDWT) before computing the loss (Eq. 6) - is a meaningful technical strength. This approach avoids the gradient instability often associated with computing MSE directly on multi-channel wavelet coefficients, which can vary significantly in magnitude. The efficacy of this spatially interpretable loss is confirmed by the ablation study in Table 4, where the removal of the IDWT step results in a 6.2% drop in Dice. The framework demonstrates a good quantitative and qualitative advantage in segmenting difficult anatomical structures. In BraTS 2024 benchmark (Table 2), the Dice for the non-enhancing tumor core showed a good improvement of 13% - result validates the paper’s hypothesis that explicit detail-bearing supervision is crucial for low-capacity models. The proposed DCD method is used only during the training phase and easily integrates into existing U-Net pipelines (e. g. , nnU-Net). As demonstrated in Table 3, the student model achieves a 16x reduction in parameters (6.38M vs. 101.9M) and significantly lower TFLOPs without introducing any additional inference-time overhead (no DWT/IDWT needed at deployment). This makes the approach well-suited for clinical workflows and resource-constrained hospital hardware.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The major weak points are: Statistical insignificance and misleading representation of results. The paper employs bold font to highlight its results, even when the performance gain over existing baselines is statistically marginal or non-existent (!). Exaples below: a. Table 1 (ISLES 2022): The proposed mDice of 73.95±2.70% is highlighted as the best, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from Feature [14] at 72.70±2.90%, given the overlapping standard deviations. Furthermore, the proposed method actually underperforms CWD [17] in HD95 (12.95 vs 9.48 mm) and Feature [14] in NSD (83.47% vs 83.58%), yet these deficits are not addressed in the text. b. Table 2 (BraTS 2024): For the Enhancing Tissue (ET) class, the proposed method (62.55±2.36%) is inferior to IFVD [21] (63.95±2.34%). In several other categories (SNFH, RC), the performance is nearly identical to prior work when accounting for variance. The superiority of the method on the ISLES dataset, in particular, remains questionable. The ablation study is incomplete, as the core theoretical contribution - Proposition 1, which advocates for the exclusion of the “noisy” S (HHH) band - is not experimentally validated. While Table 4 shows that distilling only the S band yields poor results, the authors fail to compare their proposed D (details-only) strategy against a D+S (all high frequencies) baseline. Without proving that the inclusion of the S band actively degrades performance, the claim that noise-filtering is essential for MRI distillation remains an unverified hypothesis. In Section 2.2 it is stated that l=3 levels of DWT decomposition are applied across all encoder stages. However, in standard 3D U-Net architectures (like nnU-Net), the spatial resolution often drops to 8^3 or 4^3 voxels at the final encoder stages. It is mathematically impossible to perform 3 levels of DWT—which requires a reduction by a factor of 8 - on a 4×4×4 tensor without significant and potentially detrimental padding. This technical discrepancy is not addressed, which calls into question the implementation details for deeper layers. The framework focuses exclusively on stage-wise encoder distillation. In image segmentation, the decoder (paired with skip connections) is primarily responsible for synthesizing high-resolution details and refining boundary masks. Given that the paper’s objective is “detail-consistent” segmentation, the omission of the decoder from the distillation process appears to be a critical architectural misstep that likely limits the method’s overall potential. Ther is a lack of practical efficiency benchmarks. Authors motivate the paper by citing constraints in inference latency and memory footprint, yet they only report FLOPs and parameter counts (Table 3). In 3D medical imaging, FLOPs are often a poor surrogate for actual wall-clock time due to data I/O bottlenecks and sliding-window inference overhead. Without reporting peak VRAM consumption and real inference latency on standard hardware, the claim of improved efficiency is not fully substantiated for clinical deployment scenarios. The proposed DCD framework is based on the (Eq. 1), which states that the representational gap between the teacher and student models is significantly larger in the high-frequency domain than in the low-frequency one. While this assumption is conceptually supported by general (spectral bias) literature, the authors do not provide direct empirical evidence - such as a spectral energy analysis or a frequency-wise distance plot - performed on the actual feature maps of the models. Without verifying that a disproportionate spectral gap indeed exists in the baseline student’s features before distillation, it remains unclear whether the observed performance gains are a direct result of narrowing this specific spectral gap or broader regularization effects.

title: Discovering Heterogeneous Neurodegenerative Disease Patterns From MRI Data for Improved Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: The major strength of the paper is that the proposed method is simple and generalizable: it proposes to add a mixture of expert models after an MLP acting as a router to different experts. The method beats what is generally considered state-of-the-art for tabular data, namely, random forests. The paper is well written, and the ablation study is well performed.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: One “weakness” is that the method is applied only on tabular data: the authors should discuss how we can apply such a framework to a representation space coming from self-supervised learning of imaging data. The other weakness is the relationship between the experts and the actual labels: the loss (1) forces the subjects having the same subtype label to belong to the same cluster. However, there is a lengthy discussion on the optimal number of experts: is it not expected that it equals the number of subtypes (3 if I am not mistaken)? When the authors state that there are 4 experts (figure 3 of page 8), the authors should add the proporition of the actual subtypes for each expert for clarity.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Innovative integration of prediction and clustering via a MoE architecture tailored for heterogeneous neurodegenerative disease data. Use of multiple regularization losses to stabilize training and prevent degenerate solutions. Comparisons to strong baselines and state-of-the-art models in classification and survival prediction tasks.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Dataset and MCI case selection: The paper states that for classification, 668 MCI subjects with baseline MRI were selected and categorized as stable or progressive based on dementia progression within three years. For progression risk prediction, 1,243 MCI subjects with baseline MRI and multiple follow-ups were used. It is not clear how these subjects were selected. Optimal cluster number determination: The authors report that performance peaks at four experts, suggesting four natural subtypes. However, relying exclusively on prediction metrics to select cluster number is weak (the difference in performance is extremely narrow) which may not fully capture the biological or clinical validity of subtypes Clustering evaluation: Clustering performance is quantitatively assessed on the semi-simulated dataset using ARI and NMI, showing improvements with the MoE framework. However, the real-world clustering quality is not directly evaluated, and no comparison to alternative subtyping methods is provided in the real data setting. Comparison to baselines: The paper compares predictive performance against baselines for classification/risk prediction. However, comparisons against other subtyping or clustering strategies, especially those designed for neurodegenerative disease heterogeneity, are missing. This would clarify the added value of the MoE approach for subtype discovery. Interpretation of atrophy patterns: The four identified subtypes show distinct atrophy patterns consistent with disease stages (e.g., mild atrophy in early MCI subtype, severe atrophy in late-stage subtype). While this supports clinical plausibility, it raises the question of whether the method primarily captures disease severity rather than novel subtype heterogeneity. Further exploration of subtype-specific clinical or biomarker profiles would enhance interpretability.
