author_feedback: We thank reviewers for their constructive feedback. Following meta-review, we focus on main concerns and then address reviewer-specific comments. Q1: Expert/subtype interpretation, severity, and confounders [R2,R3,Meta] We agree that learned experts should not be overinterpreted as biological subtypes without further validation. We interpret them as data-driven disease groups. With a small K (e.g., 2), the model may capture a mild–severe atrophy axis, leading to poorer prediction performance (Table 1). With K=4, experts show spatially distinct atrophy patterns, including medial-temporal-predominant and diffuse cortical patterns, suggesting heterogeneity beyond severity alone (Fig. 3). Assessing clinical records of Subtype 1 (S1) and S3 showed similar conversion rates (~20%) and comparable cognitive decline, despite their distinct spatial patterns. A similar pattern was observed for S2 and S4, which both showed ~50% conversion and comparable cognitive decline. Including age and sex as additional inputs yielded similar prediction performance. Nevertheless, we agree that explicit age/sex comparisons across subtypes and additional clinical profiling would further strengthen interpretation and is an important future work. Q2: Experts number K [R1-3,Meta] Since no ground-truth disease subtype labels exist, we use prediction performance as a surrogate indicator. We agree it is insufficient alone for selecting K when differences are small. Evaluating current subtyping results with clustering stability (ARI) and quality (Calinski-Harabasz Index) provided additional insight (K=2-5; ARI: 0.896, 0.840, 0.822, 0.525; CH: 195.2, 113.4, 116.1, 98.8, respectively). Although K=2 was most stable, it mainly separated mild from severe atrophy. In contrast, K=4 provided the best balance among prediction performance, stability, and heterogeneity. Q3: Expert separation and routing enforced [R1,R3,Meta] Each expert represents one subtype, while the router learns subtype assignments that minimize prediction loss. Expert separation is encouraged by a load-balancing term preventing collapse to one expert and sparse routing to assign each subject to a single expert. Thus, experts are encouraged to specialize while maintaining balanced usage. Q4: Evaluation relative to baselines and clustering methods [R2,R3,Meta] Our goal is not standalone clustering, but joint learning of subtypes and prediction in a unified framework that is not hinged on specific prediction or clustering backbones. Table 1 shows that, even with simple MLP experts, our method is competitive with or improves over TabPFN and DeepSurv. Table 2 shows that MoE improves clustering performance over alternatives. In response to R3, MoE significantly improves over Single and Single*, with all p-values <0.01.We agree that additional comparison with other methods on real data would further strengthen biological validation, but real-world subtype labels are unavailable; therefore, following prior studies [7,24,25,26], we used semi-simulated data with known subtype structure for quantitative clustering evaluation. Q5: Additional Clarification [R2] Risk prediction used 1,243 MCI subjects with baseline MRI and longitudinal follow-up. For classification, stable/progressive MCI was defined by conversion to dementia within 3 years; subjects without sufficient follow-up were excluded, yielding 668 subjects. [R1] Semi-simulated atrophy patterns were generated by reducing selected ROI values by predefined percentages to mimic subtype-specific neurodegeneration. [R1,R3] We used ROI-level MRI features for interpretability and controlled semi-simulation, but the framework is representation-agnostic and can operate on voxel-wise imaging embeddings (discussed in P.8). [R1,R3] Random Forest hyperparameters were tuned using sklearn RandomizedSearchCV; TabPFN was evaluated zero-shot; standard deviations for Table 2 and balanced accuracy can be added. We will revise the paper accordingly for better clarity.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Reviewers mainly request clarifications on whether the identified experts truly reflect meaningful biological subtypes rather than confounders or disease severity, and why the model consistently favors four experts. They also ask for clearer explanations of the method (how expert separation is enforced and how routing works), along with clarification of evaluation choices, such as metrics, and how improvements should be interpreted relative to existing baselines. | I tend to agree with Reviewer 2’s assessment. The article presents a relatively straightforward idea, combining subgroup discovery with supervised classification, that has already been explored in the literature. In its current form, the manuscript does not provide a sufficiently thorough comparison with prior work, either from the perspective of subgroup identification or predictive modeling. In particular, the proposed approach should be compared against established subgroup discovery methods such as HYDRA, CHIMERA, UCSL, Deep UCSL, MAGIC, SuStaIn, and DeepCluster (or related deep clustering approaches). Such comparisons are essential to demonstrate whether the proposed method offers any advantage in terms of subgroup stability, interpretability, clinical relevance, or predictive performance. Similarly, stronger baselines should be included for the supervised classification and progression-risk prediction tasks. Without these comparisons, it is difficult to assess the true contribution of the method. More fundamentally, I share Reviewer 2’s concern that the methodological novelty of the work remains unclear. The manuscript does not convincingly explain what distinguishes the proposed framework from existing approaches, nor why it should be expected to outperform them either theoretically or empirically. Finally, the evaluation would benefit from the inclusion of an additional dataset, ideally one in which subgroup labels or underlying subgroup structure are known (or can be reasonably approximated). This would provide stronger evidence that the method is capable of recovering meaningful subgroups rather than dataset-specific patterns or task difficulty. Overall, the clinical utility and statistical added value of the proposed approach remain insufficiently demonstrated. The manuscript would benefit from a clearer positioning with respect to the existing literature, stronger baselines, and more rigorous validation of the discovered subgroups. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have reasonably clarified the main concerns about expert interpretation, expert number selection, and routing mechanism; while subtype validation remains limited, the revised explanation is sufficient to support acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend accepting this paper. The idea to couple identification of data-driven disease groups with predictive modelling in a Mixture-of-Experts framework is novel and interesting. Although the paper does not provide sufficient validation to claim that each expert discovers a distinct disease subtype rather then disease severity stage, during rebuttal authors provide disease progression comparison for identified groups, which do not show a linear trend. The identification of data-driven disease groups and their processing through separate experts improve predictive performance over a single-expert approach as well as other baseline methods, demonstrating that the proposed approach is both novel and effective.

title: Disentangling Prompt Dependence to Evaluate Segmentation Reliability in Gynecological MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is well written, well presented. The authors propose a solid theory on how variability or ambiguity in the prompt definition can affect the reliability of a segmentation outcome. Extensive experiments are also conducted.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The work also seem very preliminary, but very interesting. It is preliminary to me because I would have expected the experiments to include more images modalities. The theoretical work is solid, and the paper would benefit from demonstrating that it also works for other image modalities. Also while the authors already mentioned it, experiments or more details on how contrast affect the results will be great.
reviewer_1_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_2_strengths: A principled analysis of prompt sensitivity in SAM-like foundation models is crucial as these models are increasingly adopted. Specifically, the disentanglement of inter-user variability and local sensitivity are novel and provide an interesting view-point in analyzing the robustness and sensitivity of foundation models to changes in inputs. The specific mathematical grounding of these two aspects of robustness is well explained in the paper. The results, in terms of negative correlation between the two above-mentioned aspects of model sensitivity provide additional support to the disentanglement argument. This aspect is also potentially interesting utilizing the learned p(b|x) as augmentations during training.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The theoretical framework of the paper is well articulated. However, the evaluation of prompt ambiguity is not satisfactory. Lack of evaluation in a setting where the prompt model is known a priori weakens the empirical evidence. While the proposed metric exhibits an inverse correlation with segmentation performance, this observation alone is insufficient to substantiate the theoretical claims. The purpose and intended contributions of the paper are not clear. The sensitivity of promptable segmentation models to prompt choice is already well recognized in the literature. The analysis presented is informative. However, the work appears largely exploratory without a clearly defined objective or downstream use case.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: As prompt dependence is a central challenge in clinical adoption of foundation models, the proposed work is timely and clinically relevant. Therefore, the paper is highly relevant to the wider MICCAI community. The work builds upon both, clinical observation and theory inspired approximations, yielding a well structured study, with clearly motivated design choices (e.g. the MDN for approximating the distribution) that make the method and comparisons easy to follow. Moreover, the idea to quantify U_amb is of high clinical value as it can be leveraged to indicate intrinsic variability vis a vis a misbehaving model / failed prediction.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The connection between idealised decomposition of the prompt variance, and the connection with the empirical estimator is ambiguous. Based on the law-of-total-variance the paper suggests the decomposition of the perturbed prediction, and suggest to approximate the expectation E_Delta with S(I,B) for sufficiently small perturbations, which already presumes local regularity of the prompt-to-mask map (so this is more than empirical). However, the empirical quantities introduced are not the two variance terms from this decomposition: the proposed ambiguity score is a prompt-space dispersion measure, while local sensitivity is operationalized as a finite-perturbation stability margin via threshold. That is, while the theory is built on a local smoothness approximation in mask space, the empirical method replaces the resulting variance terms with prompt-space covariance and a thresholded stability margin. The paper’s own first order approximation shows a dependence on both covariance and local Jacobian. Hence, U_amb is not an estimator of the theoretical prompt ambiguity. Therefore, the work should reflect under which assumptions these proxies are faithful, and soften the claim that they are “computable estimators” of the theoretical components. This is especially relevant, given the known behaviour of SAM models. The low mutual correlation between the terms is not a sufficient condition for disentanglement; the paper lacks a sanity check to prove the metrics do not correlate with confounding variables. To truly validate U_amb as a measure of “clinical uncertainty” the authors needed to demonstrate that it specifically predicts inter-observer variance. Instead of proving that cases with high inter-rater variance yield a high U_amb (and evaluating this against a baseline like aleatoric entropy), the authors settle for dataset-wide proxies. Consequently, the metrics feel like noisy proxies for general image difficulty rather than a clinically validated disentanglement of error sources.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their feedback and for recognizing the relevance of our work on prompt dependence in SAM-like models. We address the major concerns raised by R2 and R3.1.Faithfulness of empirical proxies R2 and R3 question whether our empirical metrics faithfully estimate the theoretical variance terms. We agree that they should not be interpreted as exact estimators. Instead, our goal is to build a prompt model that is theoretically motivated and practically computable from frozen models and images. Exact computation would require access to the true distribution of valid prompts and the local Jacobian of prompt-to-mask mapping, neither of which is observable in our setting. We will rephrase U_amb and δ* as theory-motivated operational proxies rather than computable estimators. Their interpretation relies on assumptions: i) pθ(b|x) captures dominant modes of plausible prompts; ii) the prompt-to-mask mapping is locally regular within these prompts; iii) perturbations reflect realistic user imprecision. Under these assumptions, U_amb captures image-driven ambiguity in prompt definition, while δ* captures local model robustness around a plausible prompt. R3 also notes that low correlation is insufficient to prove disentanglement. However, in Fig. 3, we observe not only a low correlation but also a stronger lack of mutual information between the metrics. This is sensible as, by design, the metrics capture distinct mechanisms: U_amb is an image property; δ* depends on the model-mask combination. This is further confirmed by cross-dataset behaviors: U_amb is higher in UT-EndoMRI, while δ* dominates in MOGaMBO. With respect to the effects of contrast and other image properties, the datasets present two use cases: low contrast and diffuse boundaries in UT-EndoMRI, and high contrast in MOGaMBO. This observed cross-dataset behavior is therefore preliminary evidence that contrast affects prompt dependence. 2.Validation of prompt ambiguity modeling R3 suggests validating U_amb against inter-rater variability, and R2 questions the absence of evaluation against a known prompt distribution. Repeated prompts from multiple users would be ideal, but not available in these open datasets. Thus, we use a computational surrogate from multi-rater segmentation masks (1-3 expert masks per image). Thus, pθ(b|x) is grounded in real inter-observer variability rather than artificial jitter. This allows us to model two sources of prompt variability: multiple prompts encoding similar masks, and those encoding different plausible masks. We provide two forms of validation for pθ(b|x): the MDN reaches an NLL of -2.5, indicating a good fit. Fig. 3 (bottom) shows functional validation: uncertainty maps sampled from pθ(b|x) reach AUC=0.98, outperforming D0 and jitter. D0 (non-conditional distribution) serves as an aleatoric prompt-entropy baseline, showing that our model captures image-specific ambiguity beyond generic prompt variability. 3.Downstream objectives R2 asks for a clearer downstream objective. The novelty is not to observe prompt sensitivity, which is already known, but to i) make it actionable per image and ii) separate it into two distinct sources that can be measured and regulated independently. First, unlike aggregate robustness metrics, U_amb and δ* are image-level. This is necessary for problems in which the factors of interest (e.g., specific sequences, patient demographics, etc.) are not a priori known and more flexibility is needed for future analysis. For example, Fig. 3 (top) shows that these metrics yield meaningful groups on MOGaMBO: Dice differs ~2.5× between low- and high-risk images (0.73 vs 0.29). Secondly, δ* reflects model-level robustness, improvable through model design or regularization. U_amb reflects image-user ambiguity, addressable through operator guidance or expert review. By disentangling the two metrics, our framework helps identify not only whether a sample is at risk, but also why and how to mitigate it.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper is deemed timely and addressing an important current problem of foundation models with what seems a solid theoretical framework. The rebuttal should however clarify the objective of the paper and address / justify what appears as shortcomings of the evaluation framework with respect to the current claims of the paper | The authors’ rebuttal addresses well the key concerns raised during the review clarifying the perspective of the work which will hopefully create fruitful discussion. The relevance of the topic makes it pass the acceptance threshold Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors provide a strong rebuttal that meaningfully improves the clarity and positioning of the work. The most important revision is the explicit correction of the theoretical framing: the proposed quantities are no longer presented as exact estimators of a variance decomposition, but rather as theory-motivated operational proxies built under clearly stated assumptions. This clarification resolves the central concern raised across reviewers regarding the faithfulness of the proposed measures and significantly improves the conceptual rigor of the paper. The authors further clarify the modeling assumptions behind the prompt distribution (learned via MDN) and the local regularity of the prompt-to-mask mapping, and they appropriately acknowledge that these assumptions are necessary for interpretation rather than empirically guaranteed properties. In addition, they provide clearer justification of the experimental design, including the use of multi-rater masks as a surrogate for prompt variability and the evaluation protocol used for stability and uncertainty estimation. These clarifications address key concerns regarding methodological ambiguity and strengthen confidence in the validity of the reported analysis. Concerns regarding limited dataset size, absence of explicit inter-observer prompt distributions, and lack of external baselines remain, but these are inherent limitations of the current study setting and are not issues that can be resolved within the rebuttal. Importantly, reviewers no longer identify these as disqualifying weaknesses after the rebuttal clarifications. Remaining limitations related to proxy validation and statistical completeness are now appropriately acknowledged and do not undermine the main contribution. Overall, the rebuttal successfully resolves the major conceptual misunderstandings and improves transparency around assumptions and empirical design. The work provides a timely and relevant contribution to understanding prompt sensitivity in SAM-like segmentation models, with a clear decomposition into image-dependent ambiguity and local robustness components. Given the strengthened clarity, improved methodological framing, and converging reviewer opinions, the paper meets the acceptance threshold for MICCAI. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After the rebuttal round, this one is a clear accept. I encourage authors to implement the promised changes and clarifications in the camera-ready.

title: Disentangling Uterine and Bladder Activity in Paired EHG-MRI Data Using Anatomy-Guided Multicluster Beamforming
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.A core strength of this paper is the specificity of the task and the success of the tailored approach to a challenging problem, given the heterogeneity and diversity in the population studied. 2.This paper also includes a comprehensive evaluation with good statistical analysis and clear discussion of the the actual implications of the findings in the clinical environment, acknowledging the present limitations of the study. 3.The paper is well-written and logical with a clear motivation and story presented. 4.The composition of the dataset, while small, shows thoughtfulness in the inclusion of male participants for a “control” comparison without a uterus and the assessment of different menstrual phases in a small portion of the cohort.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.A primary weakness of the paper is the size of the human dataset which contains only 10 participants of which only 7 had a uterus and only 3 were evaluated longitudinal to consider the effect of menstrual phase, as acknowledged in the Discussion. 2.There is no mention in this paper of reproducibility factors, such as source code or dataset access.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper targets uterus–bladder source disentanglement in paired EHG–MRI, a niche but meaningful problem where simple spectral filtering is insufficient because the signals overlap in frequency. The anatomy-guided multicluster LCMV formulation is well motivated: subject-specific MRI geometry is used to define clustered uterus/bladder steering directions and organ-specific pass/null constraints, which is a sensible way to inject anatomy into a difficult inverse problem. The method includes clustered steering, constrained beamforming, and leakage subtraction in a logically consistent framework, with subject-level diagnostics showing strong target response and cross-organ suppression. A notable finding is that uterine cluster compactness, rather than gross uterus–bladder separation angle, appears to be the main driver of pass-direction stability, which could be useful for future sensor-placement and modeling design. The paper provides cohort-level and subject-level analyses, including PSD trends, compactness/stability correlations, leakage metrics, and dynamic examples, making the proposed mechanism relatively interpretable. The paper demonstrates stable constrained beamforming with only 8 electrodes is practically appealing and supports the claim that anatomical priors can compensate for limited sensors.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper lacks convincing comparisons with meaningful baselines, such as simpler frequency-based separation, standard beamforming without multicluster constraints, no-null versions, or no-leakage-subtraction versions. This makes it hard to judge the true added value of each component. Most reported evidence is internal or model-based, such as pass/null gains, residuals, correlations, and energy ratios. These support engineering consistency, but they do not fully verify that the recovered signals are truly organ-specific physiological sources. The dataset contains only 10 paired recordings, with 7 female and 3 male volunteers and only 3 longitudinal acquisitions. All appear to be healthy participants, which limits the strength of the biological and clinical claims. The paper explains the framework reasonably well, but several practical details appear insufficiently specified for full reproduction, including some clustering/regularization choices and preprocessing specifics. Some claims may be overstated. Very strong suppression numbers and leakage improvements are reported, but without independent physiological validation, they should be interpreted more cautiously as method-internal evidence rather than definitive organ-level separation.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: the clinical problem is well motivated and relatively underexplored. Separating uterine activity from bladder-related activity in non-invasive EHG is important because both organs can contribute low-frequency signals, and simple frequency filtering may not be sufficient. the use of subject specific MRI anatomy is a strong and interesting aspect of the work. Instead of treating EHG as only a multichannel surface signal, the authors use MRI-derived segmentations of the uterus, bladder, and electrodes to guide the source separation. to me this is a nice formulation because the uterus and bladder are deep, spatially close organs, so anatomical priors are important for good separation. next the authors do not represent each organ as a single source, but instead define multiple spatial clusters for the uterus and bladder. overall framework is coherent and shows how anatomical imaging and surface electrophysiology can be combined in practice. the work provides an initial in-vivo feasibility demonstration. Although the cohort is small, the authors include 10 paired EHG-MRI datasets, including both female and male volunteers, and show that the method can be applied with only 8 EHG channels.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: i do have a few minor concerns; for example the validation of true uterus–bladder separation is still indirect. The authors show that the beamformer satisfies pass/null constraints and that leakage subtraction reduces correlation between reconstructed signals, but these are mainly internal technical checks. There is no independent physiological reference, such as bladder filling, urodynamics, uterine pressure, cine MRI motion, or expert-labeled uterine activity, to confirm that the separated signals truly come from the intended organs. This is important because the paper claims robust in-vivo uterus–bladder separation. some key implementation details are missing or unclear. The paper describes MRI-based steering dictionaries, clustering, LCMV beamforming, covariance shrinkage, and overlap-add reconstruction, but does not clearly specify details such as the number of clusters, clustering method, window length, overlap, preprocessing steps, shrinkage selection, and the exact bladder-pass/uterus-null formulation. These details are important for reproducibility. But i think this limitations can be easily resolved by making the code public. simple baselines or ablations are missing. As the main claim is that anatomy-guided multicluster beamforming is needed, it should be compared with simpler alternatives such as frequency filtering alone or single-cluster beamforming lcmv without null constraints
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and the meta-reviewer for their constructive feedback and recognition of the work’s novelty and clinical relevance. Below we address the main concerns grouped by theme. P1 — Dataset size (R1, R2, R4): While the cohort consists of 10 volunteers, the 3 longitudinal participants each contributed 2 sessions (follicular/luteal), resulting in 13 recordings total. Simultaneous EHG-MRI acquisition is resource-intensive, requiring MRI facility access, custom synchronization, and extended patient preparation. Data collection is ongoing. P2 — Physiological validation (R2, R4): We acknowledge that independent physiological validation was not included in the current study and agree this is an important limitation. We clarify that the ~−155/−158 dB null suppression values quantify mathematical constraint satisfaction — how accurately the LCMV enforces pass/null directions — not physiological organ-level purity. The practically relevant cross-organ suppression is the null gain (0.10–0.48, Table 1). Similarly, Δr and energy ratios are engineering consistency metrics confirming the mathematical operations work as intended, and should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of organ-level separation. We will make this distinction more explicit in the camera-ready. The simultaneously acquired EPI dynamic MRI contains bladder filling information over time, which we plan to incorporate as an independent physiological reference in future work. P3 — Baselines and ablations (R2, R4): We agree explicit comparisons would strengthen the evaluation. While the Methods establish theoretically why frequency filtering alone is insufficient, we acknowledge this does not substitute for empirical comparison. We note that the leakage subtraction component is partially evaluated through the Δr and energy ratio columns in Table 1, which quantify its effect across all sessions. A full ablation against frequency filtering and single-cluster LCMV without null constraints remains an important direction for future work. P4 — Implementation details and reproducibility (R1, R2, R4): The full code will be released publicly upon publication. The camera-ready will clarify missing parameters (number of clusters, window length/overlap, shrinkage β selection). Participant data will be shared in accordance with institutional and ethical guidelines. We confirm the study received appropriate institutional ethical approval and all participants provided informed consent. P5 — Additional questions (R4): Segmentations were obtained manually from T1-weighted MRI; variability across sessions/operators was not assessed but is recognized as important for future work. Electrode positions are registered within the same simultaneous session, ensuring geometric consistency; soft-tissue deformation was not modeled and will be investigated in future work. Manual segmentation takes ~3 hours per subject (uterus being most challenging); full pipeline timing will be reported in the camera-ready. Near-real-time processing is not feasible due to prior MRI segmentation requirements, but same-session beamforming is achievable once the anatomical model is built. P6 — Minor clarifications (R1): We will rename “Results” to “Experiments and Results.” “Repeated sessions from the same volunteer” refers to the 3 longitudinal subjects scanned across menstrual phases, not same-day repeats. We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer once more for their valuable input. The camera-ready will incorporate clarified implementation details and code release.

title: Diverse Normal Prototypes-Guided Contrastive Reconstruction for Medical Anomaly Detection
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper is generally well-motivated, with clear experimental validation and solid presentation. 2.The paper includes sufficient ablation experiments to evaluate the contribution of each component.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Using teacher-student feature discrepancy at the patch level to generate anomaly maps is not well justified. [3] Roth et al., “Towards total recall in industrial anomaly detection”, CVPR (2022). reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clear Motivation: The authors provide a profound analysis of why existing reconstruction methods struggle with medical images. The proposed momentum update and diversity-aware alignment loss are logically coherent solutions to the issues of pre-trained feature mismatch and the loss of representational diversity caused by coherence objectives. 2.Convincing Architectural Evolution: The method derivations and ablation studies (e.g., the progression from M0 to M1, M2, and finally M2+ in Fig. 3) clearly demonstrate why direct fine-tuning is infeasible and justify the necessity of the momentum encoder.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient Verification of the Momentum Encoder (M2+) Applicability: Replacing the frozen pre-trained encoder with a momentum-updated encoder is theoretically sound. However, this strategy is currently only integrated and evaluated within the INP-Former architecture. If the authors claim this is an effective solution for medical image domain shifts, it is highly recommended to adapt and validate this momentum strategy on other baseline reconstruction-based methods (e.g., RD4AD, ReContrast, Dinomaly). This would provide stronger evidence of its value and generalizability. 2.Lack of Discussion and Comparison with the Core Baseline (M2): The motivation and network architecture of the proposed M2 framework are similar to the frozen-encoder+trainable-encoder of ReContrast. However, the authors did not to provide any comparison or explanation of this relationship in the main text. Please clarify: Is M2 same as the arch used in ReContrast, or are there specific architectural innovations? 3.Given the rich modalities and high variability of medical images, evaluating on only three public datasets is somewhat limited. It is recommended that the authors perform additional experiments on a more comprehensive medical anomaly detection benchmark, such as the BMAD benchmark (which includes sub-datasets from 5 different modalities), to solidify their empirical conclusions. 4.In Fig. 3(b), which shows the performance trends over training iterations, the authors provide the curves for OCT2017 and ISIC2018 under the M2+ framework, but omit the M2+ results for APTOS2019.Is this because the M2+ framework performs poorly (e.g., fails to converge or drops in performance) on the APTOS dataset?
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers (R) and the Meta-Reviewer (MR) for their constructive feedback. As rebuttals are limited to 4,000 characters and text-only, we provide concise clarifications below. === Response to R1 and MR === 1.Rationale of the anomaly map -Principle: Follows prior works [6,8,9,10,14,18], which assume a network trained only on normal data poorly rebuilds anomalous regions, thus giving larger rebuild errors there. We measure this error by cosine distance, then resize and apply Gaussian smoothing to get the final anomaly map. -Empirical: Localization quality is shown by heatmaps (Figs. 4–5) and pixel-level metrics (Table 2). On our in-house dataset, we further compare predicted maps with masks (Fig. 5), where high-response areas overlap well with real lesions. 2-3.Number of prototypes and updating -Following INP-Former [14], we fix prototype number M=6 across all datasets. In practice, smaller M under-represents normal diversity, while larger M mainly increases computation with marginal gains. -As in Sec. 2 & Fig. 2(c), prototypes P = E(F_Q, {t_m}) are dynamically generated via cross-attention with encoder features and optimized end-to-end by L_total (Eq. 6). 4.Backbone fairness We faithfully follow each baseline’s original backbone: ViT-Small/14 (35.13M): Ours, INP-Former, Dinomaly WideResNet50 (136.28M): RD4AD, ReContrast ResNet50: EDC (34.64M), EA2D (49.06M) Our improvements are clear against baselines with the same backbone (INP-Former, Dinomaly) or comparable parameters (EDC, EA2D). Against larger-backbone baselines, we still outperform despite using fewer parameters. We will clarify the backbone of all methods in the final draft. === Response to R2 and MR === 1-2.Additional baselines We compared the most directly related SOTA methods, e.g., EDC [9] (IEEE TMI 2024), EA2D [18] (IEEE TMI 2025) within the page limit. Since rebuttal guidelines preclude new experiments, we will discuss the methods you mentioned in related-work section. As for PatchCore’s performance, one may refer to Recontrast [8] (Table 5), which reports generally moderate results. 3.Methodological details -Multi-layer aggregation: following [10], we adopt group-to-group supervision, summing features from layers 2–5 and 6–9 of ViT-Small into two groups. Cosine similarity is computed between the encoder and decoder feature groups, and then taking the average. -In Eq. 4, S is cosine distance. -The bottleneck module is a two-layer MLP. 4.DINOv2 vs DINOv3 (i) When this work was conducted, DINOv3 and its evaluation ecosystem were not yet mature; (ii) for fair comparison, ViT-based competitors (INP-Former, Dinomaly) all use DINOv2; (iii) the framework is backbone-agnostic and can be directly migrated to DINOv3. The above and other issues (typo ‘MIR’, Fig. 1d output, figure font size, table order, appendix ref) will be corrected in camera-ready. === Response to R4 and MR === 1.Applicability of M2+ We agree with the suggestion to apply this to other baselines. M2+ is method-agnostic by design: it only modifies the teacher-update rule (Eq. 2) and is decoupled from the rest of the framework. Systematic studies on other baselines will be pursued in future work. 2.Relation to ReContrast/M2 M2 shares the asymmetric twin-path philosophy of ReContrast [8], but is presented only as an intermediate ablation in Sec. 2.1/Table 3a, not as our contribution. Our contribution is M2+ and tackling prototype collapse from a long-tail perspective. 3.Datasets Our datasets follow the protocol of EDC [9] and EA2D [18], and our private brain MRI dataset, i.e., BrainMRI. We note that rebuttal guidelines preclude new experiments; extension to the BMAD benchmark is planned as future work. 4.APTOS curve in Fig. 3b Fig. 3b is intended to illustrate the limitation of M2: it cannot keep improving with iterations on some datasets (OCT2017, ISIC2018), which M2+ resolves. On APTOS2019, M2 already improves monotonically, while M2+ further achieves higher AUC.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes DNP-ConFormer for medical anomaly detection, using prototype-guided reconstruction, a momentum-updated encoder, and a diversity-aware alignment loss to address domain gap and prototype collapse. Reviewers generally recognized the clear motivation, solid presentation, useful ablation studies, and the potentially valuable insight of adapting DINOv2 to medical images with EMA. However, several recurring concerns should be addressed in rebuttal. Reviewers requested clearer justification of the anomaly scoring strategy based on teacher–student patch-level discrepancy, more details on how prototypes are learned or updated, and analysis of the critical prototype number hyperparameter. Multiple reviewers also raised concerns about limited comparisons, including missing reconstruction-, embedding-, and KD-based baselines, and insufficient discussion of the relationship to core baselines such as ReContrast/M2.Further clarification is needed on methodological details and comparison fairness. A focused rebuttal addressing these and other reviewer-raised points would help reassess the contribution. | DNP-ConFormer addresses domain gap and prototype collapse in medical anomaly detection via a momentum-updated EMA teacher and a diversity-aware alignment loss. Reviewers found the motivation clear, the presentation solid, the ablations useful, and the DINOv2-EMA adaptation insight valuable beyond anomaly detection; R2 upgraded to Accept post-rebuttal. The rebuttal reasonably clarified the in-scope concerns, including comparison fairness, prototype generation, anomaly-scoring rationale, method details, and the relationship to ReContrast. Remaining limitations, including M2+ being validated only within INP-Former, evaluation on three datasets, and lack of sensitivity analysis for M, are real but non-fatal. The authors are encouraged to address these in the camera-ready where possible, particularly by more carefully scoping claims about M2+ generality and incorporating the rebuttal clarifications. Recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal addressed several of the main methodological concerns and improved the clarity of the paper, especially regarding the anomaly scoring rationale, the prototype mechanism, and implementation details. Although some concerns remain about comparison completeness and methodological justification, the overall post-rebuttal assessment is positive. I therefore support acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper received Weak Reject (no post-rebuttal submitted), Accept, and Weak Accept (no post-rebuttal submitted). The authors’ rebuttal addressed shared methodological concerns, such as anomaly-map rationale, prototype mechanism, multi-layer details, backbone fairness, and ReContrast positioning. title: Dual-Registration Reciprocal Super-Resolution for Prior-Guided Real-Time 4D-MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: Highly Novel Clinical Integration: The framework identifies a critical bottleneck in real-time 4D-MRI (the lack of perfect ground truth) and elegantly solves it by repurposing underutilized clinical assets—diagnostic T1w scans for anatomical guidance and breath-hold HR scans for training supervision. This marks a significant paradigm shift from conventional single-image super-resolution to prior-guided reconstruction. Methodological Soundness: The reciprocal design of HRMNet ensures that registration and super-resolution mutually reinforce one another at each resolution level; improved SR yields better spatial matching, which in turn provides more accurate anatomical priors for further SR refinement. Additionally, the ARC loss intelligently addresses the geometric distortions typical in GAN-based models by assessing similarities on the warped input rather than the direct SR output. Strong Quantitative and Visual Results: The method is rigorously benchmarked against state-of-the-art models (AST, ATD, A2-CDic, DANCE), showing consistent and substantial improvements in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, particularly at aggressive acceleration factors up to ×32.Extensive ablation studies (evaluating recursive depths and individual training losses) systematically validate the efficacy of both HRMNet and ACMT.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Limited Clinical Dataset Size: The real-world clinical evaluation relies on an in-house 4D-MRI dataset comprising only 26 liver cancer patients. Validating the model on a larger, multi-centric cohort would be necessary to confidently ensure generalizability across diverse anatomies and cancer morphologies. Reliance on Synthetic Deformations for Public Data: For the experiments conducted on the public CHAOS dataset, inter-fraction misalignment resulting from respiration was simulated using synthetic Gaussian deformations. This synthetic approximation may not fully encapsulate the complex, non-linear respiratory and peristaltic motions encountered in real patients. Unverified Real-Time Latency: The manuscript explicitly notes that real-time imaging protocols demand a stringent sub-300 ms latency. While the method achieves excellent visual fidelity, the text does not detail the inference speed of the complex, multi-level recursive HRMNet. It remains unclear if the framework can reconstruct images fast enough during deployment to meet the strictly defined real-time radiotherapy gating requirements. Errors in Fig. 1.Input of the registration and SR modules should be k+1 instead of k-1. Typo. The first sentence of subsection 2.1 should be “As shown in Fig. 1,”

reviewer_2_strengths: (1) This work addresses the SR problem for 4D MRI, which represents a clinically significant task with substantial practical implications. To my knowledge, prior research specifically targeting 4D MRI SR (and image restoration) remains limited. (2) The proposed HRMNet architecture and ACMT training strategy exhibit good methodological innovation. The experimental results on two datasets show performance improvements over existing approaches. The authors should be aware that excessive use of inline expressions can affect the readability of paper. (2) Also, the figures contain many arrows and symbols. Figure 1 includes the “K-2” case, which appears unnecessary and could be simplified. (3) Questions for experimental design: 3A) The paper appears to process each frame (i) independently. Have the authors considered incorporating temporal correlations between frames, or estimating inter-frame deformation fields? Typically, single-modality registration within the same MRI sequence is easier than cross-modality (e.g., between R and S) and cross-scale (between R and L) registration. 3B) Is the number of patients (26) of the in-house dataset sufficient for model optimization? 3C) The backbone network utilized for LPIPS metrics is not specified. 3D) The undersampling method of MRI data in CHAOS is not mentioned. (4) Based on point (3), this work appears to address a broader image restoration (IR) problem, rather than super-resolution (SR), i.e., the input I^L has a spatial resolution of (H W D) that is equal to I^H, although anatomical details are corrupted during the undersampling.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.For the challenges of no ground truth for supervision, the paper proposed to use the breath-hold scans to serve as the pseudo-ground-truth. 2.The paper proposes to use anatomical scans (T1 scans) as a reference to enhance the SR details. 3.The paper proposes to jointly train SR and registration modules in the model.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The training and evaluation are both on the pseudo-ground-truth by the HR breath-hold scans, which may raise concerns about the validity of the results. Although it is understandable that true ground truth is generally unavailable, the authors should at least discuss the reliability of using such pseudo-labels or conduct a reader study to assess the clinical quality of the SR results. 2.The qualitative results should show different time frames across the scan to show the effectiveness of the SR results, considering this is a 4D scan. 3.Some more recent generative-based SISR methods like diffusion models should be included in comparison.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers (R1, R3, R4) for their constructive comments. We provide our responses to major concerns below and will correct all minor issues (typos, Fig.1) in the camera-ready version. 1: Limited 4D-MRI Data (R1, R3) As 4D-MRI is not yet clinical routine, it’ s extremely scarce and current studies typically enrolled ≤30 cases (e.g., Refs [1, 25, 27] in the paper). Nevertheless, each 4D-MRI contains 72 temporal frames, providing sufficient data for model optimization, as confirmed by converged validation loss. For rigorous evaluation, all experiments were repeated five times with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests in Table 1, and a public 3D MRI dataset (CHAOS) was used for additional evaluation. 2: Synthetic Deformations in CHAOS (R1) We wish to clarify that our main results (in-house 4D-MRI dataset) were obtained with real inter-scan deformations, validating performance on actual respiratory motion. Further incorporating public CHAOS data with synthetic deformations provides pixel-wise ground truth for quantitative evaluation, which is a widely used approach in related literature (Refs [3, 11] in the paper). 3: Real-Time Latency (R1) We apologize for missing this information. Our method meets real-time requirements (total ≤500 ms, MRI imaging ≤300 ms to allow reconstruction) [25]. Ours finished reconstruction in 252 ms (k=4) for ×4 4D-MRI (~173 ms), totaling ~425ms latency—well within the limit. 4: Unclear Presentation (R3) Given the extra half-page space in the camera-ready version, we plan to explicitly define ambiguous variables (e.g., Φ_R→L, Φ_S→H) and avoid inline-formatted losses (e.g., L_adv, L_smt, L_recon) to improve readability. Also, we will provide additional implementation details with our open-source code for better reproducibility. 5: Incorporating Temporal Correlations (R3) We’d like to note that our work focuses on prior-guided SR, which is crucial for real-time 4D-MRI under heavy undersampling because it is extremely difficult to recover lost structures based solely on 4D-MRI information. We agree that incorporating temporal correlations is also promising for 4D-MRI, but there also exists a concern that reliance on inter-frame correlations may lead to error accumulation, where reconstruction errors from previous frames can accumulate to the current one. We will further explore this in future studies as this is a non-trivial topic beyond the scope of this work. 6: LPIPS backbone & MRI Undersampling Method (R3); More Visualization (R4) Backbone network for LPIPS is AlexNet, and undersampling method in CHAOS is radial undersampling, which will be added to the camera-ready version. Visualization of different time frames will be provided in online resource with our code. 7: Image Restoration (IR) or Super-Resolution (SR)? (R3) We respectfully suggest that undersampled MRI reconstruction is typically defined as a SR problem, consistent with existing RefSR and multi-contrast SR works (e.g., Refs [3, 5, 11-14] in our paper). 8: Pseudo Ground-Truth (GT) of 4D-MRI (R4) Hardware limitations prevent acquiring fully aligned GT for 4D-MRI. To address inevitable misalignment in pseudo GT, we proposed ACMT for training (mitigating SR-HR spatial mismatches via a registration module) and used Elastix for rigorous pre-registration during evaluation. The latter evaluation protocol is widely used in related literature where GT is inherently missing (Refs [23, 27] in the paper). In addition, as mentioned in Q1/Q2, we also adopted the CHAOS dataset with simulated deformations for rigorous quantitative assessment against real pixel-wise GT. We agree that reader study would strengthen clinical validation and will include this as future work. 9: Compare with Diffusion-based SOTA (R4) As suggested, we add a comparison to Diffusion-based InvSR (CVPR’25) and observe that our method still outperforms it with statistical significance (e.g., 20.11 vs 22.04 in PSNR, 85.01 vs 92.34 in SSIM for ×4 4D-MRI, p < 0.001).

title: Dual-Space Cold-Start Active Learning Guided by SAM3 for Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper presents an innovative combination of representative-based and coverage-based methods for sample selection. By leveraging masks generated by the zero-shot foundation model SAM3 (via text prompts) to construct a diversified description space, the proposed method effectively addresses the common issues of existing approaches, which often select redundant similar samples or overly focus on boundary cases. 2.The overall organization of the manuscript is clear. The motivation is well-justified, and the proposed approach demonstrates a solid level of technical novelty. 3.The experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves strong, state-of-the-art performance in terms of the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) compared to existing baselines. Furthermore, the authors provide relatively comprehensive ablation studies to validate their network design choices.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The scale of the experiments is somewhat limited. The evaluation is conducted on a relatively small number of datasets, which significantly weakens the persuasiveness regarding the generalizability and robustness of the proposed method. To make the claims more convincing, the authors are encouraged to evaluate their approach on more diverse and larger-scale datasets. 2.The manuscript lacks a thorough discussion on the scenarios where the proposed method underperforms. Specifically, the quantitative results show a disadvantage compared to some baseline methods under the Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD) metric, but the authors fail to provide any insights or explanations for this. A detailed analysis of this limitation is necessary.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem in medical image segmentation, namely cold-start active learning under limited annotation budgets. The proposed dual-space design is intuitive and technically reasonable, combining representative sampling in feature space with morphology-aware diversity in pseudo-mask space. The experiments cover two public datasets, include multiple baselines and an ablation study, and show clear gains in Dice score under low-budget settings.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper does not compare with the most relevant recent SAM-based CSAL baseline, especially SUGFW [15], which weakens the claim of state-of-the-art performance. The methodological novelty appears moderate, since the main design combines representative sampling and diversity sampling ideas that are already central in prior methods such as TypiClust [6], BAL [9], and Core-set [19]. The empirical gains are more convincing in Dice than in boundary quality: ASSD is not consistently improved and is worse than several baselines in some settings. Reproducibility is limited because several key details are unclear, including SAM3 prompt construction, the exact quality-score computation, feature extraction settings, and how the two spaces are normalized and combined.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper is generally well-written, with a clear structure and coherent presentation. The figures effectively illustrate the key ideas of the proposed framework. 2.The proposed modules are well-motivated, and the overall framework is technically sound. The dual-space design is conceptually consistent, and the Cluster-Balanced Penalty provides a reasonable mechanism to alleviate redundancy in the Centroid Affinity Scoring process. 3.The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on two public datasets, demonstrating its empirical effectiveness.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.It would strengthen the paper to include ablation studies across different versions of SAM models, to better understand the robustness and generalizability of the proposed framework. 2.Additional visualizations illustrating the effect of the Cluster-Balanced Penalty in the feature space would improve interpretability and provide more intuitive insights into its contribution.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing the motivation (R1/R2), design (R1/R2/R3), and performance (R1/R2/R3) of our method. We address the main concerns below: *Novelty(R2) While representative sampling is a general CSAL principle, CSAL methods differ in definition of representativeness. Unlike existing methods[6,9,19] purely define it based on global image feature we further introduce object morphology-aware representativeness to encourage size/shape diversity based on SAM3 text-prompted pseudo-masks (Sec.2.1). We also introduce CBP to obtain a better feature-based representative score, and combine them in a unified score (Sec.2.3) for better sample selection. *SUGFW comparison(R2) The source code of SUGFW was not actively maintained. We attempted to reproduce SUGFW under our segmentation backbone, but due to some unresolved issues in data preprocessing and hyper-parameter tuning, we failed to get results. We will contact the first author of SUGFW for help and encourage the author to fix the issues. *ASSD analysis(R1/R2) Compared with Dice, ASSD is highly sensitive to small distant false-positive regions, which can disproportionately increase the surface distance. To diagnose the higher ASSD in the 15-sample PROMISE12 setting (Tab.1), we applied largest-connected-component post-processing as an auxiliary analysis. ASSD decreases from 6.15 mm to 2.83 mm, suggesting that the higher raw ASSD mainly comes from scattered disconnected false positives rather than poor segmentation of the main prostate region. This is consistent with our morphology-aware acquisition, which improves Dice by prioritizing structurally diverse foreground samples, but may yield more aggressive foreground predictions under limited budgets. As the budget increases, our method achieves the best ASSD with 100 samples. We will briefly explain this. *Reproducibility(R2/MR) Following MedSAM3[13] and standard prompt template of SAM3, we prompt SAM3 with “skin lesion” for ISIC 2018 and “prostate” for PROMISE12 for reproducibility. For feature extraction, we use the penultimate layer of the SAM3 image encoder and spatial pool it for CAS. As described in Sec 2.2, the quality score is derived from SAM3’s final image-text cross-attention map[10] by projecting their attention to the spatial grid, taking the maximum token probability at each position, and averaging spatially. For normalization, centroid-affinity scores and morphological descriptors are min-max normalized over candidates, and mask-diversity distances are dynamically normalized at each greedy selection step before being combined. We will release the code for reproducibility. *Dataset scale and SAM-variant robustness(R1/R3) Small sample size is an important and common challenge in medical image analysis, which motivates adapting pre-trained models like SAM/SAM3 to downstream medical image tasks. This work shows a cold start active adaptation of SAM3 for two medical image segmentation tasks with smaller dataset size than natural images. However, too small dataset will reduce the reliability of results, so we chose Prostate12 (100 cases) and ISIC 2018 (2594 cases) that are moderate to ensure reliable conclusion. SAM1/SAM2 were not included since their target-specific masks require point/box prompts, which conflicts with CSAL setting where no mask is provided beforehand. We use SAM3 because its text-prompted, concept-driven zero-shot inference enable obtaining pseudo-masks without additional annotation cost. *Visualization of the CBP(R3) Due to space limits and the high-dimensional feature, a 2D visualization is difficult to include in the current manuscript. We therefore support this module through detailed ablation studies, where adding the penalty consistently improves performance. We will explore toy-data visualizations in an extended version to show how CBP avoids over-selection from dominant clusters.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper is borderline-positive (scores 3–5), with reviewers recognizing a practical and well-motivated dual-space active learning framework, clear presentation, and strong Dice improvements. The rebuttal should mainly address the missing comparison to the closest recent SAM-based CSAL baseline, clarify the novelty beyond combining representative and diversity sampling, explain the weaker ASSD/boundary results, and improve reproducibility by detailing SAM3 prompts, quality scoring, feature extraction, and space normalization/combination. It would also help to comment on robustness across SAM variants and dataset scale. Overall, the concerns are focused and addressable, so a clear rebuttal could strengthen the case for acceptance. | Prior to the rebuttal, the paper received a single negative rating (WR). However, this reviewer did not provide any follow-up comments after the authors’ rebuttal. In contrast, the rebuttal successfully addressed the concerns raised by the other reviewers and led to a more favorable overall assessment. Based on the reviewers’ feedback and the authors’ responses, the AC recommends acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This submission somehow received mixed scores, with reviewers mainly questioning the actual novelty, and clarifications on results and reproducibility. After carefully reading authors rebuttal, I believe that these concerns were satisfactorily addressed, and thus recommend the acceptance of this paper. I encourage the authors to incorporate these clarifications and improvements into the camera‑ready version Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I recommend rejection. The paper addresses an important problem, namely cold-start active learning for medical image segmentation, but the current submission has several significant weaknesses. First, the methodological novelty is limited. The proposed framework mainly combines existing ideas: centroid/typicality-based sampling, cluster balancing, farthest-point-style diversity sampling, and pseudo-mask descriptors from a foundation model. The paper does not clearly establish why this combination is technically new beyond an engineering aggregation of known components. Second, the use of SAM3 is insufficiently justified and under-specified. The method relies heavily on SAM3 features, pseudo-masks, and cross-attention-based quality scores, but the paper does not clearly define the prompting strategy, the mask-generation protocol, or why the proposed attention-based uncertainty is a reliable proxy for medical segmentation quality. This is particularly problematic because the self-training baseline shows highly unstable pseudo-mask quality, especially on ISIC 2018. Third, there are important technical ambiguities in the acquisition function. The figure includes a weighting parameter between the image-space and mask-space scores, but the final equation omits it. The normalization of the mask distance, initialization when no sample has been selected, the choice of the number of clusters, and the computation of the quality score are not sufficiently specified. These details are critical for reproducibility. Fourth, the experimental evidence does not strongly support the claimed superiority. Many reported improvements are small relative to the very large standard deviations. For example, on ISIC 2018 with 100 samples, the DSC gain over strong baselines is marginal, while the ASSD is worse than several methods. On PROMISE12 with 15 samples, the proposed method has the best DSC but a relatively poor ASSD. Therefore, the claim of consistent and substantial improvement is overstated. Finally, the evaluation scope is limited. Only two datasets are used, and the annotation unit is not fully clear for PROMISE12, where 2D slices are selected but 3D volumetric evaluation is reported. The paper would also benefit from stronger statistical testing, clearer baseline implementation details, and broader validation across more medical modalities.

It would be helpful to briefly explain what is meant by “pseudo-break transformations” early ion the text as they are referenced multiple times before Section 2.2. From the text and Figure 1, it is not entirely clear at which points pseudo-break transformations are incorporated into the M1 and M2 model training.

reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Continual test-time adaptation for 3D vessel segmentation is an important yet underexplored setting, especially given the practical challenges of domain shift in medical imaging and the structural sensitivity of vascular segmentation. The paper identifies a meaningful gap between existing generic CTA methods and the specific demands of vessel analysis. 2.Continual test-time adaptation for 3D vessel segmentation is an important yet underexplored setting, especially given the practical challenges of domain shift in medical imaging and the structural sensitivity of vascular segmentation. The paper identifies a meaningful gap between existing generic CTA methods and the specific demands of vessel analysis. 3.The pseudo-break transformation is a meaningful way to simulate topology-damaging perturbations and encourages the model to learn structurally robust adaptation. reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.While the teacher and student roles are reassigned online based on entropy, the actual optimization in Sec. 2.3 still becomes a one-way supervision scheme within each iteration, where the lower-entropy model is treated as a fixed teacher. Since lower entropy does not necessarily imply a more correct prediction under domain shift, the method may still inherit overconfident teacher errors. This point deserves deeper analysis and clearer empirical validation. 2.The method involves several task-specific settings, such as the binarization threshold for pseudo masks, the dilation setting in Eq. (4), the patch size and Gaussian scale in the pseudo-break transformation, and the persistence threshold used in Eq. (8). While these choices are reasonable, the paper would benefit from a bit more discussion or sensitivity analysis to help readers better understand their impact on performance and robustness. 3.The paper claims improvements in preserving vessel topology and reducing structural errors such as disconnections or false branches. reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Important and timely problem setting. The paper addresses continual test-time adaptation for 3D vessel segmentation, which is highly relevant for real-world medical deployment under cross-center and cross-device distribution shifts. This is a meaningful extension of CTA to a clinically relevant structured segmentation problem. Clear technical novelty. The proposed method is not a minor variant of existing CTA pipelines. The dynamic collaborative mechanism challenges the common assumption that the teacher is always more reliable than the student, which is particularly reasonable in complex 3D vascular segmentation. This is a well-motivated and interesting design choice. Topology-aware formulation is well aligned with the task. The pseudo-break transformation and the topological regularization are both tailored to the structural characteristics of vessels. Rather than relying only on generic entropy minimization or pixel-level consistency, the method explicitly targets connectivity preservation and the reduction of topology-breaking artifacts such as disconnections and spurious branches. Strong empirical evaluation. The paper provides experiments on both cerebrovascular and cardiovascular datasets and reports consistent improvements over a broad range of CTA baselines. The long-term adaptation experiment is also valuable, as it directly addresses error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting, which are central concerns in CTA. Good overall paper quality. The method is conceptually coherent, the ablation study supports the contribution of each component, and the submission also provides an anonymized code link, which further strengthens reproducibility.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper is strong overall, and my concerns are relatively minor. First, the computational overhead and memory/runtime cost of DyCo-CTA are not analyzed in sufficient depth. Since CTA is an online adaptation setting, efficiency is important for practical deployment, especially in 3D medical imaging. Second, although the paper argues that this is the first CTA work for 3D vessel segmentation, the final version could better position itself with respect to prior topology-aware tubular segmentation and topology-enhanced adaptation literature, for example recent topology-preserving tubular segmentation and topology-aware TTA works. A sharper discussion of what is fundamentally new here beyond extending teacher-student CTA to 3D vessel data would make the contribution even clearer. Third, some implementation details could be explained more thoroughly, such as the sensitivity to the pseudo-break construction strength, the choice of the persistence threshold, and the robustness of the dynamic switching criterion. These points mainly affect completeness and reproducibility, rather than the validity of the core idea. Overall, these weaknesses do not undermine the main contribution or the empirical strength of the paper.
