author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the importance of ASL-specific representation learning, the value of the large multi-site ASL dataset, and the potential utility of ICHOR as a reusable ASL encoder. Reviewers noted that the work addresses an important gap, uses one of the largest ASL datasets to date, and demonstrates improved performance across downstream tasks. The reviewers also raised thoughtful critiques and questions, which we have organized into the following themes and address below. Contribution, positioning, and novelty (R1, R2, R3). We appreciate that reviewers recognized the timeliness and practical impact of developing a representation model for ASL CBF. Reviewers also noted that MAE, ViT, and LoRA are established components rather than new modeling techniques. We acknowledge this point, and emphasize that the contribution is best viewed as an application and resource contribution: integrating these components for ASL CBF at scale, supported by a curated dataset of 11,405 scans from 14 studies and validated across four downstream tasks. ICHOR is intended as an ASL-specific pretrained encoder, rather than a modality-agnostic foundation model. This distinction is central because ASL CBF maps encode physiological perfusion rather than anatomical contrast, and no comparable pretrained backbone currently exists for this modality. Rationale for MAE-based ASL pretraining (R1). R1 raised an important question about why MAE-style pretraining is suitable for ASL CBF maps. ASL CBF maps are low-SNR, spatially structured physiological images affected by acquisition variability. Reconstructing masked 3D regions from visible context encourages the model to learn distributed perfusion structure and global spatial dependencies, rather than relying only on local intensity patterns. This is particularly relevant for heterogeneous multi-site ASL data, where robust representations must capture shared perfusion structure across variable acquisition conditions. Evaluation design and downstream task relevance (R1, R2, R3). We appreciate that reviewers recognized the breadth of downstream evaluation, while also noting that some labeled cohorts are small. Limited labeled data is a fundamental constraint in ASL and is a primary motivation for self-supervised pretraining. To reduce instability from small samples, we used nested 5-fold cross-validation with held-out test folds rather than a single split. R2 also raised a question about the clinical relevance of the Aβ task, noting that ASL is not typically used to evaluate amyloid positivity in clinical practice. Our goal is not to propose ASL as a standalone clinical amyloid test. Rather, this task evaluates whether ICHOR captures disease-relevant perfusion patterns that distinguish CU Aβ− controls from cognitively impaired Aβ+ participants, consistent with prior evidence that ASL CBF is sensitive to AD-related neurodegeneration. Adaptation strategy and additional comparisons (R2, R3). R2 and R3 raised helpful points regarding comparison to existing ASL tools and the choice of LoRA for downstream adaptation. ICHOR is designed as a reusable pretrained encoder, and LoRA was chosen as a parameter-efficient adaptation strategy for limited-label settings and to provide a consistent adaptation protocol across downstream tasks. We agree with R3 that full fine-tuning would be an informative additional comparison and is an important direction for future work. Regarding comparison with ASLPrep and related ASL quality tools (R2), these methods are primarily designed for preprocessing or quality assessment, whereas ICHOR is intended to learn representations that can transfer across multiple task types. Therefore, comparison across diagnostic tasks would not be appropriate. However, a targeted comparison on the ASL quality prediction task would be valuable in future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): Strengths: The paper makes a strong practical contribution by assembling a very large ASL CBF dataset and introducing an ASL-specific self-supervised masked-autoencoder pretraining framework that shows useful downstream performance with lightweight fine-tuning and promises reusable pretrained weights. Weaknesses: There are some minor concerns of the details of the method, since MAE/ViT/LoRA are established components, ambiguity about whether the goal is a foundation model or ASL-specific feature extractor, small downstream task datasets, and the need for clearer guidance on replication and use by other researchers. The work might be accepted after some minor corrections.

reviewer_2_strengths: Clear motivation and clinical relevance: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem in dynamic LGE MRI, namely reducing motion artifacts associated with conventional motion-compensated LGE. Technical contribution: The proposed framework formulates LGE as a dynamic reconstruction problem and incorporates inception modules and physics-based priors for highly accelerated reconstruction. Comprehensive evaluation: The paper includes comparisons against four baseline methods, ablation studies, and evaluation on two clinical datasets. Additional robustness analysis: The inclusion of free-breathing data and noise robustness experiments further supports the evaluation.

The introduction would be strengthened by discussing these related studies and clarifying how the proposed method differs from them. Please clarify whether the PSIR data were acquired under segmented breath-held conditions or free-breathing conditions. A small schematic of the acquisition protocol would improve clarity. More complete reporting of model configuration, optimization settings, hyperparameters, and evaluation details would improve reproducibility. [1] Sultan, Muhammad Ahmad, et al. “An unsupervised method for MRI recovery: deep image prior with structured sparsity.” Magnetic Resonance Materials in Physics, Biology and Medicine, 38.5, 2025, 859–871.[2] Vornehm M., Chen C., Sultan M.A., et al. “Multi-dynamic deep image prior for cardiac MRI.” Magnetic Resonance in Medicine, 2025;94(6):2668–2679.doi: 10.1002/mrm.70000.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.While deep unrolling networks are established in MRI reconstruction, the integration of Inception modules into the iterative loops is a novel architectural contribution. This design effectively enhances multi-scale feature representation, allowing the network to simultaneously capture global structural context and fine-grained local details during each iteration. 2.The paper proposes a clever reformulation of the problem by treating conventional static Late Gadolinium Enhancement (LGE) MRI as a dynamic multi-frame reconstruction task. By partitioning sequential k-space acquisitions into temporally localized subsets, the authors exploit temporal redundancy without extending scan time. This approach is clinically significant as it directly targets motion robustness by leveraging temporal consistency rather than relying solely on spatial priors. 3.The validation strategy is a strong aspect of this work. The authors utilized a large-scale dataset comprising 100 subjects from 3T clinical scanners, supplemented with additional 5T data. This scale is substantial for deep learning MRI studies and enhances the statistical power of the results. Demonstrating consistent improvements over state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines across different field strengths (3T and 5T) suggests that the method is not only effective but also generalizable across different hardware configurations, which is crucial for clinical translation. 4.The paper provides a thorough ablation study that clearly isolates the contributions of key components: Architectural Impact: Comparing the full model against variants without the Inception module validates the specific benefit of multi-scale representation. Training Strategy: Evaluating the impact of the mixed-data training strategy helps understand the role of data diversity in model performance. Motion and Noise Robustness: The inclusion of synthetic noise experiments (varying SNR) and, most importantly, validation under free-breathing conditions demonstrates the method’s practical utility. Showing superior performance compared to standard single-frame static LGE imaging in the presence of motion artifacts strongly supports the claim of improved clinical feasibility.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The authors describe the method as “physics-guided,” yet the manuscript lacks sufficient technical detail regarding how the physical forward model is integrated into the network architecture. Is it just data consistency (DC) layer or there is another physics learned. Without this clarification, it is difficult to assess whether the method truly leverages physics-based constraints to ensure fidelity to acquired data, or if it relies primarily on data-driven priors. This distinction is vital for understanding the method’s robustness to out-of-distribution sampling patterns or hardware variations. 2.The proposed method relies on Inception modules within a deep unrolling framework to handle the “dynamic” multi-frame nature of the reformulated LGE problem. However, the authors do not sufficiently justify why this convolutional-based multi-scale approach was chosen over established sequence modeling architectures such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), or Vision Transformers (ViT). 3.The paper does not provide adequate details on the k-space undersampling (acceleration) scheme used during training and evaluation. Key parameters such as the acceleration factor, the type of mask (e.g., random Cartesian, variable-density Poisson disk, radial, or spiral), and the centering strategy (number of auto-calibration signal lines) are either missing or vaguely described. Furthermore, it is unclear if the same masking strategy was applied across both the 3T and 5T datasets. 4.The authors claim that their “parameter-shared fixed-point implementation reduces memory consumption,” but this assertion is not supported by empirical evidence.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: Thank all reviewers and the Meta-reviewer for the constructive comments. 1.Novelty and design rationale: We clarify that our framework is a task-specific design for ultra-high-accelerated (R>11) dynamic LGE reconstruction rather than a simple combination of existing modules. Therefore, our primary novelty lies not in introducing isolated network components, but in establishing a dynamic reconstruction methodology specifically tailored for highly accelerated PSIR-LGE acquisition. 1) From Static Recovery to Dynamic Reconstruction. Conventional motion-compensated LGE methods fuse multiple shots into a single static image. In contrast, we reconstruct each PSIR shot as an independent frame without explicit motion compensation or shot fusion, while exploiting temporal redundancy across shots during reconstruction. This reformulation converts motion from an artifact source into a resolvable reconstruction dimension. 2) Task-Specific Multi-Scale Prior for Dynamic LGE. LGE reconstruction under R>11 simultaneously requires the preservation of small structures like hyperenhanced scar and the suppression of globally distributed aliasing artifacts. The Inception module provides complementary receptive fields for these two competing requirements, while LSTM or ViTs may struggle to simultaneously preserve local features and suppress global aliasing under extreme acceleration. 3) Fixed-Point Unrolling for Dynamic Reconstruction. For high-resolution 2D+t reconstruction, naive deep unrolling becomes computationally prohibitive due to the large memory consumption associated with storing intermediate variables across iterations. We therefore adopt a fixed-point implementation with Jacobian-free backpropagation. It enables memory-efficient iterative reconstruction for dynamic data within practical GPU memory constraints. The physics-guided component corresponds to explicit data consistency using the multi-coil forward model. Unlike recent DIP-based dynamic LGE methods requiring subject-specific optimization during inference, our supervised framework enables fast and efficient inference. 2.Acquisition and implementation clarification: The reconstructed “phases” do not correspond to conventional cardiac phases or respiratory phases. Instead, they are generated from independently acquired PSIR shots collected across adjacent R-R intervals. We employed a time-interleaved Cartesian undersampling strategy (TGRAPPA-style sampling). Time-averaged central ACS lines (14–22 depending on orientation) were used for coil sensitivity estimation. The same undersampling strategy was applied to both 3T and 5T datasets. Typical imaging parameters were TR/TE(ms)=4.3/1.82 (4CH), 5.2/2.13 (3CH/2CH), and 4.2/1.73 (SAX), with 5–8 shots depending on acquisition orientation. The model was trained using a combined MAE and perceptual loss with equal weighting. Due to page limits, these details were omitted; code will be released upon acceptance. 3.Experimental clarification: 1) To better show the reconstruction quality of myocardium, we tightly cropped the reconstructed images with only cardiac region remaining. Our method performs better in artifact suppression and detail preservation of myocardium, and shows less phase-inconsistency-related distortions in the full image. The arrow annotations to Fig 2 and full images of Fig 3 will be added to highlight our advantage. 2) The counter-intuitive observation (CS outperforming MoDL in SSIM) was primarily due to an inconsistency in the intensity normalization protocols during the initial metric calculation. We have now re-evaluated all baselines using a unified, strictly consistent normalization framework. The corrected results now show consistent superiority of deep learning methods over traditional CS. We apologize for this oversight and have updated Tables 1–2 accordingly. 4.Discussion: Current reconstruction quality may degrade under more aggressive acceleration, which will be discussed in the revised manuscript.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The manuscript addresses a clinically relevant problem in accelerated dynamic LGE MRI and reports promising results on a large 3T cohort with additional 5T validation. However, the novelty over prior motion-resolved/free-breathing LGE reconstruction and recent dynamic MRI reconstruction methods is not clearly established, and the technical contribution appears to mainly combine known components. The rebuttal should focus on clarifying the specific methodological novelty, explaining the LGE acquisition and k-space-to-frame partitioning, justifying the baseline choices, and providing the missing implementation details needed for reproducibility. The authors should also clarify the reported baseline behavior and temper claims that are not directly supported by the submitted experiments. | The paper addresses an important clinical problem and reports promising reconstruction results. However, the rebuttal does not fully resolve concerns about novelty relative to prior dynamic/motion-resolved LGE and existing unrolled reconstruction methods. The clarification that the reconstructed frames are PSIR shots rather than conventional cardiac or respiratory phases also weakens the paper’s original framing. In addition, the acknowledged normalization error in the submitted quantitative comparisons reduces confidence in the reported performance gains. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and presents a technically interesting framework for motion-robust dynamic LGE reconstruction with reasonable experimental validation. Reviewers were split: two recommended acceptance while one recommended rejection, based on limited methodological novelty, outdated baselines, and missing implementation details. The rebuttal larified the key design rationale, acquisition protocol, and corrected a normalization inconsistency in the baseline comparison. The remaining concern regarding novelty over prior dynamic LGE reconstruction work is noted, but does not outweigh the overall merit. title: Interpretable Local-to-Global Estimation of Brain Aging Speed From Morphological Changes Using Longitudinal Structural MRI Data
reviewer_1_strengths: The approach is novel and interesting to model longitudinal morphological trajectories based on a diffeomorphic registration framework. The results are strong, especially for cross-site generalization compared to previous state-of-the-art.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The first part of your model (deep learning-based diffeomorphic image registration) follows exactly the VoxelMorph pipeline. Is it trained along with the actual regressor of aging speed based on the Jacobian determinant map? If yes, do you observe a correlation between the registration accuracy and the speed aging prediction accuracy? (Suggestion) In your model, you only consider time difference (t2-t1) between two scans, implicitly assuming the morphological changes do not depend on the initial timepoint t1 (i. e. original age). According to current brain charts [Bethlehem, Nature 2022], we know this is not true because brain morphology typically evolves non-linearly with time (and is even different across sex). I wonder whether including the original timepoint t1 (and maybe sex) as input to the model (in addition to the two scans) would refine the quality of the brain aging speed estimation.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Well-motivated and clearly presented idea: The paper is built on a clear and intuitive premise that longitudinal data can better capture aging dynamics compared to cross-sectional approaches. In addition, the use of localized (patch-level) information is well justified, as it enhances both interpretability and predictive performance. Meaningful use of morphological information: Leveraging morphology derived from diffeomorphic registration is a strong design choice, as it focuses on biologically relevant changes rather than relying solely on intensity-based features. Comprehensive experimental validation: The experiments are generally sufficient to support the main claims, including comparisons between morphology vs. intensity features and localized vs. global modeling. Evaluation on downstream clinical tasks: The inclusion of experiments on diseased populations strengthens the practical relevance of the work and demonstrates potential clinical utility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: While the combination of morphology-based features and patch-level modeling is well motivated, each component has been explored in prior work (e.g., registration-based morphometry and patch-based learning). The paper would benefit from a clearer articulation of what is fundamentally new beyond this integration, and how it advances the state of the art. Missing details on hyperparameter weighting: The paper does not specify the hyperparameters that control the relative strength of each loss term. Unexpected generalization behavior: The model achieves lower error (MAE and RMSE) on the external test set than the internal set, which is counterintuitive.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important limitation of brain age delta by explicitly modeling aging dynamics through longitudinal data, which is a meaningful and relevant direction. 2.The use of deformation fields and Jacobian determinants as representations of structural change is technically sound and biologically meaningful compared to intensity-based differences. 3.The patch-wise regression framework is an interesting design choice that enables spatial interpretability while maintaining a global prediction. 4.The paper includes: -comparisons with cross-sectional and longitudinal baselines, -ablation studies (without morphology / without local prediction), -evaluation on internal and external datasets.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Figure 3 presents trends of aging speed across different diagnostic progression groups (e.g., CU-to-CU, MCI-to-AD), computed as averages within age bins. However, the manuscript does not report: -the number of samples per group -the number of samples per age bin -any measure of variability (e.g., standard deviation, confidence intervals, or error bars) This is a critical limitation, as the observed trends may be strongly influenced by differences in sample size across groups or bins. In particular, progression groups are likely smaller and unevenly distributed across age ranges, which can lead to unstable estimates and misleading trends. As a result, it is difficult to determine whether the reported differences reflect genuine biological effects or are artifacts of sampling variability. 2.The paper concludes that progression groups exhibit higher aging speed based on the trends in Figure 3.However, no statistical test is reported to compare these groups, and no uncertainty estimates are provided. Given the lack of quantitative support, these conclusions appear overstated. 3.The proposed aging speed metric is central to the contribution, yet its validity is not rigorously demonstrated. In particular, the paper does not show: -correlation with clinical outcomes or cognitive measures, -comparison with established biomarkers (e.g., brain age delta) beyond qualitative trends, -robustness or stability of the metric across subjects. As a result, it remains unclear whether the proposed measure captures meaningful biological aging dynamics or primarily reflects model-specific behavior. 4.The method relies entirely on deformation fields obtained via diffeomorphic registration. However, no analysis is provided regarding: -sensitivity to registration errors, -robustness across different registration approaches, -potential artifacts introduced by misalignment. Given that the Jacobian determinant maps are the core input to the model, this is an important missing validation.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. Following meta-review, we first address the methodological and statistical concerns, then respond to additional points. Q1: Statistical rigor of group comparisons (Fig. 3) [R4-C1,C2; Meta-Review] We appreciate this important concern. We have amended Fig. 3 to include 1) sample sizes per group and per age bin, and 2) Wilcoxon rank-sum test results between converter and non-converter groups, overall and within each age bin. Brain age delta showed significant differences (p < 0.01) between two non-converter groups of different disease severity (CU->CU vs. MCI->MCI) across all age bins and overall. For aging speed, MCI->AD differed significantly from both non-converter groups across all age bins (p < 0.01), while CN->MCI differed significantly in the 60-64 age bin. Crucially, the non-converter groups (CU->CU vs. MCI->MCI) showed no significant aging speed differences across most age bins, confirming that aging speed captures disease progression rather than severity, unlike brain age delta. Q2: Age and sex as confounders [R1-C2; Meta-Review] We agree brain morphology changes nonlinearly with age and differs between sex. In our framework, the Jacobian determinant maps may already implicitly encode age-dependent atrophy patterns. Incorporating t_1 as an input feature at the output layer of regressors yielded comparable performance on CU subjects (MAE :1.15, R2: 0.67 internal test; MAE: 0.72, R2: 0.58 external test), suggesting Jacobian maps already capture substantial age-related information. However, more advanced conditioning methods (e.g., FT-Transformers or FiLM) may further improve predictions, which is a promising future work, and we will discuss this limitation in the revised manuscript. Q3: Validation of the aging speed metric [R4-C3] Spearman correlations between the estimated aging speed and longitudinal cognitive change (on ADNI CU test + all ADNI MCI/AD subjects) were statistically significant: MMSE (-0.23), CDR (0.28), FAQ (0.24), ADAS13 (0.23), all p < 0.001.These further confirm aging speed captures clinically meaningful cognitive decline, not merely model-specific behavior. Q4: Registration robustness [R1-C1, R4-C4] Our framework is end-to-end and jointly trained; registration and regression errors decrease simultaneously, with registration converging first. The registration part is a within-subject registration task, which is inherently easier than cross-subject registration, reducing susceptibility to large misalignment. Also, Table 2 (rows 5–6 vs. 2–3) consistently shows improvements over methods without morphological features, demonstrating the utility and robustness of deformation-based representations. Nevertheless, we agree that a systematic comparison across registration methods is a valuable future work. Q5: Novelty [R3-C1] Our contribution addresses two limitations of prior works: 1) intensity-based methods are sensitive to imaging noise and variability, whereas within-subject registration-derived Jacobian determinants provide morphology-driven, noise-robust features reflecting anatomical aging; 2) existing methods predict a single global aging speed, whereas our patch-wise prediction with learned aggregation explicitly models spatial heterogeneity, improving both prediction accuracy (Table 2) and interpretability (Fig. 4). Their integration within a jointly optimized framework is, to our knowledge, novel. Q6: Hyperparameter details [R3-C2] Default hyperparameters were used for registration, similar to prior studies [5]. The full loss is: 1.0 L_reg + 0.01 L_smo + 1.0 L_local + 1.0 L_global. These details will be added to the manuscript. Q7: Lower external test error [R3-C3] This reflects dataset characteristics: AIBL has a narrower age range and smaller longitudinal intervals (\Delta t) than ADNI/OASIS (Table 1). All comparison methods achieved lower external errors, confirming a dataset-level rather than model-specific effect.

title: Interpretable Longitudinal Disease Forecasting with Graph-Based Multimodal Encoding and Population-Aware Language Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: Strength 1: Novel Integration of MLMs for Interpretable Clinical Forecasting This is pioneering work bringing multimodal language models to longitudinal disease forecasting with structured interpretability, addressing a critical gap in medical AI where most models are “black boxes. “ The hierarchical explanation structure (VI, RC, LC, PG) is clinically meaningful and mirrors how physicians reason about disease progression - considering current status, recent changes, long-term trends, and expected trajectory. The dual-task learning (forecasting + explanation generation) is elegant: the model learns better disease representations by being forced to generate clinically grounded explanations, not just predict labels. Strength 2: Sophisticated Handling of Missing and Heterogeneous Data The bipartite graph encoding (BGE) is technically sound for handling incomplete multimodal longitudinal records - a ubiquitous challenge in real clinical data. Graph structure naturally represents variable-time relationships with missingness encoded in connectivity patterns, more principled than simple imputation or loss masking. The method handles three types of variables (time-variant tabular, time-invariant tabular, imaging patches) in a unified framework using GNN with multi-head attention. Strength 3: Strong Empirical Results with Comprehensive Evaluation Impressive improvements over strong baselines: 84.2% accuracy vs. 76.4% for best baseline (UniLM), 89.3% AUC vs. 89.0% for GraFITi. Outperforms recent LLM/MLM methods (DTGPT, NoteLM, ViT-LM) across all metrics, demonstrating the value of the proposed architectural innovations. Multi-faceted evaluation: quantitative forecasting metrics (ACC, SEN, SPE, F1, AUC), NLG quality metrics (BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L, BERTScore), LLM-based judge evaluation, AND clinician evaluation across 6 dimensions. Comprehensive comparisons: 9 baselines covering single-modality, multi-modality, and VLM approaches. Qualitative analysis (Fig. 3) shows the model generates more accurate, structured, and clinically coherent explanations compared to strong baseline (NoteLM).
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Weakness 1: Questionable Quality of GPT-Generated Teaching Labels Issue: The entire hierarchical interpretation structure (VI, RC, LC, PG) is generated by GPT-5.2 and used as teaching supervision. The paper states “To avoid manual summarization, we provide GPT-5.2 with the complete four-visit longitudinal records. . . “ However, there is no validation mechanism to verify the correctness of these GPT-generated annotations. This is problematic because: (1) The model is learning from potentially hallucinated or inconsistent explanations, (2) GPT-5.2 may not have medical expertise to accurately interpret normative deviations and generate clinically appropriate explanations, (3) No gold standard from actual clinicians is used for comparison. The reviewer asks (from focus points): “What are the mechanisms put in place for verifying the annotation given by ChatGPT considered as reference for the teaching for the different annotation VI, RC, LC, PG?” - This critical question is not addressed in the paper. Specific references: For concerns about LLM-generated medical data: Thirunavukarasu et al. , “Large language models in medicine,” Nature Medicine 2023; Singhal et al. , “Towards Expert-Level Medical Question Answering with Large Language Models,” arXiv 2023. Weakness 2: Missing Statistical Significance Testing Issue: No statistical significance tests are reported for the forecasting results in Table 1.While the proposed method shows improvements (e. g. , 84.2% ACC vs. 76.4% for UniLM), there are no p-values, confidence intervals, or significance tests (e. g. , DeLong test for AUC comparisons, McNemar’s test for accuracy). Given that results are reported on a test set of only 297 clips, statistical testing is crucial to establish whether observed differences are significant or could occur by chance. Reviewer’s focus note: “Need statistical test DeLong for AUC” Specific references: DeLong et al. , “Comparing the areas under two or more correlated receiver operating characteristic curves: a nonparametric approach,” Biometrics 1988. Weakness 3: Inconsistent and Unexplained Baseline Comparisons Issue: The reviewer notes “Why is LaTIM missing in the Visit missing comparison?” suggesting that some baselines are not consistently evaluated across conditions. Some baseline methods (DTGPT, NoteLM) are given an unfair advantage by providing ground-truth volumetric measurements directly as input, while other methods must extract this from imaging. The paper acknowledges this (“DTGPT and NoteLM are unable to process MRI images, instead ground-truth volumetric measurements are directly provided”) but doesn’t fully account for this advantage in interpretation of results. The paper claims improvements over NoteLM on explanation quality, but NoteLM has access to privileged information (ground-truth volumes), making the comparison less meaningful.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The authors introduced a graph-based multimodal encoder tailored to irregular, missing longitudinal data by treating time and variables as a bipartite graph with edge embeddings for observed values and a query-time aggregation mechanism.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The authors mentioned that their main contribution is to design Bipartite graph encoding (BGE). However, the authors have not emphasized the good points of this module. What is the novelty of this module? In addition, what is L_da^i loss in equation (1)? How is it computed? 2.I wonder if there is some data leakage. Why 399 participants but have 2342 clips. If one participant has more than one clip. I wonder if these clips from same participant appear in both training and testing sets. The author should clarify this 3.The author mentioned that this is multimodal longitudinal forecasting framework but looks like they only use MRI scan along with tabular data. I think we should not consider tabular data as a modality. 4.What feature do tabular data contain (age, sex, education level, gene, …)? 5.The author mentioned the limitation of existing method are irregular and incomplete multimodal data. But it’s not clear how the authors solve this problem. How about a subset of MRI scan or tabular data are missing? 6.Figure 1 is also not very clear for readers to understand how the proposed model work. The author should redraw it. 7.In Table 3, using only image without tabular data, the accuracy and F1 score drop ~30% compared to the use of image and tabular data. Could the authors explain this? Does the model dominate tabular data? 8.The authors lack of compare the proposed method with SOTA method in multimodal longitudinal predictions with missing data such as: +https://doi.org/10.1016/j.inffus.2022.11.028 https://doi.org/10.1109/JBHI.2024.3472462 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2022.102643
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The forecasting result itself is the cleanest piece of evidence and looks genuinely strong. The visit-4 diagnostic label is an objective ground truth independent of the language modeling, and a jump from 0.764 to 0.842 accuracy over the best baseline is not trivial. The robustness experiments under missing tabular variables and missing visits (Fig. 4c, 4d) are a sensible addition and the model appears to degrade gracefully. The bipartite graph formulation for handling irregular and incomplete longitudinal records is a reasonable design choice and builds on a defensible line of prior work (GraFITi, GRAPE). The motivation — that visualization-based interpretability via image synthesis demands expert reading, while structured language explanations are more directly useful — is well-taken.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Circularity in the explanation evaluation. This is my main substantive concern, and it runs through several parts of the evaluation in a way that is not adequately acknowledged. The reference explanations used as training targets are written by GPT-5.2 from the structured input data. The same GPT-5.2 is then used as the LLM-judge to score candidate explanations across the six clinical-correctness dimensions in Table 2.The model under evaluation is, to a meaningful extent, being trained to imitate the judge’s writing on inputs the judge has already seen in structured form, and is then graded by that judge. The first row of Table 2 makes this concrete: “GPT (GT)” is itself scored and receives 4.04–4.96 across the six dimensions, i.e., the judge rates its own outputs as near-ceiling. The authors do not comment on this, and the implications for the relative ordering of methods in Table 2 are unclear. The clinician evaluation in Fig. 2 is the right instrument for breaking this loop, but as reported it cannot do that work. Ten explanations, across five methods, scored on six dimensions by two clinicians, with no inter-rater agreement statistics, no confidence intervals, no significance tests, no rubric beyond the one-sentence definitions in the text, no statement on blinding or order randomization, and no information about the clinicians’ subspecialty or experience reading ADNI-style cases. With those gaps, the radar plot in Fig. 2 is suggestive at best. I would want to see, at minimum: the full prompt and rubric used by the LLM-judge (in supplementary); inter-rater agreement (Cohen’s κ or ICC) for the clinician panel; a substantially larger clinician sample and ideally a blinded pairwise preference protocol rather than absolute Likert scores, which are notoriously poorly calibrated across raters; and explicit discussion of the circularity introduced by using GPT-5.2 as both supervisor and judge. Asymmetric baselines for explanation quality. DTGPT and NoteLM are given ground-truth volumetric measurements as text input, while image-based methods (including ENIGMA) must extract this from MRI. The authors note this and treat it as a handicap they overcome, but it cuts in both directions: the text-only baselines lack feature-extraction noise, which should favor their explanation quality, but they also lack any mechanism to identify imaging findings the volumetrics don’t capture. It is hard to read Table 2 cleanly given this asymmetry, and a more apples-to-apples baseline — say, NoteLM given the same MRI features ENIGMA extracts — would strengthen the case. Single-cohort evaluation. All results are on ADNI, with one preprocessing pipeline (FreeSurfer + MNI152), one LLM backbone (Qwen3-4B), and an exclusion criterion (no pre-visit-4 converters) that selects for slower progressors. There is no external cohort validation. For a paper whose central claim includes “population-aware” forecasting, the absence of any out-of-distribution test is notable. Minor / Clarification Questions The notation nn.Embedding should be spelled out (it’s a learnable lookup table); calling it by its PyTorch class name will not be transparent to all readers. The phrase “L = 4 layers GNN using multi-head attention blocks” deserves a sentence clarifying that the GNN is attention-based message-passing rather than convolutional, since “GNN” is overloaded in the literature. The w-score concept is used heavily but never defined; one sentence (“residual from a covariate-adjusted normative model, divided by residual SD”) would help readers outside the normative-modeling community. The rationale for selecting α_cl = 2.0, α_ca = 1.0, the 25% router sparsity target, and the memory length of 64 (Fig. 4a is shown but the criterion is unstated) should be made explicit. The footnote deferring “detailed implementation documentation” to a post-camera-ready GitHub release is a familiar dodge, and given how much methodological detail is unspecified in the main text, I would want to see at least a methods supplement at review time.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers/ACs and clarify key concerns below: Dataset [R2Q2Q4/R4Q3]: We split dataset in participant level (319 train/41 val/39 test), yielding clips with no participants overlap. Tabular variables include 6 demographics (e.g. Sex/Age/Edu/Ethnicity/Race/Marry), APOE4, and 6 cognitive scores. MRI data are complete for all samples, whereas 22% records exhibit tabular missing values. GT-reliability [R1/3/4Q1]: We construct GT similarly to how junior doctors are taught to trace evidence given target status. We also invite two senior clinicians to recognize GT’s quality across all 6 dims (CS 4.8 HF 4.9 PF 4.6 SS 4.7 HP 4.5 HL 4.8) together with Fig 2, suggesting GT’s reliability. Notably, similar GT-summary setups have been adopted in recent medical reasoning works, such as GEM(NIPS25) and ClinRaGen(ACL25), which supports our design. LLM-judge circularity [R3Q1]: Using same LLM in GT-summary and LM-judge is adopted by prior works (GEM) since two stages are independent with different contexts and tasks. LM-judge‘s prompt instructs LM to rate candidate hieratically using given data, stats, rubric and output format, e.g. “You are a clinical reasoning evaluator. Input… Evaluate quality on… Output STRICT JSON…”. Rubric emphasizes objective evidence, e.g. “missing a key V1-V3 trend should score 3” in historical fidelity (full prompt and rubric in anonymized link). We further use Sonnet-4.6 as LM-judge across metrics, GPT-summarized GT achieves avg score of 3.86 as upper bound and ENIGMA ranks best among all methods (3.70 vs. suboptimal ViTB-LM 3.51). Human evaluation [R3Q1/R4Q2]: Beyond GT text matching, the evaluation also includes historical and prognostic fidelity in both the LM-judge and clinician rubrics. Specifically, we include two clinicians’ blinded ratings for 10 cases, providing them with full records, labels, normative stats and shuffled text candidates. Two clinicians achieved high agreement (Cohen’s κ 0.79). Fairness [R1Q3/R3Q2]: DTGPT/NoteLM cannot read MRI, we provide volumetric features as a realistic upper-bound proxy, and we also include MLM baselines, e.g. ViTB-LM, with MRI encoders and structured tabular for symmetric comparisons. BGE novelty [R2Q1/5]: Unlike prior pre-visit fusion or missing completion works, BGE models fine-grained cross-time interactions in a unified graph. It is trained directly with missing value and irregularity thanks to edge disconnection design and learnable time encoding. L_da^i is a cross-entropy loss aligning the representation of visit i with disease status. Reproducibility [R3Q4]: Full settings/code are online (sent to ACs due to Rebuttal Guide). Some important details are shared below. Experiments use 1 L40S GPU and cost 3.4h pretraining (batch size 16/100 epochs) and 2.0h finetuning (batch size 4/6 epochs) with lr=3e-5 and anneal decay. Checkpoints are selected by validation AUC with early stopping. We empirically search αcl from 1 to 3, αda in 0.5 1.0 1.5, sparsity 1/8 1/4 1/2. Statistic significance [R1Q2]: McNemar tests (p<0.05) are conducted to assess statistical significance showing ENIGMA significantly improves accuracy. Modality ablation justification [R4Q5]: First panel in Table 3 presents an ablation study of the multimodal encoder (BGE) under different modality inputs, rather than the full MLM pipeline. which leads to AUC difference. Tabular data domination [R2Q7]: Experimental results indicate that tabular data contribute more, likely due to their closer relevance to AD diagnosis (e.g., cognitive scores). However, MRI still provides complementary anatomical cues. Visit missing comparison [R1Q3]: Fig 4 tests extra input missing at inference stage. As LaTiM utilize the single record for inference, it is not directly comparable in this setting. Related work [R2Q8]: Direct comparison is limited as W1/W2 lack public code. We compared W3 by adjusting into status prediction without PET, obtaining F1=0.652/AUC=0.796.We will discuss W1–3 in Related Work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents an ambitious and potentially impactful multimodal language model framework for interpretable longitudinal AD forecasting, with one reviewer strongly supporting acceptance while others provide mixed assessments (scores: 5 / 4 / 3 / 2) . While reviewers acknowledge strong empirical performance and novelty in combining forecasting with structured explanation generation, several critical concerns remain. In particular, the reliance on GPT-generated supervision without validation, potential data leakage in longitudinal splits, and circularity in explanation evaluation (e.g., using the same LLM for supervision and judging) need to be carefully addressed. Additional issues include unclear methodological details, baseline fairness, and reproducibility; the authors are encouraged to respond to these points in the rebuttal to clarify the validity and robustness of the proposed approach. | After the rebuttal, two reviewers recommended acceptance, one reviewer suggest reject, and one reviewer did not respond (with the original rating 2). Most of the concerns are raised due to clarity and reproducibility, which may not be easy considering the complexity of the method. The authors should try to improve the figures and descriptions, and include the discussions in the rebuttal in the revision. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After carefully reviewing the authors’ rebuttal, I have revised my initial assessment to Accept. The authors have provided a thorough, evidence-based response that directly addresses the core concerns raised by the reviewers, including participant-level split to prevent data leakage, validation of GPT-generated ground truth via clinician assessment, mitigation of evaluation circularity using Sonnet-4.6 as an independent judge, high clinician inter-rater agreement (Cohen’s κ = 0.79), statistical significance testing with McNemar tests, clarification of AUC inconsistencies, and provision of an anonymized code repository for reproducibility. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal substantially alleviates the key concerns on participant-level data leakage, GPT-generated supervision reliability, LLM-judge circularity, statistical testing, and reproducibility, and although some issues about future-information-dependent explanations and table consistency remain, the strong empirical performance and positive post-rebuttal assessments support acceptance.

title: IntraStyler: Intra-Domain Style Synthesis for Cross-Modality MRI Domain Adaptation
reviewer_1_strengths: the definition of source and target domains in I2I is often vague and embeds high heterogeneity. it is thus very sound to try to tackle domain variations in an unsupervised fashion. CrossMoDA is an appropriate setting as the target domain is heterogeneous in style. Method is very well described and sound and results clearly show the ability of the approach to generate diverse styles while preserving the structural fidelity of the original T1 image. Quantitative results are also very good. It is overall a very well written paper of outstanding quality, that could be applied in a variety of other image to image translation setting.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: -The contrastive learning mechanism relies on synthetic data augmentation. The selection, relevance and relative importance of these have not been explicitly discussed by the authors. Applied synthetic transformations are global to the image. I suspect this explains that, From Fig. 3, it seems that the applied style is global, i. e. the VS appearance in the synthetic image (to the right) does not follow the VS appearance in the reference #2 image, i. e. the VS is hypersignal in the reference, but hyposignal in the target, as the synthetic transformation seemed to have applied a global darkening of the style. The variability in target appearances in crossMoDA has been previously discussed in another top performing method Salle et al. TBME 2024.The authors propose a more local alteration by only changing tumor appearance. Could such more local data augmentation solve the suspected problem of global contrast change ? I think that point could be mentioned as future evolution of the work or simply discussed.
reviewer_1_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The observation that institute-level sub-domain labels are too coarse to capture genuine intra-domain variability is well-supported by Figure 1 and the experimental design. The problem of sub-domain label dependency is a real bottleneck for clinical deployment, and the proposed solution is principled. 2.Defining positives as same-image crops with different anatomy, and negatives as intensity-perturbed versions of the positive, is a clean and annotation-free strategy for learning style-invariant-to-anatomy embeddings. The fact that the encoder trained on synthetic perturbations generalizes to discriminate real MRI scanner differences (Fig. 4) is a notable and non-obvious finding.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.IntraStyler is explicitly built upon the CrossMoDA challenge-winning method and the primary modification is the addition of a style encoder with contrastive training and DIN injection. The core synthesis backbone, discriminator, PatchNCE loss, and segmentation pipeline are all inherited. While the results are strong, the methodological novelty relative to prior style-conditioned synthesis work (e.g., StarGANv2, AdaIN) is incremental, and the paper’s framing as the “first 3D unpaired image translation method for sub-domain-free style synthesis” requires more careful qualification given the breadth of existing style transfer literature. 2.All experiments are conducted on a single benchmark (CrossMoDA) involving one specific anatomy (posterior fossa), one translation direction (ceT1→T2), and one imaging modality pair. The paper acknowledges that intensity perturbation functions may require modality-specific tuning for CT or PET, but provides no evidence of transferability beyond brain MRI. The generality claim in the conclusion is therefore unsupported. 3.At inference time, IntraStyler uses K-means clustering with silhouette analysis to select 7 representative reference images. The number of selected references (7 vs. 3 for sub-domain methods) is not controlled for in the comparison. It is unclear whether the performance gain comes from the quality of the style encoder or simply from using more diverse references. An experiment fixing the number of references or sampling randomly would help disentangle these factors.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper explicitly targets intra-domain variability within the target modality, which is often implicitly ignored in image-level domain adaptation methods. The avoidance of predefined sub-domain labels such as institute or scanner identifiers makes the approach practical as such labels may often be challenging to acquire reliably in practice. The visualization and clustering of learned style embeddings provide qualitative evidence that the model captures meaningful appearance variations beyond anatomy. The method is implemented by extending a rather strong existing image translation backbone rather than redesigning the full pipeline. This allows for a simple incremental contribution.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The novelty of the proposed style modeling is limited relative to prior work in image style transfer and multi-style image translation. The idea of extracting a per-image style code and using it to condition synthesis is well established in the computer vision literature, e.g. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-58580-8_13 , https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV48922.2021.01389 The manuscript would benefit from a clearer discussion of what is fundamentally new in the proposed formulation. The contrastive learning formulation for style extraction appears simplistic and only weakly justified. Positives and negatives are derived from the same target image via spatial cropping and intensity perturbations, which raises questions about what enforces consistency of style representations across different images that share similar acquisition characteristics. Emergent capabilities may arise from such training but this aspect is not well discussed. The clustering of style embeddings plays a central role in selecting representative styles for downstream segmentation training, yet this step is treated largely as a post hoc procedure. The sensitivity of the results to the clustering method, the number of clusters, or the style selection strategy is not explored, and comparisons against using all target images (thus avoiding clustering entirely) as style references are missing.

meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a 3D unpaired image translation framework for cross-modality MRI domain adaptation that eliminates the need for predefined site/scanner labels using a contrastively trained style encoder. Reviewers acknowledge that the paper is addressing a real-world clinical bottleneck: modeling intra-domain variability without relying on coarse sub-domain labels. The contrastive learning strategy is principled, and the method successfully outperforms a highly competitive baseline (the CrossMoDA challenge winner). To be addressed in final version: 1.Explicitly acknowledge the limitation of evaluating on a single dataset/modality pair (ceT1→T2) and the potential need for modality-specific tuning in other applications. 2.Better position the method relative to prior computer vision literature on style-conditioned synthesis (e.g., StarGANv2, AdaIN) and temper overly broad novelty claims (e.g., “first 3D unpaired…”). 3.Explicitly define all terms in the loss functions (specifically $L_{Adv}$ and $L_{PatchNCE}$). 4.Discuss the impact of the k-means clustering strategy and the uncontrolled number of reference images used (7 vs. 3). 5.Update the captions and context for Figures 3 and 4 as suggested by R3 and R4.

title: Joint Imaging–ROI Representation Learning via Cross-View Contrastive Alignment for Brain Disorder Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper has several strengths. First, it proposes a unified framework that integrates global imaging and ROI-based graph representations through cross-view contrastive alignment, which is a reasonable and well-motivated approach beyond simple fusion methods. Second, the study provides a controlled comparison of imaging-only, ROI-only, and joint models under the same training setting, which is valuable for understanding their relative contributions. Third, the method is evaluated on two well-known datasets (ADHD-200 and ABIDE) and shows consistent, albeit modest, performance improvements across different model backbones. The large sample size is also a strength.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper has several notable weaknesses. First, both the imaging and ROI-based graph representations are derived from the same underlying data, raising concerns about whether the two views provide truly complementary information or largely redundant representations. This limits the strength of the multi-view learning claim. Second, the novelty of the method is somewhat limited, as cross-view contrastive learning and multi-modal alignment have been widely studied in prior work (e. g. , contrastive representation learning frameworks such as SimCLR, MoCo, and CLIP). The paper does not clearly demonstrate what fundamentally new methodological contribution is introduced beyond applying these ideas to this specific setting. Third, the reported performance improvements are relatively modest (e. g. , around 1–2% AUC, ADHD 72.73 vs 70.92, ABIDE 64.08 vs 62.84), making it unclear whether the gains are meaningful. Fourth, given the use of subject-level contrastive alignment, it is important to clarify whether strict subject-level data splitting was enforced. Without this, there is a risk of subject-level leakage, especially in multi-site datasets such as ADHD-200 and ABIDE (the datasets are known for significant heterogeneity and is highly noisy). Finally, although interpretability analyses are included, the paper does not clearly identify which specific features or brain regions drive the classification performance, limiting the neuroscientific insight of the work.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses the challenge of different types of ways to input structural brain data - using the original imaging volume vs the popular ROI-based methods. Considering both representation methods jointly allows for leveraging advantages of differing representations. 2.The proposed cross-view contrastive alignment is an interesting approach for the representation learning. The idea is that the learned embedding for the imaging and ROI information for the fMRI sample should be aligned in the learned representation space. 3.The experiments are performed on 2 public datasets and compared multiple different encoder backbones, under five-fold cross-validation. This helped show the generalizability of the proposed approach. 4.The ablation study on different ways to combine or fuse information from the two imaging and ROI representations helped to show the contribution of the proposed contrastive learning approach. 5.The experiments included a study to see the effect of removing a single branch input (imaging or ROI), simulating the case of “missing” data. The bounded drop as the amount of missing data was increased helped to verify that that the cross-view representation was effective in learning robust representations.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Missing ablation on loss contribution The method has a lambda term to weight the loss of the the contrastive learning vs brain disorder classification terms. The setting for lambda is not included. In addition, an ablation varying lambda would be informative to understand the loss contribution (I believe the case for no contrastive loss was included in the experiments for the “simple concatenation” setting.) 2.No statistical testing for differences in model results. I appreciate the reported variance across five-fold cross-validation. Additional statistical testing to show which methods / model settings are significantly different (i.e. in Table 1 and 2) would give stronger evidence for the better performance of the proposed approach. 3.Incorrect reference Ref. [25], which should be for the ABIDE dataset, is incorrect. It should cite Di Martino et al., “The autism brain imaging data exchange: towards a large-scale evaluation of the intrinsic brain architecture in autism,” 2014.Please check and correct this.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper proposes to leverage the complementary nature of image and graph representations for improving the performance. The proposed fusion protocol provides improvement in performance compared to imaging-only or ROI-only configurations as shown in ablation studies. An attempt is also made to incorporate interpretability into the analysis—showing that different configurations capture distinctive patterns for decision-making.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: As cross-view or cross-modal contrastive learning is a well-established paradigm, using bidirectional subject-level contrastive objectives to brain imaging is not conceptually very novel. The statement—Existing fusion approaches are typically task-specific—is neither clarified nor comparatively analyzed against them. While the overview of the proposed framework indicates that diverse imaging modalities can be used, all the experiments are based only on the anatomical MRI datasets. Abstract mentions a bidirectional contrastive objective that encourages representations from the same subject to converge while separating those from different subjects. This is standard instance-discrimination contrastive loss. It’s unclear what “bidirectional” adds—whether the loss operates symmetrically across both branches or introduces some asymmetric cross-view alignment. To assess robustness under missing views, the experiments are conducted to simulate view absence by zero-masking one branch for a random subset of subjects. However, the only case that is realistic is the image being available and the ROI missing due to preprocessing failure. ROI availability and missing images don’t make sense; ROI-based features (parcellations, connectivity matrices, and graph nodes) are derived from the same underlying brain image. Lastly, comparison with the state of the art is not quite fair or comprehensive. The significance of the proposed InfoNCE loss should have been demonstrated in comparison with other contrastive losses (like triplet loss and decoupled contrastive loss) and other non-contrastive losses.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their constructive feedback and clarify key points below. Review 1 & Review 3 – Methodological novelty We agree that our method builds on established contrastive learning. Our contribution is not a new loss, but a unified and controlled framework for jointly modeling volumetric imaging and ROI-graph representations. Prior fusion approaches are often architecture-specific and lack systematic analysis. In this work, we provide: (i) cross-view alignment between global volumetric and ROI-level graph features, (ii) controlled comparisons (imaging-only, ROI-only, joint) across multiple backbones, and (iii) interpretability analyses revealing complementary neuroanatomical patterns. This establishes a principled framework for imaging–ROI complementary learning. Review 1 – Performance & complementarity Although absolute gains over imaging-only and ROI-only baselines are modest, the improvements are consistent across datasets, encoder choices, and evaluation metrics. As shown in Table 1, we observe dataset-specific trends: imaging-based models perform better on ADHD, whereas ROI/graph-based models perform better on ABIDE. Despite these differences, the proposed joint framework consistently achieves the best overall performance on both datasets, further supporting the complementary nature of the two representations rather than simple redundancy. Review 1 & Review 2 – Statistical significance We conducted paired t-tests on (subject-level) Accuracy and DeLong’s tests on AUC, both confirming statistical significance. We will include these results in the revision. Review 1 – Subject-level leakage in contrastive alignment Strict subject-level splitting was enforced in 5-fold cross-validation, with each subject assigned exclusively to either the training or test set. Contrastive alignment was performed only within the training set, and test subjects were never involved in optimization. Therefore, subject-level leakage is strictly prevented. Review 1 – Interpretability Our interpretability analysis aims to assess whether the two branches capture complementary patterns. We agree that deeper region- and feature-level interpretation would strengthen the neuroscientific insight. The framework is backbone-agnostic and can be combined with more advanced interpretable imaging and graph models in future work. Review 2 – Hyperparameters (λ) Hyperparameters were optimized via Optuna. The loss-weight λ was searched in [0.05, 0.5], with optimal values 0.48 (ADHD) and 0.2 (ABIDE), indicating moderate alignment strength. The “Concat” setting in Table 2 corresponds to λ = 0, serving as an implicit ablation of the contrastive objective. We will clarify it in the revision. Review 2 – Clarifications 1.We will update the ABIDE reference (Ref. 25) to Di Martino, A. et al., 2014.2.Stratification is diagnosis-label based at the subject level. 3.The dotted blue line should indeed originate from p_img (not z_img); we will update Fig. 1 accordingly. Review 3 – Additional clarifications 1.“Task-specific fusion” refers to methods tied to specific architectures or pipelines, where performance gains may reflect model complexity rather than representation quality. In contrast, our approach focuses on studying the complementary contributions of imaging and ROI feature representations under a unified setting. 2.“Bidirectional” refers to the symmetric matching formulation in Eq. (5), where contrastive matching is computed in both directions between the imaging and ROI branches. The two directional losses are averaged over the mini-batch, and no additional asymmetric alignment component is introduced. Review 3 – Loss comparison We agree that broader loss comparisons would be valuable. However, our goal is not exhaustive benchmarking but validating a unified framework under controlled settings. InfoNCE is used due to its suitability for subject-level pairing. We will clarify this scope and discuss extensions as future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem with a reasonable and technically sound framework, and reviewers acknowledge its promise across datasets and experimental settings. However, concerns remain about limited methodological novelty, modest and potentially insignificant performance gains, unclear independence between representations, and possible subject-level leakage. The rebuttal should specifically clarify: (1) statistical significance of the reported improvements, (2) safeguards against subject-level leakage, and (3) the extent of true complementarity between views. | This paper presents a technically sound and interesting application of cross-view contrastive learning to brain MRI, with consistent though modest empirical gains. Given the generally positive consensus among reviewers and the rebuttal’s clarification of key methodological concerns, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After rebuttal, R1 changed from Weak Reject to Reject, while R2 maintained Accept and R3 remained Weak Accept. Although authors clarified concerns regarding subject-level leakage, statistical testing, and the motivation for cross-view alignment, concerns remained about the limited methodological novelty, modest performance gains, lack of external validation, and insufficient evidence that image and ROI representations provide truly complementary rather than redundant information. Given these unresolved issues, I recommend Reject. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper is technically sound and provides a controlled framework for jointly modeling volumetric imaging and ROI-graph representations. Although the novelty is incremental and the gains are modest, the rebuttal addresses the key concerns about subject-level leakage, statistical significance, loss weighting, and bidirectional alignment. The final version should tone down broad novelty claims and clarify the limits of the complementarity analysis.

title: Joint Segmentation and Graph-Based Skeletal Representation Learning with Geometric Priors
reviewer_1_strengths: The problem formulation is compelling and well-motivated. The existing s-rep fitting pipeline is a major bottleneck for clinical adoption of skeletal shape analysis, as well as necessitates a prior structural segmentation. Replacing it with a learned single-forward-pass approach directly from MRI data is a practical and valuable contribution. The architectural design is well-done. The combination of a variational encoder for global shape context, a differentiable skeletonization module for medial priors, learnable positional embeddings with cross-attention for node-specific decoding, and a graph convolutional decoder that respects fixed s-rep topology is a principled pipeline where each component serves a clear purpose. The geometric loss terms (spoke direction and orthogonality) are well-formulated and address genuine domain-specific constraints rather than generic regularizers. The main novelty is in the overall framework, as well as the geometric loss terms that are specific for skeletal representations, spoke direction consistency and spoke-boundary orthogonality . The ablation study is informative and shows a clear trade-off: adding geometric, skeletal constraints improves skeleton-specific metrics (medialness, angle, orthogonality) at the cost of raw coordinate RMSE. It shows that the geometric constraints push the model towards better skeletal representations even if point-wise error increases. The downstream classification experiment (Table 2) demonstrates that predicted s-reps retain discriminative power comparable to the existing pipeline in a hippocampus study of AD vs. NC classification (ADNI dataset). Finally, the results also show that the proposed joint segmentation & skeletal representation framework also improves segmentation accuracy, particularly in data scarce settings. Incorporating s-rep supervision improves Dice & H95 scores.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Minor: Limited anatomical diversity. The framework is evaluated exclusively on hippocampal s-reps, which have a relatively simple slab-like geometry. It is unclear how the approach would generalize to other anatomical structures with more complex shape (e. g. , thin-walled or spreading organs, or structures with more branching medial sheets). Missing comparisons with recent learning-based methods. The paper compares primarily against the evolutionary s-rep pipeline. However, the most relevant competitors, as discussed in the introduction— HybridGNet/HybridVNet and the GNN-based s-rep fitting method of Gaggion et al. — are discussed in the introduction but not included as experimental baselines. Since the paper’s central claim is to improve upon existing approaches, a direct comparison against these methods is essential.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: S-reps plays a critical role in statistical shape analysis. The good correspondence and rich geometric features provided by s-reps allow for statistical understanding of shape data. This research chose a good direction and proposed a computationally efficient method that connects image segmentation and s-reps fitting in a supervised fashion. The paper introduced (1) a learnable position embedding and (2) cross-attention layer to connect image segmentation and GNN-based s-rep computation framework. These components act as a bridge that allows the two tasks (i.e., segmentation and s-rep computation) can be trained jointly. But to confirm the effectiveness, it is necessary to look deeper into the performance of each task. The research showed with experiments that the s-rep computation improves the learning efficiency of segmentation in sparse data scenarios. The shape information encoded in s-reps provides explicit structural priors and thus helps the image segmentation task.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper is largely well-written. But the notations are not clearly explained. For example, in section 2.2, the lack of notations such as R^{M\times d} can lead to confusions. As the paper integrates image segmentation and s-reps fitting, it is clearer to visualize the “goodness” of each. For example, a reader may wonder how the training dynamics (e.g., learning curves) look like given the small to medium data size? More practically, how to tune the parameters in equation (1) to achieve good results from both segmentation and s-reps fitting. It is not clear what features the authors have used from evolutionary s-reps and Liu’s s-reps regarding the experiments shown in Table 2. S-reps fitting with Cross Attention and GNN: 1) About the loss function regarding skeletal geometry: a. the loss of spoke directions should take into account the skeletal radial curvature, as detailed in Damon, Smoothness and geometry of boundaries associated to skeletal structures, II: Geometry in the Blum case. It is important to leverage Damon’s mathematical tool to produce valid spoke direction vectors. b. It should also account for the distance between spokes’ ends and the corresponding boundary, see the paper Liu et al., Fitting unbranching skeletal structures to objects. 2) The evaluation needs to show the quality of the correspondence in the context of more statistical analysis. S-reps is designed to facilitate the statistical shape analysis via good correspondence across objects. Different from Liu’s diffeomorphism-based method of s-reps, the proposed method in this paper maps image all the way to geometric primitives of s-reps driven by the loss function that takes some skeletal geometry into account. Regardless to the quality of the segmentation, it is natural to ask if the resulting s-reps can help statistical tasks such as classification, hypothesis testing, etc. The relevant evaluation of s-reps in this paper is the classification results in Table 2, showing on-par-with performance with the diffeomorphism-based fitting methods. It can be more convincing to have more relevant evaluation and metrics, see the paper as an example Liyun T. et al., Skeletal Shape Correspondence Through Entropy. 3) I wonder if the authors have tried 2-stage framework separating the segmentation and the s-rep fitting.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The method targets an important geometric task and combine the segmentation and skeleton extraction into a unified framework. 2.It achieves great performances compared to recent SOTA methods. 3.paper is well written, well illustrated with good literature coverage. 4.Efficiency improvement.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.author could visualize example(s) of the generated skeleton overlaid with the hippocampus volume in 3D for presentation. 2.Downstream task performance didn’t indicate a necessary performance advantage over other methods. 3.The segmentation evaluation is missing from experiment.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments and for recognizing the strengths of our work, including the joint segmentation/s-rep learning framework, domain-specific geometric losses, improved segmentation performance, and over 1000× speedup over conventional fitting pipelines. We will incorporate the feedback into the camera-ready revision. Below, we respond to the main comments. To R#1: We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestions. (a) We agree that the current evaluation is limited to hippocampal s-reps. While the hippocampus is an established testbed for s-rep analysis, our framework can in principle be adapted to other structures with appropriate s-rep templates, including thin-walled or sheet-like organs. Structures with branching medial sheets or variable topology are more challenging and will require topology-adaptive skeletal templates or graph generation mechanisms, which we view as important future work. (b) HybridGNet/HybridVNet are important related works using hybrid graph neural networks for landmark and surface mesh prediction. They motivate the broader direction of learning anatomical geometric representations from images, while our work directly predicts s-rep primitives jointly with segmentation. Since these methods mainly target surfaces, meshes, or landmarks rather than s-rep primitives, the settings are not directly comparable. (c) Following the meta-reviewer’s suggestion, we will also discuss CM-Rep as a continuous medial shape modeling alternative to discrete skeletonization in the revised version. To R#2: We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments on s-rep geometry and statistical shape analysis. (a) The loss weights in Eq. (1) were selected to balance segmentation accuracy and s-rep geometric validity. We observed that overly large s-rep-related weights could degrade segmentation performance. The final weights were selected by reducing the relative contribution of s-rep losses and performing grid search. (b) For downstream classification, all s-rep-based classifiers used the same skeletal features following “Interior Object Geometry via Fitted Frames”: 61 interior skeletal points and 24 skeletal fold points per hippocampal s-rep, yielding an 8,076-dimensional Euclideanized feature tuple, reduced by PCA to 177 dimensions. (c) Regarding Damon’s radial curvature condition and valid spoke directions, we agree that these are more rigorous theoretical constraints and important future work. We also agree that spoke-end-to-boundary distance is meaningful. We experimented with such an objective, but found it less stable during backpropagation in the current training pipeline. (d) For correspondence, our fixed-topology GNN decoder, node-specific positional queries, and downstream AD/NC classification provide indirect validation that predicted s-reps preserve statistical utility. More systematic entropy/correspondence analyses will be included in follow-up work. (e) We agree that a separated two-stage learning baseline is valuable; however, such designs may introduce additional optimization and error-propagation challenges. We will explore end-to-end learned two-stage variants in future work and revise unclear notations, including dimensions and symbols in Sec. 2.2. To R#3: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestions. (a) Table 2 is not intended to claim superior AD classification, but to verify that predicted s-reps preserve discriminative anatomical information comparable to fitted s-reps while enabling orders-of-magnitude faster inference. (b) We clarify that segmentation evaluation is reported in Fig. 3 using Dice and HD95, including the low-data setting where s-rep supervision improves segmentation accuracy. (c) We will add a 3D qualitative visualization showing the generated skeleton overlaid with the hippocampal volume, and strengthen the efficiency discussion, including comparison with Liu et al. in Table 3.
