title: Maximizing Domain Generalization in Automated Fetal Brain Biometry
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper presents several strengths. First, the methodological design is well developed and carefully thought out, resulting in a novel framework for test-time adaptation. In particular, the approach combines different self-supervised objectives that not only leverage landmark heatmap predictions but also incorporate their relationships with biometric lengths and their expected positions along structural edges. Additionally, a structural prior based on an atlas is used to enforce anatomical plausibility. Another strength is the comprehensive evaluation. The authors train the backbone model(s) on a single dataset and perform two types of evaluations, each across two different datasets: a quantitative evaluation (analyzing biometric measurement errors) and a diagnostic evaluation (assessing the final diagnostic performance of the method in conditions such as ventriculomegaly and germinal matrix hemorrhage). They also compare their method with state-of-the-art approaches for the quantitative evaluation and with observer variability for the clinical assessment. Finally, another strength is the application of the proposed method in a web-based system, demonstrating the authors’ intention to translate the approach into clinical practice.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Concerning the weaknesses, despite the strong evaluation presented by the authors, where two out-of-domain datasets were used for quantitative assessment, in one of the datasets only three measurements were evaluated (LFC), whereas 11 measurements were considered in the other (FeTA). Although this still allows the assessment of the method across different datasets, this lack of uniformity in the analysis may raise questions about how the method would perform across a broader set of measurements on the LFC dataset. Another weakness is the modest discussion of the results. While the authors present the results and their main conclusions, the discussion lacks depth and could be improved by adding comprehensive insights.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper tackles an important problem in FeTA biometry and adopts a reasonable constraint setting, namely source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation. The use of a length consistency loss to design a biometry-aware TTA framework is a clear methodological contribution. In addition, the authors attempt to move beyond laboratory-style AI evaluation by comparing BioTTA with clinical experts, which reflects an interest in practical clinical utility. Finally, the ablation study is well designed and clearly shows the contribution of the main components of the proposed method.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main weakness of this paper is that the comparison framework is not sufficiently fair. In domain adaptation, different paradigms allow access to different kinds of information, and comparison methods should therefore be matched under the same information constraints. For clarity, one can distinguish four settings: (A) OOD detection, which aims to identify whether an input is outside the source distribution; (B) UDA, which uses target data during training; (C) TTA, which uses target input during inference; and (D) SDG, which assumes no access to target information at all. This paper clearly belongs to (C), namely source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation, so the core evaluation should be organized within that setting. Major weakness 1.Essential baselines for source-free unsupervised TTA are missing In this setting, I believe the following comparisons are necessary for a fair evaluation. (i) Source Model This is the basic baseline and is required to show how the source-pretrained model performs on the target domain without adaptation. (ii) A generic source-free TTA baseline TENT is the most direct example. The authors are clearly aware of it and mention it in the paper, yet it is omitted from the reported comparisons. I would be interested in hearing the authors’ reasoning here. For a paper proposing a source-free test-time adaptation method, comparison against a generic baseline such as TENT appears highly relevant unless there is a clear reason why such a comparison would not be appropriate in this setting. (iii) Common source-free TTA methods used for medical brain image inputs Although this paper uses dense spatial prediction through heatmaps and landmark localization rather than segmentation, it would still be strongly desirable, or at least worth discussing explicitly, to compare against source-free TTA methods that are commonly used in medical brain imaging. Examples include Karani et al., “Test-time adaptable neural networks for robust medical image segmentation,” atlas-guided TTA for 3D medical segmentation, and one-pass or plug-and-play medical TTA methods such as TestFit. Even if the authors believe that these methods cannot be applied directly to FeTA biometry, the paper should explain why they were not considered appropriate. At present, such an explanation is not provided. (iv) A source-free TTA method with a similar key idea or with the same target domain, i.e., FeTA This point is particularly important. Through reference [10], the authors are already aware of a TTA study that is directly related to FeTA or fetal brain MRI morphometry. That study shares substantial overlap with the present paper: fetal brain MRI morphometry, target domain = FeTA, TTA, and the use of anatomy or atlas priors. It is therefore a strong comparable method and should be included experimentally. Differences in backbone, annotation protocol, or exact label setting may exist, but such differences are usually not sufficient to justify complete exclusion. At minimum, the paper should explain why this comparison was not performed. (v) Ablation over the proposed components I mention this only to complete the evaluation framework. This is not a weakness. On the contrary, the authors handled this part well. By contrast, the methods that are actually reported do not match the proposed paradigm. FetalSynthGen [24] is based on synthetic data augmentation to improve robustness during training. It is not an inference-time online adaptation method(C), and therefore it does not belong to the same source-free TTA setting as the proposed approach. (maybe this is B or D) DGMLD [8] uses 10 labeled target samples and is therefore target-supervised. It may serve as an upper-bound reference, but it is not an appropriate core baseline for source-free unsupervised TTA. (this is B) In other words, the key baselines in (ii), (iii), and (iv) are missing, while the reported comparisons mostly involve methods that do not share the same information constraints as the proposed method. As a result, the current experiments do not convincingly show how competitive BioTTA is as a source-free TTA method. Instead, they read more like a list of methods from different paradigms placed in the same table. Major weakness 2.Table 2 is interesting, but it does not directly validate the claimed advantage of the TTA method Table 2 is clinically interesting. In our field, it is important not only to compare technical metrics, but also to demonstrate actual clinical usefulness. If designed rigorously and fairly, this kind of evaluation could add substantial value even if the purely technical comparisons were somewhat limited. For that reason, I view Table 2 as potentially very meaningful. However, as currently described, it is not fully clear to me what exactly this table is validating, and I would be interested in the authors’ clarification. From the paper, my understanding is the following: BioTTA predicts landmarks and biometric measurements. Those biometrics are then converted into VM diagnosis, VM grading, and GMH grading using rule-based clinical criteria. The radiologists, in contrast, directly interpret the MRI scans. If this interpretation is correct, then Table 2 may not directly test the advantage of BioTTA as a TTA method. Rather, it would compare a full TTA-based biometry pipeline against human readers. That is a different question. In that case, the table would read more as an AI-pipeline-versus-human-reader experiment than as a controlled validation of the proposed TTA method itself. This would not make the evaluation unimportant, but it would make its role in the paper different from what I initially expected. A fair TTA-oriented evaluation would require at least the following comparisons: source model biometry → rule-based diagnosis generic TTA biometry → rule-based diagnosis BioTTA biometry → rule-based diagnosis This would allow the reader to assess whether the proposed TTA actually improves downstream diagnostic usefulness relative to other TTA methods or to the source model alone. From a clinical workflow perspective, an even better comparison would be radiologist alone versus radiologist + model measurement assistance. As it stands, Table 2 appears potentially interesting and important, but I am not yet certain how it should be interpreted in relation to the central TTA claim. I would therefore welcome clarification from the authors. Minor weakness The authors partially explain why they chose setting (C), but they do not fully answer why this setting is more appropriate than (A), (B), or (D) for the actual clinical deployment scenario. Questions remain, such as: how many optimization steps are acceptable per patient at test time; whether this conflicts with real-time or near-real-time workflow; whether per-patient online updating is operationally acceptable; and whether the setting assumes a continuous target stream or independent one-shot patients. That said, I do not regard this as a major weakness in a short paper, and this point alone would not lead me to reject the submission.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) The methodological innovation is substantial and task-specific. The sparse weighted differentiable landmark detector resolves the gradient-blocking issue in converting heatmaps to coordinates, and the length consistency loss leverages the task-specific geometric structure of biometry by enforcing consistency between inter-landmark distance and regression output. This regression-to-heatmap distillation is the core algorithmic contribution rather than a simple combination of existing losses. The integration of atlas priors is also reasonable, as the gestational-age-matched fetal brain atlas provides structural constraints to keep landmarks within anatomically plausible regions. 2) The experimental validation is extensive and forms a relatively complete evidence chain. The method is evaluated on 259 images from five centers using two target-domain datasets, FeTA and LFC. It is validated on both a CNN backbone (BioCNN) and a Transformer backbone (BioFormer), suggesting that the approach is not dependent on a specific architecture. The ablation study supports the central claims, with the full framework achieving a 47.12% error reduction over the source-model baseline. Moreover, without target annotations, the method reaches performance comparable to or even better than supervised fine-tuning with 10 labeled target samples. 3) The paper has clear clinical deployment value. The problem definition targets a real bottleneck in fetal brain biometry, namely domain shift in practical cross-center deployment, rather than a purely academic setting. The source-free formulation is well aligned with clinical requirements because it avoids access to source data and target labels, thereby reducing privacy-compliance and annotation-cost barriers. In addition, the paper goes beyond reporting measurement errors and evaluates diagnostic performance on ventriculomegaly diagnosis and germinal matrix hemorrhage grading against three radiologists with different levels of experience, which supports its clinical relevance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) The core assumption is insufficiently validated, and the potential impact of registration on individualized structural characteristics is not analyzed. The paper assumes that the regression branch is more robust to domain shift than the heatmap branch, but does not provide direct experimental evidence for this claim. More importantly, the atlas registration process may alter individualized brain structural characteristics through nonlinear deformation, potentially distorting morphological measures such as gray matter volume or cortical thickness. The paper does not analyze the effect of registration error on biometry accuracy, nor does it discuss whether degraded registration quality in pathological brains, such as ventriculomegaly or germinal matrix hemorrhage, may introduce systematic bias. 2) The technical boundary with related work is not sufficiently clear, and the novelty requires further clarification. Li et al. (MIDL 2025) has already presented a highly similar anatomy-guided test-time adaptation method for automated fetal brain MRI morphometry that also uses atlas registration to constrain heatmap prediction. Although BioTTA differs in its TTA mechanism and self-supervised loss design, the use of atlas priors is highly overlapping, and the paper does not adequately clarify the technical distinction and contribution difference. In addition, the entropy minimization loss and boundary gradient loss are largely direct applications of the TENT paradigm and common edge-based constraints, respectively, which limits their novelty. 3) The diagnostic evaluation remains limited in scope, and the potential for normative reference construction is not explored. The paper validates only ventriculomegaly diagnosis and germinal matrix hemorrhage grading, without evaluation on other common fetal brain abnormalities such as agenesis of the corpus callosum, cerebellar maldevelopment, or neural tube defects. More importantly, although the adapted model could in principle support automated biometry on unlabeled data from new centers and potentially enable gestational-age-specific normative reference construction, the paper does not discuss this direction or evaluate sensitivity for abnormality detection. 4) The experimental validation and statistical rigor are still limited. The ablation study is conducted only on BioCNN, without corresponding ablations on BioFormer or analysis of interactions among the loss terms. The reported improvements are not accompanied by statistical significance testing, so some smaller gains may not be significant. The fairness of some comparisons is also unclear, for example when DGMLD is used outside its intended metric scope. In addition, the target-domain sample size is limited, with only 50 cases each in FeTA and LFC.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: # R1: LFC metrics: Only 3 cerebellar measurement labels are available in the LFC public dataset, which limits our evaluation scope. BioTTA on OoD-GMH: The OoD-GMH dataset (SS/TSE sequences, NesVoR recon) exhibits a larger domain gap from the source domain in acquisition parameters and reconstruction methods, resulting in more pronounced distribution shift. Nevertheless, BioTTA’s diagnostic results remain comparable to senior radiologists, validating its cross-domain generalization and clinical utility. # R2: Regarding the comparison framework: (ii) TENT is a source-free TTA baseline that updates BN parameters by minimizing entropy. Our method adopts the same update strategy while designing three self-supervised losses: length consistency, entropy minimization, and boundary gradient. Consequently, the ablation setting with only entropy minimization is equivalent to TENT, which alone actually increases error. The next revision will explicitly note that TENT is already included in the ablation framework. (iii)The method of Karani et al. targets segmentation tasks and is not applicable to landmark heatmap regression-based biometric measurement. Unsupervised TTA methods for brain biometry are extremely scarce. We tested DGMLD [8], a TTA method specifically designed for fetal cerebellar measurement that exploits the cerebellum’s regular geometric contour for boundary pre-training. However, DGMLD’s direct TTA version performed much worse than the source model, likely due to large imaging parameter differences, so we adopted its supervised fine-tuned version. (iv) To comply with the double-blind policy, we cannot discuss the relationship with the reference [10]. Technically, [10] is equivalent to our atlas-constraint only ablation setting, and our results confirm that the proposed additional losses yield significant improvements over this baseline, which will be explicitly clarified in the next revision. Regarding Table 2: (1) BioTTA’s quantitative advantage over other methods is demonstrated in Table 1; (2) Table 2 validates clinical usability by comparing with radiologists; (3) We appreciate this suggestion and will supplement other methods’ diagnostic performance in the next revision. “Preliminary experiments confirm that the source model achieves an accuracy of 0.921 and F1 of 0.924 for VM Diagnosis, and an accuracy of 0.908 and F1 of 0.912 for GMH Grading on the OoD-GMH dataset, both inferior to BioTTA (Acc 0.932, F1 0.934 and Acc 0.919, F1 0.922, respectively). # R3: Regression branch robustness: In segmentation domain adaptation, auxiliary prediction of global quantities such as region proportions has been shown to be effective and domain-invariant (Bateson et al., 2020). Inspired by this, we introduce a length regression branch to model more global structural relationships among landmarks (Song et al., 2024). Empirically, this branch provides stable structural guidance for the heatmap branch and improves robustness under domain shift. Atlas registration constraint: We warp atlas landmarks to the test image space with a 4 mm radius soft constraint to prevent outlier heatmap maxima, which only provides a search region without strictly confining predictions or relying on fine structural details. MIDL short paper: To comply with the double-blind policy, we cannot discuss the relationship with that paper. Our ablation study demonstrates that the additional losses significantly improve performance over using the atlas alone. Space limitations: (1) Standard developmental curves with gestational-age-specific percentiles have been constructed but omitted due to space; they will be publicly released with the codebase. (2) Larger-scale validation with broader pathological coverage and more rigorous ablation experiments is planned for future work. (3) OoD annotation is highly time-intensive, requiring experts to manually label anatomical landmarks; we currently annotated 50 cases and will expand in subsequent studies.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The reviewers find merit in this paper - particularly regarding the importance of the application and novelty (sparse weighted differentiable landmark detector and length consistency loss, task-specific geometric structure) as well as the cross-center aspect and general performed validation. The source-free test time framework is adapted well to clinical need. There are however major weaknesses / points to be addressed: more in-depth discussion of the results (incomplete experimental and statistical analysis), insufficient validation of the core robustness assumption, unclear novelty boundaries relative to closely related prior work (BioTTA, missing groups in table 2) | The authors have addressed some of the concerns and there was feedback and discussion with the reviewers. While one reviewer continues to recommend acceptance and mentioned that some concerns have been addressed, they specify themselves that the criticism re lack of depth, more critical analysis were not appropriately addressed and that the acceptance recommendation is mainly based on the topic being highly relevant and the methodology being interesting. The other reviewer engaged intensively with the rebuttal and maintained (even stronger then before) the recommendation reject arguing similarly that the main concern about methodological clarity and a lack of proof about the main contribution, supervision free TTA. In summary, significant strengths remain important application with possible future impact interesting methodological contribution, Identified WEAKNESSES remain lack of proper comparison to the state of the art insufficient methodological clarity with regard to the exact contributions lack of critical evaluation/discussion of the results Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviews are mixed, with two reviewers recommending acceptance and one reviewer maintaining rejection after rebuttal. I agree that Reviewer 2 raises a substantive concern: for a paper positioned as source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation, the comparison framework should more clearly separate no-adaptation, domain generalization, supervised adaptation, and true source-free TTA baselines. The rebuttal only partially resolves this, and the authors should explicitly clarify the TENT-equivalent ablation, the relationship to the atlas-only prior, and the role of Table 2 as clinical-usability evidence rather than direct evidence for the TTA component. However, I do not consider this issue sufficient for rejection. The paper addresses an important clinical deployment problem in fetal brain biometry, proposes a task-specific and technically meaningful framework, including differentiable landmark extraction and length-consistency-based adaptation, and provides multi-center validation with two backbones, ablations, and clinically oriented diagnostic evaluation. Reviewers 1 and 3 judge the work to be relevant and above the acceptance threshold, and Reviewer 2 also acknowledges the merit, clinical relevance, and meaningful technical design, despite disagreeing on the sufficiency of the validation. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After rebuttal, R2 remains a reject, finding the TENT explanation inconsistent with the reported ablation numbers and the radiologist comparison incapable of isolating the TTA-specific gain. Because of these unresolved fundamental issues, the recommendation is therefore Reject.

title: MedRAG-SCA: A Retrieval-Augmented Self-correcting Agent for Clinically Compliant Cross-Modality MRI Synthesis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Strong and clinically meaningful problem formulation. A major strength of the paper is that it explicitly distinguishes visual plausibility from clinical validity. This is an important point for medical image synthesis, and the authors motivate it convincingly with concrete examples such as CSF suppression failures that may not be captured by standard similarity metrics. 2.Novel protocol-grounded framing of MRI synthesis. This paper introduces protocol-aware synthesis by grounding generation and refinement in retrieved imaging guidelines. The idea of translating qualitative clinical protocol language into quantitative pixel-space constraints is interesting and clearly differentiated from standard GAN/diffusion synthesis papers. 3.Well-designed multi-component framework. The Retrieve–Verify–Refine loop is well structured and easy to follow. The Protocol-Aware RAG Consultant, the Source-Anchored Tri-Critic Committee, and the Targeted Refinement Controller have distinct roles that fit together coherently. The Geometry–Intensity Decoupling principle is also well articulated and clinically intuitive. 4.Good attention to pathology preservation. The pathology-preserving shield and the Geometric Fail-safe are thoughtful additions. They address an important failure mode of synthesis/refinement systems, namely improving apparent modality fidelity at the cost of altering lesion boundaries or edema structure. This adds credibility to the clinical framing of the work. 5.Strong clinical evaluation beyond pixel-level metrics. A particularly notable strength is the inclusion of blinded neuroradiologist evaluation with CAR as the primary clinical endpoint. This is much stronger than relying solely on PSNR/SSIM/FID and directly supports the paper’s central claim that protocol-aware synthesis improves clinical acceptability.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Scope is still limited to neuro-oncology MRI synthesis. The results are strong for the stated task, but the broader generality of the method is not yet established. The framework may not transfer directly to other organs or other protocol families without considerable adaptation of the retrieval knowledge base and the constraint extraction machinery. 2.Comparison is strongest on clinical compliance, but pixel-level tradeoffs remain. The paper argues, plausibly, that slight reductions in PSNR/SSIM may reflect protocol-correct synthesis rather than model weakness. Still, this makes the evaluation somewhat harder to interpret, and the reader must largely accept the paper’s clinical framing to fully endorse the tradeoff. More direct downstream task validation (such as segmentation and classification) would make this argument even stronger.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Novel Clinical Grounding: First work to integrate retrieval-augmented generation for clinical protocol adherence in image synthesis, converting text-based ACR guidelines into verifiable pixel-space intensity ratios (e.g., CSF/WM ∈[3.5,4.2]). This addresses a real clinical need often ignored in synthesis literature. Rigorous Clinical Validation: Unlike most synthesis papers relying solely on pixel metrics, this work employs blinded evaluation by three board-certified neuroradiologists (ICC=0.81), establishing CAR as the primary endpoint. This sets a high bar for clinical utility assessment. Technical Innovation: The Tri-Critic Committee architecture elegantly separates concerns—geometry (Anatomist), modality fidelity (Radiologist), and pathology preservation (Diagnostician)—enabling unsupervised, ground-truth-free quality assurance. The Geometric Fail-safe mechanism for complex edema cases shows sophisticated handling of clinical edge cases. Practical Impact: Directly addresses the clinical bottleneck of incomplete MRI acquisitions due to contraindications/motion, with demonstrated protocol transfer to healthy subjects (IXI dataset) without retraining. Comprehensive Evaluation: Multi-dataset validation (BraTS 2024, IXI), ablation studies confirming each component’s contribution (RAG provides largest gain: +21% CAR), and pathological fidelity verification (ET Dice 0.763 vs 0.724 baseline).
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Scope Limitation: Evaluation restricted to neuro-oncology (glioma). Generalization to other anatomies (spine, abdominal) or pathologies (stroke, MS) is unverified, limiting immediate clinical translatability beyond brain tumors. Confirmation Bias in PAS: The Protocol Adherence Score (PAS) is directly optimized by the framework (via gradient guidance), making it susceptible to confirmation bias. While CAR (primary endpoint) is independent, the tight correlation between PAS and CAR (ρ=0.72) suggests potential circularity in the optimization target. Performance Degradation in Risk Zones: The Geometric Fail-safe triggers in 12.7% of cases (extensive edema), causing PAS to drop to 0.68 and requiring reduced-confidence flagging. This reveals fragility when source-target anatomy diverges significantly. System Complexity: The multi-component pipeline (RAG retrieval, MedSAM segmentation, three critics, iterative refinement) introduces multiple failure points and computational overhead that may hinder clinical deployment, despite the <50ms retrieval latency claim. Retrieval Dependency: Performance relies heavily on the curated 1,170-document knowledge base. Rare protocols or emerging guidelines may not be covered, and the parse accuracy (>90%) leaves edge cases dependent on conservative wide-range priors. Marginal PSNR Trade-off: While explained as reference non-compliance, the PSNR reduction (27.85 vs 28.30 dB) compared to SynDiff may concern practitioners prioritizing pixel fidelity over protocol adherence.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clinically grounded problem. The decoupling of pixel-level metrics from clinical validity is correctly identified. The SynDiff example—SSIM > 0.90 yet ACR CSF-suppression failure in 29/50 radiologist-reviewed cases—is a compelling motivation that aligns with recent critiques of pixel-wise metrics in medical imaging. 2.Rigorous radiologist study. Three independent board-certified neuroradiologists rated 150 images with ICC = 0.81 [0.76, 0.85]. Pre-specifying CAR as the primary endpoint and powering the study appropriately is commendable. 3.Pathology-preserving refinement. The Diagnostician critic’s expanding feature-based shield (RadImageNet ResNet50 layer-4) prevents progressive overcorrection of lesion boundaries. This is a thoughtful solution to a known failure mode in iterative medical synthesis.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The RAG claim is inflated. The system does not use generative retrieval-augmented reasoning. It retrieves documents with BioBERT + FAISS, but the actual “translation” from text to pixel constraints is performed by spaCy dependency parsing mapped through a 47-entry lookup table built from only 50 radiologist-annotated documents. This is retrieval-augmented templating, not RAG. The title and abstract mislead readers into expecting end-to-end LLM reasoning over retrieved guidelines. 2.The ablation conflates retrieval with any textual guidance. Removing “RAG” (replaced with static prompts) drops CAR from 92% to 71%, but this compares the full system against no protocol text at all. 3.Confirmation bias in PAS. PAS is directly optimized via the hinge protocol loss (Eq. 2). The authors admit this bias, yet they still foreground PAS improvements (0.94 vs. 0.79, including per-constraint breakdowns in Table 2) rather than treating PAS strictly as a training signal. CAR partially mitigates this, but PAS should be de-emphasized in the results. 4.Validation scope is too narrow. Only BraTS 2024 (challenge data) and IXI (healthy subjects). No real clinical PACS data, no multi-vendor scanners, no non-glioma pathology, no cross-ethnic cohorts. For a paper claiming clinical compliance, this gap is too large. Recent contrast-enhancement work has demonstrated validation across multiple external datasets, vendors, and clinical sites; this paper’s footprint is substantially narrower. 5.Parser generalization is questionable. “>90% parse accuracy on held-out validation” with only 50 documents implies a tiny test set (likely ~10 documents under a standard 80/20 split, or ~5 under a 90/10 split).
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments and positive evaluation of our work. We are grateful that the reviewers recognized the clinical motivation of distinguishing visual plausibility from clinical validity, as well as the value of protocol-aware synthesis, the tri-critic verification design, pathology-preserving refinement, and blinded radiologist evaluation. We will carefully revise the manuscript for clarity in the camera-ready version, including refining the description of the retrieval-augmented protocol-grounding mechanism, clarifying the role of PAS as a mechanistic measure rather than an independent clinical endpoint, and improving the discussion of validation scope, Risk Zone behavior, and deployment considerations. We also appreciate the suggestions regarding future extensions to broader anatomies, pathologies, vendors, and clinical datasets, and will discuss these limitations and future directions more explicitly in the final version where appropriate.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses the important problem of cross-modality synthesis aligned with clinical imaging protocols focusing on the context of euro-oncology. All reviewers highlighted the clinical relevance of the contribution and the novelty of the proposed approach. It appears however that there may be some degree of circularity in the proposed evaluation that should be clarified.

title: Memory-Guided Random-Direction Feature Disentanglement Model for Multi-phase MRI Translation
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper presents an interesting and technically coherent framework, with a reasonably novel random-direction disentanglement design and a segmentation-guided memory mechanism that is well motivated for improving region-level fidelity in medical image translation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The model does not explicitly incorporate the physical properties of multi-phase imaging, such as temporal dynamics across phases. Since phase progression in contrast-enhanced MRI follows an underlying physiological and temporal pattern, ignoring this characteristic may limit the model’s ability to capture more realistic cross-phase relationships. It is unclear whether segmentation is required at test time. If so, the method has a clear dependence on segmentation priors and a pre-trained segmentation model, which reduces its general applicability and weakens the claim of being a lightweight translation framework. The method is designed in a 2D manner, whereas medical imaging data are inherently 3D. This may limit the model’s ability to preserve volumetric consistency and exploit inter-slice contextual information, which are often important in medical image translation.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Elegant geometric formulation for disentanglement: The core idea of selecting content and style points along a random 1D line using density-based criteria is mathematically clean and intuitive. The content point as the joint density maximizer and style points as density discrepancy extrema provide a principled geometric interpretation of content-style separation. The closed-form solution for the content point (Eq. 2) and the differentiable soft-argmax for style points (Eq. 4) make the approach both analytically grounded and end-to-end trainable. Architectural simplicity and parameter efficiency: By using a single shared VAE encoder instead of multiple domain-specific encoders and content discriminators, the method achieves a compact inference footprint (13.15M parameters), approximately 8× smaller than TransUNet or ResViT while achieving competitive or superior performance. This is practically meaningful for medical imaging deployment scenarios. Well-motivated memory bank design with region-level evaluation: The segmentation-guided style memory bank addresses a real limitation of global style representations, as different anatomical regions respond differently to contrast agents. The ablation study supports its effectiveness with consistent improvement from RDFD-only to MG-RDFD. Furthermore, the authors go beyond standard full-slice metrics by reporting ROI-level PSNR and MAE for liver and lesion regions, which is clinically relevant.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Lack of repeated experiments despite stochastic nature of the method: RDFD fundamentally relies on random sampling from the two posteriors to construct the 1D line along which content and style points are selected. Despite this inherent stochasticity, all results in Table 1 are reported as single values without standard deviations from multiple runs. Given that the reported improvements over baselines are often marginal (e.g., 0.2–0.5 dB in PSNR), it is difficult to assess whether these gains reflect genuine methodological advantages or simply favorable randomness in a single training run. Data split strategy is not specified: The paper states that approximately 32k paired slices are split into training/validation sets at a 4:1 ratio, but does not clarify whether this split is performed at the subject level or the slice level. If slices from the same patient appear in both sets, data leakage could inflate the reported metrics. This is a critical detail for assessing the validity of the experimental results. Insufficient ablation studies: The ablation only demonstrates the incremental effect of adding RDFD and the memory bank on top of FDA-VAE. However, the method introduces numerous critical hyperparameters — κ (search range), τ (soft-argmax temperature), G (grid resolution), the number of memory slots per region Mk, and momentum μ — none of which are analyzed for sensitivity. Similarly, the memory bank design choices (K=16 regions, the role of the global cross-entropy loss Lglob) and the loss weighting scheme in Eq. 10 (8 terms) are not ablated. Without such analysis, it is unclear how robust the method is to these design decisions. Inconsistent SSIM results are not adequately discussed: Adding RDFD to FDA-VAE causes a notable SSIM drop on the Pre→CA task (80.40 → 78.59), and even the full MG-RDFD model does not recover the baseline SSIM on this task (79.99 vs. 80.40). This suggests that the proposed disentanglement may introduce structural distortions in certain translation scenarios. The paper does not analyze or explain this trade-off, which undermines the claim of consistent improvement. Validity of the single-input inference assumption is not analyzed: At inference time, the method constructs a pseudo-target posterior by flipping the mean of the source posterior while keeping the variance unchanged. This is a strong assumption that relies on the symmetry encouraged by FDA during training. However, the paper provides no analysis of how well this pseudo posterior approximates the true target posterior, nor does it discuss under what conditions this assumption might break down. Evaluation on a single dataset: All experiments are conducted on the LLD-MMRI 2023 dataset only. While the limited availability of multi-phase paired CE-MRI data is acknowledged, evaluation on a single dataset makes it difficult to assess the generalizability of the proposed method to other anatomical regions, imaging protocols, or institutional settings.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: -The random-direction latent geometry to jointly determine content and styles via density overlap/discrepancy along a sampled 1D subspace is an elegant and interpretable mechanism that explicitly couples shared and domain-specific factors, avoiding multiple encoders or explicit content discriminators. -A closed-form solution for the content anchor (via maximizing joint log-likelihood) and a bounded, differentiable soft-argmax/min search for style anchors are technically sound and differentiable. -The segmentation-guided memory bank with momentum-updated, region-wise content keys and domain-specific style values (plus regional and global CE regularizers) is a principled way to stabilize regional appearances and mitigate texture confusion. -Evaluations include three clinically relevant phase-translation directions, full-slice and ROI metrics (liver/lesions), and parameter counts for inference. -Comparisons span both high-capacity end-to-end translators and disentanglement models; ablations (FDA-VAE backbone vs RDFD-only vs memory-augmented MG-RDFD) isolate the contribution of the proposed components.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: -The clinical applicability and practical value of the work remain insufficiently demonstrated. Multi-phase liver MRI translation is clinically meaningful only if the synthesized phases preserve diagnostically relevant enhancement patterns and can support real downstream interpretation. The current evidence is still mainly based on PSNR, SSIM, and ROI-level MAE/PSNR, which measure pixel-level fidelity but do not establish whether the generated images are clinically reliable or useful. -The paper does not provide downstream task validation. Given that the dataset contains liver-lesion annotations, it would be important to evaluate whether synthesized phases improve or preserve performance in lesion segmentation, lesion-type classification, or other clinically relevant tasks. Without such evidence, it is difficult to determine whether the reported ROI improvements translate into meaningful diagnostic utility. A segmentation Dice evaluation, lesion-wise detection/recall, enhancement-pattern consistency analysis, or classification performance under missing-phase settings would substantially strengthen the paper. -The methodological novelty, while interesting, should be better positioned against recent generative modeling literature. The paper builds upon an FDA-VAE-style framework, and the gains over this strong backbone appear relatively modest. In the current medical image synthesis landscape, diffusion models and latent diffusion models have become strong baselines for structure-preserving image translation and conditional generation. The paper only briefly discusses such methods and does not provide a direct comparison or a convincing rationale for excluding them. This makes it difficult to assess whether the proposed latent-geometry and memory-bank design remains competitive against more recent diffusion-based approaches. -Several practical aspects are underexplored. The inference process may involve stochastic sampling, yet the paper does not clearly state whether deterministic latent means are used at test time or whether output variability is evaluated. The per-pixel grid search used in RDFD and the memory-retrieval mechanism may introduce non-trivial computational overhead, but runtime, latency, and GPU memory usage are not reported. The method also appears to rely on segmentation masks during inference, but the source of these masks and robustness to segmentation errors are not quantified. Since the experiments are conducted on a single dataset with 2D slice-based training, cross-site, cross-scanner, and 3D volume-level generalization remain open questions. Overall, the paper is technically promising and addresses a relevant missing-phase MRI synthesis problem, but its current form does not fully establish clinical utility or practical deployability. The contribution would be much stronger if the authors added downstream clinical task evaluations, clarified inference-time dependencies, reported computational costs, and compared against or more carefully justified the exclusion of recent diffusion/LDM-based MRI translation baselines.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their recognition and suggestions. Our responses are as follows. Phase-time information and RDFD rationale (R1): Explicit temporal modeling could introduce stronger clinical priors. However, LLD-MMRI does not provide precise acquisition time steps, and we focus on a general content-style disentanglement mechanism rather than temporal modeling. For the RDFD rationale, the content anchor is not merely a visually overlapping point: density-overlap selects the point that best represents both phase posteriors, while density discrepancy selects phase-preferred style anchors within the same latent geometry. Mask dependence and patient-level data split (R1&R2): Our model needs organ and lesion labels from pretrained models during both training and inference. It’s a low-cost structural/clinical prior. Mask downsampling to feature-map resolution attenuates pixel-level errors. We split patient volumes 4:1 with lesion-distribution stratification before slicing, avoiding patient-level leakage. We will state this in the Experimental Setup. 3D training and computation (R1&R4): 3D training can improve volumetric consistency. Our code can be easily extended to 3D, but we used 2D training considering computational cost and a fair 2D-baseline comparison. RDFD has no learnable parameters and runs on low-resolution feature maps, so its overhead is much smaller than learnable modules. Since FDA-VAE reports a positive active-parameter/latency relation, active inference parameters are a practical efficiency proxy. Stochastic sampling and variability (R2&R4): RDFD is stochastic, but the content anchor is less variable than raw VAE samples because it maximizes joint density in the overlap of two close posteriors(Fig.3); sampling mainly defines the search direction. Internal repeated trainings/validations varied mainly at the second decimal place, close to/below Table 1 precision. We agree formal multi-seed std would be stronger and will clarify this limitation without overstating small gains. Ablation scope and hyperparameter choices (R2): Our ablation tests overall RDFD and memory-bank effectiveness. Preliminary grid search selected RDFD hyperparameters: G trades style search resolution for compute/memory; κ sets the style search range, too small misses extrema and too large dilutes grid precision; τ controls soft-argmax sharpness, too small is hard/unstable and too large over-smooths extrema. K=16 comes from automatically available regions: major organs, seven lesion types, abdomen, and border. Loss/memory settings follow FDA-VAE/MGUIT. SSIM discussion (R2): We will revise the analysis to clarify possible causes of the Pre->CA SSIM drop. All phases are registered to CV, and all predicted segmentation labels are also defined in the CV reference space; thus, Pre/CA->CV benefits from direct alignment, whereas residual Pre-CA misalignment can be penalized by SSIM and may affect RDFD/memory via structural anchors and labels. FDA gain and LDM rationale (R2&R4): Compared with FDA-VAE, RDFD provides statistical disentanglement and alleviates late-training over-overlap (Fig. 3(c)); 0.2-0.5 dB PSNR gains are meaningful in this domain. Diffusion/LDMs are strong but rely on iterative sampling with high computational costs and long inference time, while our goal is a lightweight, interpretable, single-pass disentanglement framework with low active parameters. Single-dataset and clinical tasks (R4): LLD-MMRI is a lesion-rich paired multi-phase MRI dataset with 498 unique patients covering 7 different liver lesion types and multiple MRI phases/sequences. We use three clinically relevant CE phases (Pre, CA, CV), providing paired lesion-level supervision. This is richer for our task than many two-modality translation datasets with only tens of subjects. The dataset lacks expert pixel-level gold labels, making downstream evaluation difficult; we will consider lesion classification/detection and enhancement-pattern consistency in future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers pointed out several concerns. Key issues include the lack of incorporation of multi-phase imaging’s inherent temporal dynamics, the unclear dependency on segmentation at inference time, and the limitations of the 2D model design for inherently 3D medical data. Furthermore, ablation studies are insufficient, and critical details such as data split strategies and computational costs are underexplored. The reviewers also noted that the single-dataset evaluation limits the generalizability of the method, while clinical utility remains inadequately demonstrated. | The proposed method is technically thoughtful and shows parameter efficiency with promising results. The key concerns raised by reviewers focus on the clarity and novelty of the methodological contributions relative to prior work, the modest experimental gains without statistical significance, and insufficient practical validation for clinical applicability. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): While R1 suggests acceptance, praising the random-direction disentanglement design, the majority of the reviewers raised critical concerns regarding empirical rigor and clinical validation. R2 and R4 highlighted that the statistical significance of the marginal gains cannot be verified, as the authors provided no run-to-run variance estimates despite the framework’s inherently stochastic sampling design. Furthermore, the core inference-time deployment mechanism remains unvalidated, with no analysis supporting the strong symmetry assumption used to construct the pseudo-posterior. Finally, the clinical utility of the synthesized multi-phase MRIs remains unproven, as the evaluation relies entirely on pixel-level metrics rather than downstream clinical task validation (e.g., lesion segmentation or classification performance), while the model’s sensitivity to its numerous hyperparameters and test-time dependence on segmentation masks remain unquantified. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents an interesting idea of random-direction disentanglement. Although two reviewers gave rejection after the rebuttal, the main concern is about the lack of comprehensive validation and implementation details. So I think this is a broadline paper with an interesting methodology contribution. I am leaning toward accepting it.

title: MiGAD: Gut Microbiota-informed Genetic Surrogates for Multimodal Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: (1) Novel Methodological Formulation: The paper innovatively proposes “Microbiota-informed Genetic Surrogates” to capture gut-brain axis signals. By leveraging Mendelian Randomization on GWAS data, it bypasses the instability of direct microbiome profiling, using stable host genetic variants as reliable proxies for AD diagnosis. (2) Clinical Deployability via Distillation: The proposed Multimodal-to-MRI knowledge distillation strategy effectively addresses data scarcity in real-world screening. The distilled MRI-only student model significantly outperforms baseline imaging models (AUC 0.825 vs. 0.910), demonstrating strong practical utility where peripheral data is unavailable. (3) Robust Cross-Modal Alignment: The integration of an explicit InfoNCE contrastive learning objective ensures semantic consistency across heterogeneous modalities. Ablation studies confirm that this alignment mechanism is critical for maximizing the performance of the hierarchical Transformer fusion architecture. (4) Rigorous Large-Scale Validation: The method is evaluated on 6,500 participants from two distinct cohorts (UK Biobank and ADNI). This large-scale, cross-cohort validation demonstrates the model’s robustness and generalizability across diverse demographic and clinical populations.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) Fundamental Flaw in Causal Logic and Surrogate Validity: The core premise relies on the unproven assumption that selected genetic variants effectively proxy for gut microbiome composition. However, reverse causality is a significant confounder: AD pathology may influence microbiome composition via changes in diet, medication, or behavior. The paper fails to empirically validate that these variants predict actual microbial profiles in the study cohort. If this link is weak, the “microbiota-informed surrogates” are merely standard AD-risk loci, rendering the proposed mechanistic innovation illusory. (2) Modality Gap in Knowledge Distillation: Stage III forces an MRI-only student to mimic multimodal teacher representations (h_T). However, MRI captures structural changes, whereas genetic/clinical data reflect systemic states. It is questionable whether structural imaging alone can truly reconstruct these peripheral signals. The performance gain may stem from fitting the teacher’s output distribution rather than learning genuine gut-brain mechanisms, a claim unsupported by interpretability analysis linking student attention to biologically relevant regions. (3) Unfair Comparison with Multimodal Baselines: The evaluation in Table 3 is methodologically inconsistent. Only MADDi integrates three modalities (imaging, tabular, genetics), while HyperFusion and DAFT use only imaging and tabular data. Comparing MiGAD—which leverages genetic surrogates—against baselines lacking genetic input fails to isolate the specific benefit of the proposed selection strategy. A fairer assessment would require baselines that also incorporate genetic data (e. g. , PRS-enhanced models). (4) Insufficient Experimental Details: Key reproducibility details are omitted, including the dataset splitting strategy (e. g. , random or site-based) and specific MRI data augmentation techniques. (5) Poor Readability and Undefined Notations: The manuscript lacks clarity in its mathematical formulation. Several notations are introduced without explicit definitions, such as the classification loss L_cls(Eq. 6), the projection function fm(*) (Eq. 4), etc.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: This work goes beyond typical MRI + tabular data by introducing biologically motivated genetic features. Specifically, using a microbiota-informed genetic surrogate approach is relatively novel. title: Missing Modality-Aware Calibration for Trustworthy Brain Tumor Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The main strengths of this paper lie in its clinically relevant problem setting and its focus on an often overlooked yet important issue in missing-modality segmentation, namely the reliability of model confidence under incomplete modality conditions rather than segmentation accuracy alone. Methodologically, the novelty of MMA-LTS stems from its combination of modality-combination awareness and spatially adaptive calibration. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on modality count or global temperature assumptions, the proposed method explicitly models which modalities are missing via learnable modality tokens, capturing fine-grained modality dependencies. In addition, it introduces a voxel-wise difficulty score (VDS) to characterize spatial uncertainty and generates a voxel-wise temperature field for locally adaptive calibration, which is better suited to address modality-specific and spatially heterogeneous miscalibration. The method is implemented as a post-hoc module without requiring retraining of the segmentation backbone, making it practically appealing from an engineering perspective. Experimentally, the paper provides relatively comprehensive validation across multiple datasets, segmentation backbones, and modality combinations, along with ablation studies supporting the effectiveness of each component. Overall, the strengths of this work lie in a well-motivated problem, a targeted methodological design, and reasonably thorough empirical evaluation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: In its current form, the paper does not yet meet the publication bar. The main concern is that the proposed contribution is largely confined to a specific calibration module rather than representing a broader architectural or methodological advance. MMA-LTS is essentially built as a post-hoc extension on top of an existing segmentation backbone, and the claimed novelty mainly comes from combining modality-aware tokens, FiLM conditioning, and voxel-wise temperature scaling within this narrow module. As a result, the work appears more like a task-specific engineering adaptation of existing calibration techniques than a genuinely new framework that advances missing-modality segmentation at the network level. The method does not introduce a new representation learning strategy, a new missing-modality learning paradigm, or a new backbone design; instead, it refines confidence correction after prediction. This makes the overall contribution somewhat limited for a top-tier venue. A related concern is that the practical applicability of the method seems highly restricted to the specific setting studied in the paper, namely brain tumor MRI datasets such as BraTS 2020 and FeTS 2024.The proposed design is strongly tied to the characteristics of multimodal brain MRI, where different sequences have relatively well-understood and complementary roles for different tumor subregions. It is therefore unclear whether the same formulation would remain effective for other anatomical sites, other imaging modalities, or more heterogeneous multimodal clinical settings where the relationships among modalities are less structured. Since all experiments are conducted only on heavily standardized brain MRI benchmarks, the paper does not provide sufficient evidence that the method is broadly useful beyond this narrow application domain. More generally, the paper overstates the scope of its contribution. While the problem of calibration under missing modalities is important, the current solution is specialized to a particular post-hoc module and validated only in a very specific experimental context. Without stronger evidence of architectural generality, cross-task transferability, or applicability beyond BraTS-style brain MRI benchmarks, the impact of the work remains limited. For these reasons, I do not think the paper, in its current form, provides a sufficiently broad or substantial advance to justify acceptance.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1) This paper points out that existing methods for missing-modality segmentation often ignore the issue of confidence calibration. More importantly, the authors observe a clinically meaningful phenomenon in brain tumor segmentation: the difficulty of prediction depends more on which specific modality is missing than on the total number of missing modalities. 2)To address this, the paper introduces a spatially adaptive temperature field, predicted using modality availability tokens and voxel-wise difficulty scores. The design is logically sound and well tailored to the anatomical characteristics of brain tumor segmentation. 3)The experimental validation is thorough, covering comparison experiments, ablation studies and analyses of hyperparameter sensitivity.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1) It is recommended to include failure case analyses to enhance the clinical interpretability of the model. 2) Although the method encodes different modality combinations via modality availability tokens, effective calibration still requires exposure to specific combinations in the validation set during training. The generalization capability for extreme modality combinations not encountered during training has not been sufficiently validated. It is suggested to do more experiments to validate the superiority of this method.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. Following the meta-reviewer’s suggestions, we clarify below the key concerns raised by the reviewers. (Reviewer #2) VDS Implementation: As stated in Section 2.1, GT labels are used only during offline estimation of class-conditional statistics (µₗ, Σ) from D_train, after which these statistics are fixed. At inference time, predicted labels serve as pseudo-labels to compute the RMD without requiring GT labels. This is feasible because the pretrained segmentation model F has frozen weights, keeping the feature space invariant, such that the distribution statistics estimated from training data remain valid reference points at inference. We will provide a more explicit description of the inference procedure. (Reviewer #2) Novelty and Generalizability: The core contribution lies in the problem formulation itself: the observation that calibration error in brain tumor segmentation varies by which modalities are absent rather than how many has not been addressed in prior work. Although individual components are standard, their combination is essential for solving this problem, as demonstrated by our ablation study. We recognize that extension to anatomical sites beyond brain tumors remains an important direction, and will consider this in future work. (Reviewer #2, #3): Failure Cases and Limitations: Explicit failure case analysis would strengthen the paper, and we will add a discussion focusing on residual overconfidence in boundary regions. We acknowledge the absence of additional reliability metrics and validation in real clinical settings as limitations of the current work. (Reviewer #3) Generalization to Unseen Modality Combinations: The modality availability token encodes each modality’s status independently and combines them linearly (Eq. (3)), allowing unseen combinations to be naturally represented at inference. We nonetheless recognize that calibration performance may degrade when certain combinations are entirely absent from D_val. Due to rebuttal constraints, we could not include new experimental results, but we will explore enforcing full combination coverage in D_val or generalization validation for unseen modality combinations as potential mitigation strategies. (Reviewer #5) External Validation and Statistical Comparison: Consistent improvements across two independent benchmarks (BraTS 2020 and FeTS 2024) provide evidence for the applicability of our method. We agree that additional external validation and formal statistical comparison of performance metrics would further strengthen the work, and will look to address these in future work. We will make every effort to incorporate the reviewers’ suggestions into the final version.
