title: S2GAIN: Spatio-Spectral Guided Affinity Imputation Network for Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis with Incomplete Modality
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The overall presentation of this paper is clear. 2.Missing PET is a crucial task in AD diagnosis. 3.Experiments are reasonable and presented clearly.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Ablation studies should not be limited to lambda, alpha, and beta. 2.On page 7, 1 line and Table 2 are not aligned nicely.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The methodological innovation is well targeted. The authors identify two critical limitations in existing missing-modality approaches and design corresponding solutions accordingly. First, most feature completion methods focus only on spatial-domain alignment, even though the discrepancy between MRI and PET lies not only in spatial structure but also in texture patterns and frequency components. Second, many studies implicitly assume that MRI can recover the full spectrum of PET information, whereas part of the metabolic information in PET is not reliably predictable from MRI; forcing such components to be fitted may introduce noise and further blur the classification boundary. To address these issues, the authors propose S2JA and AGRW. S2JA extends alignment from the spatial domain to a joint spatial-frequency framework by incorporating amplitude-spectrum constraints, while AGRW uses affinity to estimate the reliability of cross-modal completion, emphasizing more trustworthy correspondences and suppressing noise from inherently unpredictable components. The main novelty lies not merely in the use of FFT or weighting, but in a more refined modeling perspective: distinguishing how modality differences should be aligned and which components should not be forced to be learned. 2.The experimental evaluation is convincing, particularly the cross-cohort validation. This is another major strength of the study. Many related works rely solely on splits within a single dataset, which may yield strong performance but provide limited evidence of robustness under distribution shift. In contrast, this study conducts a bidirectional cross-cohort evaluation on ADNI-1 and ADNI-2, training on one cohort and testing on the other, and then reversing the setting. This design is substantially more rigorous than conventional random splits and offers stronger evidence of generalization. The stronger experimental protocol, together with results that closely match the methodological motivation, makes the overall empirical support more compelling.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The applicability of the proposed method remains relatively narrow. Although the title claims to address the general problem of incomplete modalities, the study focuses primarily on a single missing-pattern setting, namely the availability of MRI with missing PET, and all experiments are conducted under this assumption. While this scenario is clinically meaningful, the paper does not establish whether the method would remain effective in more complex incomplete multimodal settings, such as simultaneous absence of multiple modalities or varying missing rates. The authors do acknowledge in the conclusion that future work should extend the framework to more challenging missing-modality scenarios. 2.The reliability weighting mechanism still depends on supervision from real PET data. The idea of AGRW is reasonable, yet during training it requires the affinity between completed features and ground-truth PET features to generate reliability weights. In essence, this means that the mechanism still relies on the availability of true PET supervision at the training stage. Therefore, although effective under the current experimental setting, the paper does not clarify whether this module would retain the same advantage in scenarios where paired PET data are scarcer and supervision is weaker. 3.The validation of completion quality is still not sufficiently direct. A central goal of this study is to recover PET representations from MRI, and the authors further introduce image-domain reconstruction regularization to encourage the completed representations to better approximate the metabolic distribution and structural consistency of real PET images. However, the experiments mainly report downstream classification results, together with ablation studies and parameter sensitivity analyses, without providing more direct evidence of completion quality, such as quantitative similarity metrics between completed and real PET or visual comparisons of representative cases. As a result, the current findings demonstrate more clearly that the method benefits classification, while offering less direct support for the claim that it produces more faithful PET representations. 4.Although the paper compares the proposed method with several advanced missing-modality imputation approaches, it omits a particularly important baseline: a strong MRI-only classifier. Without reporting the performance of a model trained directly on MRI alone, using either a standard backbone such as ResNet or the paper’s own 3D Dense Block, it is difficult for readers to assess the absolute performance gain brought by the proposed cross-modal completion framework over a single-modality MRI setting. 5.Some writing issues are also present in the manuscript. On page 3, in Contribution 1, there is a missing space before “spectrum”. In Contribution 2, the ending period is missing. On page 6, after DfpetL, there should be a space following the period.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A major strength of the paper is that it explicitly addresses the inherent heterogeneity between MRI and PET when synthesizing missing modalities, including differences in texture patterns, frequency characteristics, artifacts, and noise. Rather than relying solely on image-space information, the method jointly leverages spatial-domain and frequency-domain information, which is a well-motivated design for improving heterogeneous representation alignment across modalities. This design is meaningful because multimodal AD diagnosis often depends on effectively integrating complementary MRI and PET information under missing-modality settings.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: One important limitation is that the paper mainly evaluates the generated features through diagnostic performance, without sufficiently examining their interpretability or modality-specific validity. As a result, it remains uncertain whether the generated representations faithfully capture the characteristics of the target modality or simply act as useful auxiliary signals for prediction.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Reviewer 1.Thank you for the suggestion. We selected λ1, λ2, λ3, α, and β for sensitivity analysis because they directly correspond to the three core objectives of S²GAIN, i.e., S²JA, AGRW, and R², and control the balance between spatial and spectral alignment. Thus, they are the most relevant objective-level hyperparameters. We agree that other factors, such as temperature τ, stage number L, imputer capacity, and PET decoder configuration, are also worth studying. However, they are mostly internal or structural hyperparameters, and changing them would affect model capacity, computation, and memory simultaneously. Due to the page limit, we prioritized the loss-related parameters and will study more settings in future extended work. We also thank the reviewer for pointing out the layout issue of Table 2. Reviewer 2.Thank you for the comments. We agree that this work focuses on the clinically common setting where MRI is available but PET is missing. MRI is generally more accessible and less costly, whereas PET is more likely to be absent due to cost, equipment requirements, and radioactive tracers. Thus, our goal is to impute PET-related latent representations from MRI for PET-missing AD diagnosis. More complex cases, such as multiple missing modalities, different missing patterns, or varying missing rates, are not covered here. We will explore them in future extended work, e.g., missing both fMRI and PET after introducing additional modalities. Regarding AGRW, we agree that it uses real PET features during training. Our method follows a supervised cross-modal imputation setting: paired MRI-PET data are used to learn the MRI-to-PET mapping, while only MRI is required during PET-missing inference. AGRW does not remove PET supervision; instead, it uses the affinity between imputed and real PET features as a reliability weight to emphasize predictable cross-modal associations and suppress non-inferable components. Regarding completion quality, we agree that similarity metrics or visual comparisons would provide more direct evidence. However, our goal is not PET image synthesis for visual inspection, but PET-related feature imputation for diagnosis. Thus, the current evaluation focuses on diagnostic performance, cross-cohort generalization, and module ablation. R² is an auxiliary regularizer rather than a standalone synthesis module; Table 3 shows that removing R² decreases performance, suggesting its benefit for structural consistency and diagnostic usefulness. The current results mainly support diagnostic effectiveness rather than pixel-level PET recovery. We will study direct completion metrics and visual comparisons in future extended work. Regarding the MRI-only baseline, we agree that it is important. The current comparisons focus on incomplete-modality learning and imputation methods under a similar setting. Table 3 shows that removing S²JA, AGRW, or R² degrades performance, indicating that the gain is not solely from the backbone. Still, these ablations cannot replace a direct MRI-only baseline. Due to the page limit, this comparison is not included, and we will add it in future extended work. We also thank the reviewer for pointing out the writing issues. Reviewer 3.Thank you for the important comment. We agree that diagnostic performance alone cannot fully demonstrate interpretability or modality-specific validity. In S²GAIN, S²JA constrains MRI/PET features in spatial and frequency domains; AGRW uses feature affinity to focus on PET-related components inferable from MRI; and R² encourages deep PET-related features to preserve image-domain spatial structure. These designs encourage PET-consistent representations, but do not fully establish interpretability or target-modality validity. The current experiments mainly show diagnostic usefulness, and we will further study interpretability and modality-specific validation in future extended work.

title: SAGEAgent: A Self-evolving Agent for Cost-Aware Modality Acquisition in Multimodal Survival Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: Novel methodology
reviewer_1_weaknesses: lack of external validation Lack of statistical analysis of model performance metrics.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1) The paper extends the optimization objectives of prior work beyond predictive accuracy by incorporating clinically important requirements, including modality acquisition order constraints, multidimensional clinical burden such as economic cost, invasiveness, and turnaround time, and decision auditability. This provides a new modeling direction for clinical multimodal decision support research. 2) The proposed fully decoupled predictor-agent architecture balances predictive stability and decision interpretability. The frozen Transformer-based multimodal predictor preserves the predictive stability of static fusion models, while the LLM-based decision agent with dual memory modules addresses the black-box nature of prior reinforcement-learning-based dynamic acquisition approaches. Its reasoning is based only on quantified predictions, similar historical cases, and standardized clinical rules, which makes the decision path traceable and reduces the risk of hallucination at the mechanism level. 3) The training and evaluation pipeline is more aligned with realistic clinical scenarios. The modality-dropout strategy combined with partial-modality patient data augmentation improves robustness to common missing-modality settings, and the MCDA framework enables a more comprehensive evaluation of multidimensional clinical burden than prior approaches that only use the number of acquired modalities as the evaluation metric. 4) The validation results on a public mixed glioma cohort show initial clinical application potential. The method reduces average clinical burden by 42.7% with only a non-significant 0.013 decrease in C-index, and the modular decoupled design allows rapid replacement of the multimodal predictor and decision rules without global retraining. The fully auditable decision pipeline may also reduce barriers to clinical compliance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1) The experimental comparison and generalization validation are insufficient. The method is validated only on a single-disease public glioma cohort and does not cover other cancer types or multi-center clinical settings. In addition, the set of comparison methods in dynamic modality acquisition is incomplete, since the experiments only compare against a basic reinforcement learning baseline and a full-modality static fusion baseline, without including more recent agent-based dynamic modality acquisition methods, making it difficult to fully establish the effectiveness of the SAGEAgent architecture or its cross-scenario generality. 2) The study lacks support from real clinical data. All experiments are based on retrospective offline analyses using public datasets, without prospective validation in real clinical workflows or verification on independent multi-center clinical cohorts. As a result, the actual clinical deployment effect and clinician acceptance remain to be validated. 3) There are unresolved gaps regarding training reliability and pathological validity. The lightweight Transformer-based multimodal survival predictor is trained with Cox survival loss and survival metrics under high-dimensional multimodal inputs and limited sample size, which introduces a substantial risk of overfitting, and the paper does not demonstrate at the principle level that the model truly learns core pathological features that are strongly related to survival outcomes. At the same time, similar-case retrieval in the episodic memory module is based only on vector similarity of input modality features and does not consider intrinsic heterogeneity in the pathological microenvironment, especially the tumor microenvironment. Therefore, feature-level similarity may differ substantially from true pathological similarity, which may reduce the clinical value of the retrieved cases. 4) The optimization design may not align with the underlying logic of clinical decision-making. Clinical diagnosis is a complex process that depends heavily on expert experience, and diagnostic accuracy, examination cost, and invasiveness are naturally in tension with one another. Integrating them into a single weighted objective may lead to performance degradation on both types of goals. The notes argue that a more appropriate design would treat diagnostic accuracy, examination cost, and invasiveness as three independent objectives and optimize them through a cooperative multi-agent game framework rather than the current weighted single-objective formulation. 5) Reproducibility and ablation validation are incomplete. The authors do not disclose the training data, parameters, or performance of the pretrained modality feature extractors, so third parties cannot independently verify the quality of multimodal feature encoding or fully reproduce the reported results. In addition, the ablation study does not include validation of modality contribution, and therefore cannot establish the actual contribution of different modalities such as genomics and imaging to the final predictions.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Problem framing is genuinely novel and clinically well-motivated. 2.Architecture is coherent and well-grounded. 3.Interpretability is real, not performative. 4.Rule-discovery analysis (Table 3, Sec. 3.5) is the interesting empirical result. The finding that stopping rules converge in 1–2 reflection cycles and persist, while acquisition rules churn and often get deprecated, is a genuinely useful observation about what self-reflective agents can and cannot learn reliably. 5.Experimental protocol is rigorous for the scale.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.SAGEAgent’s C-index of 0.813 is below Self-Attention Fusion (0.825), MMD (0.822), MCAT (0.817), Reflexion (0.823), and even the ablation’s Base LLM (0.827), showing that every component added reduces C-index relative to Base LLM, and the contribution is squarely on the accuracy–cost trade-off (captured by HV), not accuracy preservation. 2.No statistical significance testing. Standard deviations are ~0.04–0.05, and differences between the six top methods (0.812–0.825) are well within one std. Without paired tests across folds, claims like “competitive with full-modality” and “only method that achieves meaningful burden reduction without compromising accuracy” are not statistically supported. 3.Missing critical baseline: uncertainty-threshold stopping. The calibrated uncertainty head already achieves AUROC 0.908.A naive rule, “stop when u_t < τ”, would test whether the LLM, tools, and dual memory actually add value beyond the uncertainty estimator. Without this baseline, I cannot tell if the semantic rules are doing real work or just reformulating thresholds. Given that the discovered stopping rules all boil down to “uncertainty is low, stop,” this is a serious omission. 4.Comparison with LLM-based acquisition is weak. Only Reflexion is compared. Hager et al. (Nature Medicine 2024, ref [13]) and Nori et al. (ref [18]) are cited but not benchmarked, even though they are the most direct LLM-based-diagnosis competitors.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their feedback and for recognizing that “the work is meaningful and promising”-R4 and “rule-discovery analysis is a real contribution worth publishing”-R5. Common concerns: 1) Statistical significance testing (R3:W2, R5:W2). Paired bootstrap (1000 reps, 170 patients) on ΔC-index, ΔBurden, and ΔHV (SAGEAgent vs comparator) for every Table 1/2 method with C > 0.8: ΔC-index: every 95% CI contains 0 (all p ≥ 0.30). Concat Δ=−0.001 [−0.040,+0.035]. MCAT −0.005 [−0.037,+0.030]. MMD −0.010 [−0.053,+0.029]. Self-Att −0.013 [−0.050,+0.027]. Reflexion −0.011 [−0.047,+0.025]. Base LLM −0.014 [−0.050,+0.022]. ΔBurden: every 95% CI strictly below 0 (all p < 0.001). vs B=1 methods Δ=−0.549 [−0.589,−0.505]. Reflexion −0.420 [−0.473,−0.364]. Base LLM −0.346 [−0.395,−0.295]. SAGEAgent has no significant C-index loss but significantly lower burden and higher HV than every C > 0.8 method. RL excluded due to substantial accuracy drop. 2) External validation (R3:W1, R4:W1). To our knowledge, TCGA-LGG/GBM + BraTS is the only public cancer cohort where 170 patients carry all four modalities. These 170 form our evaluation set, while the 792 partial-modality patients serve as predictor augmentation via modality dropout. Our task uses pre-extracted multimodal features and requires a multimodal predictor. Reflexion and SAGEAgent operate above this predictor via text-translated signals, decoupling agent reasoning from input format. Hager et al. (Nat Med 2024) and Nori et al. (2025) operate end-to-end on raw clinical text with no feature-level multimodal pipeline, and cannot ingest our setting without substantial redesign. meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): (1) The authors should provide paired statistical tests or bootstrap confidence intervals for C-index, burden, and hypervolume when comparing SAGEAgent with Self-Attention Fusion, MMD, MCAT, Reflexion, and Base LLM. In particular, the claim that SAGEAgent is “within 0.012 C-index” of full-modality fusion should be statistically supported, preferably with a predefined non-inferiority margin; otherwise, the claim of “no accuracy compromise” should be softened. (2) The authors should add an uncertainty-threshold stopping baseline. (3) The authors should clarify why Base LLM achieves a higher C-index than SAGEAgent, and explicitly present SAGEAgent as improving the accuracy–burden trade-off rather than pure predictive accuracy. (4)The authors should either include adapted LLM-based acquisition baselines or justify why prior LLM diagnosis methods such as Hager et al. and Nori et al. cannot be directly benchmarked. (5)The authors should clarify that the reported evaluation is based on 170 complete-modality patients, while the remaining 792 partial-modality patients are used for training augmentation. (6)More implementation and reproducibility details should be provided, including feature extractors, prompts, decoding parameters, random seeds, threshold tuning, FAISS retrieval features, reflection prompts, and the Qwen2.5/Qwen3 citation issue. | All reviewers who provided post-rebuttal opinions recommend acceptance. The rebuttal adequately addresses the main empirical concerns, including statistical support for the accuracy–burden trade-off, the uncertainty-threshold stopping baseline, and the role of the LLM/tools/dual-memory components. Reviewers also recognize the clinical relevance and novelty of agent-based clinical examination decision-making. Remaining concerns, especially the lack of external validation, limited generalizability, and data scarcity, should be clearly discussed as limitations, but they do not outweigh the paper’s methodological and clinical interest. The authors should provide the full open-source implementation to improve the reproducibility and broader impact of the paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Congratulations! Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper truly introduces a valuable contribution to the state-of-the-art. title: SAMoCo: A Learning-Initialized and Physics-Refined Framework for Sampling-Agnostic Motion Correction in MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The sampling mask is used as a dynamic routing mechanism to extract per-shot PE lines before Bi-GRU temporal modeling, allowing a single trained network to generalize across varying shots, ACS lines, and acceleration factors without retraining — directly addressing the fixed-trajectory limitation of prior methods. 2.Most existing methods assume perfectly known sensitivity maps, which is unrealistic under simultaneous undersampling and motion corruption. SAMoCo incorporates sensitivity estimation into an alternating inner-outer optimization loop alongside motion refinement, treating the two as a principled coupled estimation problem. 3.The ablation quantifies motion parameter MAE directly (>70% reduction after autofocusing), disentangling each component’s contribution beyond image metrics alone. Testing on unseen FLAIR contrast and a different-vendor scanner further supports cross-contrast and cross-site generalization.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Major Concerns: 1.It is unclear how well the motion estimation network generalizes beyond the training shot-number distribution. Since the method emphasizes sampling-agnostic motion estimation, it would be important to evaluate whether the network remains stable when the number of shots at test time exceeds or differs from the training range. 2.The sensitivity of the full pipeline to initialization quality is not sufficiently analyzed. Since the method is explicitly learning-initialized and physics-refined, the paper should better clarify how robust the final reconstruction is to different qualities of initial motion estimates. 3.The contribution of joint sensitivity-map updating is not sufficiently isolated. In particular, it would be helpful to show how much performance is lost if the method refines only motion parameters while keeping the sensitivity maps fixed. Minor Concerns: 4.The paper should describe the sampling-pattern-guided shot-wise feature extraction more clearly. In particular, the aggregation operation used to form shot-wise feature vectors is not sufficiently specified. 5.The computational cost of the iterative refinement is not clearly reported. Since the method relies on inner/outer optimization loops, reporting the number of iterations, convergence behavior, and runtime overhead relative to the baselines would improve the practical assessment. 6.The motion-correction evaluation remains relatively limited in scale, especially given the strong claims on generalization.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The work is relevant, well-motivated and well-organized, and free of grammatical errors and typos Figures are neat and legible
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The motion simulation method is not explained in sufficient detail. Non-cartesian sampling patterns are not considered, and no justification for exclusion is presented. Robustness of the method on pathological data is not evaluated. Downstream performance evaluations are not considered. For example, does segmentation performance on the motion-corrected data approach that of the ground truth?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The DL-part is only used as an initialization for motion parameter estimation. The motion corrected reconstruction is performed using physics-based formulations such as autofocus. Thus there is no hallucination risk, which could be a real risk if it were an end-to-end DL approach. The DL-network for motion estimation uses a spatial-temporal framework which may aid to estimate reasonable motion parameters in a temporally consistent manner from the retrospective measurements (although this aspect is not described in the paper). The method is shown to work on more than one contrast (eg: simulated multi-shot T1 and T2 datasets).
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The proposed method is fundamentally limited to multi‑shot or segmented MRI acquisitions where motion is approximately rigid and constant within each shot. The standard T1/T2 datasets are not multi-shot acquisitions, where the key assumptions of this paper breaks down. What the paper demonstrates on T1/T2 are simulated cases where a single shot acquisition is split into a multi-shot acquisition retrospectively and does not reflect a standard MRI acquisition. More realistic multi-shot methods would have been multi-shot EPI or non-Cartesian methods (eg: multi-shot spiral, radial), where the feasibility of the method is not demonstrated. The method is stated to be sampling agnostic, however the description makes it clear that the method is sampling aware and is a strict constraint. It is not clear how multiple contrasts or orientations will recast the method as sampling-agnostic.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers and the meta-reviewer for their positive reviews and constructive feedback, which have been very helpful in improving the quality of our work. Below, we address their main comments as follows: (1) We agree with R3 that our proposed method is limited to multi-shot or segmented MRI. However, we would like to clarify that the term “multi-shot” in our work includes segmented acquisitions in which multiple k-space lines are acquired within one TR, such as T1-weighted MPRAGE, T2-weighted TSE, and FLAIR sequences. These sequences are widely used in standard clinical scans. In fact, the T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and PD-weighted images from the IXI dataset were acquired in a multi-shot manner, with echo-train-lengths of 208, 16, and 16, respectively. We have added the following text to the revised paper to clarify this point: “Notably, all images were acquired in a multi-shot manner with varying echo-train-lengths.” Additionally, we revised the opening sentence of Section 2.1: “We focus on the retrospective motion correction problem in 2D multi-shot MRI, such as in common sequences like fast spin echo.” (2) We agree with R3 that the term “sampling-agnostic” may be imprecise, as the initial motion estimation takes sampling patterns as input, making the method “sampling-aware”. Our intended meaning was that SAMoCo is not limited to a single fixed sampling pattern; the same trained network can handle variable shot numbers, ACS lines, and acceleration factors without retraining. In future publications, we will replace “sampling-agnostic” with more precise terminology, such as “sampling-flexible”, to better describe the ability of the framework to generalize across different sampling schemes. (3) We thank R1 and R2 for their valuable suggestions regarding real-motion validation, generalization to shot numbers beyond the training distribution, non-Cartesian sampling, pathological data, and downstream clinical tasks. We plan to investigate these issues in our future work. In addition, we will follow R1’s suggestion to further analyze the influence of initial motion estimation and joint sensitivity map updating through additional ablation studies.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The reviewers agree that the paper presents a well-motivated and technically sound hybrid framework that combines learning-based initialization with physics-driven refinement for MRI motion correction. The method is clearly described, shows consistent improvements over strong baselines, and demonstrates promising generalization across datasets and acquisition settings. While concerns remain regarding evaluation scale, realism of motion settings, and some claims (e.g., sampling-agnostic behavior), these are viewed as limitations that can be addressed in future work rather than fundamental flaws. Overall, given the solid methodology, empirical gains, and potential clinical relevance, I recommend acceptance.

title: SAR-Net: Sample-Agnostic Retrieval Network for Robust Brain Tumor Segmentation with Missing Modalities
reviewer_1_strengths: The use of Gram matrices to represent style and the separation between structural and statistical components are well-motivated, and the integration with contrastive learning is reasonable. The component-wise and loss-wise ablations support the contribution of each module, and the incremental gains from retrieval and contrastive learning are demonstrated. The experiments consider all missing-modality combinations. Gains in more challenging regions (TC/ET) are more than those of WT, suggesting the method may indeed improve boundary precision.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The method largely combines existing ideas (Gram matrix-based style transfer, memory banks with MoCo-like contrastive learning, and feature modulation via AdaIN). The assumption that Gram matrices capture modality-specific style independent of anatomy is borrowed from natural image literature. However, in MRI, intensity distributions are not just stylistic, and scanner/protocol variability, as well as pathology, may be entangled. The selected baselines are reasonable, but recent studies in diffusion-based imputation or foundation models with multimodal learning are not addressed. Given the added architectural complexity (memory bank, contrastive learning, retrieval, transformer), the improvements achieved over the baseline are relatively small. The paper criticizes generative models for being computationally expensive, but does not provide runtime comparisons, memory consumption, or training stability discussion. No cross-dataset evaluation is provided to show how well this generalizes to unseen distributions or whether performance depends on dataset-specific factors. The paper argues that retrieval avoids hallucination, but does not provide qualitative evidence (e. g. , failure cases, visual comparisons). The paper lacks implementation details to ensure reproducibility. Several aspects are missing, including training hyperparameters (learning rate schedule, batch size, number of epochs), memory bank configuration (size, update frequency, queue length per modality), momentum coefficient, and temperature in contrastive learning, details of data preprocessing and augmentation, and architectural specifics (e. g. , encoder backbone, feature dimensions, transformer configuration).
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: This paper demonstrates several key strengths. 1.First, it proposes an innovative retrieval-based approach to solve the missing modality problem, designing specialized feature extraction and retrieval methods tailored to the specific challenges of missing modalities in medical segmentation tasks. 2.Furthermore, in the context of multi-modal medical image segmentation, the authors accurately identify the distinction between structural information and modality-specific styles, developing a corresponding disentanglement module. To efficiently maintain the memory bank, the study introduces contrastive learning to further enhance the separability and distinctiveness of different modality styles. 3.Finally, the paper is well-structured and logically coherent, and the experimental results robustly demonstrate the excellent performance of the proposed model.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: However, the manuscript still has several weaknesses that warrant further clarification. 1.Missing Loss Function Weights: The paper does not specify the weighting coefficients for the various loss functions. The authors should discuss how different weighting ratios might affect the model’s performance. 2.Inconsistent Dataset Usage: There is a discrepancy in the datasets used for evaluation: the ablation study is conducted on the BraTS 2018 dataset, while the SOTA comparison uses the BraTS 2020 dataset. Even though these datasets share some overlapping cases and exhibit domain similarity, this experimental design choice lacks a proper justification. 3.Limited Reproducibility: The paper lacks comprehensive implementation details and does not provide reproducible source code, which hinders the overall reproducibility of the method.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Methodological contribution is novel. Framing missing modality imputation as style retrieval rather than generation is well-motivated. 2.Disentanglement with Gram matrix is more explicit than adversarial or implicit alignment methods. Visualizations confirm that. 3.Comprehensive evaluation reported. All 15 missing modality combinations were reported with both DSC and HD95 showing consistent gains in clinically critical TC and ET regions.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The authors claim to have tested on BraTS 2024, but there is no result shared in the paper. 2.TMFormer [24], KMD [9], and CCSD [18] are cited but not compared against despite being directly relevant and recent. (citation indexes from paper). 3.Table 1 is the BraTS 2020 results. But ablation is on BraTS 2018.The standard convention is to share results across all datasets and to show ablation results on a subset. That is not followed here, and the claim that it surpasses all BraTS 2018, 2020, and 2024 is not supported.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for your valuable comments to improve our work. To Meta Reviewer: Below we have provided clarify experimental discrepancies, BraTS 2024 results, and methodological novelty. BraTS dataset inconsistency (R1,R2,R3): (1) using BraTS 2020 for SOTA comparison and BraTS 2018 for ablation is aimed to show more datasets results within limited space. (2)The mention of BraTS 2024 in the abstract was an editing error, for fine-grained six-label BraTS 2024, we have additional evidence: in a large-scale six-region evaluation, SAR-Net improves over M2FTrans, with DSC gains of +0.5/+0.9/+0.4/+1.0/+0.5/+0.8 for WT/TC/ET/NETC/SNFH/RC and mean HD95 reduced from 7.78 to 6.58 mm. Following rebuttal policy, we do not provide more results here.. Reproducibility and code (R1,R2): Key settings are Adam, lr=2e-4, weight decay=1e-4, poly LR decay, batch size 1, 1000 epochs, seed 1024, and 128^3 crop with rotation/intensity/flip augmentation. Memory bank uses 250 entries per modality-layer, 10 warm-up epochs, momentum 0.995, and 4/128 positive/negative samples. Gram-layer temperatures are 0.5/0.45/0.4/0.35/0.3, with weights 0.3/0.25/0.2/0.15/0.1.Total loss is unit-weighted Lcon+Lrec+Lreg+Lds+Lseg. Code will available after accept. Novelty and Gram/style statistics (R1): Our approach is not a mere heuristic but a genuine innovation grounded in a deep understanding of the missing modality segmentation problem. SAR-Net uses mature components, but not as a simple stack: Gram prototypes summarize modality statistics, contrastive learning organizes the bank, retrieval selects sample-agnostic prototypes for missing modalities, and feature modulation injects them into segmentation features. We agree MRI intensity distributions are entangled with scanner/protocol variations and pathology, and are not “style” in the natural-image sense. Here, “style” is a proxy for modality-specific statistical cues, including modality appearance, protocol-related intensity variations, and distributional information. We do not claim perfect anatomy-independent disentanglement; because complete disentanglement remains difficult, SAR-Net uses Gram prototypes to aggregate these statistics as feature-level compensation cues, rather than reconstructing images or treating prototypes as anatomical representations. We will weaken “style” wording to avoid equating MRI intensity differences with natural-image style, and discuss limitations. Complexity, efficiency, and hallucination (R1): Although average gains may appear moderate, the results highlight robustness in extreme missing-modality cases and difficult tumor regions, the focus of clinical missing-modality scenarios. SAR-Net is slower than lightweight CNN/fusion baselines due to memory bank, retrieval, and Transformer modules, but avoids iterative image-level synthesis and is algorithmically more efficient than diffusion-style imputation. At inference, it uses one feature extraction pass and compact Gram-memory lookup, without generating missing MRI images. Thus, this is a cost-benefit/algorithmic-efficiency argument, not a runtime benchmark. We will clarify this tradeoff. Here, “mitigating unreliable feature hallucination” refers to avoiding image-level hallucination from synthesized missing-modality images; SAR-Net performs feature-level retrieval/compensation, so there is no image-level hallucination issue. Uncompared related works (R3): We thank R3 for noting TMFormer, KMD, and CCSD. Our baselines focus on reproducible representative methods from different paradigms under comparable missing-modality settings. KMD is a plug-and-play Koopman module, TMFormer refines Transformer via token merging, and CCSD appeared very recently and was not included. SAR-Net focuses on retrieval-based training/architecture using sample-agnostic style prototypes. Fair comparison requires unified implementation/protocol, which cannot be added in rebuttal. We thank the reviewers again and will incorporate these clarifications.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): While Reviewer 2 strongly recommends acceptance, Reviewers 1 and 3 raise significant concerns regarding the inconsistency of experimental datasets, missing results for BraTS 2024, and lack of comparison with recent relevant baselines. The authors should clarify these experimental discrepancies, provide the missing BraTS 2024 results, and justify their methodological novelty against existing style-transfer and retrieval methods to secure acceptance. | All reviewers suggest to accept this submission. title: Segment Anything Model with Symmetric Spectral Uncertainty Gating for Generalizable Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) Strong clinical motivation and relevance: The paper targets the issue in real-world clinical practice: domain shifts caused by variations in data acquisition protocols and equipment-based biases. By explicitly addressing how these acquisition-based variations degrade the performance of foundation models in single-domain generalization settings, the authors provide a clear, clinically valuable motivation for their proposed framework. 2) Plug-and-play versatility: The proposed uncertainty-aware symmetric channel gating module is a lightweight plug-in component used in SAM. This module can be readily utilized in other models featuring Transformer mechanisms, which significantly broadens the potential impact and applicability of this work beyond just SAM. 3) Comprehensive experimental design: The evaluation is strong and convincing. The authors thoroughly validate their method across completely different anatomical regions and imaging modalities (Fundus 2D images and Prostate 3D MRIs) using multiple generalization datasets. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics are standard and reasonable, the selected baselines are both abundant and up-to-date (including recent SAM-based SDG methods), and the ablation studies prove the effectiveness of each individual component (SME, USCG, and HDC).
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) The assumption about feature channels is too simple: The method assumes we can simply turn off “style” channels without losing “anatomy” information. However, in deep neural networks, a single channel usually contains both. If we completely turn off a channel to remove noise, we might accidentally delete important medical details (like small lesions). This is risky for clinical diagnosis. The authors should discuss this problem. 2) Potential high computational cost for real clinical use: The paper claims the module is “lightweight,” but the overall training process uses a dual-branch design and Fourier transforms. Since SAM is already a very large model, running two branches at the same time will cost a huge amount of memory and computing power. The paper needs to provide an analysis of the training time and memory usage to show if real hospitals can actually run this model. 3）Sub-optimal performance on specific metrics and missing failure analysis: Although the method achieves the best overall average performance, it does not get the best results on certain sub-tasks. For example, in Fundus Disc segmentation (Domain 2), The proposed method’s ASD score is worse than existing methods like MaxStyle and SLAug. The paper does not explain why the framework struggles in these specific situations. Furthermore, even though the table caption briefly mentions a significance test (p-value < 0.05), the text does not provide details on the exact statistical method used (for example, which specific test was applied to compare the models).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: It addresses the issue of generalization degradation of SAM in medical image segmentation under the single-domain generalization andfocuses on mitigating style sensitivity and overfitting within SDG foundation model architectures.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The integration of the method description and the research motivation is relatively weak, such as the summarized modules and the issue of style sensitivity in SDG is not directly evident in the Introduction, and the experimental section lacks sufficient analysis of the results.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The three modules form a coherent and well-structured framework: SME simulates style variations, USCG identifies and filters style-sensitive channels, and HDC enforces consistency between the original and augmented images. 2.The paper compares traditional data augmentation methods with state-of-the-art domain generalization approaches for SAM, demonstrating superior performance on two challenging datasets and providing compelling empirical evidence.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The novelty of the approach appears limited. Amplitude perturbation in the frequency domain for data augmentation is a well-established technique in medical image domain generalization. The method primarily combines this operation with exponential moving average (EMA) for statistical extrapolation. USCG and HDC can be interpreted as variants of attention mechanisms and feature consistency regularization, which are commonly used in multi-view contrastive learning. The integration of these existing techniques within the SAM framework appears to constitute incremental engineering-level innovation. 2.SAM is inherently a prompt-driven model. It is unclear how prompts are obtained during the testing phase. Specifically, it is not specified whether ground-truth bounding boxes are used or whether the model operates without prompts. The paper only states that the prompt encoder is “fully fine-tuned with default embeddings,” which remains insufficiently specified. Given that SAM’s performance is highly sensitive to prompt design, this lack of detail raises concerns about the fairness and validity of the quantitative comparisons. 3.SME reconstructs the image within a band-limited region; however, the definition of this region is not clearly specified.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the meta-reviewer and reviewers for their constructive comments and for recognizing the clinical relevance (R2), coherent design (R4/R5), and solid empirical results (R2/R5) of our work. We clarify the main concerns below: *Prompt configuration and fair comparison(R5) In our method, we aim at automatic segmentation of medical images, and SAM was used with its everything mode, so no human interaction or Ground-Truth-derived prompt (bounding box, point, or text prompt) is needed. This ensures a fair comparison with the competing methods that do not use human interaction as well. *Soft uncertainty calibration, not hard channel removal(R2) We agree that a channel may contain both anatomical and style-related information, and do not assume a binary separation of “style” and “anatomy” channels. Instead, we quantify each channel’s sensitivity to style change (Eq.2) and use soft and progressive reweighting to calibrate each channel (Eq.3), rather than hard deletion. HDC further constrains both calibrated intermediate features and final embeddings, encouraging anatomical priors to remain robust throughout the entire encoding process. *Systematic novelty beyond simple integration(R5) We acknowledge that spectral perturbation, gating, and consistency regularization have been studied individually. However, S²UG is not a simple aggregation of generic techniques; it is a synergistic closed-loop system tailored to counteract source-style overfitting in PEFT-adapted SAM under SDG. Specifically, SME is not a passive or random amplitude perturbation: it estimates source spectral statistics in log-radial space and extrapolates along the statistical envelope to actively probe distribution boundaries (Eq.1). USCG is also not generic channel attention; it is an uncertainty-aware gate explicitly conditioned on the original/SME-branch response divergence for symmetric channel calibration inside the SAM encoder. Together with HDC, these modules form a coupled cycle of active style probing, sensitivity calibration, and anatomy-preserving regularization, rather than a simple combination of existing modules. *Computational cost and deployment efficiency(R2) Note that FFT/IFFT-based SME and the augmented branch with consistency regularization are only needed for training. As a result, our method does not increase computation or memory cost for inference: only the original image is processed through the standard branch with the learned USCG modules, and no manual/GT prompts are needed. In Fundus inference, S²UG runs at about 0.35s/case with the GPU memory footprint of 1.87 GiB, which makes it easy for clinical deployment. *Implementation details and statistical clarification(R2&R5) In SME, the band-limited region is the low-to-mid FFT amplitude band with normalized radius ρ∈[0.25,0.45], where amplitudes are extrapolated using the estimated spectral envelope while out-of-band amplitudes and the original phase are preserved. Statistical significance was computed using a two-sided paired t-test on per-case Dice/ASD scores between S²UG and the second-place method, with p<0.05 considered significant, which will be clarified in the final version with minor modification. *Sub-metric analysis and overall robustness(R2&R4) Due to the complexity of segmentation objects and inter-domain variation, there is no single method that always achieves the best value on all evaluation metrics in all domains on all datasets. S²UG achieves the best average Dice/ASD values on both datasets, demonstrating its general robustness. In some domains, such as Domain 2 in Table 1, the relatively large ASD is mainly due to the fact that ASD is sensitive to noise (false positives far from the foreground). We will clarify this limitation in the revised manuscript and provide a more detailed case-wise discussion in a future journal extension.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important problem (single-domain generalization for SAM in medical imaging) and shows solid empirical results across multiple modalities. Two reviewers assign Weak Accept (4), one assigns Weak Reject (3). The main concerns are: (1) unclear SAM prompt configuration during testing, which is critical for fair comparison; (2) the novelty is primarily integrative, combining existing techniques within the SAM framework; (3) missing computational cost analysis; and (4) oversimplified assumption about style/anatomy channel disentanglement. These concerns are addressable during rebuttal, though the prompt configuration issue is critical and must be clarified. The paper should proceed to rebuttal with a clear expectation that the authors address these points. | The paper presents a well-motivated S²UG framework to improve SAM’s single-domain generalization via spectral uncertainty gating, with solid experiments on fundus and prostate MRI. Reviewer #2 and #4 gave Weak Accept (4), and Reviewer #5’s Weak Reject (3) concerns (prompt configuration, novelty, computational cost) were adequately addressed in the rebuttal by clarifying the automatic prompt-free mode, soft channel calibration, and inference efficiency (0.35s/case, 1.87 GiB). The overall positive consensus supports acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper addresses an important and timely problem: single-domain generalization for SAM-based medical image segmentation. The proposed S2UG framework is coherent: SME actively probes spectral style shifts, USCG performs soft response-divergence-based channel calibration, and HDC enforces multi-level consistency. The experiments cover two distinct benchmarks, include recent SAM-based SDG baselines, report Dice/ASD with statistical testing, and show consistent average improvements. The rebuttal satisfactorily resolves the most critical concern by clarifying that SAM is used in automatic “everything” mode with no GT-derived prompts, ensuring fair comparison. It also clarifies that USCG performs soft calibration rather than hard channel removal, that SME is training-only, and specifies the spectral band and statistical test. While novelty is partly integrative and some sub-metric failures deserve more discussion, the technical design and empirical evidence are sufficient for acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I have read the paper, reviews (2 positive, 1 negative), and the rebuttal. Despite the positive scores, critical flaws remain. The evaluation lacks comparisons with traditional (non-SAM) domain generalization methods, making it impossible to validate the clinical viability of the results. Furthermore, the core FFT-based frequency method lacks novelty (extensively explored in prior work like FedDG), and the proposed architecture appears to be an ad-hoc, unmotivated combination of existing modules.

title: Self-Supervised Implicit CEST Reconstruction via Physics-Informed Lorentz Encoding
reviewer_1_strengths: By replacing generic positional encodings with Lorentz Encoding, the method explicitly incorporates the underlying CEST physics into the reconstruction process. This mechanism effectively reduces noise, promotes consistency with the physical model, and achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art methods across multiple metabolite maps, including APT, NOE, and MT.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: There are two major concerns. First, the training details are insufficiently described. For the 18 subjects, the manuscript should clarify the criteria used to split the data into training, validation, and testing sets. It should also report the image dimensions and the number of slices included in the analysis. For the 2D model, it remains unclear whether all slices were used for training or whether a selection strategy was adopted, such as restricting training to middle slices or slices with higher image quality. Second, it would strengthen the paper to include an ablation study that evaluates the two parallel encoding modules separately. Such an analysis would better illustrate the contribution of each module and help clarify whether spatial or spectral feature is more critical to the overall model performance.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The proposed Lorentz Encoding method is clearly novel for this application, also the concept with the decoupling of the spectral and spatial appears to be novel in approach for CEST MRI. Overall the presented work is well described and in a very understandable language. The description of the method has enough details and at the same time is not very convoluted that is can be understood by a person with a bit of experience in CEST MRI. The presented experiments are well designed, easy to follow and to understand what is going on in the results themselves. The limitation section identifies correctly issues of the method.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There are a few weaknesses of this work. My biggest concern is about the reference which the authors use for the calculation of the PSNR/SSIM metrics in their Table 2.Based on the desciption in the text above I would understand that the calucations are performed against the maps/results from the Direct MPLF applied to the undersampled spectra. Such an approach would be wrong as the observed effects would be affected by the decreasing performance of the MPLF on the undersampled spectra. However in the Figure 3 the authors provide reference maps which are clearly obtained from direct MPLF on the fully sampled spectra. As such it’s not clear to me what is the final set up in these results. Please clarify this aspect of the results. Also a missing aspect of the work is how was the training performed and how were the testing cohorts created.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in CEST MRI, namely reducing acquisition burden while preserving spectral fidelity. The proposed Lorentzian encoding of the frequency dimension is a reasonable way to introduce CEST specific prior knowledge into an INR framework, and this is the most interesting part of the method. The reported results against the baselines included in the paper are consistently strong across the three sampling settings, both for reconstructed spectra and for the derived APT, NOE, and MT maps. The manuscript is also generally readable, and the overall motivation is clear.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The technically new part is the Lorentzian encoding of the frequency dimension. The broader ideas of using INR for CEST reconstruction, or of treating spatial and spectral dimensions differently, are not new. More importantly, closely related CEST papers have already addressed recovery or quantification from sparsely sampled data using deep learning, including Chen et al., MRM, 2024, and Cheema et al., MRM, 2025.These are more relevant comparisons than several baselines currently included in the paper, yet no direct comparison is provided. Terms such as “Lorentzian manifold,” “physical subspace,” and “manifold-constrained optimization” are stronger than what is actually defined. What the paper clearly specifies is a learnable Lorentzian feature map for the frequency coordinate, followed by a general INR decoder. I think the paper would be stronger and more precise if it described the method as a physics-informed spectral encoding rather than a fully constrained manifold model. The learning objective and optimization problem are not stated clearly enough for a methodological paper. The paper gives the forward mapping and an (L_2) loss over the sampled set, but it remains unclear how the training is organized in practice, what exactly is optimized, and how the slice-by-slice optimization mentioned later relates to the earlier mathematical description.

author_feedback: GENERAL RESPONSE TO ALL REVIEWERS We thank the reviewers for recognizing our Lorentzian spectral encoding as a novel, meaningful contribution to INR frameworks. We prioritize addressing every clarification below. All conceptual clarifications will be incorporated into the final manuscript to ensure theoretical completeness. 1.COMMON MAJOR CONCERNS: 1.1 TABLE 2 REFERENCE METRICS (ADDRESSES R2-Q1) All quantitative metrics in Table 2 are computed against the reference maps derived from the FULLY SAMPLED (97-offset) spectra, matching the reference maps in Figure 3.The “Direct MPLF” (fitted directly on under-sampled data) is included purely as a minimum baseline. It serves as a lower bound to guarantee that all evaluated interpolation methods yield positive improvements over direct sparse fitting, preventing any negative degradation. We have modified the manuscript to clarify this rationale. 1.2 TRAINING DETAILS AND DATA SPLIT (ADDRESSES R1-Q1, R2-Q2) Regarding the data split, our framework follows the subject-specific optimization paradigm inherent to Implicit Neural Representations (INR). An independent continuous mapping f(x, y, ∆ω)→I is trained from scratch for each individual subject. DATA: For all 18 participants, magnetic resonance images were acquired in the axial plane, with the field of view (FOV) specifically positioned to cover the midbrain region. A single 128x128 slice with matrix of 128x128 and 97 frequency offsets was acquired per patient. SPLIT: Models are trained independently per subject using sparse offsets (21, 29, or 39 points; Fig. 2). A 21-offset strategy provides 344,064 training pairs (128x128x21). Remaining offsets form the test set. OPTIMIZATION: Training involves 10,000 epochs and the final epoch model is used for evaluation. 2.SPECIFIC REVIEWER CONCERNS: REVIEWER 1 ABLATION STUDY: To clarify module contributions while adhering to MICCAI policy, we performed an internal check on a randomly selected single case under the 29-offset sampling condition. Ablating Spatial MHE (using Fourier PE+LE) degraded boundaries and caused PSNR to drop to 52.20 dB. Conversely, ablating Spectral LE (replacing it with generic MHE + Fourier) dropped PSNR to 42.03 dB. Our proposed joint MHE+LE approach achieves the highest fidelity (54.44 dB) on this case. These empirical findings validate our decoupled design, and we will explicitly discuss the orthogonal contributions of both modules in the revised text. REVIEWER 3 COMPARISON WITH PRIOR WORK: We compared our approach with previous works using a 5-fold cross-validation on an 18-subject dataset with 29-offset acquisition. First, Cheema’s 2D U-Net struggled on our single-slice data (PSNRs ~20 dB vs ours >31 dB) without their larger cross-slice training cohorts. Second, to evaluate Chen’s 1D spectral U-Net, we heavily augmented our data to match their massive training pool. While this fully-supervised U-Net achieved slightly higher Z-spectra interpolation fidelity (PSNR 57.94 dB vs our 56.53 dB), our strictly unsupervised approach generated highly competitive parameter maps (APT PSNR 31.60 vs 31.54 dB) without requiring any external training data or ground-truth labels. Importantly, the parameter maps produced by the 1D U-Net are quite noisy, whereas our unsupervised Lorentzian prior acts as a natural physical regularizer to effectively denoise the output. We will explicitly highlight this paradigm contrast in the revised text. OPTIMIZATION OBJECTIVE: The objective minimizes the point-wise L_2‭‬ loss between the INR prediction and acquired sparse Z-spectra. For our slice-by-slice 2D implementation, the network takes 2D spatial coordinates (x, y) and frequency offset ∆ω ‭‬‭‬as inputs. The weights are optimized exclusively over the acquired sparse coordinates of that specific slice. The explicit loss equation and step-by-step training process will be added.‬‬‬‬‬‬

author_feedback: R1: Novelty of the model architecture Our contribution is methodological rather than purely architectural. Although Hierarchy Flow serves as the backbone, the proposed Sequence-Aware Affine Network (SA) introduces a physics-driven multi-channel conditioning mechanism. SA processes each contrast channel (T1w, T2w, PDw) through dedicated sub-networks that learn non-linear relationships between pulse-sequence parameters (TR/TE/ES) and signal intensity. We will clarify this distinction in the Introduction. R1: The physical model We agree that the current MR signal model does not account for RF pulse profiles, stimulated echoes, or mixed contrast effects caused by turbo-spin echo acceleration, T2 decay, and phase-encoding order. However, this study focuses on feasibility evaluation for self-supervised phantom generation. The analytical approximation remains suitable for TSE sequences because image contrast is mainly determined by the effective echo filling the central k-space. We agree that more advanced modeling is required for greater robustness, and future work will incorporate the MRZero simulator. R2: Adaptation to other pulse sequences The framework is generalizable to pulse sequences with known analytical signal equations, provided the inputs contain distinguishable T1, T2, and PD contrast information. R2: Scaling, parameter counts, and training dynamics Scaling to 4096 corresponds to the 12-bit dynamic range of DICOM MRI. Compared with normalization to [0,1], this scaling avoids vanishingly small losses and improves numerical stability in flow-based optimization. Model complexity: Baseline: 1.02M params / 64 ms inference / 11.96 MB memory; EF: 1.04M / 65 ms / 12.18 MB; FF: 1.08M / 74 ms / 12.71 MB; SA: 1.06M / 215 ms / 12.51 MB. Training on an NVIDIA RTX 5070 (12 GB VRAM) required ~80 minutes for all models. The learning rate and “17 + 50 epochs” schedule were selected empirically from pilot experiments and loss curves. Convergence was defined as a loss change <0.0001 over five consecutive epochs. R2: Downstream task evaluation Evaluation on downstream tasks (e.g., segmentation trained on synthetic vs. real data) is an important next step but falls outside the scope of the current submission. Conference guidelines also prevent adding new experiments. R2: Table 1 formatting and precision Highlighting both EF and SA was a formatting mistake. With 4-decimal precision, MS-SSIM on the real test dataset is: Baseline 0.9825/0.9386/0.9640, FF 0.9844/0.9436/0.9682, EF 0.9897/0.9360/0.9812, SA 0.9915/0.9464/0.9771 for T1/T2/PD, respectively. R1, R3: Limited evaluation and imaging scenarios Healthy volunteer data was used to validate technical feasibility; evaluation on pathological open datasets is planned as immediate future work. We report MS-SSIM and PSNR on synthesized weighted images because the primary objective is anatomically faithful MRI augmentation rather than direct quantitative-map estimation. Quantitative maps were verified against ground truth on synthetic data during development, but submission rules prohibit adding these results. Since this work is a feasibility study, we selected representative pulse sequences. While SE sequences are easier to approximate analytically, they are less common clinically. R1, R2, R3: Comparisons with other methods Direct comparison with prior approaches is difficult because existing methods address different constraints. Our framework simultaneously generates three quantitative maps from conventional weighted MRI in a self-supervised manner without ground-truth data, while explicitly incorporating pulse-sequence parameters and maintaining efficient training and inference. To our knowledge, none of the reviewed methods satisfy all these conditions simultaneously. Regarding MRI2QMap, the method was designed for MR fingerprinting and highly undersampled 3D MRI acquired with a TGAS–SPI–MRF sequence. In contrast, our approach targets standard pulse sequences available on clinical scanners.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a sequence-conditioned hierarchical flow-based framework for digital phantom generation in MRI. The reviewers agree that the pairing-free formulation and sequence-conditioned design are practically valuable, that the writing and figures are clear, and that the problem has broad potential impact for qMRI reconstruction and synthetic MRI dataset generation. Scores split 3/4/4.The AC finds that R1 provides the deepest concerns. Eq. 1 omits stimulated echoes from imperfect 180-degree refocusing and T2 weighting along the TSE echo train, which is a non-trivial physics omission; evaluation is narrow (only normal tissue, only SSIM/PSNR, no quantification-error reporting, no SOTA comparisons); and testing is confined to TSE with tight parameter ranges. R2 adds concrete reproducibility concerns — unjustified LR and epoch counts, undefined convergence criterion, no wall-clock time, unjustified intensity scaling to 4096, missing parameter/memory comparisons across the three integration strategies, Table 1 formatting issues. R3 asks for baseline positioning against MRI2Qmap (Golbabaee et al. 2024), FID-style generation metrics, and a round-trip qMap evaluation. On the weaknesses, the AC also finds R1 and R3 disagree on novelty framing. R1 views the architecture as Hierarchical Flow with marginal changes; R3 treats the sequence-conditioned phantom-generation formulation as novel. R1 explicitly notes that some concerns are not rebuttal-tractable. Given the slightly positive score and the mix of tractable and non-tractable concerns, I recommend inviting the authors to respond in rebuttal before a final decision, with attention to reproducibility, the physical-model assumptions, and baseline positioning. | The AC thanks the authors and all three reivewers for the active engagement in the rebuttal phase. T1/T1c/T2/FLAIR provide complementary cues for WT/TC/ET, so missing scans remove region-specific evidence and induce uncertainty. This motivates Gaussian partial embeddings, the full-modality anchor, and subset–superset uncertainty ordering. We will clarify that σ perturbs incomplete evidence to regularize μ during training, while μ is used for deterministic prediction. For related work, we will add [1–4] and clarify the differences. Specifically, [1] addresses missing-modality gaps via KD/style transfer, [2] targets sequential modality acquisition, and [3,4] focus on fusion/predictive uncertainty, whereas ours directly regularizes representation-level uncertainty for arbitrary partial-modality sets. (9) is piecewise differentiable, analogous to ReLU/hinge-style objectives. On one side, what the authors called uncertainty is typically what is currently modeled by the covariance in (hierarchical) multimodal VAE. (2019) is not included as a baseline because it follows modality completion, whereas our method is imputation-free.” This approach both synthesizes missing images (modality completion) and segments observed images simultaneously; segmentation is not performed after modality completion. Covariances are there to capture this uncertainty. The authors proposed regularizing the latent spaces $zi$ to align with the full modality setting, which could have been formulated as a KL divergence. Therefore, I agree that the maths are poor and that the authors seem to ignore some of the literature. author_feedback: We thank all the reviewers for their constructive feedback and positive assessment of our method, highlighting a considerable advance over previous approaches (R1, R2), well-motivated and appropriate use of eikonal equation to encode user interactions (R2, R3) and soundness of the framework (R2). Please find our responses to the reviewers’ feedback below. Guidance Signal / User Interaction (R1-W1, R2-W1,W2,W3,C2,C4,C5): As discussed in Sec. 2.3, the WGDT signal propagates guidance along sulci using mean curvature of the white matter surface (“curv”) in the speed function. Compared to “sulc” and “inflated.H”, “curv” better preserves narrow sulcal structures while reducing signal leakage into adjacent gyri. We used a simulated interaction during training and evaluation to maintain a controlled and reproducible setting, consistent with prior interactive segmentation studies (Sec. 2.2). While robustness to real-user or suboptimal interactions is an important future direction, our primary goal was to evaluate whether the proposed guidance signal better reflects expert annotator intent. Regarding computational cost, our framework is designed for real-time interaction. Both the SPHARM-Net backbone and the fast marching solver efficiently process high-resolution cortical surfaces (> 100k vertices), achieving end-to-end inference within well under a second per interaction in our implementation. Problem Formulation / Architecture (R2-W5,W6,C5): We agree that extending the framework toward unified multi-sulcus interactive segmentation is an important direction. However, extending interactive refinement from a single sulcus to multiple anatomically variable structures is non-trivial, since user interactions occur across different sulci in arbitrary order and require simultaneous refinement of multiple targets. Therefore, as described in Sec. 2.1, we trained separate models for individual sulci to provide a controlled setting for evaluating the proposed WGDT guidance signal across distinct sulcal morphologies. Although a full multi-class framework remains challenging, we agree that integrating morphologically similar sulci within a shared model would be a meaningful intermediate direction. Evaluation Protocol (R2-W7,W8,C3,C5,R3-W1,W2): The ground-truth sulcal labels were manually identified on individual cortical surfaces by multiple trained raters and subsequently reviewed and finalized by a neuroanatomist. Due to the labor-intensive nature of fine-grained sulcal labeling, constructing large-scale datasets remains challenging, as discussed in Sec. 1.We appreciate the suggestions regarding parameter analysis and evaluation metrics. For WGDT, multiple settings of the modulation parameter k were explored (Fig. 6), while the maximum propagation distance was fixed empirically. We agree that a more systematic analysis of propagation-related parameters, as well as additional evaluation metrics beyond Dice score (e.g., boundary-aware or interaction-efficiency measures), would be important future directions. Scope / Generalization (R2-W4,W9,C5): Fine-grained sulcal labeling is becoming increasingly important as neuroimaging studies move beyond coarse parcellations to capture subtle morphological variability that differs across individuals, making fully automatic approaches less reliable and motivating interactive refinement (Sec. 1). Our experiments assume well-reconstructed surfaces and healthy participants. In pathological or excessively noisy cases, manual labeling itself becomes difficult and the task itself might be anatomically ill-posed. While such extreme conditions may affect curvature-based propagation, the WGDT signal remains effective within our experimental setting. Typos / Minor Issues (R2-C1): We will carefully review the manuscript for minor issues such as typos, acronym definitions, and notation consistency. We will do our best to address these aspects thoroughly to ensure a clear and unambiguous presentation.

title: Shape-Scale Aware Diffusion Models for Weakly Supervised Medical Image Anomaly Detection
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed Direction-guided Multi-Scale (DMS) module enhances modeling of lesion shape and scale via directional decomposition and multi-scale aggregation. This offers a clear innovation over traditional isotropic U-Net convolutions, better capturing the irregular and directional nature of medical lesions. Addressing the high inference costs of diffusion models, this work introduces a lightweight PDS-Conv backbone. The reported reduction in complexity without sacrificing performance ensures the method is viable for resource-constrained, real-world medical deployments. The evaluation is robust, spanning BraTS 2021, BraTS-PEDs 2024, and ATLAS v2.0.By utilizing diverse metrics (Dice, IoU, AUPRC) across Mixed and Unhealthy settings, the results are comprehensive. Systematic ablation studies further confirm the effectiveness of the DMS module, ASSF, and the lightweight architecture.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Despite strong results across multiple datasets, the analytical depth remains somewhat limited. For instance, while the paper claims the DMS module improves directional and multi-scale modeling, it lacks a detailed analysis of which specific lesion types, anatomical structures, or boundary complexities yield the greatest performance gains. The innovation of this work lies primarily in task-specific architectural integration and optimization, rather than in a fundamentally new algorithmic paradigm. Key components, such as dilated convolutions, SE-style feature recalibration, gated feature fusion, and lightweight design, are all closely related to existing ideas. Consequently, while the overall design is well targeted to the problem setting and appears empirically effective, the methodological novelty is more likely to be viewed as incremental rather than fundamental.
