author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for your valuable comments for improving our work. To Meta Reviewer: In our Rebuttal, we have provide dclarifications on the methodological details and ablation studies to address the concerns raised. To Reviewer #1: Q1: There is a lack of analytical depth on specific lesion types, anatomical structures, or boundary complexities. A1: Regarding analytical depth, we clarify that the DMS module yields the most significant performance gains on irregular lesions with highly variable shapes and sizes, such as pediatric tumors in BraTS-PEDs and complex jagged stroke boundaries in ATLAS. Existing methods often keep generic U-Net denoisers lacking medical structural awareness, whereas we provide a morphology-aware denoising backbone. Q2: The methodological novelty is incremental. A2: Our novelty is not in claiming each operation is entirely new, but in redesigning and integrating them into a task-specific structural inductive bias based on the inherent deficiencies of current diffusion models for medical anomaly detection. Specifically, we emphasize three points: (1) Task-specific innovation: DMS is not a simple stacking of dilated convolutions, but a structural design oriented towards directional, multi-scale, and boundary-sensitive modeling of medical anomalous regions. (2) Framework adaptability innovation: The modules are embedded into the AnoFPDM forward-process anomaly scoring, aiming to enhance the capability of modeling differences between guided and unguided trajectories. (3) Efficiency-performance trade-off innovation: The lightweight structure is not merely compressing parameters, but reducing inference costs while maintaining anomaly detection performance. To Reviewer #2 Q1-Q2: The method is evaluated exclusively within AnoFPDM, making it hard to assess the efficacy of the architecture away from this inference scheme. A1-A2: We appreciate this insightful and highly necessary recommendation. We fully accept this valuable suggestion and will incorporate these cross-framework validations into our future work. Q3: The top layer of Table 2 is unclear. A3: All ablations in Table 2 keep the AnoFPDM forward inference, training protocol, and data split fixed, only changing backbone components. The first row is the original AnoFPDM result. The following rows show the effects of adding DMS to different layers and further incorporating ASSF. Thus, Table 2 is a controlled ablation showing that improvements are attributable to the proposed shape-scale-aware backbone components, not the AnoFPDM inference scheme alone. Q4-Q6: Other concerns including comparison with ConvNeXt, brief description of AnoFPDM, and dense Fig. 1.A4-6: We will incorporate cross-framework validations (like ConvNeXt) into our future work. Regarding presentation issues such as Fig. 1, please refer to our unified response to R3-Q2~Q7.To Reviewer #3 Q1: The evaluation metrics become worse in Table 3 after using the lightweight architecture. A1: We agree that our wording should be more precise. PDS-Conv is not intended to further improve accuracy, but to provide a practical trade-off between performance and computational cost for iterative diffusion inference. Compared with the full backbone, PDS-Conv causes only a slight performance drop, while reducing parameters from 97.89M to 46.12M and GFLOPs from 65.00 to 14.75.Thus, the lightweight version substantially reduces computational cost with only minor accuracy loss. In future versions, we will describe this more accurately. Q2-Q7: Presentation and clarity issues, including explanations for “Weakly” supervised, full name of AnoSSP, usage of c_ctx and h_dec, AnoDDPM(G/S), and figure readability. A2-7: We thank the reviewer for pointing these out. h_dec denotes the current decoder feature; c_ctx is obtained by global average pooling on h_dec to generate modulation parameters in ASSF. In future versions, we will fix these issues carefully and thoroughly.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The empirical results are strong across three datasets and the efficiency gains are well-documented. The authors should address the most important points raised by the reviewers, especially with regard to whether the performance gains are attributable to the proposed architectural components or to the AnoFPDM inference scheme, the performance degradation under the lightweight architecture visible in Table 3, and the novelty positioning relative to existing directional convolution and gated skip connection designs. | The paper addresses an underexplored aspect of diffusion-based anomaly detection, the denoising backbone architecture, with consistent empirical improvements across three datasets. The rebuttal adequately addressed the three main concerns raised: the within-framework ablation in Table 2 provides controlled evidence that gains are attributable to the proposed components rather than the AnoFPDM inference scheme alone, the lightweight architecture performance degradation is reframed appropriately as a compute-performance tradeoff with concrete efficiency numbers, and the novelty is positioned as task-specific structural integration. Cross-framework generalizability remains an acknowledged limitation that should be discussed in the final version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After considering the rebuttal and updated reviews, I recommend rejection. The rebuttal does not sufficiently resolve the concern that the observed gains may be difficult to attribute specifically to the proposed architectural components, and several components appear to be incremental combinations of existing operations. Given these unresolved concerns about contribution attribution and methodological novelty, I do not think the paper sufficiently crosses the acceptance threshold in its current form. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): While the proposed method demonstrates its superiority across three datasets, and the integration of existing components could be, up to some extent, seen as novel, there are important limitations that undermines the impact of the proposed work. First, I believe that the empirical validation is limited, with several important works on anomaly detection that appeared during 2025 missing (including papers at MICCAI’25). Furthermore, one of the critical issues is the concept of weakly supervised, which is not explained in the paper (rather referred to be explained in a further revision). Similarly, I found the use of the wording Shape a bit overstated: authors frame their approach as shape-aware, but there is nothing that supports why this is the case. Given all these concerns, in addition to several concerns from reviewers which remain unresolved, I recommend the rejection of this work in its current form.

title: Shared Gaussian Geometry for Brain MRI Spatial Resolution Harmonization Without External Training
reviewer_1_strengths: The objective of the paper and the motivations are clear. The methodology is cohesive, with all necessary mathematical background provided. The overview figure is a clear visual summary of the paper’s methodology as well. Experiments are thorough, and there is a decent combination of 3 cited datasets, 4 scanning modalities, and two degradation techniques. Overall, great presentation and the methodology is compared about recent state of the art methodologies. Finally, excellent vocabulary and phrasing of the science behind the MRI acquisition and inverse problem.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Some aspects of the methodology don’t seem to contribute enough to spark discussion. In the ablation study it appears that the peristance topology loss and the latent appearance does not have a significant impact compared to LR Consistent Fusion which should be explained more thoroughly. Also, functional scans such as DWI and ASL might not be the optimal target modalities for this methodology. Finally, notation in equations is not defined before usage in a few cases cases.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Novel Geometry-Guided Harmonization Framework: This paper introduces a novel zero-shot MRI spatial harmonization framework that leverages shared Gaussian geometry learned from isotropic structural MRI to guide reconstruction of heterogeneous target modalities. By explicitly disentangling anatomical geometry from modality-specific appearance, the proposed method offers an interpretable and structurally grounded alternative to conventional interpolation or contrast-agnostic implicit reconstruction methods. Continuous Representation Design: The proposed deformable Gaussian-based continuous representation extends standard Gaussian splatting by modeling nonlinear through-plane anatomical continuity and modality-specific appearance separately. This design enables arbitrary-view rendering and continuous super-resolution while preserving structural consistency across modalities, representing a technically meaningful extension of Gaussian-based medical image reconstruction frameworks. Well-Motivated Physics-Aware Optimization Objectives: The training objective incorporates slab-aware thick-slice integration, topology-preserving persistent homology loss, and latent appearance regularization. These components are carefully designed to reflect MRI acquisition physics and anatomical structural priors. Multi-dataset Validation:he method is evaluated across multiple datasets (UKBB, GBM, ABCD), MRI modalities (FLAIR, T2w, DWI, ASL), degradation factors, and pathological settings including glioblastoma cases. This broad experimental setup demonstrates the generalizability of the proposed framework across diverse acquisition protocols and clinical scenarios.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Absence of Real-world Evaluation: The experimental validation is conducted primarily on synthetically degraded low-resolution inputs generated from originally high-resolution volumes, while quantitative evaluation on truly real-world clinical thick-slice acquisitions is absent. As a result, the practical robustness of the method under realistic scanner-dependent slice profiles, motion artifacts, and noise characteristics remains insufficiently verified. Insufficient Analysis of Failure Cases and Modality-Specific Limitations: While the paper reports broad experimental results across multiple datasets and modalities, it provides limited discussion of cases in which the proposed method underperforms or offers only marginal improvement. For example, the relatively weak performance on DWI is not meaningfully analyzed, and the paper does not clarify under what modality conditions the shared Gaussian geometry prior is reliable or when it may become a source of bias. This lack of deeper error analysis reduces the interpretability of the empirical findings. Terminology and Task Framing Clarity: While the paper addresses an important problem of cross-protocol MRI spatial resolution alignment, the terminology used throughout the manuscript may cause conceptual confusion within the medical imaging community. Specifically, the term “spatial harmonization” is not commonly used in the MRI harmonization literature. In general, MRI harmonization refers to reducing non-biological variability across scans acquired under different scanners, institutions, protocols, or imaging settings while preserving underlying anatomical and pathological information, rather than specifically denoting spatial resolution matching or super-resolution. Given this established convention, the current terminology may be somewhat misleading. It may improve clarity and consistency with prior literature to describe the task more explicitly as “spatial resolution alignment for multi-contrast MRI harmonization”, thereby clarifying that the proposed framework focuses specifically on resolution standardization rather than broader MRI harmonization. Minor Notation Clarity and Typo: Several abbreviations are introduced before being properly defined. For example, “FN” appears in Eq. (3) before its formal explanation is provided near Eq. (4), which may hinder readability. In addition, minor typographical issues are present, such as the duplicated comma following “(Fig. 3 left)” in the Qualitative Results subsection of Section 3.A careful revision of notation ordering and manuscript proofreading would improve the overall readability of the paper.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.It introduces GS to MRI resolution harmonization, employing a novel two-stage training strategy where a geometric scaffold is first learned from isotropic T1w scans, then used to fit the appearance of other modalities. 2.The zero-shot approach operates within a single subject without external training data, leveraging existing clinical T1w images as a basis for knowledge transfer, which is highly practical for clinical use. 3.It demonstrates state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity across diverse datasets, critically preserving tumor lesions accurately and mitigating interpolation artifacts, thus proving its clinical reliability. 4.Capabilities like arbitrary-view generation, potential for in-plane super-resolution, and an interpretable Gaussian-based representation offer significant extensibility to various future applications in medical image analysis.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper is technically interesting and the overall idea is promising. However, I believe the manuscript has several important weaknesses that should be more clearly acknowledged. 1.The term zero-shot is used, but it’s fundamentally a per-subject optimization. While it doesn’t require external training data, it still requires a full, high-resolution isotropic T1w scan and subsequent training for each new subject. This is a crucial distinction. It’s not a pre-trained model that can be instantly applied to any new patient. This significantly limits its scalability in a high-throughput clinical setting. 2.The paper claims “zero-shot adaptation of volume appearance” but this adaptation takes 20 minutes per subject. This is not “adaptation” in a practical sense. It’s per-subject training. 3.The method assumes that different MRI modalities can share the same geometry while differing mainly in appearance. However, modalities such as FLAIR, DWI, and ASL reflect substantially different signal mechanisms, not just intensity contrast. It remains unclear whether the proposed appearance representation is expressive enough to capture these modality-specific properties. 4.The inclusion of linear and cubic interpolation is reasonable, but these are relatively weak baselines compared with a learned multimodal reconstruction framework. Additional comparisons with stronger learning-based cross-modal reconstruction or super-resolution methods would make the empirical validation more convincing. 5.The proposed 2D+t Gaussian framework includes many interacting parameters and dynamic components, which makes the model highly flexible but also potentially difficult to optimize and control. The manuscript does not sufficiently discuss regularization, optimization stability, or sensitivity to noise and initialization.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and area chairs for their careful review and valuable comments. In this response, we would like to clarify several unclear phrasings and claims in our submission, and discuss details and potential future directions based on our experimental findings and ablation studies. To Reviewer #2: 1.The latent appearance and topology persistence losses in our method mainly contribute to improved visualization quality and suppression of speckles and unrealistic point clouds caused by the Gaussian Splatting (GS) representation. Specifically: The latent appearance loss significantly reduces random speckles and noise from the T1-guided scaffold, especially in clinically important ROIs (white matter, basal ganglia, etc.). The topology persistence loss helps reduce point clouds with limited contribution to the shared geometry and improves robustness to small anatomical shifts across modalities. We’d like to include an expanded ablation table with additional metrics reflecting geometry preservation, anatomical fidelity, and speckle/noise suppression. 2.For the DWI and ASL experiments, generally we noticed that GS-based methods are more sensitive to deformable distortions in diffusion and perfusion imaging. Some of these artifacts can be alleviated when the modalities are non-rigidly registered to structural modalities in other organs (e.g., prostate imaging). We did not include these experiments in the submission because they are not part of the core methodology of this paper. However, we consider distortion management an important future direction toward ultra-high-resolution and functional harmonization. We also thank the reviewer for pointing out the typos and organizational issues. These comments are very helpful for improving the Methods section. To Reviewer #3: We agree with your comment regarding the absence of real-world evaluation, and we will consider this an important direction for future work. We used the term “spatial harmonization” to emphasize the potential ability of our method to align multimodal imaging data with arbitrary spatial resolutions onto a shared structural reference, which extends beyond conventional “super-resolution” or “registration.” Your comments regarding notation clarity are also very valuable. To Reviewer #4: 1.Our method is designed for a common clinical setting in which structural isotropic T1w scans are routinely available. We agree with your concern regarding the justification of the term “zero-shot.” We used this phrasing to emphasize that our method naturally adapts to most brain MRI modalities without requiring external training data for the target modalities. 2.Regarding the assumption of “shared geometry,” we believe that TSE-based FLAIR generally shares the same geometry because it is also a structural imaging modality. We did observe structural bias in diffusion and perfusion imaging (see response 2 to Reviewer #2). However, in brain MRI this bias is relatively limited, and our method remains competitive with the baselines. We will gladly include further discussion of this issue as a future direction. 3.Most components of our GS algorithm are derived from MedGS, which we gratefully acknowledge as one of the baselines. From our perspective, MedGS is among the earliest works introducing Gaussian Splatting methods into medical imaging. We compared against most SOTA INR- and GS-based methods that do not require external training data. In contrast, many state-of-the-art deep learning methods are designed mainly for in-plane reconstruction or require a fixed super-resolution factor, which is not fully compatible with our setting. 4.In this work, we did not perform extensive ablation studies on hyperparameters because, for most subjects, 10k iterations were sufficient for all loss terms to converge adequately. We would like to evaluate more settings and include this analysis in future work, which may also help reduce the processing time per subject.

title: SHINE: An Entropy-Guided Digital Twin Framework for 3D Myocardial Scar Reconstruction from Sparse CMR
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses the reconstruction of 3D myocardial scar from sparse and anisotropic LGE-MRI, which is a well-known limitation in clinical cardiac imaging. The focus on recovering fine-scale structures relevant to ventricular tachycardia (VT) ablation highlights the potential clinical importance of the work. 2.A key strength is the reformulation of scar reconstruction from a discrete voxel-based interpolation problem to a continuous function learning task defined on a patient-specific anatomical manifold. This perspective is conceptually appealing, as it naturally avoids discretization artifacts and enables resolution-independent modeling. 3.The framework leverages anatomical information derived from Cine MRI and a statistical shape model to constrain the reconstruction. This is a meaningful design choice, as it helps regularize the ill-posed problem by embedding prior knowledge about cardiac geometry. 4.The adoption of a SIREN-based implicit neural representation is well-suited for modeling continuous spatial fields and capturing high-frequency geometric structures. This is particularly relevant for representing narrow conducting channels that may be smoothed out by conventional CNN-based approaches.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The primary challenge of this task lies in reconstructing structures within large inter-slice gaps where no direct measurements are available. However, the evaluation mainly relies on slice-wise validation (e. g. , leave-one-slice-out) and indirect geometric consistency, which do not fully assess reconstruction accuracy in truly unobserved regions. As a result, it remains unclear whether the recovered fine-scale or “sub-voxel” structures correspond to anatomically accurate features. While Fig. 2 provides intuitive qualitative comparisons, the absence of a reference or ground truth makes it difficult to determine whether the reconstructed structures reflect true anatomy. 2.The figures throughout the manuscript are generally difficult to interpret and would benefit from improved clarity and more detailed annotation. For instance, Fig. 1 (Overview of the SHINE framework) lacks sufficient explanatory details and textual labeling, making it challenging to follow the data flow and understand the role of each component in the pipeline. Key elements such as inputs, intermediate representations, and model outputs are not clearly defined. In addition, Fig. 5 is not clearly explained and is not referenced in the main text, making its purpose within the paper unclear. The intended message of the figure, particularly regarding the interpretation of uncertainty and its clinical relevance, is difficult to discern from the current presentation. 3.The study uses a cohort of 40 patients. It may be insufficient to demonstrate robustness across different MRI scanner and variations in LGE acquisition protocols. In addition, important details about the dataset are missing. For example, the spatial resolution of the LGE-MRI data (both in-plane and through-plane) is not consistently or clearly reported. Given that the proposed method specifically addresses highly anisotropic data. 4.Furthermore, the manuscript lacks sufficient implementation details for key components of the method. 5.While SHINE achieves strong numerical results, its technical novelty is incremental, representing an application-level integration of established methods such as SIREN, Bayesian uncertainty estimation, and Statistical Shape Models (SSM) rather than a fundamental algorithmic breakthrough. The framework’s performance is heavily dependent on the accuracy of the initial anatomical prior; any errors in the SSM fitting or automated segmentation of atypical cardiac morphologies could propagate into significant spatial biases in scar reconstruction. (Li, Lei, et al. 2024; Zou, Rongjun, et al. 2025)
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Novel continuous reconstruction formulation: The paper reformulates scar reconstruction as a continuous function learning problem on a patient-specific anatomical manifold. This is interesting because it overcomes limitations of discrete voxel interpolation and enables resolution-independent, topology-preserving reconstruction. Use of Bayesian SIREN for high-frequency detail recovery: The adoption of a Bayesian SIREN architecture effectively addresses spectral bias and allows modeling of fine-scale structures such as conducting isthmuses. This is important for capturing clinically relevant micro-structures that are typically lost in standard CNN-based approaches. Entropy-guided adaptive regularization: The proposed entropy-weighted Dirichlet energy loss is a strong contribution, as it uses uncertainty to adaptively balance smoothness and detail preservation. This helps prevent unrealistic hallucinations in data-sparse regions while maintaining fidelity where data is available. Integration of anatomical priors via digital twin modeling: The use of a Statistical Shape Model and multi-view cine MRI to construct a patient-specific anatomical manifold provides a strong geometric constraint, improving reconstruction consistency. Strong quantitative and qualitative performance: The method shows clear improvements over interpolation and deep learning baselines in both Dice score and volumetric accuracy, supported by convincing qualitative results. Uncertainty-aware outputs for clinical safety: The inclusion of predictive uncertainty maps (“safety maps”) is a valuable feature, providing additional interpretability and potential clinical utility in identifying unreliable regions.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Limited dataset size and lack of external validation: The evaluation is conducted on a relatively small cohort (40 patients) without external or multi-center validation. This raises concerns about generalizability across different imaging protocols and populations. Potential overfitting risk due to high model flexibility: The use of high-capacity neural fields (SIREN) combined with limited training data may lead to overfitting or hallucinated structures, especially in data-sparse regions, despite the proposed regularization. Limited validation of uncertainty estimates: Although uncertainty maps are presented as “clinical safety maps,” there is no quantitative validation or expert-based evaluation showing that these uncertainty estimates reliably correspond to reconstruction errors. Clinical impact not directly demonstrated: While the method is motivated by VT ablation planning, there is no direct evaluation showing improvement in clinical decision-making or procedural outcomes. Pipeline complexity and reproducibility concerns: The framework involves multiple components (segmentation, SSM fitting, co-registration, Baayesian INR), which may complicate implementation and limit reproducibility without detailed technical documentation.
reviewer_2_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The use of a Bayesian SIREN backbone is a good choice. By using periodic activations instead of traditional functions, this framework can recover the high-frequency topological details. 2.The Entropy-Weighted Dirichlet Energy loss is a good theoretical contribution. By linking regularization directly to predictive uncertainty, it may prevents the neural field from creating hallucinations without blurring the actual observed data.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The framework’s geometric prior depends on biventricular segmentations and the fitting of a Statistical Shape Model (SSM). The paper does not thoroughly explore how errors, artifacts in this initial upstream step might cascade into the final digital twin reconstruction. 2.The author claim that the Entropy-Weighted Dirichlet Energy loss is vital for preventing hallucinations. However, Table 2 shows that Variant (a) which removes only the entropy regularisation achieves a volumetric error of 1.4%, which is actually superior to the proposed SHINE model’s 3.1%. The authors rely on the qualitative visuals of Figure 4 to argue that Variant (a) produces more artifacts which is insufficient. 3.The paper highlights a rapid inference speed. However, because the framework relies on fitting a patient-specific anatomical manifold and optimizing a Bayesian architecture via Monte Carlo for each patient, the training is likely to be computationally intensive. 4.The evaluation appears to be limited to a single clinical cohort with 40 patients.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the Area Chair for the summary. We also thank R1 for recognizing our continuous manifold and SIREN architecture, R2 for endorsing our entropy regularization and safety maps, and R3 for affirming our Bayesian SIREN backbone and theoretical loss contribution. We consolidated your concerns into 5 themes addressed in the revised manuscript: 1.”Cohort of 40 Patients” & “Robustness” (R1, R2, R3) We acknowledge that 40 patients is a relatively small cohort. However, given that our primary contribution is a methodological innovation, this dataset rigorously demonstrates robustness. It originates from two centers with different MRI scanners (1.5T Siemens Avanto vs. 3.0T Biograph mMR). Acquisitions were resampled to 1.2x1.2x8.0mm space. Our Leave-One-Slice-Out(LOSO) protocol evaluates SHINE against 455 physical slices covering extreme infarct sizes (4.7%-56.1%), validating robustness against equipment variations. To clinically validate this breakthrough, we secured a multi-center dataset of >500 cases across 3 centers for future work (Will add to Sec. 4). 2.”Truly Unobserved Regions” & Lack of Ground Truth (R1) Absolute 3D ground truth data, such as 3D single-breath-hold LGE-CMR, are not available in the current study. However, our data provides relatively dense spatial sampling (8-16 slices/patient). To address this, we used a LOSO cross-validation protocol. By withholding true physical LGE slices (isolated from optimization), we establish a surrogate ground truth. Evaluated against hidden slices, SHINE achieves high spatial overlap (DSC 0.93) and near-perfect fidelity (MSE 4.0x10^-5), proving reconstructed sub-voxel structures are anatomically accurate, not hallucinations (Will detail in Sec. 3.1). 3.The “1.4% Volumetric Error” Paradox (R3) Volumetric error without topological constraints is mathematically misleading. Evaluated on LOSO hidden slices, Variant (a) collapses micro-structurally with a high MSE (1.9x10^-3). As Fig. 4A shows, its seemingly superior 1.4% error is a volumetric coincidence driven by “salt-and-pepper” hallucinations: random over- and under-estimations cancel out, destroying conducting isthmus continuity. Conversely, SHINE’s entropy loss suppresses these artifacts (MSE 4.0x10^-5). Thus, our 3.1% error reflects strict topological fidelity essential for ablation planning; the 1.4% is a dangerous illusion of fragmented noise (Will clarify in Sec. 3.1). 4.”Error Propagation from Segmentation & SSM” (R1, R3) While recent works highlight upstream error cascades (Li et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025), our statistical analysis reveals no significant correlation (r=0.20, p=0.34) between initial segmentation/SSM geometric deviations (mean 1.59+/-0.22mm) and downstream volumetric errors. Thus, these upstream errors do not propagate into spatial biases. Mechanistically, SHINE inherently decouples anatomical geometry from pathological texture learning. Its manifold alignment effectively absorbs initial geometric noise as rigid translations without distorting the underlying scar topology (Will cite/detail in Sec. 3.1). 5.”Pipeline Complexity” & “Computationally Intensive” (R1, R2, R3) To resolve clarity and reproducibility concerns, we will overhaul Figs. 1 and 5 with explicit labels, detailing Fig. 5 in a new Sec. 3.3.We will also add Sec. 2.5 (“Implementation Details”) documenting precise hyperparameters (e.g., 4-layer Bayesian SIREN, 256 units, T=50, lambda_entropy = 5 x 10^-4) and link to our public codebase. Computationally, the ~7.5 mins/case patient-specific fitting is strictly a pre-operative process, seamlessly enabling 0.54s real-time intraoperative inference on an RTX 4090 (Will discuss in Sec. 3.3). Concluding Remarks: We will expand Sec. 1 to explicitly clarify our algorithmic advancements over standard INRs, and update Sec. 4 to outline protocols for future large-scale clinical validation and impact assessment. We sincerely thank the Area Chair and reviewers for improving our work.

title: SIGMA-VAE: Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Multi-View Autoencoder for Normative Modeling
reviewer_1_strengths: Theoretical grounded claims towards attacking VAEs limitations: The authors properly explores, discusses and provide references for the reader to better understand VAE limitations, as: chance of raising an incoherente global latent geometry (regions with roles or not sufficient represented); lack of interpretability of the learned latent representation; confusion of healthy variations given demographic factors (. e. g, age and sex) with patologies; Proposer use of literature to tackle VAEs limitations: Authors adapt to their VAE techniques as SigREG (recently proposed in the LeJEPA article), L0 regularization to select important and interpretable latent dimensions, and an uncertainty-aware W-score based on epistemic uncertainty. The use of SigREG together with L0 regularization enables the authors to enable reliable distance-based deviation measures; Interpretability: By individually disturbing each W-score, the authors also enable the visualization of the anatomical subsystem that the W-score represents; Robust validation: Authors employ strategies to evaluate in- and out-of-distribution test sets, isolating the effect of testing in samples of the same test set or scanner. They also isolate the effects of age and sex on evaluation, which is also positive, as they employ conditioning with age and sex. Lastly, W-score Q-Q plots show that the learned scores follow a normal distribution centered at 0 and with close to unit variance. —— MORE DETAILS —- **Theoretically grounded motivation. ** The authors provide a well-structured and referenced critique of standard VAE-based normative models, identifying three concrete limitations: the risk of an incoherent global latent geometry with redundant or sparsely populated (hole-prone) regions; limited interpretability of the learned latent representation; and the conflation of healthy demographic variation (age and sex) with pathological deviations. This framing effectively justifies each of the proposed contributions; **Principled use of recent literature to address VAE limitations. ** The authors adapt three complementary techniques to directly tackle the identified limitations: SIGReg, recently proposed in the LeJEPA framework, is incorporated into the VAE training objective to promote a compact, hole-free isotropic Gaussian latent geometry that supports reliable Euclidean deviation scoring; L0 regularization via learnable Hard Concrete gates enforces latent sparsity, deactivating uninformative dimensions and improving interpretability; and an uncertainty-aware W-score is derived from the encoder’s per-dimension means and variances — grounding deviation estimates in aleatoric uncertainty. The combination of SIGReg and L0 regularization is particularly well motivated, as a compact and sparse latent space is a prerequisite for distance-based deviation measures to be geometrically meaningful; **Interpretability of latent dimensions. ** By independently perturbing each latent dimension and observing the resulting changes in reconstructed anatomy, the authors enable visualization of the anatomical subsystem that each W-score dimension represents. It is a meaningful differentiator from most VAE-based normative modeling works in the literature, which typically treat the latent space as a black box; **Robust and thorough validation pipeline. ** The authors employ a rigorous evaluation strategy across multiple axes. In- and out-of-distribution test sets are assessed separately, isolating performance on the same-site data from generalization to held-out scanner data. The model’s conditioning on age and sex is appropriately reflected in the evaluation, preventing demographic variation from confounding deviation scores. Finally, W-score Q-Q plots demonstrate that the learned scores follow a normal distribution centered at zero with near-unit variance across healthy subjects, providing empirical support for the Euclidean scoring assumption that underlies the deviation metric.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Use of PoE: a review of one of the cited literature (Multi-modal Variational Autoencoders for normative modelling across multiple imaging modalities, Lawry Aguila et al. ) reveals a discussion where the PoE treating all experts as equally credible, uniform contribution from every modality (in the paper under review here the contribution of erery view), and in practice noyse, and complexity may break this assumption. In Lawry Aguila et al. , they investigate using Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) or generalized Product-of-Experts (gPoE). As the authors cited Lawry Aguila et al. , it would be valuable to add one phrase discussing this limitation of PoE and how they see it; Encoder/Decoder pairs for each view: authors choose to train a pair for each view (Cortical Thickness, Subcortical Volume, Surface Area), and state that Multi-View fusion formulation naturally handles missing views, but no tests are made towards it. In the future, as they expand across multiple modalities, how will they tackle it? Other works handle views within the same encoder-decoder pair but employ a separate encoder for each modality. Maybe a short phrase discussing this choice would be valuable; Encoder architecture: Incomplete feature attention block description. It employs a single layer? How are attention weights computed? —– MORE DETAILS —— **Use of Product-of-Experts for view fusion. ** The authors adopt a standard Product-of-Experts (PoE) formulation to aggregate the per-view encoder posteriors into a joint latent representation. As discussed in Lawry Aguila et al. (2023), a work cited by the authors, PoE treats all experts as equally credible, assuming uniform contributions from all views. In practice, differences in noise levels, feature complexity, and information content across views can violate this assumption, potentially biasing the joint posterior towards overconfident but miscalibrated experts. While this concern is somewhat attenuated here since all three views derive from the same acquisition, it will become increasingly relevant as the authors expand their framework to genuinely distinct modalities, as stated in their future work. Given that the authors cite Lawry Aguila et al. , who explicitly address this limitation via Mixture-of-Experts and generalized Product-of-Experts formulations, a brief discussion of why standard PoE was preferred over these alternatives would strengthen the paper. **Untested claim regarding missing view robustness. ** The authors state that their multi-view fusion formulation naturally handles missing views, a known theoretical property of PoE, which allows excluding absent experts from the product. However, no empirical evaluation of this capability is provided. Given that missing data is a common practical challenge in clinical neuroimaging, this claim should either be validated experimentally or explicitly hedged as a theoretical property rather than a demonstrated one. Furthermore, as the authors plan to extend their framework to additional modalities, a concrete strategy for handling missing modalities will become essential and warrants discussion. **Incomplete description of the feature attention block. ** The encoder architecture includes a feature attention block before the MLP backbone, but its implementation is insufficiently described for full reproducibility. Specifically, it is unclear whether the block consists of a single linear layer or a multi-layer MLP with a bottleneck; how the attention weights are computed and normalized (sigmoid per feature vs. softmax across features). Given that the MLP backbone dimensions [512, 256, 128] and the 32-dimensional raw latent space are clearly specified, the same level of detail should be provided for the attention block to ensure reproducibility; **Incomplete references. ** The manuscript contains several instances of unresolved references appearing as [?]. While some of these may reflect intentional anonymization of self-citations for double-blind review — a common and acceptable practice — this does not account for all cases. Notably, [?] appears in contexts where already correctly cited external methods are referenced, including SIGReg, which is cited elsewhere in the manuscript with a proper reference. Authors should ensure that all non-self-referential citations are correctly resolved in the final submission, as unresolved references to key methodological sources undermine reproducibility and make it difficult for readers to trace the theoretical foundations of the work.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers (r) and Meta-Reviewer (MR), for their feedback. Following the MR’s guidance, we address the core concerns below. 1- Evaluation Design: Ablations vs. External SOTA (R2, R3, MR) Reviewers suggest comparisons against PCNtoolkit or β-VAE. These frameworks do not address the structural failures SIGMA-VAE targets. While PCNtoolkit is the current field standard, it models features univariately; its per-region z-scores cannot be aggregated into valid multivariate anomaly scores without the geometrically valid latent space this work provides. Univariate methods lack the multivariate geometry to resolve the calibration failures inherent in current normative modelling. On the other hand, β-VAE based approaches, including Lawry Aguila et al. (2023), inherit the standard VAE limitation: per-sample KL regularization does not constrain the aggregated posterior, leaving no guarantee of latent isotropy or hole-freeness required for calibrated Euclidean deviation scoring. The calibration failure of the KL-baseline makes this concrete: even a multivariate latent model miscalibrates by over-retaining 15.5% of healthy controls at the 80% threshold. We therefore adopted a controlled ablation against the standard β=1 VAE baseline — the appropriate experimental unit to isolate each component’s contribution and demonstrate their synergy. The calibration result (Fig. 2B) directly addresses this concern: only the full SIGMA-VAE resolves the miscalibration that persists across all ablated variants. To our knowledge, this is the first normative framework to jointly guarantee latent isotropy, sparsity, and calibrated deviation scoring. 2- Reconstruction metrics (R3, MR) Reconstruction loss was monitored throughout training and remains stable across all ablation variants, confirming that L0 sparsity prunes uninformative dimensions without degrading generative integrity (avg. MSE ~0.35). We will report the reconstruction loss weight and MSE range across variants in the camera-ready version to confirm that reconstruction quality remained controlled. That said, minimizing MSE is not the objective here: VAE training involves an explicit tradeoff between reconstruction fidelity and latent-space structure, and the model with the lowest MSE is not necessarily the best model for anomaly detection. The clinically relevant question is whether latent deviations are properly scaled for inference, which calibration error (Fig. 2B) directly measures, and where the full SIGMA-VAE demonstrably outperforms all variants. 3- Tabular features and large-scale validation (R3) FreeSurfer-derived tabular features are the field standard for large-scale normative studies (n=40,000+). Beginning with tabular features allowed us to validate the framework’s geometric and calibration properties in a controlled, interpretable setting; the architecture imposes no restriction on input dimensionality. Tested on data from entirely unseen scanners, SIGMA-VAE’s consistent W-scores demonstrated scanner-robustness that smaller benchmarks did not match, setting a standard for models that generalise across acquisition environments. 4-Citation tags (all reviewers, MR) We emphasize that the bibliography is complete; the [?] tags were a technical resolution error during the final anonymization pass: L0 (ref. [14], Louizos et al. 2018) and PoE (ref. [16], Hinton 2002) will be corrected in the camera-ready version. Minor points (R1, R2) Feature attention: Implemented via channel-wise sigmoid gating. PoE/Missing views: Views originate from the same acquisition, attenuating the equal-credibility concern; the missing-view claim refers to an inherent PoE property. Disentanglement: Age/sex enter via conditioning c; low latent-demographic correlations (mean |r|=0.035, Sec. 3.2) confirm variation is not absorbed into the latent space. Interpretability: Validated via perturbation analysis (Fig. 3), mapping dimensions to neuroanatomical subsystems.

title: Single-Subject Multi-view MRI Super-Resolution via Implicit Neural Representations
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper has many strengths. The incorporation of multi-orientation information for anisotropic super-resolution is well-motivated. The restriction of training data to a single-subject addresses pathology, unique contrasts/modalities, and is clinically useful. The use of an INR to perform implicit deformable registration is very novel. The experimental suite included custom augmentations for comparison methods SMORE and ECLARE (including Table 1, demonstrating the utility of their MISR augmentations) is thoughtful and useful for the field of anisotropic MISR. The number of quantitative metrics is extensive.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: This method is both interesting and promising. Yet, I still have a few clarifying questions and some comments on the theory and experimental design, ordered by what I consider most important first. 1.How is slice thickness addressed in this work? The authors explicitly mention in Sec 2, sentence 2: “thick slices along the through-plane directions. “ This is correct for 2D-acquired MRI. However, this slice thickness is not addressed in either the methods section nor in the simulation experiment. Rather, as-is, the paper addresses sparse-slice anisotropic MRI. This is fine if the authors intend it to be so, but it should be explicitly mentioned. 2.Related to the previous comment, “resolution” is not strictly defined in this work, and this causes some ambiguity in interpreting the method. Consider two cases. A) the HR image volume has voxels of resolution a x a x a mm. The simulation approach described in Sec 3.1.sounds like the LR image volume still has voxels of resolution a x a x a mm, where slices are sub-sampled with something like cubic B-spline interpolation, linear interpolation, or slice sub-sampling. In this way, the INR network f learns to use complementary information from both views, and the theory of the method makes sense: inference-time isotropic grid sampling should yield an isotropic volume, since for all coordinates the voxel resolution learned is always a x a x a mm. Now consider the second case, B) the HR volume still has voxels of resolution a x a x a mm, but the LR volumes are truly thick-slice, with voxels of resolution a x a x b mm and a x c x a mm, where b > a and c > a. This could be simulated, for example, by convolving in 1D along the slice-selection axis with a rect or Gaussian filter with appropriate full-width-half-max. In this case, the INR network f does not learn a straightforward function. For the first view, it learns to map coordinates \Omega to voxels of resolution a x a x b mm. For the second view, it learns to map coordinates \Omega to voxels of resolution a x b x a mm. On average, one would expect the final inference-time result to produce images of voxels a x (a+c)/2 x (a+b)/2 mm. I believe some theoretical discussion of this phenomenon would greatly strengthen the paper. 3.Based on the description, my assumption is that the experiment in Sec 3.1 uses cubic B-spline interpolation to produce LR volumes 4x lower resolution simply by subsampling, not by simulating slice acquisition. Is this assumption correct? If so, does this cause a mismatch on the reported results for SMORE and ECLARE, both of which assume thick slices? 4.For the experiment in Sec 3.2, how are the pseudo-ground truth (GT) sagittal slices selected? I believe an appropriate comparison between each of the SR methods would be to simulate 3mm-thick-slices by convolving with an appropriate-width rect or Gaussian profile, then selecting the same 3mm-thick sagittal slice for SR method and pseudo-GT. This would produce results with (supposedly) similar SNR and anatomical locations. Otherwise it is difficult to trust the results reported in Fig. 3, since it is unknown were in the 3mm slice the 0.5-thick estimated slice exists. The anatomy may vary greatly in that section. 5.A small comment on the runtime of each method would be useful. In Sec 4, the authors mention “While the per-subject optimization is more computationally demanding than feed-forward approaches,” but all comparison methods here are per-subject. It would be interesting to know approximately how long SIMS-MRI takes compared to SMORE and ECLARE. 6.Some minor weaknesses: 1.Please consider using ~\ref{} (with the tilde symbol) for all in-text references, since this introduces a non-breaking space between the word and citation. 2.Section 1, paragraph 2: Typo in algorithm name (should be ESPRESO with two total S’s).
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The authors demonstrate through ablation studies that using hash encoding and FreeNeRF improves the performance of the proposed method. This provides evidence and guidance for readers should they wish to build their own INR-based super-resolution frameworks. 2.The evaluation metrics includes both conventional metrics like PSNR and SSIM, and also learning-based metrics that capture perceptual similarity. 3.The organization of the paper is great. Notations are consistent and are easy to follow.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The major weakness of the paper is its limited novelty. A similar work, with a different application (fetal imaging), is NeSVoR by Xu J, et al., IEEE TMI, 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1109/tmi.2023.3236216). The task is almost the same: multi-view super-resolution with explicitly modeled subject motion across views. The method is also similar: NeSVoR also uses INR with hash encoding. In addition to NeSVoR, there is another work named IREM that uses INR for MRI reconstruction, which appeared in MICCAI a couple of years ago: Wu Q, et al., MICCAI 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-87231-1_7). This makes the novelty of this work limited unless the authors, during rebuttal, make a strong case for why their work demonstrates non-incremental improvement over these existing methods. Some design choices are poorly justified/not supported by evidence. The authors should consider providing more clarifications during revision. 1.Regarding Phase 2: Implicit Image Registration. 1.a. Why is NCC used as the similarity measure? It is slower compared to MSE and using NCC for within-modality registration is an overkill. 1.b. Why is a non-linear deformation model used for image registration? Typically, bulk motion in brain MRI is modeled as rigid transformation (6 DOF), which is also what the authors claim to use for their simulation experiments. Non-linear deformation might be helpful for prostate MRI due to possible bowel movement which is non-linear, but most of the time affine transformation (12 DOF) is sufficient. Why not just directly learn the 12 affine transformation parameters rather than using an INR to parametrize a dense displacement field which is close to affine anyway due to the strong bending energy constraint? Using INR for an underlying transformation that is near-affine offers marginal benefit and is an overkill. 1.c. Consider reporting what \alpha for the bending energy regularization is used for the in vivo clinical prostate MRI experiment. 2.Additional experiments would be helpful for the readers to better appreciate the work. 2.a. For example, it would be helpful to see a visualization (if space permits) of the results in Table 2.It would be interesting to see what w/o FreeNeRF & w/ HE looks like since it gives slightly worse performance according to conventional metrics but slightly better performance according to learning-based metrics. 2.b. In might be helpful to also report runtime/number of parameters in Table 1 since the authors intend this work to eventually have clinical applications where speed is important. 2.c. Table 1 only reports result on a single simulated data. Consider randomly choosing a couple of (say, 10) different rotation angles and report metrics over these 10 experiments. The rationale for this suggestion is that there is no other result in the paper that test for the robustness of Phase 2: Implicit Image Registration. 3.Regarding the in vivo prostate MRI experiment. 3.a. The authors are aware of the lack of ground truth for in vivo prostate MRI experiment. However, it makes little sense to compare reconstructed slices to the closest slice in the “ground truth” just to avoid blurring introduced by registration. Doing so makes Fig. 3 very hard to interpret. 3.b. In Fig. 3, only perceptual metric from MONAI is reported. It doesn’t hurt to also report other metrics, e.g., MAE, PSNR, SSIM, along with the learning-based metrics, as long as the authors provide explanations of why some of these metrics do not necessarily reflect true visual quality of the reconstruction. There are some typographical errors, e.g., spaces in front of citations.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Decoupling the INR training and registration step seems like a good way to handle misaligned data. Furthermore, INRs excel at showing generalizability with homogeneous data – which makes the decoupled registration even more interesting. 2.Qualitative results show that SIMS-MRI has substantial improvements over prior methods. reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper sets up the problem that MRIs have poor through-plane resolution, and then goes on to propose a multiview interpolation scheme, mainly using INRs. Results, however, do not show an improvement or explicit evaluation on through-plane MRI slices – demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method, particularly with respect to the problem stated in its introduction. 2.It is unclear whether the simulation has realistic in-plane and through-plane sampling rates, and whether the evaluation for interpolation performance is happening on unsampled slices. 3.Can the authors comment on how their model performs when the in-plane: through-plane sampling ratio changes? How much information trade-off / super-resolution capability arise from dense in-plane measurements?
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank R1, R2, R3, and Rmeta for their constructive feedback and encouraging comments. All suggestions, including minor writing improvements, will be reflected in the camera-ready version as rules and space permit. We address the remaining concerns below. Novelty (Rmeta and R2): We agree on shared similarities with NeSVOR and IREM. However, NeSVOR addresses only rigid motion, and IREM requires pre-registered volumes. SIMS-MRI incorporates its own registration step, eliminating prior alignment while handling linear/nonlinear misalignment, making it more generalizable for clinical MR settings where anisotropic acquisitions are the norm. We will cite both and clarify. Slice thickness, spacing, and simulation (R1, R3 and Rmeta): For brain, we 4× downsampled isotropic images (e.g., 1×1×1 mm → 1×1×4 mm); for prostate, native slice thickness is 3 mm (Sec. 3.2). Anisotropic volumes are used as-is (no further subsampling) by converting directly to intensity point sets. The final isotropic inference grid uses the original GT grid for brain and a 1×1×1 mm subsampled grid for prostate. We acknowledge that modeling the physical slice-selection profile and through-plane PSF for simulation would produce a more realistic simulation. We see this as future work. Importantly, evaluation always uses the held-out sagittal view unseen during training, testing recovery of an unseen orientation. Runtime and parameters (R1, R2 and Rmeta): End-to-end processing could take as little as 20 min/subject on a single A100.Implementation is unoptimized. Multi-GPU support and better implementation could substantially reduce this. Parameter counts (hash encoder (268.4M), MLP (4.7M), and registration model (0.1M)) will be reported in the camera-ready. Pseudo-GT and metrics for prostate (R1, R2): We are aware of the pseudo-GT limitation and will discuss it explicitly in camera-ready. Following R1’s suggestion, we simulated 3 mm thick slices via rect and Gaussian convolution. Results were consistent with reported findings. On MAE/PSNR/SSIM, rankings are mixed across methods. In addition to misregistration, these metrics are sensitive to contrast changes, which might explain the mixed results. DISTS and MONAI metrics show SIMS-MRI significantly outperforming baselines. NCC vs MSE; non-linear deformation; bending energy α (R2): We chose NCC because MRI intensity profiles can shift across acquisitions, making MSE unreliable. Results with MSE had misalignments in neck/facial regions. For deformation, we began with 12-parameter affine registration for brain (yielding similar results), but adopted non-linear deformation to maintain a general-purpose architecture suitable for all experiments and to handle misalignments in non-brain area. For prostate, we used no regularizer (α=0). These settings are application-specific and will be noted as a tunable choice in the discussion. Additional experiments (FreeNeRF/HE visualization; additional simulation scenario) (R2): Both sets of experiments are complete. We tested randomly chosen rotation+translation combinations for brain, with results close to those reported. We will include these and the visualizations as rules permit. Additional view for better SR (R2): Great point. As follow-up work, we are working on a method to utilize all available series (views, contrasts, etc) in a study. We will mention this as future work. Through-plane clarification; anisotropy ratio study (R3): The paper reports results on through-plane slices: only LR axial and coronal views were used for training, and performance is evaluated on the held-out sagittal GT. We will revise the text to clarify. Regarding varying in-plane: through-plane ratios, conceptually, SIMS-MRI benefits most when orthogonal views provide complementary high-resolution in-plane information, and should degrade as anisotropy increases or view complementarity decreases. A systematic anisotropy ratio study is an important direction we will include in future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper received mixed reviews that should be addressed in a rebuttal. The split among the reviewers is mainly about novelty and problem formulation rather than whether the method works. The paper addresses a meaningful MRI SR setting from multiple anisotropic acquisitions using only the anisotropic image. The reviewers found the decoupled INR registration and reconstruction setup promising and the results convincing with extensive analysis. However, there are substantial concerns about the novelty of the approach, especially with regards to NeSVoR. The rebuttal should focus on this aspect. There are other, more minor, concerns that should be addressed such as the forward model definition, clarification between sparse slices and thick slices, and runtime. | This paper maintains mixed reviews after rebuttal, but the authors have provided clear and detailed explanations that address the majority of the reviewers’ concerns. Novelty remains a concern, but the motivation for the methodology is quite clear and supported by clinical and physical reality. I would argue that non-rigid motion can be accepted between modalities, especially outside of the brain, and should be considered a known quantity. However, this should be directly evaluated at a later time. The author’s rationale for using NCC is frequently cited in MRI registration literature. Given the authors’ rebuttal and their addressing of the concerns, I will recommend acceptance for this paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After rebuttal, I recommend Accept. The authors addressed many key technical and presentation concerns, including slice thickness/anisotropic spacing, held-out sagittal evaluation, prostate pseudo-GT limitations, runtime/parameter counts, and the rationale for NCC and nonlinear registration. They also added requested experiments on realistic slice-profile simulation and additional motion settings. Some weaknesses remain, particularly regarding comparison with NeSVoR/IREM. However, the paper presents a useful single-subject multi-view MRI super-resolution framework that integrates registration and fusion without large supervised datasets. Given the positive critiques from R1 and R3, improved clarity after rebuttal, and clinical relevance, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a clear single-subject multi-view INR framework with integrated registration and reconstruction. The rebuttal reasonably clarifies the relation to NeSVoR/IREM, the slice-thickness setting, runtime, and additional experiments. I also do not find the use of NCC problematic, as NCC is commonly used in MRI registration when intensity profiles may vary across acquisitions. Although the novelty is somewhat incremental and the physical slice-profile modeling could be stronger, the method is technically sound, experimentally convincing, and useful for the community, so I recommend acceptance.

title: SkepticalNet: A Safety-Aware Interactive Segmentation Framework for Neuro-Oncology
reviewer_1_strengths: For the proposed interactive segmentation pipeline, the authors introduces a “skeptical prior” through a hybrid training protocol that stochastically assigns iterations to either foreground or background supervision. This enables the model to validate user prompts against local anatomy and effectively suppress activations triggered on adjacent healthy tissue, reducing the distal Activation Rate to just 1.5%. In addition, to improve the realism of the training signal, the authors replace standard linear scribbles with a Topology-Constrained Stochastic Walk algorithm. This algorithm aims at generating scribbles which are constrained to the lesion mask and can deal with the irregular, non-convex morphologies of pathologies common in brain tumors.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The authors must clarify the binary segmentation procedure used during training, as it is currently unclear if the target class refers to individual sub-regions or combinations (e. g. , Whole Tumor or Tumor Core). This ambiguity makes it difficult to assess how the model resolves conflicting user intents. In addition, for the extremely small pediatric cohort (N=99) , the paper does not explain how the balanced dataloader avoids overfitting when operating with a batch size of only 2.Does it work by loading 1 sample per batch mostly from the pediatric set? A critical technical bottleneck is the model’s reliance on a fixed 11-channel input. The framework requires co-registered T1, T1c, T2, and FLAIR modalities to function. While the authors acknowledge this as a limitation, the current architecture lacks any mechanism for missing-modality resilience and/or miss-aligned imaging modalities. In real-world clinical settings, incomplete MRI protocols are common; the absence of even a single sequence led to failure of the whole workflow. Although the paper evaluates four distinct datasets, the experiments are limited entirely to standardized BraTS challenge datasets. These datasets are heavily pre-processed, co-registered, and skull-stripped. Moreover, size of the lesions in such tumor entities are usually large enough to be segmented well with conventional U-Net based models. Therefore, the “safety-aware” suppression has not been tested against “raw” clinical artifacts, such as patient motion, varying voxel resolutions, or extra-cranial structures and more importantly more challenging lesion such as brain metastasis. The model’s ability to suppress hallucinations in a noisy, non-standardized environment remains unproven. There is a concerning performance gap regarding safety near tumor boundaries (4 voxels). While the “skeptical prior” is highly effective at distal suppression, the global activation rate in the proximal zone remains at 36.3%, rising to 70.1% for sparse prompts. For infiltrative lesions with complex edges, this suggests the model still prioritizes user guidance over image evidence in ambiguous regions, potentially snapping to healthy peritumoral tissue and undermining the stated goal of hallucination suppression.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper provides a clinically focused approach to image segmentation and introduces some novel methods to reinforce model behavior that is conducive to clinical use as it targets common weaknesses in medical image segmentation models, specifically addressing hallucination from slightly inaccurate prompts, and generating realistic scribbles. The use of a “dual-mode” training strategy is an interesting and novel approach to add robustness to invalid prompts as it explicitly punishes the model for various “trigger-happy” outputs. The datasets and data splitting provide confidence in the presented results with its multiple dataset benchmarks. The provided safety analysis is an effective means of proving the advantage of the training protocol.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The topology-constrained stochastic walk (TCSW) algorithm is under-explored in the paper. The paper could benefit from a more direct ablation study of the TCSW algorithm. The methodology for implementing TCSW is could include more details, such as how the stochastic noise is injected into the neighbor selection process. The paper would also benefit from more baseline models for comparison, with the included baseline models (pre-trained nnInteractive model; single-modality fine-tuned variant) making it difficult to ascertain the true value of each component in the proposed framework. The datasets are all from the BraTS challenge, which despite using different benchmarks, still raises some potential concerns regarding generalizability.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and Area Chair for their constructive feedback and provide the following clarifications. Note: [CR] denotes confirmed updates to the camera-ready manuscript. 1.Methodological Clarifications (R1, R2, R4) Target Sampling & Probabilities (p) (R1, R4): We clarify that for each training sample, the binary target (c_target) dynamically samples either an atomic sub-region or a composite, ensuring all possible classes per-sample are supervised throughout training, seamlessly resolving user intent. Variable p denotes branching probabilities (e.g., 75/25 Foreground/Background) in our stochastic tree. As stated, these ratios were experimentally optimized; internal testing via grid search on the validation set confirmed that altering them degrades segmentation accuracy or robustness to invalid prompts. [CR: clarified in Sec 2.2] Dataloader (R1): Our dataloader uniformly samples two of four datasets per iteration (25% probability each), rather than forcing one pediatric sample per batch. Any re-sampled minority case is heavily modified via aggressive spatial/intensity augmentations (e.g. elastic deformations, gamma/Gaussian noise), preventing overfitting via input diversity. [CR: clarified in Sec 3.1] TCSW Details (R2): We clarify that uniform stochastic noise is added to the geodesic distance map prior to each pathfinding step, enforcing different minimal connecting paths between the start and target points. [CR: clarified in Sec 2.3] Terminology (R4): We will consolidate stricter definitions for “safety” (suppressing invalid prompts), “skeptical prior” (zero-output constraint), “snaps to” (adherence to valid pathology), and “hallucination” (used strictly within our context to denote unconstrained segmentation responses to invalid prompts). [CR: definitions added to Introduction] 2.Safety Metrics & The Proximal Gap (R1, R4) 4-Voxel Clinical Cutoff (R4): We justify that assuming 1mm voxels, a 4mm margin aligns with neuro-oncology realities where radiotherapy margins utilize 2mm-5mm uncertainty buffers for microscopic extension and inter-observer variability (ESTRO-EANO 2023 Guidelines: Niyazi et al., Radiother Oncol), effectively defining a clinically ambiguous zone. [CR: justified via Niyazi et al.] Proximal Activation is a Feature, not a Bug (R1): R1 notes a 70.1% Activation Rate for proximal sparse prompts. This is intentional. Because P_target (a precision metric over activated voxels) remains exceptionally high (88.6%), predicted activations successfully fall within true tumor boundaries instead of healthy peritumoral tissue, proving “near-miss” error correction (predicting nearby pathology) rather than unconstrained false-positives. Statistical Significance (R4): Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirm that baseline improvements are statistically significant (p < 0.01). [CR: amended Sec 4.1 to present p-values] 3.Scope, Generalizability & Baselines (R1, R2, R4) Scope & Limitations (R1, R2): Evaluating PET-CT and Head/Neck cancers falls outside our explicit clinical scope (Neuro-Oncology), representing a deliberate boundary rather than a methodological flaw. While incomplete MRI protocols occur, 4-sequence mpMRI is the standard-of-care (ESTRO-EANO 2023 Guidelines); handling incomplete protocols is a distinct research problem explicitly acknowledged as a limitation. To address generalizability (R1, R2), our limitations section will explicitly include future testing on non-BraTS cohorts with unstandardized artifacts. Baseline Choice (R2, R4): R4 asks if the results hold if nnInteractive is domain-specifically trained. Yes, our FT-T1c baseline is exactly this (nnInteractive fine-tuned on BraTS). Regarding R2’s request for additional baselines, each baseline isolates one added contribution: Native establishes the zero-shot floor; FT-T1c quantifies multi-modal fine-tuning gains; Standard Baseline isolates the Skeptical Prior’s impact — collectively providing a complete component-wise evaluation.
