title: Subject-Specific Low-Field MRI Synthesis via a Neural Operator
reviewer_1_strengths: The application of neural operators to image synthesis is a key novelty of this work. The authors claim that their model addresses limitations of prior pixel‑wise image‑to‑image translation methods, which often fail to capture realistic textures and accurately model contrast changes. By explicitly modeling the degradation process, the proposed approach provides a more principled way to approximate ULF acquisition characteristics.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the proposed approach introduces a novel use of neural operators for ULF synthesis, the empirical improvements over existing state‑of‑the‑art methods are relatively marginal. This limits the current impact of the work and suggests that the method requires further refinement to demonstrate clear advantages in real‑world settings.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: First, the paper presents a novel and well-motivated formulation by modeling HF-to-LF MRI synthesis as a continuous operator learning problem, rather than a conventional voxel-wise image translation task. This perspective is aligned with MRI physics, where field strength affects the underlying signal formation and frequency characteristics, making the formulation both principled and meaningful. Second, the proposed H2LO architecture is technically elegant and well-designed, combining a CNN-based branch network with a coordinate-based SIREN trunk to capture both spatial context and high-frequency details. The introduction of spatially varying operator coefficients allows the model to adapt locally to tissue-specific contrast changes, which is particularly important for realistic LF simulation. Third, the paper demonstrates practical relevance and downstream utility, showing that the synthesized LF images can effectively augment training data and improve LF MRI enhancement performance. The evaluation is relatively comprehensive, including both reconstruction metrics and histogram-based measures, and shows consistent improvements over traditional simulators and image-to-image baselines
reviewer_2_weaknesses: First, while the operator-based formulation is well motivated, the methodological novelty over INR and operator-learning works is somewhat limited. The proposed H2LO builds upon existing frameworks such as DeepONet and coordinate-based representations (e.g., SIREN, LIIF-style extensions ), and the contribution mainly lies in adapting these components to the HF to LF MRI setting rather than introducing a fundamentally new architecture. Second, the study relies on a very limited dataset (23 subjects) for learning the HF-to-LF mapping, which raises concerns about generalization and robustness. Although 5-fold cross-validation is used, the model may still overfit to scanner-specific characteristics or acquisition protocols, and the paper does not provide evaluation on external datasets or across different scanners/field strengths . Third, the baseline comparison, while reasonable, is not fully comprehensive, particularly with respect to recent medical imaging methods. The evaluation focuses on general I2I models (Pix2Pix, diffusion) and a classical simulator, but lacks comparison with more recent physics-informed or diffusion-based MRI translation/enhancement approaches (e.g., works such as ref 8,9,11 cited in the paper but not included as baselines), which may limit the strength of the empirical claims. Fourth, the paper does not fully establish clinical validity or realism of the synthesized LF images, beyond standard image similarity and histogram-based metrics. There is no expert evaluation or task-based assessment (e.g., diagnostic performance), making it unclear whether the generated images faithfully reflect clinically relevant LF characteristics rather than metric-level similarity. Finally, the method assumes perfect spatial alignment between HF and LF scans, which may not hold in real-world scenarios. The reliance on registered paired data simplifies the problem and may limit applicability to settings where such precise alignment is unavailable or difficult to obtain.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Novelty: This is the first paper proposing an end-to-end framework for HF-to-LF MRI image synthesis Performance: The method generally outperforms all baselines both quantitatively and qualitatively, while using the least number of parameters. Elegant: The formulation of HF-to-LF synthesis as a function to function mapping constraints the model to mathematically backed good solutions compared to pixel-to-pixel methods.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Requires paired HF-LF images to train which can be challenging to obtain in practice. It is unclear whether the proposed method can generalize to unseen HF-to-LF scenarios i.e. if a model is trained on HF dataset A, can it equally synthesis LF images from a new dataset B. Dataset B could be from a different anatomy or device. The proposed SIREN trunk is inferior to the w/o SIREN setting based on the quantitative results and ablations, and its justification is based on subjective qualitative analysis. Also, it is not clear what w/o SIREN setting exactly is. The method was only evaluated on a single dataset of healthy subjects and it remains to be seen how the method generalizes to large popultations, different devices, sites, and pathological cases.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and the meta-reviewer for the efforts in reviewing this paper and providing constructive and positive feedback. We are very encouraged by the fact that reviewers found both the methodology, neural operator, and the application venue, LF MRI synthesis, reasonable and interesting. We would like to answer some of the reviewers’ points of confusion. R1 12, paragraph 2: In histogram visualization, we compare against Arnold et al.’s method because their model is explicitly optimized for histogram-statistic matching. In contrast, our model and the other comparison models are trained with pixel-wise consistency objectives. We will clarify this point in the camera-ready version. R3 12, paragraph 3: We apologize for drawing the arrow in the wrong direction and causing confusion. title: Sulcus-Aware Hippocampal Surface Modeling with Training-Time Sulcus-Guided Learning
reviewer_1_strengths: Few papers have explicitly tackled sulcal-based modelling in hippocampal shape analysis. Thus this paper highlights a unique and commonly overlooked problem. In formulating this problem, the authors have generated a dataset of 0.33 mm isotropic sulcus masks, intially automated and then refined manually by hippocampal experts. This is a valuable dataset by itself, used for training by the authors but may also be generally useful to the community. The authors present a thorough evaluation of their idea across multiple methods. The use of signed distance fields instead of binary masks also ensures topological correctness.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the paper primarily tackles sulcus indentation aware modeling, it does not explicitly visualize the indentation. This is a major weakness. Figure 2(a) shows small lateral-view thumbnails with yellow arrows pointing to surface curvature variations, but the hippocampal sulcus is absent from these views. Thus it was harder to visualize what exactly was modeled and represented here. The sulcal mask did not explicitly directly feature in the mathematical formulation. The sulcus masks are defined in terms of soft occupancy maps, which in turn are not defined explicitly. The authors refer to the paper by Hwang et al. but omit the definition of the sulcus map from this paper. Instead they just denote these maps using the symbol P_S and P_T. Similarly the boundary point cloud B_S is not formally defined. The authors state that these maps are obtained using the block-averaging operator, but this operator is not defined either. This made the paper difficult to follow. The sulcus shape is not explicitly modeled. The main geometric features of a sulcus are it’s depth, curvature, concave/convex nature etc. are not directly represented in the formulation. One would expect a sulcus-aware method to be represented by explicit geometric features such as sulcal depth fields, curvature-based losses, or medial axis constraints that represent the shape information instead of global appearance based measures. Since the formulation of the occupancy maps was not specified, it was not clear if the signed distance fields were only used for the purpse of extraction of point clouds, or was it also passed through the alignment network? There were several weaknesses in the the experimental results. in Figure 3(b), the SPHARM-PDM representation computes alignment using a spherical harmonic parameterization while the proposed method uses template deformation. It is not clear what is being compared when calculating group differences. Is it the magnitude of the deformation field or is it vertex wise displacement to the template? Why is the ODC+smooth that yields a better hippocampal distance (Table 1) absent from the results in Figure 3(b)? An ablation study that includes the proposed method without the sulcus-aware modeling is missing. This is because for experimental purposes, a sulcus-aware template is already constructed along with the sulcal indentation information. Thus it is not clear how much gain is obtained from the sulcus-aware template itself and whether incorporating sulcal constraints later during hte semi-supervised alignment stage does make a significant difference. Thus it was not clear whether the sulcus mask supervision during training actually did anything. Similarly voxel occupancy maps or the boundary extraction step could also undergo ablation to determine the performance of the proposed method. Important papers such as HippUnfold (DeKraker, J. , Haast, R. A. , Yousif, M. D. , Karat, B. , Lau, J. C. , Köhler, S. , & Khan, A. R. (2022). Automated hippocampal unfolding for morphometry and subfield segmentation with HippUnfold. elife, 11, e77945.) are not cited. While subfield segmentation is out of scope of the proposed work, the above paper does explicitly model the SRLM (stratum radiatum lacunosum moleculare) landmarks for the hippocampal sulcus. Thus it will be useful to compare the proposed method with their work.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and technically challenging problem: preserving the hippocampal sulcus in surface reconstruction. The sulcus is narrow, highly susceptible to partial-volume effects, and routinely washed out by conventional mask-based pipelines, yet it carries morphometric signal relevant to aging and Alzheimer’s disease. Addressing this gap is of clear interest to dementia researchers. The template-based diffeomorphic deformation design is well suited to the problem, simultaneously delivering fixed topology, vertex-wise inter-subject correspondence, and stable meshes with minimal self-intersections — directly addressing a known limitation of deformation-based surface methods. The evaluation is comprehensive, combining surface-distance-based measures, mesh quality metrics, and a pilot downstream morphometry analysis in CN and AD cohorts, and demonstrates improved sulcus fidelity over state-of-the-art baselines such as SPHARM-PDM.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There is a concern that the method may attenuate clinically meaningful disease effects to fit the sulcus. In Figure 3, disease effects in the hippocampal head appear diminished relative to SPHARM-PDM and prior literature, where AD-related atrophy is consistently reported across the entire hippocampus. This raises the possibility that the template-to-subject deformation establishes noisy correspondences in the hippocampal head as a by-product of prioritizing sulcal alignment. The “semi-supervised” framing is unclear. Semi-supervised learning typically means training with a small amount of labeled data alongside a large volume of unlabeled data. If only a subset of subjects have sulcus annotations, the number of labeled versus unlabeled subjects and how they are combined during training should be explicitly reported. Important neural network details are missing, including the architecture and network hyperparameters, which limits reproducibility.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Clinical evaluation: The authors perform a preliminary clinical study, comparing vertex-wise analyses comparing AD-CN patient groups on surfaces reconstructed using different methods. While these results need further validation, they illustrate the importance of handing surface geometry on downstream analyses.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The reconstructed mesh is dependent on the quality of the sulcus-aware template While the proposed method minimizes topological errors, the registration does not guarantee no self-intersections. Fig 2c, the plots are missing axes labels on the x-axis.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We appreciate the reviewers for providing insightful comments that help us improve the quality of our paper. Please see our responses below. Sulcus representation and equations (R1). Geometric descriptors such as sulcal depth, curvature, and medial axis may benefit sulcus-aware modeling. However, reliable extraction of these features typically requires an explicit surface mesh generated by a specific surface reconstruction procedure. As a result, our model may be biased toward reproducing the characteristics of that reconstruction protocol. We instead use expert-validated high-resolution sulcus labels and convert them into two explicit supervision signals: sulcus occupancy maps and sulcal boundary points. The sulcus occupancy maps (P_S) and (P_T) are obtained by applying standard 3X3X3 average pooling (block averaging in Sec. 2.4) to the binary sulcus masks (L_S) and (L_T). The boundary points (B_S) are extracted from the SDF of the sulcus-aware mask (Y~), whereas the alignment network receives the SDF of the whole hippocampal mask (Y). Thus, Y~ is used only for boundary point extraction and is not fed into the network. We will explicitly state their math notations in Sec. 2.4. Necessity of the sulcus-aware template and sulcus-guided components (R1, R3). Since subject meshes deform from the template, its quality is central (Sec. 2.2). During method development, we found that a simple template often failed to preserve sulcal folding as smoothness and mesh-regularity constraints tended to suppress the indentation. This motivates our unique sulcus-aware template construction. Also, as discussed in Sec. 1, the sulcus is often under-resolved at typical clinical resolution (~1 mm^3). Thus, we use a “soft” sulcus occupancy map for learning since the sulcus tends to be occluded in the hippocampal hard label. The boundary points provide explicit supervision of surface geometry. In Eq. (7), the Chamfer loss computed in Euclidean domain for finer level of supervision for deformation. Resulting in over 32% reduced sulcus distance than existing methods (Table 1). Shape correspondence and clinical analysis (R1, R2). We appreciate the concern regarding possible correspondence issues. Since ground-truth landmarks are unavailable in our dataset, directly evaluating regional correspondence errors was infeasible. In Fig. 2(c), we instead evaluated correspondence using PCA-based generalization and specificity following [31]; our method achieved the lowest reconstruction errors, suggesting stable shape correspondence. We note that the improved correspondence quality influences the observed statistical differences in Fig. 3.We apologize for the confusion. The colormap in Fig. 2(b) represents Koenderink’s curvedness but not the Jacobian determinant; the striped patterns do not indicate deformation instability. The per-vertex surface-area analysis requires inter-subject shape correspondence. Thus, ODC-based methods were excluded in area analysis as shape correspondence is not provided during their surface reconstruction. Surface visualization (R1): The sulcal indentation is visible in the surface-volume overlay in Fig. 2(a). However, it is less apparent in the surface rendering due to the selected viewpoint and limited panel size. We will update the figure to better highlight the existing sulcal structure using enlarged slice-based overlays and transparent or cut-away renderings that expose the indentation. Terminology (R2): We agree that the term “semi-supervised” is ambiguous. We used this to indicate that sulcus labels are used only as auxiliary training supervision and are not required at inference. To avoid confusion, we will rename this component as training-time sulcus supervision. Minor fixes (R1, R2, R3): We will correct typos and add the missing axis labels as well as missing citations. To further support reproducibility, we will add implementation details about the U-Net architecture and release the code as stated in the abstract.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers have provided valuable feedback on the paper, which proposes a novel sulcus-aware hippocampal surface modeling framework. R3 liked clinical relevance. R1 and R2 noted mathematical inconsistencies, minor. The rebuttal has clarified all concerns. The consensus is acceptance and novelty in method. For all these reaons, and with respect to other submissions, recommendation is towards acceptnace.

title: SynHydro: Biomechanics-Driven Domain Randomization for Hydrocephalus-Agnostic, Generalizable Tissue-Ventricle Segmentation Across Age, Modality, and Resolution
reviewer_1_strengths: the most interesting idea is to proposed a mechanical driven deformation model to simulate the hydrocephalus. The similar idea has been used in other brain development research but to generate a whole brain is still interesting
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.the primary concern is how to evaluate the accuracy of the proposed synthetic model. The author didn’t provide any data or experiments to evaluate this part. It is high required and a critical part of this work. 2.the following task is not very well designed, for example only using the synthetic model to train the NN-UNET.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: -The paper presents a simple method to utilize healthy images to create a model that is robust to large anomalies in the brain. -The writing is clear and understandable. -The idea of synthesizing images with hydrocephalus anatomy with the described bio mechanical driven method is novel, and performing well (Dice score of ~0.85) to segment white matter, gray matter and ventricles in pediatric T1w MRI. -
reviewer_2_weaknesses: “Real-Augmented: Trained on 1400 augmented data synthesized from all available training labels (both longitudinal and control), representing a strong data-augmentation baseline with real pathological labels”, “Real-Augmented achieves the best performance on T1w, serving as an approximate upper bound” The usage of baseline and upper bound interchangeably is confusing. Could they consider changing this description? What is the reason for selecting only T1w sequences for testing quantitatively? The results lack the cross modality segmentation robustness. In datasets, the authors mention they have 132 longitudinal sessions and 131 control scans. Then in the implementation section, they mention having 125 longitudinal and 47 control 3D images. How did they select these subjects for annotating, is it random? HyKid dataset has ground truth segmentations available for gray matter, white matter, cerebrospinal fluid, the choroid plexus, and the lateral ventricles. What do the authors imply when they say “ground-truth labels consistent with the purpose of this study is not available” ? Both the qualitative and quantitative results show similar performance to the “Real augmented” case. The augmentations seem to capture modality differences & the resolution difference and seem to be useful looking at the qualitative improvement from real paired to real augmented. This generalization raises the question of applying augmentations to the baseline (control only) model. I believe the setting with strong spatial and intensity augmentation to control set, without explicitly creating the hydrocephalus images should be included in the results as well for a fair comparison. The results lack comparisons with segmentation methods similarly trained with domain randomization and have shown good performance over various anatomical changes [1,2]. The authors have cited the first paper yet have not included any results. I believe it would be useful to compare with the existing methods, as they are known to not fail in cases of such large enlargement of ventricles (see the results in a similar work dealing with abnormalities [3]). The title and the motivation suggests that the method is age, modality and resolution. I do not think the results are supportive of this claim. It would be useful to show results on different modalities, ages and resolutions separately to be able to claim this. Figure 3 if helpful for understanding the consistency over modalities yet it just shows “a” representative subject, which is not convincing. Table 2 shows correlation among different modalities, but without GT labels on different modalities it’s hard to judge. I could suggest using a tool like SynthSR [4] to be able to map all sequences and resolutions into the same space for evaluation purposes, and then you can compare your method with those obtained labels for example. The proposed model’s advantage is not using the labeled images with pathologies. To highlight the need for the method, it could be useful to do the ablation study at different number of labeled subjects with the pathology (i.e. does 50% control, 50% pathological subjects in the real augmented setting perform considerably worse than the real augmented upper bound presented in results?). reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper introduced an end-to-end biomechanicsdriven simulation and domain randomization framework and creates a large-scale, synthetic training dataset. Extensive experiments on demonstrate that a segmentation model trained on this synthetic data achieves performance comparable to models trained with real hydrocephalus annotations.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: There are several points in this paper need clarification: 1: The authors propose a biomechanical-driven hydrocephalus anatomy synthesis process. Is there any relevant theoretical support for this process, and can previous studies confirm that such modeling approach accurately reflects the actual progression of hydrocephalus? 2: The authors state: “Given a label map (original healthy or simulated hydrocephalus), we synthesize paired data with a domain-randomization strategy, following label-to-image paradigms [1,5,6,4].” It is recommended that the authors present examples of the synthesized label maps and the corresponding multi-contrast MRI images generated from these maps, along with a comparison to real MRI images from hydrocephalus patients. 3: Please indicate the specific modality (e.g., T1, T2) for each column in Figure 2.Additionally, clarify whether the “input” row represents images from the authors’ constructed dataset or the original images. 4: The authors mention that “the image is downsampled by a factor of 3-7 to create an anisotropic low-resolution (LR) volume.” Is this factor based on empirical experience or derived from literature? Furthermore, are the generated low-resolution data used in constructing the SynHydro dataset? 5: The training parameters of the model should be described in detail, including batch size, learning rate, and the input 3D image patch size. 6: Does the “Real-paired” training data consist of the 125 (longitudinal) and 47 (control) 3D T1w image-label pairs? 7: It is advisable to elaborate on the differences between SynHydro and the other three baselines. For instance, regarding the Baseline (Normal-Only) method, is the 1400-subject dataset obtained in a manner consistent with SynHydro but sampled from 35 healthy controls, or is it generated using conventional data augmentation techniques such as flipping and rotation? 8: If the datasets for other baselines are generated using conventional data augmentation methods and have the same dataset size, mixing a certain proportion of real healthy control scans and hydrocephalus patient scans with data augmentation might achieve better model performance than the proposed SynHydro method (as shown in Table 1). If so, what is the clinical significance of the proposed framework? 9: The authors select a 3D nnU-Net model as the segmentation model. Does the model take the patient’s full head scan as input? Additionally, is the proposed SynHydro framework also implemented in 3D?
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive comments. We will revise the manuscript to clarify the following points. [R1-Q1, R3-Q1] SynHydro is not a patient-specific biomechanical solver or a model for predicting exact hydrocephalus progression. Each synthetic case is generated from a healthy label map, so no paired real counterpart exists for voxel-wise validation. Our goal is to create diverse, controllable, anatomically plausible hydrocephalus-like deformations. Thus, validation should focus on whether synthetic data provide useful pathological supervision rather than exact mechanical accuracy. This is supported by T1w DSC, qualitative results, and volumetric consistency on unseen real data. We will clarify this and add clearer synthetic examples. [R1-Q2, R2-Q5, R3-Q7-Q9] The contribution is not simply training nnU-Net with synthetic data. We use 3D nnU-Net as a fixed backbone to compare supervision sources under the same protocol. Baseline (Normal-Only) uses healthy/control labels with the same label-to-image domain randomization, matching R2’s requested strong control-only augmentation baseline. SynHydro adds hydrocephalus-specific deformation to these labels. Real-Augmented uses real annotated healthy and hydrocephalus labels with the same synthesis pipeline. Real-Paired directly uses real 3D T1w pairs. These settings isolate generic domain randomization, explicit pathological simulation, real pathological labels, and direct real-image supervision. We will clarify that all methods operate on 3D volumes. [R2-Q1] “Real-Augmented serves as an approximate upper bound” was inaccurate. The intended in-domain T1w upper-bound reference is Real-Paired, because it is trained directly on real annotated 3D T1w pairs. Real-Augmented is a strong real-label augmented comparator. We will correct this. [R2-Q2, R2-Q7] Dice-based evaluation requires complete manual labels. In our dataset, radiologist-refined labels are available only for 3D T1w scans; other modalities and LR scans do not yet have complete labels. Thus, Table 1 reports DSC only on annotated T1w scans. Cross-modality/resolution robustness is assessed through qualitative visualization, volumetric consistency, and longitudinal trends. We agree these are not full voxel-wise multi-modality DSC, and will soften the claim to “promising robustness under heterogeneous age, modality, and resolution conditions.” More complete evaluation is ongoing. [R2-Q3, R2-Q4, R3-Q6] The 132 longitudinal sessions and 131 control scans refer to the full in-house multi-modal collection, while 125 longitudinal and 47 control cases refer to annotated 3D T1w pairs. The annotated pool was determined by usable 3D T1w acquisition, image quality, successful initialization, and radiologist refinement. A subject-level split avoids leakage, and Real-Paired uses only training cases. For HyKid, labels exist but are not compatible with our 8-class bilateral protocol; direct DSC could be misleading. We are working on label alignment and will provide our best SynHydro predictions. [R2-Q6, R2-Q8] SynthSeg-like methods are relevant because they also use label-to-image domain randomization. Our Baseline (Normal-Only) is a controlled generic domain-randomization baseline under our label protocol. Its gap from SynHydro shows that intensity/contrast/resolution randomization alone is insufficient for severe hydrocephalus; explicit pathological expansion is important. Direct comparison is complicated by label-protocol mismatch. Preliminary partial-label experiments suggest that limited pathological supervision improves performance and then tends to saturate. We will discuss these points as future/extended work. [R3-Q2-Q5] We will revise figures to show synthetic labels/MRIs and real hydrocephalus MRIs; indicate modality/resolution in Fig. 2; and clarify that “Input” contains original real scans. The 3–7× downsampling factor was empirically chosen from clinical resolution variation and used in training.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The reviews are conflicting, it would be good to clarify the key concerns from the reviewers. | The reviewers agree that the paper has clinical and techincal merits. However, evaluationsI is not sufficient enough. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): While Reviewer 2 maintained a reject score due to evaluation scope, the authors’ rebuttal successfully clarified the dataset details and the specific role of the synthetic simulation framework, leading Reviewer 3 to upgrade their rating to an Accept. Given that the framework provides valuable anatomical supervision where real pathological data is scarce, the paper is recommended for acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): First of all, I discarded R1’s and R3’s main reasons to reject the paper, since they failed to understand that the value of this work is not in the “realism” of the generated images, but in their capacity to enhance the generalisation of downstream models (see SynthSeg and domain randomisation literature). Thus, evaluating the quality/realism of the generated images is not relevant. In general, I find that the rebuttal successfully addressed concerns about the contributions/positioning of this work on biomechanics model + domain randomisation for robust hydrocephalus segmentation. It also provided much needed clarifications about the experimental set-up and the training frameworks of the tested baselines. Moreover, while R2 is right that Normal-Only is not exactly equivalent to SynthSeg (GMM parameters sampled from multi-modal Gaussians instead of a uniform distribution), I believe this difference to be negligible given the large number of modes (ie contrasts) in this distribution. I also agree with the authors that the direct comparison with the original SynthSeg model requested by R2 is not really relevant, as SynthSeg was shown to provide mixed results on younger populations. However, I do agree with R2 that quantitative evaluations on multi contrast and multi resolution is missing. I also agree with R2 that the authors could have defined some common labelling between their annotations and the HyKid’s one to at least provide quantitative scores. Right now the claims about robustness to contrast and resolution are only weakly supported by visual evidence only. Personally, I also regret the total lack of statistical testing from the experiments. Overall, this paper brings a novel and interesting contribution to pathology simulation in brain MRI (the biomechanics deformation model), but is hindered by experiments that do not fully support all the claims. Thus, this paper is borderline accept/reject. Here, I decide to recommend acceptance given the recent surge in papers about domain randomisation for segmentation of brain MRI in younger populations. The main contribution on the deformation model will also foster discussions in the broader geometrical learning community.

title: SYNPRED: A Synergistic Approach to Multimodal Learning for Clinical Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: The problem addressed in the paper, i. e. fusing modalities that can be factorised into shared and modality-specific information, is quite relevant and affects many real-world healthcare applications. The method is formulated in a generic way and does not rely on application or dataset-specific assumptions. Since it also appears relatively easy to implement, it has the potential to be easily tested on other complementary multimodal applications. The proposed method is tested against multiple baselines (single-modal models + 4 multimodal baselines) that are representative of different approaches in the literature (naïve fusion, alignment-based methods, and multimodal disentanglement).
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) Regarding the proposed method, I feel that some important design choices were not discussed or justified sufficiently: 1.1) p. 4, Multimodal Fusion: The modality-specific latent posteriors are combined using a mixture-of-experts (MoE) approach, i. e. a weighted sum. I find this choice counter-intuitive, as the goal is to extract shared information between the posteriors, and MoE is typically seen as a way to query/route to specific experts. I would have thought a product-of-experts (PoE) to be a more natural fit, since a product intrinsically models where all latent posteriors are dense. PoE is even used later in the pipeline to fuse latents for downstream predictions. Have the authors considered using PoE to combine latent posteriors, and if so why did they prefer to use MoE? 1.2) p. 4, Multimodal Fusion: The original MoE paper [R1] suggested gating networks to predict data-dependent mixture weights. However, more recent MoE-based multimodal VAEs [23,24] have gone the other direction, with fixed mixture weights corresponding to the arithmetic mean of the latent posteriors. This has been done to improve robustness and to avoid the model collapsing to a single modality. The learnable, but data-independent, mixture weights proposed here fall somewhere between these two approaches. Have the authors looked at the values of the learned mixture weights, to see whether they are balanced or if they suffer from modality collapse? 2) While the evaluation shows improvements from the proposed method over existing baselines, some of the claims made by the authors do not appear to me to be properly justified by the results. 2.1) The authors propose their method broadly for “medical modalities with limited semantic overlap” (p. 2, Contribution). However, the method is only tested on one dataset (BreastD-CEDL) with some apparent limitations (see comment #2.2). Since the authors reference other works combining radiomics and radiogenomics for non-breast cancer applications [12,26], why didn’t they test their method on the application/dataset from one of these papers? Either the evaluation should be extended, or the broad claims should be narrowed to the tested application to avoid generalizing too much from the currently limited evaluation. 2.2) p. 6, Table 1: It seems that RNA is a discriminative modality on its own, and that there is little benefit to adding IMG to it at test time. While no statistical significance results are reported, given the provided confidence intervals, I would guess multimodal SYNPRED lin. prob. is not significantly better than RNA-only SYNPRED ft. The same pattern appears on multimodal baselines. This observation does not invalidate improvements from the proposed method over baselines, but it does put some conclusions in perspective. As such, the proposed method apparently leverages multimodal data during training to better align representation for downstream prediction (c. f. improved single-modality results over unimodal and multimodal baselines). However, multimodal data not improving classification at test-time suggests BreastDCEDL is a poor benchmark of synergistic interactions between modalities (c. f. when properly pretrained, RNA is sufficient on its own to solve the task). The ablation study from Table 2 further supports this interpretation. Removing the fusion latent component does not significantly impact RNA-only and multimodal versions of the model (which can rely on the RNA component), but it affects the IMG-only version (by no longer being able to align with the RNA latent during training). Thus, claims about synergistic effects should be revised to specify train-time effects, as test-time synergistic effects have not been shown yet. 2.3) p. 8, Discussion: “This work addresses a central limitation of existing multimodal learning approaches for medical data. ” CoMM [5] (often cited in the paper) proposes an alignment-based contrastive strategy addressing the same limitation in prediction-oriented frameworks. The advantage of the proposed method is that it tackles this limitation in VAEs, a generative framework. Thus, I think the claim should be clarified to be in the context of generative models. References [R1] R. A. Jacobs et al. , “Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts,” in Neural Computation, March 1991, doi: 10.1162/neco. 1991.3.1.79.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important and underexplored setting where modalities share limited semantic overlap. The argument that alignment-based methods suppress complementary signals is clearly articulated. 2.The three-way latent factorization (fusion/uni/inst) with task-conditioned priors is simple, intuitive, and well-justified. 3.MoE for training and PoE for prediction allow test-time inference with incomplete modalities without retraining. 4.Image-only AUROC improves from 0.549 to 0.693 after multimodal training, which is clinically relevant since imaging is far more available than gene expression in practice. 5.Public multi-center dataset, clinically meaningful endpoint (pCR), five-seed runs with CIs, component-wise ablation, and saliency-based explainability analysis.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The MoE fusion of Gaussian posteriors uses simple weighted averages of means and standard deviations, which is not a standard approach for combining Gaussians and could misrepresent uncertainty. It would be helpful to discuss why this was chosen over more principled alternatives such as moment matching or MoPoE. 2.The KL regularization weight beta is very small (10^-4), which suggests reconstruction loss dominates training. This raises the question of how much the task-conditioned KL terms actually shape the latent space. An ablation over beta would help clarify this. 3.The synergy claim is central to the paper but is supported only by downstream performance gains. Some form of information-theoretic quantification (e.g., PID or conditional MI) would make this claim more concrete. 4.The unimodal image baseline (convolutional VAE, AUROC 0.549) appears weak relative to discriminative models available on BreastDCEDL (e.g., ViT-based). Including stronger baselines would help better calibrate the observed gains from multimodal training. 5.Multimodal performance for SOTA baselines is reported as the average of single-modality results, which is unconventional. Genuine multimodal inference for all baselines would improve the fairness of comparison. 6.Linear probing outperforms fine-tuning in the multimodal setting, which is surprising and not discussed. This warrants some analysis.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.address a clinical limitation in multi-medical learning: not all modalities are aligned and forcing cross-modal similarity may suppress complementary signal. This is an important question, especially for an imaging-genomics setting. 2.The decomposition into fusion, modality-unique, and instance-specific latent variables is intuitive and technically well-structured. The use of task-conditioned priors to shape the task-relevant latent space is a meaningful design choice over other superficial architecture tweaks. 3.Good performance gain, such as multi-modal AUROC is 0.725, exceeds the baseline methods, and the ablation studies also support this claim.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper is evaluated on essentially one application setting: breast MRI plus RNA for pCR prediction. This is too narrow to fully support the paper’s broader claims about multimodal medical learning with limited semantic overlap. 2.The paper repeatedly uses the term synergy, but the evidence is mostly indirect: improved multimodal performance and improved unimodal performance after multimodal training. That is suggestive, but not a rigorous demonstration. The authors should define what operationally constitutes synergy and distinguish it from ordinary regularization, auxiliary-task benefit, or representation transfer. 3.The comparison includes ContIG, MMVM VAE, DMVAE, and concatenation. This is reasonable, but still not comprehensive enough. It would be helpful to compare against stronger contemporary multimodal fusion baselines, including attention-based fusion or transformer-style fusion models, and perhaps a supervised multimodal encoder without a generative objective. Otherwise, it is not fully clear whether the gains come from disentanglement specifically or simply from a better training setup.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for constructive feedback. SYNPRED enables synergistic gains under partially observed modalities through disentangled shared, modality-specific, and instance-specific latent components. Multimodal pretraining improves the weaker but clinically deployable imaging modality from AUROC 0.549 to 0.638 (0.693 after fine-tuning). The contribution of synergy is isolated by a drop from 0.638 to 0.603 AUROC when ablating the fusion loss, while leaving RNA-only essentially unchanged. This demonstrates the impact of task-conditioned shared latents rather than generic multi-modal regularization. Aggregation Strategy & KL (R1.1, R2.1). We use MoE rather than PoE-based fusion during representation learning because of its greater robustness under missing modalities [Daunhawer et al., 2021]. While MoPoE improves robustness compared to standard PoE, it still relies on product-based aggregation. Learned MoE weights remained balanced (~0.5), indicating no modality collapse. The fused (μ, σ) serves as a moment-matched summary used only to drive L_KL-task, not a generative density. We will clarify these points in the revised manuscript. In pretraining, a small shared β avoided posterior collapse while preserving active KL regularization, as reflected by strong frozen linear-probing performance. Synergy Definition and RNA Dominance (R1.2.2, R2.3, R3.2). We evaluate empirical rather than formal information-theoretic synergy in real-world multimodal data. Synergy in [5] is defined through complementary cross-modal interactions in a synthetic-data setting. Since the underlying generative factors are unknown in real-world datasets such as BreastDCEDL, we follow [23] and assess synergy empirically through improved unimodal representations learned across multimodal observations. R1 notes that RNA-only is close to multi-modal prediction, an accurate diagnosis of where synergy matters clinically: imaging is routinely acquired, RNA rarely is. Multimodal pretraining improves image-only AUROC from 0.549 to 0.693, showing molecular information improves the weaker imaging modality via synergy even when RNA is unavailable at inference time. The ablation study further isolates this effect: removing the shared fusion latent selectively degrades image-only performance, suggesting the gains arise specifically through the shared fusion latent rather than from disentanglement or regularization alone. Dataset Scope (R1.2.1, R3.1). We agree a broader evaluation would strengthen claims and will moderate statements regarding general applicability accordingly. BreastDCEDL nonetheless combines three independent breast cancer cohorts, yielding a multi-center, multi-manufacturer dataset with meaningful clinical heterogeneity. Publicly available paired radiology-genomics datasets remain very limited. The datasets [12,26] are substantially smaller. Baselines and Evaluation (R1.5, R1.6, R2.4, R2.5, R3.3). We agree that this needs clarification in the manuscript: (1) baselines were chosen to compare contrastive alignment, disentanglement, multimodal regularization, and naive fusion effects. (2) R1.5: we agree CoMM is the more appropriate alignment baseline given our framing; ContIG was chosen for its radiogenomics specificity, and both belong to the same alignment family. We will clarify this rationale. (3) multimodal evaluation (R1.6, R2.5) needs clarification: the baselines report modality-specific evaluation and lack native multimodal evaluation under missing modalities. Following [24], we therefore report multimodal performance as an average across modality-specific evaluations. (4) a stronger image backbone (e.g., ViT; R2.4) could improve performance, but our focus was to investigate multi-modal learning effects under matched encoders Replicability (R3) Code, configurations, preprocessing scripts, and a reproducibility appendix will be released upon acceptance. Notation, missing subscript, typos, and CoMM ICLR’25 citation will be corrected. (R1)
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers found the evaluation on one specific application to be problematic and suggested that the paper may be overreaching in its claims. Please prioritize addressing these concerns, including strengthening the baseline comparisons to clarify whether the gains come from disentanglement specifically or from a stronger training setup, and more clearly defining or formalizing the claimed synergy. | The paper proposes SYNPRED, a multimodal variational autoencoder framework that factorizes information into task-relevant multimodal, task-relevant unimodal, and task-irrelevant instance-specific components. The work is well motivated and addresses an important problem in multimodal medical prediction, and several reviewers have acknowledged the potential value of the proposed formulation. The most critical concerns raised in the reviews concerned the aggregation strategy, the definition of synergy, and the limited dataset setting. The authors’ rebuttal provides reasonable clarifications on these points: they explain that the MoE aggregation is more robust than alternatives when modalities are missing, motivate the clinical relevance of using multimodal synergy during training to improve unimodal performance at test time, and commit to moderating claims regarding general applicability. While the concern about generalizability is not fully resolved, the BreastDECDL dataset combines 3 cohorts, making it multi-center, multi-manufacturer, and substantially larger than many radiology-genomics datasets. The authors’ planned clarification in the final revision appears sufficient. Overall, the rebuttal addresses the main reviewer concerns to an acceptable degree, and the remaining limitations do not outweigh the paper’s novelty and potential impact. The paper is therefore recommended for acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After carefully reviewing the authors’ rebuttal, I have revised my initial assessment to Accept. The authors directly addressed key concerns including justification of MoE over PoE for robustness under missing modalities, clarification of empirical synergy evaluation with ablation isolating the fusion latent’s contribution, moderation of generalizability claims, and improved unimodal imaging performance (AUROC 0.549→0.693) demonstrating clinical relevance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Although there are some flaws in the experiments, the novelty and motivation of the paper are recognized by all reviewers.

title: Testable Concept Bottlenecks for Pretreatment pCR Prediction in Breast DCE-MRI: Faithfulness and Reliability
reviewer_1_strengths: The clinical question is compelling and well-motivated: predicting complete response from pre-treatment MRI is a high-value problem. The choice of iSPY data is well-justified and appropriate for this question. The paper is clearly written relative to its stated intentions, well organized, stability analysis was performed, and appropriate statistics are reported.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: It is unclear whether the model is trained and tested across all iSPY treatment arms or within specific arms. Dataset composition and per-treatment group sizes are not reported, leaving a fundamental ambiguity in the experimental design. More fundamentally, the paper implies that the 13 BI-RADS-derived concepts are universal predictors of response independent of treatment, a strong hypothesis that ignores tumor biology. The link between these imaging concepts and underlying biology is not established, yet the paper proceeds as if this connection is self-evident. Such a bold hypothesis requires more supporting evidence than is provided. No sensitivity analysis was performed using treatment as a class variable, yet that is precisely the question that needs answering: is the CBM’s predictive performance independent of treatment? Without that analysis the results are difficult to interpret. The CBM does not perform meaningfully better than black-box models (Table 1), raising the question of whether the authors believe they have captured the full MRI-based predictive signal. No demographic or treatment-specific covariates were considered, which is a significant omission.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Clarity: The paper is well-written, with all methodological steps and configurations thoroughly detailed and justified. The proposed metrics are clearly formulated and investigate various aspects of faithfulness and reliability. All figures are clear and effectively support the narrative of the paper. Notably, Figure 1 is excellent, providing a highly comprehensive overview of the entire framework. Domain-Specific Methods: The framework effectively utilizes appropriate tools for the medical domain. Feature extraction is performed using a mask-guided 3D ResNet (chosen via model selection). Additionally, the concepts are derived from the well-established BI-RADS standard and converted into fixed-length embeddings using the PMC-CLIP text encoder, which is specifically trained on medical text data. Comprehensive Interpretability Evaluation: The interpretability insights provided by the framework are well-demonstrated both at a global level (Figure 2) and at a local level (Figure 3).
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Inconclusive results: The most significant weakness concerns the test-set performance during the model selection phase. All evaluated models, including the one chosen for the final framework, report F1 scores around 0.5, which is quite poor for a binary classification task. The fact that specificity is significantly higher than sensitivity clearly suggests that the model is negatively affected by the unbalanced class distribution, as positive cases represent roughly one-third of the dataset. These low performance metrics contradict the claim of the authors in the introduction of having trained “a strong end-to-end 3D ResNet baseline,” which somewhat weakens the subsequent discussion. While the primary contribution of the paper lies in the proposed framework rather than raw predictive accuracy, the authors should acknowledge these performance issues and the dataset imbalance in a dedicated limitations section. Lack of training details: Section 3.1 does not specify the train/validation/test splitting strategy. If a random split was used, adopting a stratified split could help mitigate the imbalance issue discussed above. Furthermore, critical training details, such as the number of epochs and the use of early stopping, are not provided. The poor test performance might also stem from overfitting, which the authors could easily verify by comparing training and test metrics or by analyzing the learning curves.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Focusing strictly on pretreatment (T0) imaging aligns perfectly with the real-world clinical decision point for neoadjuvant therapy, avoiding the reliance on mid-treatment scans. 2.Instance-level concept labeling is highly resource-intensive in medical imaging. The authors cleverly bypass this by freezing a heavily trained 3D ResNet backbone and using a text encoder to project features into a semantic space, requiring minimal concept supervision.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.One of the biggest drawbacks of posthoc based concept bottleneck methods is that it is not clear if the discoverd concepts are causal or not. Meaning, if the discovered concepts were actually used by the blackbox or encoder while doing the prediction in the first place. In any post-hoc based explainability our central question is to explain the blackbox. The current intervention analysis mainly shows the associational importance of concept dimensions in the linear head; establishing a causal effect of a concept on prediction is much harder and generally requires explicit causal treatment of confounding and dependencies between concepts, as emphasized by Goyal et al.’s Causal Concept Effect (CaCE) framework. 2.In addition, the method highlights influential concepts but does not learn explicit decision rules over concepts. This is a meaningful design choice, but it means the paper should better position itself relative to rule-based / neuro-symbolic concept explanation work. In particular, the paper already cites standard CBM, label-free CBM, and post-hoc CBM references, but it does not discuss rule-based concept explanation methods such as [1, 2, 3], which are directly relevant when the goal is not just to rank concepts but to expose interpretable rules over them. [1] Entropy-based Logic Explanations of Neural Networks. Barbiero et al. [2] Dividing and Conquering a BlackBox to a Mixture of Interpretable Models: Route, Interpret, Repeat. Ghosh et al. [3] Distilling BlackBox to Interpretable models for Efficient Transfer Learning. Ghosh et al. 3.The paper’s main contribution is concept-based interpretability, but there is no evaluation against expert concept annotations, even on a small subset. Without showing that the predicted concept scores agree with radiologists or correlate with known BI-RADS attributes, it is hard to trust the semantic interpretation of Fig. 2 and Fig. 3.A method can be internally decomposable without being clinically interpretable. 4.The paper compares predictive performance across backbones, but not explanation quality against relevant baselines such as post-hoc CBMs, label-free CBMs, or even Grad-CAM-based faithfulness/reliability analyses. There is also no ablation using shuffled prompts, random text embeddings, or a random low-dimensional basis. Without that, it is hard to know whether the chosen BI-RADS concept space is actually doing useful work, or whether almost any compressed linear probe on the frozen representation would behave similarly. 5.The method was evaluated on a single I-SPY2 split with 949 cases, no external validation, and no reader study. While this is a robust and standard dataset, testing the generalization of the learned concept projections on an external, multi-center cohort would solidify the reliability claims.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their thorough reading and constructive feedback. We are honored by your recognition of our work and would like to address the main concerns raised. 1.Data and treatment-arm stratification Concerns were raised regarding whether the model was trained and tested across different treatment arms. We used the eligible pretreatment T0 I-SPY2 cohort after applying our inclusion criteria, with patient-level 8:1:1 train/validation/test splits. Because treatment-arm labels are not publicly available, per-arm stratification or treatment-specific sensitivity analysis could not be performed. The evaluation was conducted on the aggregated eligible cohort to ensure representation of all treatment groups. 2.Concept interpretability and m parameter Concept contributions were evaluated using the top-m zeroing approach (Sec. 2.4, Table 2), which measured their effect on model predictions within the available data. We selected m=3 and m=5 to represent small- and medium-sized concept interventions. Coverage referred to the fraction of cases retained after ranking by mean concept stability U_mean (Sec. 2.5, Table 3). Future work will incorporate expert validation to further assess concept reliability. 3.Model performance and class imbalance The relatively low F1 (~0.5) and sensitivity were noted. CBM performance was comparable to the end-to-end 3D ResNet baseline (Table 1). The lower sensitivity resulted from class imbalance (pCR ~32.6%); we applied WeightedRandomSampler and reported AUC, ACC, F1, SEN, and SPE with 95% CIs for balanced evaluation (Sec. 3.2). The primary contribution remained the interpretability of concept-level evidence while maintaining competitive predictive performance. 4.Training details and backbone rationale Due to space limitations, detailed training settings including train/validation/test splits, number of epochs, and early stopping are not fully described in this manuscript. These details will be clearly presented in the camera-ready version. Similarly, the rationale for selecting 3D ResNet as the backbone will be emphasized earlier in the Introduction and Methods sections in the final version. 5.Decision rules, baseline comparisons, and generalization Finally, we acknowledge that explicit decision rule learning, comparisons with alternative interpretability baselines (post-hoc CBM, label-free CBM, Grad-CAM), and multi-center evaluation were not included in this study. Future work will extend the framework to learn decision rules, benchmark against other interpretability baselines, and validate concept reliability in external cohorts, enhancing generalization and practical utility.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): Reviewers feedback is mixed. However, all agreed that the paper proposed a framework with potential clinical value. The authors are encouraged to clarify iSPY arm selection, training details, and generalizability in the final version of the manuscript.

title: Text Guidance and Distance Gating Improve Detection and Segmentation of Focal Cortical Dysplasia
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) The paper makes a compelling clinical argument: in presurgical epilepsy evaluation, prior knowledge about seizure onset zone localization is routinely available (from semiology, EEG, PET, etc. ). Leveraging this non-imaging information to guide a deep learning model is a logical and underexplored direction in FCD detection. This bridges the gap between purely data-driven methods and clinical workflow. 2) The adaptation of the GuideDecoder fusion mechanism from 2D vision to cortical surface meshes (using HexUnpool and SpiralConv) is a non-trivial technical contribution. It demonstrates a careful handling of irregular graph-structured data. The distance-based gating is a simple yet highly effective inference-time post-processing step. It cleverly re-purposes an existing auxiliary output (distance regression) to address the specific failure mode (increased false positives on healthy controls) of the text-conditioned model. The quantitative impact on specificity is substantial (from ~27% to ~93% on the main cohort). 3) The evaluation strictly follows the established MELD protocol, using a large multi-center dataset with a held-out independent test cohort (Bonn). This ensures a fair comparison and assesses generalizability. The use of multiple text conditioning variants (hemisphere only, lobe only, hemisphere+lobe) and the robustness strategy of random sampling during training (including “unclear” prompts) is a thoughtful experimental design that explores the granularity of required prior information.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) The text prompts are derived from atlas-based overlap with the ground-truth lesion. In a real clinical scenario, the prior information would be provided as free text by a clinician (e. g. , “suspected left temporal lesion”). The current evaluation uses structured, clean atlas labels. The authors correctly note this as a future direction (free-form radiological narratives). It would strengthen the discussion to explicitly state that performance may degrade with noisy or imprecise clinical text and that this evaluation represents an upper-bound or “oracle” setting for text guidance. 2) The ablation in Table 4 focuses on gating aggregation rules, but does not isolate the effect of the text guidance itself versus the modified decoder architecture. The baseline is MELD. The Vision+LM model introduces both text fusion and the GuideDecoder with HexUnpool/SpiralConv. Could some of the gain be attributed solely to architectural changes? 3) The text mentions replacing standard 2D upsampling with HexUnpool and standard convolution with SpiralConv. A brief justification for why HexUnpool was chosen over simpler interpolation on the mesh would be helpful for readers unfamiliar with spherical surface processing. 4) In the References section, reference [8] (Park et al. ) appears to be duplicated or mis-cited. It is listed as a narrative review on AI for FCD, but the citation in text is for RadBERT. The actual RadBERT citation is missing. The authors should ensure the RadBERT model is properly cited. 5) The dice metirc should be used in the experiments to evaluate the performance of the proposed method.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The main strength of the paper is its potential in focal epilepsy to combine imaging-based input with other clinical information, such as radiology notes, which tend to be available for surgical candidates, but are currently not incorporated in automated lesion detection tools. In practice, pre-surgical evaluation considers a variety of sources of information, and the paper demonstrates that incorporating some of these into imaging-based localisation tools could substantially improve performance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The authors motivate the incorporation of text-based information of lesion localisation with the typical availability of prior clinical knowledge. However, in their analysis the authors generate the text input by using the MELD pipeline to predict a lesion localisation, which is then mapped to an anatomical template to generate textual descriptions. This appears to be a circular way of generating input, which is then used alongside the MELD surface features to refine localisation. What is the conceptual justification for generating text input using a model based on MRI cortical surface features, only then to combine the text input with the same model of cortical features? Instead, why not use input independent of the MELD pipeline, e.g. notes of a radiologist, or findings of EEG? 2.Another methodological consideration is the gating mechanism. Does applying a median (min/max) threshold of the distance of vertices within a cluster to its boundary not bias towards detecting small and, in particular, narrow lesions? What is the justification for using this mechanisms specifically? 3.Further, table 4 compares the novel method with all gating mechanisms to MELD with the same gating options. However, the discussion of this is very limited, e.g. the authors do not discuss that MELD with added gating mechanism outperforms their model in three out of five metrics. It is also unclear why these results are only show for the main cohort, and not the independent validation cohort.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The work tries to combine surface-based and textual data to segment lesions in the brain
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The work is not clear organized. It is hard to follow and the motivation is not clear. What advantage does the text adds to the segmentation? The authors call it segmentation but it should rather be parcellation as it is surface-based. These text-based inputs are very primitive and does not provide enough information as the results are quite inferior in general; huge portions of the legions are missed. Why was surfaces used? Can we use volumetric segmentations (without the graph-based framework) and then check the results with that; perhaps an ablation study might be good? The gating mechanism lacks technical grounding what is the use of computing the SDF? The different loss functions need ablation studies to see what is the true effect of each loss. reviewer_3_rating: (1) Strong Reject — must be rejected due to major flaws
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer. The meta-review highlights three themes (text generation, gating, evaluation choices), grouped below. [1] Text input: source and realism (R1, R2, MR) R2 raises a concern that the text appears circular (MELD predictions re-fed into MELD). We respectfully clarify this is not the case: textual descriptions are derived from ground-truth lesion masks registered to template space via AtlasReader (Sec. 3.1), following MELD’s localization procedure but using GT, not model output. The goal is a methodological proof of concept that text representations of coarse anatomical priors can guide detection. We agree this setup is an upper-bound evaluation, performance may degrade with noisy clinical text, and radiology notes or EEG findings are the natural next step. Such data was not consistently available across the 23-center MELD cohort. This is discussed in Sec. 5 and we will make it more explicit, as requested by R1. [2] Distance gating: rationale and bias (R2, R3, MR) The gating uses the existing MELD signed-distance head (Sec. 2.3): inside lesions distances are negative, outside they are positive and grow with distance from the boundary. FP clusters in healthy cortex retain high positive distances and are filtered, while true-lesion clusters contain near-/negative-distance vertices and are kept. The Youden’s J threshold is positive on our data; therefore, as long as distance predictions are accurate, true-positive clusters are not filtered regardless of lesion size. Empirically, sensitivity is largely preserved on both cohorts (Tables 2-3) while specificity rises from 27.5% to 93.3% (main) and 37.3% to 94.0% (Bonn). [3] Evaluation choices and ablations (R1, R2, R3, MR) R3 states evaluation is on a single dataset. We respectfully note Sec. 3.1 describes two cohorts: the multi-center MELD cohort (23 centers, 1.5T/3T) and the independent Bonn cohort as external test set. Improvements over MELD are consistent on both, supporting generalizability. R2 notes MELD+gating outperforms Vision+LM on some specificity metrics (Table 4). Our objective is improved sensitivity, the clinical bottleneck in FCD detection. Vision+LM detects more lesions and yields higher IoU, particularly on Bonn (sensitivity 78.0% vs 69.5%, IoU 0.306 vs 0.218); we view this as a sensitivity-specificity trade-off and will frame it as such in the revision. R1 asks whether gains stem from text or from the modified decoder. In an unreported ablation, Vision+LM with “unclear” prompts at inference (no localization content) shows no consistent gains over MELD; gains appear only with informative prompts, indicating the contribution is not purely architectural. If permitted, we will add a note on this ablation to the final version. Reviewer-specific points R1: HexUnpool preserves the icosphere mesh correspondence during upsampling, ensuring consistent feature propagation across resolutions and integrating naturally with SpiralConv, unlike generic interpolation. The RadBERT citation was a preparation error and will be corrected. IoU and Dice are monotonically related (Dice = 2*IoU/(1+IoU)); we used IoU per the MELD protocol for direct comparability. R3: The surface formulation follows MELD and is motivated by FCD manifesting as subtle cortical morphological/signal changes along the cortical sheet; the model performs vertex-wise lesion prediction, a segmentation task in surface-based neuroimaging, not parcellation. The loss exactly follows MELD (Sec. 3.2) for fair comparison. IoU values are in line with published MELD on this challenging task; the relevant signal is consistent improvement on both cohorts. We will improve methods clarity and will release code upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes the ingenious idea to combine text and images for the detection of FCD. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This has been a difficult choice as I have some mixed feelings after reading the paper and checking all comments post-rebuttal.
