In International conference on pattern recognition (pp. 475-489). Cham: Springer International Publishing. [2] Roth, K., Pemula, L., Zepeda, J., Schölkopf, B., Brox, T., & Gehler, P. (2022). Towards total recall in industrial anomaly detection. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition (pp. 14318-14328). [3] Tan, J., Hou, B., Day, T., Simpson, J., Rueckert, D., & Kainz, B. (2021, September). Detecting outliers with poisson image interpolation. In International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (pp. 581-591). Cham: Springer International Publishing. [4] Schlüter, H. M., Tan, J., Hou, B., & Kainz, B. (2022, October). Natural synthetic anomalies for self-supervised anomaly detection and localization. In European Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 474-489). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. Since the paper has been provisionally accepted, we will use the revision to clarify the following modeling choices and limitations. [R4] Independence between $x_{t_k}$ and $m$. We agree that $x_{t_k}$ may retain residual information about anomalies. However, following DAPS, the noisy diffusion state $x_{t_k}$ is only introduced as an auxiliary variable to approximate the intractable image prior $p(x_0)$ via the conditional diffusion prior $p_k(x_0 \mid x_{t_k})$. We additionally assume independence from $m$ as a tractable approximation. The empirical performance across both datasets suggests this approximation does not critically impair the method in practice. We have made this approximation explicit in the revised manuscript. [R4] Approximate the forward model. We would like to clarify the distinct roles of the two components of our forward model. While Eq. 3 utilizes an isotropic Gaussian likelihood, this is only one component of our model. The spatial structure of anomalies is explicitly captured by the random Gaussian field prior on the mask $m$. As shown by the ablation without spatial regularization in the mask prior (Table 3-(C)), the isotropic Gaussian likelihood alone struggles to capture structured anomalies, highlighting the importance of the structured prior. [R3] Annealed likelihood variance. Unlike standard inverse problems with a known forward model, both the reconstruction and the anomaly mask are uncertain in our setting. Inspired by DAPS, we use a sequence of intermediate likelihoods whose variance evolves jointly with the conditional diffusion prior across scales. A larger variance in early iterations allows broader exploration of reconstruction-mask pairs, while a smaller variance later enforces closer consistency with the measurement. The algorithm targets the final annealed approximate posterior associated with the last variance level. The fixed-variance ablation in Table 3-(B) supports the usefulness of this annealing. [R3] Scale-dependent $\lambda_0$. Since the likelihood term scales as $1/r_k^2$, keeping $\lambda_0$ fixed would change the relative strength of the likelihood and mask regularization during annealing. We adapt $\lambda_0(k)$ across scales to maintain a consistent balance between these terms in the intermediate posteriors. This is part of the annealed approximation used for sampling, rather than a claim that the underlying Bayesian prior itself is scale-dependent. [R3-R4] Langevin step sizes. As in DAPS, the effective step size decreases as the intermediate posteriors become sharper. Since the energy gradients with respect to the healthy image $x_0$ and the mask unconstrained logits $a$ can have different scales, we adapt the step sizes $\eta_x$ and $\eta_a$ inversely to the gradient of the energies $|\nabla x_0 U_k|2^2$ and $|\nabla a U_k|_2^2$, respectively, with clipping for numerical stability. [R4] PET evaluation and additional MRI sequences. We agree that synthetic PET anomalies do not capture the full clinical variability of real disease. However, our goal was to complement the BraTS FLAIR tumor experiments with a different modality and disease pattern: FDG PET with Alzheimer-like hypometabolism. The synthetic setting provides ground truth and enables quantitative comparison, while still revealing differences between methods.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): Two reviewers were strongly positive. R4 is weakly negative, but raises issues that may be addressed. However, I also agree that R4’s raised issues limit scope and impact.

title: VCDA-Net: Graph-Guided Voxel-Cluster Density Attention for Global-Regional Brain Age Gap Estimation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The core idea of coupling global morphological context with local geometric cues via the novel Voxel-Cluster Density Attention (VCDA) mechanism is highly interesting. This approach effectively addresses the limitations of traditional regional volume metrics by mitigating inherent segmentation noise and capturing stable, fine-grained structural variations. 2.The quantitative evaluation is solid and persuasive. The proposed VCDA-Net demonstrates competitive performance by outperforming several established baselines (including SFCN, ResNet50, and DenseNet121), achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.71years on a multi-cohort normative dataset. 3.The methodology thoughtfully incorporates a linear bias correction step to mitigate the well-known regression-to-the-mean effect in age estimation. This crucial adjustment not only improves the overall accuracy of the brain age predictions but also ensures that the resulting Brain Age Gap (BAG) reliably isolates true neurodegenerative changes from systematic prediction errors.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The review of related work in the Introduction could be better structured. The current narrative feels slightly disjointed. It would be highly beneficial to reorganize this section to explicitly tighten the connection between existing multimodal learning strategies, global-local brain age prediction paradigms, and the specific methodological gap that VCDA-Net aims to fill. 2.The multi-attributed graph utilizes three specific metrics for edge construction (dot product, Euclidean distance, and cosine similarity). The manuscript lacks a clear justification for selecting these exact three. Given that they measure overlapping concepts of geometric similarity, there is a high risk of information redundancy. Furthermore, the ablation study (Table 2) only evaluates individual metrics against the full combination; it lacks experiments evaluating pairwise combinations (e. g. , using only two metrics) to definitively prove that all three are strictly necessary and non-redundant. 3.While the evaluation is extensive, several of the primary comparison baselines (e. g. , ResNet50, DenseNet121, and SFCN) are relatively dated. To robustly validate the framework as a state-of-the-art approach, the authors should include comparisons with more recent and highly representative architectures in this domain, such as Global-Local Transformer-based brain age models. 4.The authors are strongly advised to double-check the statistical values reported in Table 3.Some of the mean and standard deviation values for the clinical groups (e. g. , specifically the magnitude of standard deviations relative to the means) warrant a careful verification to ensure there are no typographical errors in the calculations or reporting. 5.A fundamental aspect of the methodology requires further clarification: how is the “ground truth” age for individual anatomical regions determined? While chronological age serves as a global label, the manuscript does not explicitly detail the biological or mathematical assumptions used to assign or approximate target ages for specific local brain structures during training, especially concerning the physiological differences between healthy controls and pathological subjects.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The main strength of the paper is its novel methodology, which uses a graph-guided voxel-cluster density attention mechanism to improve brain age gap estimates. The guidance seems to improve age gam predictions, and the fact that it relies on voxel-clusters instead of segmentations masks potentially improves the quality of the regional brain age predictions.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main weakness of the paper is that its methodology is hard to follow based solely on the manuscript. Fortunately, the authors provided the anonymized code. For example, in Figure 1 (a), where the regional brain age is coming from? It appears in Figure 1(b) (“regional brain age estimator”), but it is unclear where it fits within VCDA-Net workflow. I missed a figure showing the regional age predictions for the MCI and ADS groups. Were the models that VDCA-Net compared against retrained on the same data? I believe the data has sex and not gender information.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The VCDA mechanism captures local morphological details, whereas existing DL models often ignore heterogeneous information within specific structures. 2.The proposed method is able to localize neurodegenerative changes to specific anatomical structures (e.g., hippocampus and ventricles in AD), greatly enhancing method interpretability.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.While the paper utilizes a large-scale dataset containing 1,710 MRI scans, there is a lack of an unseen dataset for validation, and the generalization of the model needs to be verified in future studies. 2.More decimal places are needed in Table 1 to differentiate the R2 and r values among methods.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the strengths of our work, including the “novel methodology” with a “highly interesting mechanism” (@R1, R2), the effective “voxel-cluster density attention” for “capturing local morphological details” and “greatly enhancing interpretability” (@R2,R3), and the “crucial adjustment” of bias correction to “reliably isolate true neurodegenerative changes”(@R1). Q1.Non-redundancy(@R1): Cosine Similarity, Euclidean Distance, and Dot Product capture complementary geometric perspectives: orientation, magnitude, and their composite relationship. Orientation identifies shape patterns, while magnitude captures scale-specific morphological changes. To prevent redundancy, Gated Fusion dynamically filters these inputs, ensuring only non-overlapping features are integrated. Table 2 proves this synergy: single-metric models using Euclidean (MAE:4.42), Dot product (MAE:4.40), or Cosine (MAE:5.82) underperform VCDA-Net (MAE:4.22). This MAE reduction confirms that multi-edge attributes provide unique information that Gated Fusion prioritizes, validating the framework’s necessity for capturing complex structural variations. We agree that pairwise ablation studies would further highlight the specific contribution of each metric pair. Q2.Statistical Verification(@R1,R2): We confirmed the accuracy of the reported Mean+/- SD values. The high variance reflects inherent biological heterogeneity typical in multi-site neuroimaging. Crucially, in Table 3, the 95%CIs for clinical groups (e.g., ADNI AD [3.06, 5.11]) remain clearly distinct from zero and the HC group [-0.74,0.74], confirming that observed BAG increases are statistically significant indicators of pathology. Furthermore, negative BAG values in Fig. 3 represent normal biological diversity; by centering the HC mean at zero, these values identify brain regions that appear younger than their chronological age. Q3.Assumptions for Regional Ground Truth(@R1,R2): We clarify that chronological age serves as the indirect ground truth for all 32 regional decoders (Eq.3,4), based on the established assumption that healthy regional development aligns with chronological time. By fitting our accelerated aging analysis framework exclusively on Healthy Controls, we establish a normative reference that effectively decouples systematic prediction bias from true pathological signals. As detailed in Section 3.3 (p.8), our results confirm that this strategy successfully isolates neurodegeneration: despite training on global labels, VCDA-Net identifies significant localized deviations in AD groups, particularly in the Right Hippocampus (BAG=2.11±8.08,p<.005) and Right Lateral Ventricle (BAG=3.94±7.39, p<.001). These gaps quantify region-specific “accelerated aging” as deviations from the normative trajectory, providing a robust proxy in the absence of regional biological labels. Q4.SOTA Comparison & Impact(@R1): VCDA-Net was benchmarked against established 3D CNNs (SFCN, ResNet) and modern Transformer-based SOTA (Voxel-level BA using Swin UNETR) alongside specialized frameworks (SynthBA, Ordinal-DR), covering both gold standards and the global-local paradigms requested. The bias correction is integral; its efficacy is evidenced by significant AD findings (Sec 3.3). We value the suggestion on longitudinal trajectories; while this study builds a robust cross-sectional foundation, extending the framework to track disease progression is a key priority for future development. Q5.Refinement & Generalization(@R1,R2,R3): We will slightly refine the Introduction and update technical terms (e.g., changing “Gender” to “Sex”) and Table 1 precision as suggested. Regarding generalization, our multi-site dataset (1,710 scans) provides robust evidence of model stability. While all benchmarks were evaluated under identical conditions for fair comparison, we agree that validation on an unseen dataset is a valuable direction for future expansion.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviews stated different recommendations, with R1 and R2 recommending weak reject and R3 recommending accept. All reviewers raised concerns about the paper that should be addressed in the rebuttal. The major points addressed by the reviewers include clarifying the regional brain age pipeline and its supervision signal, addressing comparison fairness, justifying the choice of metric, and addressing and stating any other missing information requested by the reviewers. | Following the rebuttal, all three reviewers agreed to accept the paper, after the authors clarified the regional brain age pipeline, the supervision signa and the methodology, which R1 and R2 had initially found insufficiently explained. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal successfully addressed most methodological concerns, resulting in post-rebuttal support for acceptance by all reviewers and leading to my recommendation of acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces a multi-scale brain age estimation framework that utilizes a graph-guided voxel-cluster density attention mechanism for both global and regional predictions. In the rebuttal, the authors clarified that chronological age serves as an indirect ground truth for regional decoders to establish a normative reference. They also justified the complementary nature of the chosen geometric metrics and the statistical validity of their results. Convinced by these clarifications, both Reviewers 1 and 2 upgraded their scores, leading to a unanimous agreement that the paper is a strong methodological contribution suitable for MICCAI.

title: VecHeart: Holistic Four-Chamber Cardiac Anatomy Modeling via Hybrid VecSets
reviewer_1_strengths: This work proposes a novel implicit cardiac four-chamber shape reconstruction framework, enabling effective four-chamber shape completion from sparse or partially observed input. The proposed VecHeart framework achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple cardiac four-chamber shape reconstruction and generation tasks.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: It would be interesting to explore if contrastive learning approaches could further improve modality alignment in the latent space. Fig. 1 is somewhat small, which may affect its clarity and readability.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Strong improvement over baselines in the reported quantitative evaluation. Interesting methodological contribution: a conditioning approach intended to mitigate sparsity and variability in input configurations. The methods section appears to include sufficient detail to reproduce the approach, at least at a high level.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Incomplete-data / missingness evaluation is not well-motivated clinically. As the authors state in the introduction, in typical CMR protocols, the information content for the atria is fundamentally limited: SAX stacks often do not cover the atria well, and LAX views provide only sparse 2D delineations. Given this, it is unclear what evidence supports the claim that there is sufficient patient-specific information to reconstruct detailed atrial geometry. In practice, completion in these regions is likely dominated by learned priors and correlations with other structures. Insufficient engagement with the existing cardiac reconstruction literature. The introduction and related work do not adequately situate the contribution within recent work on (i) multi-class point-cloud based four-chamber reconstruction/completion (e.g. HeartFormer: Semantic-Aware Dual-Structure Transformers for 3D Four-Chamber Cardiac Point Cloud Reconstruction, arXiv:2512.00264) and (ii) anatomically/topologically consistent mesh reconstruction constraints (e.g. Topology-Preserving Loss for Accurate and Anatomically Consistent Cardiac Mesh Reconstruction, arXiv:2503.07874). This weakens the novelty claim and makes it harder to interpret what is genuinely new beyond architectural choices. Intended use is too unfocused to evaluate clinical relevance. If the goal is shape completion for downstream simulation (e.g., finite element modelling), then a strong learned prior could be appropriate. If the goal is patient-specific anatomical measurement/analysis from sparse CMR, then hallucinated structure may be misleading. The manuscript does not clearly commit to a particular use case; there is only one comment in the introduction that “These constraints severely limit their clinical utility,” but it does not elaborate further on the intended clinical use. Residual atrial errors appear too large for realistic use (for measurement). Even if the method improves over baselines, the reported LA/RA CD errors under missingness (e.g., ~9.2 mm and ~7.9 mm) are far above typical MRI voxel sizes (~2 mm) and likely beyond what is usable for patient-specific quantification. Generation / anatomical realism is not addressed. A major concern in anatomy generation is concordance with known clinical distributions and anatomical variability; the paper does not meaningfully discuss or evaluate this. Overall, the organisation and writing of the paper would benefit from significant improvement, which might clarify some of the issues mentioned.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: First, this article design the method by introducing the correlation of multichambered correlations and the they can captures the motion correlation between each part of the heart. Second, this article focus on the complete inputs and 3d+t generations and it seems reasonable to me to include these tasks since this is related to an issues that sometimes might encounter. Third, this article have some graphs to help understanding the detail of the articles as well.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: First, in [Table 2] there is a systematic gap in validation. Author only reports the synthetic SAX and LAX reconstruction results of LA and RA, however for its “Real Dataset”, it didn’t show the results of LA and RA. This will inevitably leads to a validation error since synthetic LAX usually use displacement algorithm. Usually in real LAX and SAX dataset, there is always breath noises and image quality issue in LAX images, so I think using only synthetic LAX is lack of solid validation of model performance. Second, the way author used to get ground-truth meshes are likely to may lead to proxy reference. In the article they stated that “we register and fit a Statistic Shape Model to segmentation masks predicted by a publicly available method to generate ground-truth cardiac meshes.” However, this leads to inherent biases that ground-truth meshes uses the SSM model, which is a statistical model that will introduce model-based proxy. The SSM model has a potential generating bias that ground-truth meshes might be embedded in template-like anatomy. The results of using these generated ground-truth meshes lead to weakening this article’s statement of model results comparison. Third, in the ablation study, the article ablation still have a validation gap between their results and their conclusions. In the article, the authors states that “ VecHeart outperforms the baselines in both complete and missing data scenarios, validating our HPT and ACM designs”.However, the ablation experiment in “Table 1” and “Table 2” does not contain the design ablation for “HPT”, “ACM”. If the author still simultaneously contains these three parts together in the ablation study, then it will be difficult to see whether individual module are effective enough. Fourth, In the quantitative analysis part (Figure 2) the author only provide results for 1 or 2 samples. However, usually for the quantitative analysis it is important to provide the worst, medium, best result to demonstrate the generalizability of the model. It is especially in this type of missing part and SAX-only conditions, since the model received sparse information input. If the author only demonstrated selected cases, then there is a potential of cherry-picking result, which leads to gaps in validation examinations. Fifth, for the (3D+t) tasks, there is a validation gap of using only two metrics (vFID and Cycle-CD). The first reaons is that these metrics is indirect to clinical application, some more clinical-related metrics should be used such as ejection fraction and volume curve of the heart. Furthermore, the author should also compared with other published 3D+t reconstruction pipeline.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: [R1] We appreciate the advice and will explore it. [R2] Formulation, motivation: Our motivation, as detailed in the first two paragraphs of the Intro, is to propose a better multi-part 3D latent representation to address the limitations of prior implicit methods: restriction to single-part modeling or reliance on complete surface and slow test-time optimization. Accurate multi-part modeling is important and a prerequisite for downstream tasks like index analysis and cardiac simulation. By introducing HPT, ACM, MA, VecHeart achieves SOTA performance across widely studied benchmarks, including better representation capacity with faster inference (Tab 1 Top) and better visible part reconstruction from sparse slices (Tab 2). “limit their clinical utility” means prior implicit methods’ performance and speed limitations on the fundamental shape representation problem. Regarding the learned prior: even standard SAX MRI is sparse and necessitates anatomical priors. Incorporating prior is common in SOTA methods [19,32,33,34,37]. [R2] Missingness Evaluation: The missingness experiment is designed to probe the model’s ability in extreme scenarios without requiring architecture modification, rather than to show immediate clinical relevance. This evaluation highlights the model’s ability to produce plausible outputs on unobserved parts under severe data constraints, rather than representing its only intended use. We acknowledge the reconstruction of unobserved anatomy is not perfect, but this shows VecHeart’s potential for application like conditioned generation (e.g., via volume or pathology). The model’s SOTA reconstruction performance on visible parts, which is a well-established and standard setting, shouldn’t be overshadowed by its currently imperfect handling of extreme tasks, where it shows potential despite not being fully mature. We shouldn’t be penalized for exhibiting new abilities absent in previous methods. Regarding “usable”: CD is computed as the standard sum of pred-to-gt and gt-to-pred squared L2 distances, and is thus not directly comparable to the 2mm threshold. Using the comparable mean surface distance instead yields 3.02/2.51 mm, indicating strong potential despite these parts being completely missing. [R2] Literature: Requiring comparison with unpublished preprints is inappropriate, especially HeartFormer was released only 3 months before deadline. Moreover, given the fact that we do things these unpublished methods do not fully cover, we don’t see how they diminish our work’s novelty. [R2,R3] 3D+t Generation Experiment: We clarify that this experiment evaluates mesh sequence generation via diffusion model, not reconstruction (3D+t reconstruction is in Tab 2, Real SAX). Following the setting of CardiacFlow, the current SOTA for 3D+t generation, VecHeart shows better volume preservation and periodic consistency. We agree by including analysis with clinical-related distributions and metrics can further strengthen the evaluation. [R3] Real Evaluation of LA/RA: It’s impossible to evaluate 3D LA/RA quality as we can’t get 3D GT from LAX, which is just a 2D image. Also, the real dataset we use only has SAX. Thus synthetic evaluation is the only viable proxy for 3D LA/RA accuracy. [R3] GT mesh: 1060 shapes are directly derived from expert CT annotations, ensuring no proxy bias. SSM is only used to obtain bi-ventricle GT for real SAX MRI. Our evaluation against SSM GT is zero-shot (no SSM bias during training), yet we still achieve SOTA. Ours-finetune proves adapting to SSM bias indeed improves metrics. [R3] Ablation Study: Ours-Sep serves as an ablation for HPT, proving modeling inter-part relationship is beneficial. Excluding ACM can keep performance on visible parts, but it won’t produce any meaningful results on missing parts, which we mention in the main text as: “cant extend to missing-input”. We will clarify. [R3] Visual Results: Due to space limit, more visualization will be provided in a possible journal extension.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I totally agree with the reviewer #2 that the motivation/fomulation of this study is not quite convincing. The authors should explain this clearly in the rebuttal stage. | The motivation is still not fully convincing to me. The paper claims that multi-part latent representation improves clinical utility, but the link between reconstruction accuracy and downstream clinical tasks such as index analysis or cardiac simulation is not sufficiently demonstrated. Therefore, the work appears more like an incremental improvement over existing implicit/shape-prior methods rather than a clearly motivated methodological advance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal clarified the motivation and intended use as a multi-part latent representation rather than a clinical end-application, reframed the missingness study as a probe of new capabilities, and resolved the evaluation concerns, leading R2 to move from a reject to accept while R1 maintained acceptance. On balance, the methodological contribution is good enough, and I therefore recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers generally agreed that the proposed VecHeart framework provides meaningful methodological contributions, particularly in modeling multi-part cardiac structures under sparse and incomplete input settings, and achieves strong performance across multiple reconstruction and generation benchmarks. The main concerns were related to the clinical motivation and interpretation of the missingness experiments, the evaluation of anatomically unobserved regions, and the clarity of the intended downstream use case. The rebuttal clarified that the missingness setting is primarily designed to evaluate representation robustness and conditional completion ability rather than immediate clinical deployment, and also addressed concerns regarding proxy bias, ablation design, and the role of anatomical priors.

title: WaveDiT: Distribution-Aware Wavelet Flow Matching for Efficient 3D Brain MRI Synthesis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper is generally well written and easy to follow. The motivation is clear, and the overall framework is reasonably presented. 2.The paper studies a meaningful problem in 3D medical image generation, i. e. , how to generate high-quality 3D volumes efficiently while keeping the training complexity manageable. The overall design, combining wavelet modeling, uncertainty-aware optimization, and efficient attention, is thoughtful and well motivated. 3.The method contains some interesting technical designs. In particular, the analysis of wavelet-band statistics during flow matching provides reasonable support for the band-aware design, and the uncertainty-aware conditioning is also a novel part of the framework. 4.The experimental evaluation is fairly comprehensive. In addition to image generation results, the paper also includes brain age prediction and ROI analysis on generated volumes, which makes the evaluation more convincing.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The overall framework contains several components, so it is sometimes not easy to fully understand the contribution of each individual design choice. In addition, the introduction of several advanced modules makes the paper a bit harder to follow in some parts. These aspects could be further clarified with more detailed analysis if possible. 2.The uncertainty-aware formulation is interesting, but its role could be better discussed. In particular, it would be helpful to further explain how the learned uncertainty contributes to the final improvement.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1. Well-justified use of the wavelet domain. The paper makes a convincing case for why wavelets are attractive for 3D MRI synthesis: they reduce spatial dimensionality while preserving invertibility and avoiding learned compression artifacts. This is especially relevant in neuroimaging, where subtle cortical and anatomical details matter. The empirical analysis showing that the approximation band contains most energy, while high-frequency bands are sparse and heavy-tailed, provides a solid statistical basis for the proposed design. 2. Efficient architecture for full-resolution 3D synthesis. The proposed factorized spatio-depth attention is practically important. Full 3D self-attention at this resolution would be infeasible, and the paper provides a concrete complexity analysis demonstrating large computational savings. The design—local 2D neighborhood attention at higher resolution and deeper factorized spatial/depth attention—appears sensible and aligned with volumetric anatomy. 3. Strong practical efficiency. A notable strength is that the method supports full-resolution 3D generation on a single H100 GPU , with training in about 26 hours and inference in about 1 second for 10 steps . In this problem domain, practical accessibility is a meaningful contribution, since many high-quality 3D generative methods remain difficult to use outside highly specialized compute settings. 4. Comprehensive evaluation beyond standard generative metrics. The evaluation is stronger than many generative imaging papers because it does not rely only on FID-like metrics. The authors follow a multi-level evaluation protocol : global distributional alignment (FID, MMD, MS-SSIM), a clinically relevant downstream task ( brain age prediction ), and ROI-level anatomical analysis using segmentation-based metrics. This is important because global image metrics can miss anatomically meaningful errors. The ROI and downstream analyses make the empirical case substantially more convincing.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1. The uncertainty model is relatively coarse. Morpheus predicts band-wise log-variance from global summary statistics per channel rather than finer-grained spatial uncertainty. Given that heteroscedasticity is argued to vary strongly across space, especially near tissue boundaries, a spatially resolved uncertainty model might be more faithful to the stated motivation. The current design is elegant and lightweight, but potentially limited. The paper does not deeply analyze whether band-wise uncertainty is sufficient compared with more localized alternatives. 2. Evaluation remains limited to one modality and one task setting. The study focuses only on T1-weighted brain MRI . This is a reasonable starting point, but it limits generalizability. It is unclear whether the gains would transfer to: other MRI contrasts, pathological populations, or other 3D medical imaging modalities such as CT. The authors acknowledge this limitation. 3. Potential concern about downstream evaluation interpretation. The brain age prediction improvement is interesting, but the causal interpretation should be made carefully. Better augmentation performance does not necessarily imply that the generated images are clinically realistic in all relevant respects; it may partly reflect task-specific regularization or data balancing effects. The paper is reasonably cautious, but this point is worth emphasizing.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in scalable 3D brain MRI synthesis, where voxel-space diffusion is expensive and latent compression may lose anatomical detail. The wavelet-domain formulation is well motivated, and the analysis of band-wise statistics provides a reasonable basis for the Morpheus uncertainty module. The paper also includes many relevant baselines, ablations, efficiency comparisons, and downstream evaluations such as brain age prediction and ROI-level anatomical analysis.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weakness is the evaluation protocol. Although the paper is framed as a 3D medical image synthesis method, it does not report commonly used image synthesis metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS, making it difficult to assess voxel-level fidelity and perceptual image quality. The authors argue that global volumetric metrics can be biased by background voxels, but this does not fully justify omitting foreground-masked or ROI-based PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS comparisons. In addition, the downstream brain age prediction result may not directly reflect synthesis fidelity, since improved BAP performance could come from distributional or demographic augmentation rather than anatomically accurate image generation. Finally, the model is still relatively large, around 142M parameters, and requires an H100 for training, which somewhat weakens the claim of broad accessibility despite its faster inference.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. R2 (W1) “Several components … difficult to disentangle individual contributions.” Each component corresponds to a distinct design axis isolated in the ablations: Voxel-space (representation), w/o Morpheus (uncertainty), RFM/OTFM/CFM (flow objective). The architecture mirrors two distinct observations: local HF structure (neighborhood attention) and cross-slice consistency (spatio-depth attention). We will make this mapping explicit. (W2) “Role of uncertainty.” Morpheus contributes through both loss reweighting (Eq.1) and conditioning, introducing band-wise precision aligned with the heteroscedastic statistics of wavelet subbands. Its removal degrades global (FID, MMD), downstream (BAP), and ROI metrics simultaneously (Tables 2b, 3), indicating a structural rather than cosmetic contribution. R3 (W1) “Band-wise uncertainty is coarse.” The dominant heteroscedasticity is between bands (Table 1), spanning up to 90x in kurtosis, which motivates a band-wise formulation. Dense voxel-wise uncertainty at 224^3 would require a decoder comparable to the backbone, undermining efficiency. Spatial selectivity is nonetheless captured implicitly through: conditioning on higher-order moments, local neighborhood attention focusing on high-frequency regions, AdaRMSNorm modulation, which translates band-wise signals into spatially adaptive activations. (W2) “Evaluation limited to T1w brain MRI.” We agree, and this is explicitly acknowledged in Sec. 4.T1 is the standard benchmark in the existing 3D MRI generative literature, enabling direct comparison with prior work. We will extend the framework to other modalities. (W3) “BAP gains may reflect distributional effects rather than anatomical realism.” The ROI metrics in Table 3 are designed for exactly this concern. Unlike BAP, iMAE, KLD, and Dice are computed on independently segmented regions and are insensitive to demographic balancing. WaveDiT-CFM is best across all ROI metrics together with BAP. R4 (W1) “Absence of PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS is a limitation.” We appreciate this point and clarify our methodological position. WaveDiT addresses age-conditional synthesis, not reconstruction: each sample is drawn from p(x|age) with no one-to-one correspondence to any real volume, so paired PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, are not well-defined in our setting. The closest paired analogue already in Table 2 is intra-set MS-SSIM, designed precisely to avoid this issue. To engage the concern directly, we conducted an intra-cohort, age-matched study over 500 within-cohort pairs. The real reference is PSNR 15.93 ± 1.48 dB, SSIM 0.715 ± 0.030, LPIPS 0.204 ± 0.035.The aim is not to maximise these metrics but to match the real cohort’s own intra-similarity distribution, so deviations acquire a diagnostic interpretation: positive ΔPSNR with negative ΔLPIPS signals mode collapse (pairs too self-similar); negative ΔPSNR with stable SSIM/LPIPS points to additive noise or artefacts; strongly negative ΔLPIPS with otherwise normal PSNR/SSIM indicates perceptual collapse. WaveDiT-CFM is closest to the real reference on all three metrics: ΔPSNR = +0.76 dB, ΔSSIM = +0.004, ΔLPIPS = −0.020.By contrast, MOTFM exhibits mode collapse (ΔPSNR = +5.10, ΔLPIPS = −0.077), MD homogeneous collapse (ΔPSNR = +4.13, ΔLPIPS = −0.044), and MLDM perceptual collapse (ΔLPIPS = −0.105) despite a “normal” PSNR/SSIM. (W2) “BAP improvement may not reflect synthesis fidelity.” See R3(W3): ROI metrics (Table 3) measure anatomical consistency independently of demographic effects, and WaveDiT-CFM leads across all of them. (W3) “142M parameters and H100 weaken accessibility.” WaveDiT runs in ~12 GB VRAM at batch size 1 (e.g., 4060ti). The H100 was used only for hardware parity across baselines, since WDM, MLDM, and BS exceed 24-48 GB at full resolution. At 142M parameters WaveDiT is the lightest full-resolution 3D MRI generator among the compared models.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a technically interesting and well-motivated framework for efficient 3D brain MRI synthesis. The problem is meaningful, and the proposed combination of an HDiT backbone with the Morpheus state-aware uncertainty scheduler is promising. Also, the paper is well-written, and the evaluation is fairly comprehensive. The main concerns are the absence of standard image-quality metrics, such as PSNR, and the need for a more detailed analysis of the individual model components. The authors should carefully address these points, along with the other concerns raised by the reviewers, in the final version.

title: When Brains Disagree: Biological Ambiguity Underlies the Challenge of Amyloid PET Synthesis from Structural MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: This is exactly the kind of paper MICCAI needs more of. We are forever formulating new problems and publishing a solution to that problem; leading to a cascade of other people trying to publish better solutions later on. No one seems to ask whether the problem was ever solvable to begin with; what the upper bounds of performance are. Answering the solvability question would tell us when new attempts to squeeze better performance out of a new algorithm are unlikely to be fruitful. Because the solvability question is rarely addressed, we waste untold person-hours on algorithms that are unlikely to push the field forward. This paper addresses solvability and that is commendable.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The only weakness I see is that the presentation of plasma Alzheimer biomarkers as “complementary” information to the amyloid PET scans is confusing. Blood and PET are different, that is true, but both of them are estimates of the same underlying biological construct which is brain amyloid burden. I would prefer the blood markers to be presented as a second measurement of amyloid rather than something that is truly “complementary. ”
reviewer_1_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_2_strengths: This paper present an important, hypothesis-driven analysis of a popular neuroimaging problem of interest. Rather than proposing yet another synthesis model, it asks a fundamental question about why existing approaches fail and designs controlled experiments to answer it. The hypothesis is clearly stated, biologically grounded in established AD progression models, and testable. The stratification into concordant and discordant training subsets cleanly isolates the effect of biological ambiguity. The two distinct model architecture further strengthen the argument for architecture-independence. The large test set (n=1,720) with bootstrap confidence intervals provides statistically reliable estimates. The concordant/discordant models achieving ~82–85% balanced accuracy in-distribution but collapsing out-of-distribution is strong evidence for the ambiguity hypothesis. The paper is well-written with a logical flow from motivation to hypothesis to experiments to conclusions.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The N-intermediate cases, which likely constitute a substantial fraction of the data, are excluded from the stratified analysis but presumably included in the Baseline. How many subjects fall in the N-intermediate category? For an apples to apples comparison in Experiment 2, it would be helpful to train/test the MRI-only model on exactly the same 589 pairs that have the plasma biomarkers and compare the results. Similarly, the work would also benefit from training a plasma-only prediction model from completeness.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The authors presented a well-organized experimental setup to prove their research questions. The concept of combining biomarkers and MRI images is not novel but it serves well the purpose of directing image generator to derive accurate images.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Some concepts presented are a little redundant. It is a bit questionable whether it is then needed to synthesize PET images when, maybe your information can be maybe derived by the blood markers already.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their very positive and constructive feedback. We are particularly pleased that the reviewers found the hypothesis and experimental design regarding the solvability of MRI-to-amyloid PET synthesis meaningful and well-supported. We also appreciate the reviewers’ valuable suggestions. We summarise our responses below. R1: “the presentation of plasma Alzheimer biomarkers as “complementary” information to the amyloid PET scans is confusing” Response: We agree that the wording could be clarified. Our intention was not to describe plasma biomarkers as complementary to amyloid PET, since both reflect the same underlying biological process. Rather, we meant that plasma biomarkers provide information complementary to structural MRI. We will revise the wording accordingly. R2.1: “How many subjects fall in the N-intermediate category?” Response: A total of 447 subjects (36%) in the Baseline training and 672 subjects (39%) in the full test set fell into the N-intermediate category. These cases lie between the two neurodegeneration extremes and therefore contribute to ambiguity in a more continuous manner than our defined N-/N+. We verified that including or excluding these cases does not change the overall behaviour or conclusions of the study. Nevertheless, we retained them because they represent a substantial and clinically realistic portion of the data. R2.2: “in Experiment 2, it would be helpful to train/test the MRI-only model on exactly the same 589 pairs that have the plasma biomarkers and compare the results” Response: We agree this would provide a more direct comparison and will consider it in future work, though it would substantially reduce sample size and may affect statistical power and stability. R2.3: “the work would also benefit from training a plasma-only prediction model from completeness” Response: We appreciate this suggestion and agree that such an experiment would be informative. Our primary goal with Experiment II was not to demonstrate the superiority of multimodal prediction in itself, but rather to test whether it could reduce ambiguity. However, we agree that a plasma-only model would generally help to directly quantify the relative contributions of MRI versus molecular biomarker information. We will explore this in future work. R3: “It is a bit questionable whether it is then needed to synthesize PET images when, maybe your information can be maybe derived by the blood markers already.” Response: This is an important point, and we agree that plasma biomarkers raise a broader question regarding the utility of PET synthesis. In this work, however, the primary role of plasma biomarkers was to test the biological ambiguity hypothesis, rather than to justify the clinical necessity of PET synthesis itself. At the same time, we believe PET synthesis may still provide clinically useful spatial information that is not directly available from plasma alone, and hence remain valuable from an interpretability perspective Once again, we sincerely thank all reviewers for their valuable feedback and encouraging comments.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): I will follow the decision of all the reviewers. R1 recommended a strong acceptance, while R2 and R3 recommended acceptance. Except of some minor fixable weaknesses the reviewers state that the the work is well-executed and statistically credible.

title: XTinyU-Net: Training-Free U-Net Scaling via Initialization-Time Sensitivity
reviewer_1_strengths: Interesting idea that has potential for real-world acceleration in finding the best UNet configuration for a given task. Well-written paper. Easy to follow, and there was clearly effort put into communicating the intuition. Large number of datasets and baselines. Also a large number of evaluated configurations to ensure the proposed method works. Overall, enough evidence to convince me that this method generally works.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: It is not fully clear whether UNeXt, Tiny U-Net, etc. , have been evaluated within the nnUNet framework. If not, this is not a fair comparison, and it is then no surprise to see these performance differences. Considering the qualitative results, all of these methods perform well enough; the main question of interest here would have been robustness. If we reduce parameters significantly but then lose robustness, we do not really gain anything. Regarding Figure 4b (Effect of initialization), the authors mention that it is quite robust against initialization, but I would not agree with this. Jumping between three model configurations that are orders of magnitude apart is definitely not robust. What if you have a configuration where the peak (assuming there always is one) is in between two points? 4b) This would have benefited from a more extensive statistical analysis. Right now, it is not clear if these few data points give us the right idea in terms of robustness.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The authors propose a training-free method for optimizing UNet architecture by scaling its width (channel count). By utilizing a Jacobian sensitivity measure, the approach identifies the ‘empirical collapse boundary’, the point of minimum parameter count just before model accuracy sharply declines. This allows for the pre-selection of the most efficient model size without compromising performance metrics such as Dice or HD95
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper is technically solid and, within the limited space, has provided sufficient empirical evidence to support its methodology. Additional comments are provided in section 12.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper has several notable strengths, even though I remain below the acceptance threshold overall. The strongest aspect of the submission is that it focuses on a highly practical and often overlooked problem in medical image segmentation: efficient model configuration selection. A large portion of recent literature concentrates on proposing new architectures, yet in real deployment settings many practitioners still rely on strong baselines such as U-Net or nnU-Net and need principled ways to reduce model size for resource-constrained environments. By addressing the question of how aggressively a standard U-Net can be compressed for a specific dataset before performance degrades, the paper tackles a relevant and deployment-oriented problem rather than introducing architecture novelty for its own sake. A major strength is the conceptual reframing of lightweight model design. Instead of asking which new compact network should be invented, the paper proposes that a canonical architecture may already be sufficient if scaled correctly. This is an interesting perspective because it challenges the common assumption that efficiency must come from handcrafted lightweight blocks, token mixers, or architectural redesign. The suggestion that intelligent configuration search can outperform bespoke compact models is both practical and thought-provoking for the community. Another important strength is the proposed training-free model selection strategy. The method uses initialization-time Jacobian sensitivity to estimate the smallest stable U-Net configuration without fully training every candidate model. This is appealing because exhaustive train-and-evaluate sweeps are computationally expensive, especially in medical imaging where experiments often involve large volumes, heavy augmentations, and cross-validation protocols. A selection mechanism that only requires random initialization plus a few forward and backward passes can significantly reduce experimentation cost. Even if the method requires further validation, the overall idea is novel and operationally useful. The empirical observation of a two-regime scaling pattern is also a meaningful contribution. The paper shows that as U-Net width decreases, segmentation accuracy often remains on a broad plateau across many compressed configurations, followed by a sharp collapse once capacity becomes too small. This phenomenon is interesting because it suggests that many segmentation models are over-parameterized relative to dataset complexity. Framing model scaling as a plateau-to-collapse transition rather than a smooth monotonic degradation is a useful insight that could motivate future work in compression and neural scaling laws for medical imaging. A further strength is the use of Jacobian sensitivity as a collapse detector rather than simply as a generic zero-cost ranking metric. Existing zero-cost NAS approaches are often designed to compare unrelated architectures, whereas this paper focuses on a structured family of width-scaled U-Nets. The idea of using local input-output sensitivity to identify instability near the representational boundary is creative. Even if the theoretical underpinnings could be strengthened, it is an original application of initialization-time analysis to dense prediction model scaling. The breadth of evaluation is another positive aspect. The paper reports experiments across six public datasets spanning diverse imaging modalities and tasks: breast ultrasound, echocardiography, dermoscopy, retinal vessel segmentation, brain tumor MRI, and cardiac MRI. This is stronger than many papers that validate only on one or two benchmarks. The diversity of modalities suggests the method may capture a general property of U-Net capacity scaling rather than overfitting to one domain. The reported efficiency gains are also impressive. XTinyU-Net is claimed to achieve performance comparable to nnU-Net while using approximately 400x to 1600x fewer parameters depending on the dataset, along with substantial FLOP reductions. If these results hold under broader testing, they would be practically meaningful for edge deployment, mobile inference, portable imaging systems, and institutions with limited hardware resources. The ability to reduce a standard nnU-Net style model from tens of millions of parameters to tens of thousands while maintaining competitive Dice scores is an attractive result. Another strength is the comparison against contemporary lightweight baselines such as UNeXt, CMUNeXt-S, and TinyU-Net. The paper does not only compare to the heavy nnU-Net upper bound but also to models specifically designed for efficiency. This makes the evaluation more relevant because it tests whether architecture search through scaling can compete with dedicated lightweight design. The ablation analysis adds additional value. The authors test robustness of the proposed selection criterion to batch size and random initialization, and compare against existing zero-cost metrics such as NASWOT and SWAP. Showing that the chosen architecture remains relatively stable under different initialization seeds and even with a small number of input samples is encouraging. This kind of robustness analysis is important for methods that rely on initialization statistics. The paper is also clearly written and easy to follow. The motivation is intuitive, the method is mathematically simple, and the main figures communicate the plateau-collapse phenomenon effectively. The overall narrative is coherent: identify redundancy, detect collapse boundary, and choose the smallest safe model. From a translational standpoint, the work has potential clinical relevance because resource-efficient segmentation models are increasingly important. Portable ultrasound devices, point-of-care scanners, low-power hospital systems, and real-time embedded applications often cannot support heavy nnU-Net style deployments. A training-free route to generate compact dataset-specific models could therefore be useful in practice. Finally, the paper has strong practical elegance. It does not rely on complex multi-stage distillation, pruning, quantization, or expensive NAS pipelines. Instead, it proposes a simple structured family of U-Net variants and a lightweight sensitivity criterion. This simplicity may help adoption and reproducibility if validated further. Overall, although I have concerns that place the paper below threshold, the submission has genuine strengths: it targets a practical problem, offers a creative training-free selection framework, provides broad empirical evaluation, and challenges the assumption that new lightweight architectures are always necessary. These aspects make it an interesting and worthwhile contribution.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper has several strengths, but there are also important weaknesses that prevent me from rating it above the acceptance threshold in its current form. My main concerns relate to novelty, rigor of validation, fairness of comparisons, methodological assumptions, and practical deployment claims. The first major weakness is limited methodological novelty. The paper does not introduce a fundamentally new segmentation architecture, learning objective, or optimization framework. Instead, it proposes selecting channel-scaled U-Net variants using an initialization-time proxy score. While practical, this places the contribution closer to model selection heuristics or zero-cost NAS adaptation than a substantial new medical image segmentation method. Training-free architecture scoring at initialization has already been explored extensively in the broader NAS literature through methods such as NASWOT, SynFlow, SNIP, Zen-NAS, and SWAP. The paper acknowledges some of these works, but the methodological jump beyond prior zero-cost proxies is moderate. The main change is applying Jacobian sensitivity to detect a collapse point within a family of width-scaled U-Nets rather than ranking unrelated architectures. This is useful, but somewhat incremental rather than a major conceptual advance. A second weakness is that the central claim of a plateau-then-collapse scaling law is not fully established. The paper shows six datasets where Dice remains stable over a range of widths and then drops sharply. However, six datasets are still limited relative to the diversity of medical segmentation tasks. It remains unclear whether this behavior consistently holds for highly imbalanced segmentation, large 3D volumetric tasks, noisy labels, pathology images, longitudinal imaging, or highly multi-class dense labeling. The claim may be valid for the tested settings, but broader generalization is not yet sufficiently demonstrated. Relatedly, the datasets are somewhat heterogeneous but mostly moderate-scale and standard benchmarks. The study lacks validation on larger and more demanding tasks where nnU-Net is widely used, such as MSD benchmarks, full 3D abdominal organ segmentation, large CT cohorts, or multi-center clinical data. Since the method is framed around nnU-Net scaling, stronger evidence on more canonical nnU-Net challenge datasets would strengthen the case. A third weakness is that the proposed Jacobian sensitivity metric lacks strong theoretical grounding. The paper argues that under-parameterized networks become more sensitive to input perturbations near the capacity boundary, and therefore Jacobian norms can detect collapse. While intuitive, this connection is not rigorously justified. Jacobian norms at random initialization are known to depend on initialization scheme, activation function, normalization layers, depth, input resolution, and scaling constants. It is unclear whether the measured peaks truly correspond to representational insufficiency or simply reflect optimization dynamics specific to the chosen implementation. A deeper theoretical or empirical analysis would help justify why this metric should generalize. Another concern is sensitivity to implementation details. Since the method depends on random initialization behavior, seemingly minor changes such as He versus Xavier initialization, normalization placement, residual versus plain blocks, deep supervision, or preprocessing may alter the sensitivity curve. The paper shows some robustness to seeds and batch size on one dataset, but does not study robustness across initialization schemes or architecture variants. This limits confidence in broader applicability. The fairness of comparisons also deserves scrutiny. XTinyU-Net is compared against UNeXt, CMUNeXt-S, TinyU-Net, and nnU-Net, but these baselines may not all be equally optimized under identical training budgets. Some lightweight methods may require architecture-specific tuning rather than default nnU-Net style settings. If all baselines are trained under one common recipe that favors standard U-Net style models, then the comparison may advantage XTinyU-Net. Stronger fairness would require reproducing each baseline under its recommended protocol or reporting official numbers alongside standardized retraining. A related issue is that only a limited set of lightweight baselines is included. There are many recent efficient medical segmentation models such as Mobile U-Net variants, EfficientUNet derivatives, lightweight transformers, pruning or distillation approaches, MedNCA, LeanUNet, and other task-specific compact architectures. The comparison space therefore feels selective rather than exhaustive. This weakens the claim that XTinyU-Net consistently outperforms the state of the art in lightweight segmentation. Another weakness is the use of parameter count as a dominant efficiency metric. While reducing parameters from 33M to 20K is striking, parameters alone do not fully capture deployment efficiency. Real inference speed depends on memory access patterns, hardware utilization, operator fusion, precision mode, and tensor shapes. Very narrow networks can sometimes underutilize GPUs or NPUs. Although FLOPs are reported, wall-clock latency, throughput, CPU or mobile inference time, and memory footprint are not comprehensively benchmarked. Since the paper is motivated by deployment, practical runtime evidence would be important. The clinical feasibility narrative is also somewhat indirect. The paper argues that lightweight segmentation is useful for portable and decentralized settings, which is true in principle, but no actual embedded deployment, point-of-care experiment, mobile benchmark, or clinician-facing use case is demonstrated. Thus, the practical significance is plausible but not directly validated. Another concern is that the method optimizes only width scaling while keeping depth and topology fixed. This simplifies the search space, but may also limit achievable efficiency. Many successful lightweight models derive gains from changing kernel sizes, stage depth, skip pathways, separable convolutions, decoder simplification, or attention placement. Restricting the search to width alone may miss better Pareto-optimal architectures. Therefore, the conclusion that a properly scaled U-Net is superior to custom lightweight designs may be overstated. The reported results also raise some questions. In several datasets XTinyU-Net slightly exceeds nnU-Net despite having orders of magnitude fewer parameters. While possible due to reduced overfitting, such dramatic compression with equal or better performance across many datasets is surprising and merits deeper analysis. Confidence intervals are given, but only three runs are used. More seeds, cross-validation, or statistical significance testing would strengthen confidence that these gains are robust rather than variance-driven. Reproducibility is moderate but incomplete. The method description is understandable, yet exact implementation details for candidate family generation, sensitivity computation overhead, image sampling strategy, preprocessing consistency, and integration into nnU-Net versions could be more explicit. Since the paper claims training-free rapid selection, reporting actual selection runtime compared with conventional sweeps would also be useful. Finally, the paper’s impact may be narrower than it first appears. If the method mainly works for U-Net width scaling inside nnU-Net-like pipelines, then it is a useful engineering tool but not necessarily a broad methodological advance for MICCAI. Overall, the paper is interesting and practically motivated, but the novelty is moderate, the evidence base is narrower than the claims suggest, comparisons could be stronger, and the theoretical justification remains underdeveloped. These issues collectively place the work below threshold for me in its current form.

meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The reviewers found that the paper is interesting and easy to follow. As pointed out by a reviewer, the authors put effort into communicating the intuition. The authors performed experiments on six datasets, covering MRI, ultrasound, and fundus images, and performed different evaluations to show the advantages of the proposed method. On the other hand, the reviewers also raised concerns regarding the experimental details and the presentation of the results. Reviewer #4 provided some useful comments. However, the AC disagrees with some of the weaknesses raised by the reviewer. For example, the reviewer considered proposing the Jacobian-based metric to be incremental. In contrast, the AC believes that establishing a simple yet functional metric for pre-training assessment, if successful, is an important contribution to the community. Reviewer #4 also commented on the comparison models and the datasets. The AC considers some of these suggestions are infeasible for an 8-page MICCAI paper. As noted by other reviewers, although the paper is not flawless, it provides sufficient evidence that the proposed method is promising. Overall, the paper meets the MICCAI standard in its current form.
